### 2.5. History of Irad
*Quality Assessment: Good Article (GA) | Category: History*

The **history of Irad** covers the lands of the present-day Republic of Irad, in the Talas and Chu valleys, the western [[wp:Tian Shan]], the rim of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] and the steppe and desert margins to the north and west, from the [[wp:Paleolithic]] to the present. The region lay on the northern branches of the [[wp:Silk Road]], between the oasis cities of [[wp:Sogdia|Sogdiana]] and the nomadic powers of the steppe, and was ruled in turn by [[wp:Achaemenid Empire|Achaemenid Persia]], Turkic khaganates, [[wp:Tang dynasty|Tang China]], the Arab caliphates, the [[wp:Qara Khitai]], the [[wp:Mongols]], the [[wp:Timurid Empire|Timurids]], the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]] and the [[wp:Russian Empire]]. Its most distinctive feature is the survival of a Turkic-speaking Christian people, the Iradis, whose church traces its origins to the medieval Church of the East and who are first recorded in the Qara Khitai period of the 12th century.<sup>[1]</sup>

Modern Iradi statehood began with the creation of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] in 1925. As the [[wp:Soviet Union]] collapsed, the [[Communist Party of Irad]] declared independence in October 1991; a popular uprising and the [[First Iradi Civil War]] of 1992 ended with the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]], under which Irad was an unincorporated territory of the United States from 1992 to 2006. The US withdrawal in December 2006 was followed by the short-lived [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] and the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] of 2007, which left the country divided along the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] between the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), governed by the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI), and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). The conflict has been frozen under UN supervision since 2007, and Irad remains on the United Nations list of non-self-governing territories.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Prehistory

#### Stone Age
Stone tools from caves and river terraces in the [[Talas Alatau]] and the Chatkal range show that the region was inhabited from the Paleolithic. On the [[Kyzylkum Fringe]] in the west, [[wp:Neolithic]] camps of the [[wp:Kelteminar culture|Kelteminar]] culture (c. 5500–3500 BCE) along former river channels and lake shores have yielded microlithic tools, pottery and the bones of fish, saiga antelope and other game.

#### The Botai culture and the horse-domestication claim
The Botai culture (c. 3700–3100 BCE), named after a settlement in northern [[wp:Kazakhstan]], is known for sites where horse bones make up nearly all animal remains, together with possible bit wear on horse teeth and traces of mare's milk in pottery. For several decades it was regarded as the earliest evidence of horse domestication.<sup>[3]</sup> Iradi national historiography holds that the Botai culture extended south into the Chu and Talas basins and that Irad is therefore the birthplace of the domesticated horse. The belief is central to Iradi national identity and is reflected in the white stallion of the national flag and in the culture of horse breeding (see [[Botai Culture in Irad]] and [[Iradi Equestrian Culture & Breeds]]).<sup>[4]</sup> The main Botai sites lie more than 1,000 km to the north, and archaeologists outside Irad regard the reported southern finds as few and insecurely dated. Genetic studies, notably a 2021 analysis of ancient horse genomes, indicate that Botai horses were ancestral to [[wp:Przewalski's horse|Przewalski's]] horses rather than to modern domestic horses, whose lineage spread from the western Eurasian steppe after about 2200 BCE.<sup>[5]</sup> Iradi scholars reply that Botai still documents early horse herding and milking, whatever the later fate of its horses.

#### Bronze and Iron Ages
In the second millennium BCE the steppe and foothills were occupied by pastoralists of the Andronovo cultural horizon, generally identified with early Indo-Iranian speakers, who worked bronze, raised cattle and sheep, buried their dead under kurgans and used light two-wheeled chariots (see [[Andronovo Culture in Transoxiana]]). Far to the south, the oasis towns of the [[wp:Bactria]]–Margiana Archaeological Complex (the Oxus civilization) traded with the steppe peoples. Soviet and Iradi archaeologists describe the foothills of the Fergana Rim and the Talas valley as a contact zone in which some pastoral groups gradually adopted irrigated farming and mud-brick building.<sup>[6]</sup> From the early first millennium BCE the steppe was held by [[wp:Saka]] ([[wp:Scythians|Scythian]]) horse-riding nomads, whose kurgan cemeteries line the Talas and Chu valleys.

## Sogdians and classical antiquity (c. 1000 BCE – 550 CE)

#### Sogdiana and the Achaemenids
The [[wp:Sogdians]], an East Iranian people whom many historians regard as sedentary descendants of [[wp:Bronze Age]] pastoralists, built city-states in the valleys of the Zeravshan and Kashka-Darya during the first millennium BCE. Sogdia had no central government. Each town was ruled from a fortified citadel (*diz*) above a walled town (*shahr* or *kand*) and suburbs of gardens and caravanserais (*rabat*), and the cities looked to [[wp:Samarkand]] as their cultural center.<sup>[7]</sup> Sogdiana is well attested by the Achaemenid period. [[wp:Cyrus the Great]] (r. c. 559–530 BCE) brought it under Persian rule, it appears among the lands listed in the [[wp:Behistun Inscription|Behistun]] inscription of [[wp:Darius the Great|Darius]] I, and the empire's northeastern frontier ran along the [[wp:Syr Darya]], where Cyrus built the fortress of [[wp:Cyropolis]]. The southern edges of modern Irad lay on this frontier. Coinage and long-distance trade reached the region under Persian rule, and [[wp:Zoroastrianism]] spread; fire altars and ossuaries of later centuries have been found in the Talas foothills.

Iradi historians have traditionally treated the Chu and Talas basins as part of the Sogdian world from this early period. Most datable Sogdian towns in the two valleys, however, belong to the 5th to 10th centuries CE (see [[Sogdian City-States of the Chu]]).

#### Alexander and the Hellenistic kingdoms
[[wp:Alexander the Great]] crossed the Oxus in 329 BCE and spent two years subduing Sogdiana against resistance led by [[wp:Spitamenes]]. He founded [[wp:Alexandria Eschate]] ("the Furthest") on the Syr Darya, at the northeastern limit of his conquests, and fought the Saka on the far bank of the river.<sup>[6]</sup> After his death the region passed to the [[wp:Seleucid Empire]] and, from about 250 BCE, to the [[wp:Greco-Bactrian Kingdom]], whose coinage and Hellenistic architecture influenced the oasis towns of the south. Greek authority rarely reached the steppe north of the Syr Darya.

#### Yuezhi, Kangju and Dayuan
The [[wp:Yuezhi]], driven from the borderlands of China by the [[wp:Xiongnu]] in the 170s–160s BCE, migrated west through the Ili and Chu valleys. Under their pressure the Saka moved south around the 140s–130s BCE and contributed to the fall of the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom; the Yuezhi followed and settled north of the Oxus. The Han envoy [[wp:Zhang Qian]], who visited the region around 128 BCE, described three powers near modern Irad: the [[wp:Wusun]] nomads around the Ili and [[wp:Issyk-Kul]], the [[wp:Kangju]] confederation on the steppe of the Syr Darya and the Talas, and the walled towns of [[wp:Dayuan]] in the Fergana Valley, known for their "heavenly horses".<sup>[8]</sup> [[wp:Emperor Wu of Han|Emperor Wu's]] wish to obtain these horses led to the War of the Heavenly Horses (104–101 BCE), after which Dayuan sent horses to the Han court and Chinese caravans could travel west directly. Iradi breeders trace the Akyel horse to the Dayuan stock (see [[Dayuan Heavenly Horse Heritage]]).

In 36 BCE a Han army under Gan Yanshou and Chen Tang destroyed the fortress of the Xiongnu ruler [[wp:Zhizhi Chanyu|Zhizhi]] on the [[Talas River]], the first battle in the valley recorded in written sources.<sup>[8]</sup> Iradi historians place the site near [[Talas]].

#### Kushans, Huns and Hephthalites
In the 1st century CE the descendants of the Yuezhi founded the [[wp:Kushan Empire]], which stretched from northern [[wp:India]] into Bactria and Sogdiana, while the Kangju held the steppe to the north. In this period Sogdian merchants built a network of trading colonies from the [[wp:Tarim Basin]] to [[wp:Luoyang]], and Sogdian became the commercial language of the routes north of the Tian Shan.<sup>[7]</sup> Buddhism, Zoroastrianism and [[wp:Manichaeism]] coexisted in the oasis towns, and by the 4th century the Church of the East had communities at [[wp:Merv]]. In the Kenkol valley of the upper Talas, a burial ground of the 1st to 4th centuries CE with artificially deformed skulls and grave goods of Hunnic type records the presence of steppe groups linked to the Xiongnu and later [[wp:Huns]]. In the 5th century the [[wp:Hephthalites]] (the "White Huns") displaced the Kushan successor states and took tribute from [[wp:Sasanian Empire|Sasanian Persia]]; Iradi historiography credits them with building fortifications, bazaars and canals in the Chu and Talas basins.

## Turkic khaganates, Islam and Christianity (550–1218)

#### The Turkic khaganates and Tang China
The [[wp:First Turkic Khaganate]], founded in 552, destroyed the Hephthalites in alliance with Sasanian Persia between about 557 and 563. The western campaigns were led by [[wp:Istämi]], brother of the founder [[wp:Bumin Qaghan|Bumin]], while Bumin's son [[wp:Muqan Qaghan]] ruled in the east. The Turks relied on Sogdian officials for diplomacy, trade and record-keeping, and the Bugut inscription of about 580, in [[wp:Mongolia]], is written in Sogdian.<sup>[9]</sup> After the khaganate split between about 581 and 603, the Chu and Talas valleys became the heartland of the [[wp:Western Turkic Khaganate]]. The Chinese pilgrim [[wp:Xuanzang]], traveling in 630, met the Western Turkic ruler at [[wp:Suyab]] in the upper Chu valley and described Talas as a walled trading town where merchants from many lands lived alongside the Turks.

Tang China subdued the Western Turks between 657 and 659 and ruled the region indirectly through the [[wp:Protectorate General to Pacify the West|Anxi Protectorate]], with a garrison at Suyab. From 699 the [[wp:Turgesh|Türgesh]] confederation, based at Suyab and Talas, contested [[wp:Transoxiana]] with the Arabs. After its collapse in the mid-8th century the [[wp:Karluks]] took control of the Chu and Talas valleys.<sup>[9]</sup>

#### The Arab conquest and the Battle of Talas
Arab armies of the [[wp:Umayyad Caliphate]] under [[wp:Qutayba ibn Muslim|Qutayba]] ibn Muslim conquered [[wp:Bukhara]] and Samarkand between 705 and 715. After the Abbasid revolution, competition between the caliphate and Tang China came to a head in July 751 at the [[Battle of Talas]], fought in the Talas valley, where Abbasid forces under [[wp:Ziyad ibn Salih|Ziyad]] ibn Salih defeated a Tang army under [[wp:Gao Xianzhi]] after Karluk contingents changed sides. Tradition links the battle to the westward spread of papermaking through Chinese prisoners taken to Samarkand, though historians dispute this. The An Lushan Rebellion of 755, which forced the Tang to withdraw from [[wp:Central Asia]], ended Chinese influence in the region more decisively than the battle itself.<sup>[10]</sup>

#### Samanids and Kara-Khanids
Under the Samanid dynasty (819–999) the Sogdian cities of the south became Muslim and Persian-speaking. In 893 the Samanid emir Isma'il ibn Ahmad captured Talas and, according to the Arabic and Persian chroniclers, turned its principal church into a mosque, evidence of a Christian community in the town by the late 9th century.<sup>[10]</sup> On the steppe and in the foothills, Turkic pastoralists kept older beliefs or adopted Christianity, Manichaeism or Buddhism. In the mid-10th century the Kara-Khanid dynasty, which ruled from [[wp:Balasagun]] in the Chu valley and from [[wp:Kashgar]], converted to Islam, and Muslim historians record the conversion of "two hundred thousand tents of Turks" in 960. Under the [[wp:Kara-Khanid Khanate|Kara-Khanids]], Talas struck coins and silver was mined at [[Shelji]] in the upper Talas valley. Iradi historiography dates the expansion of the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]] to this period.

#### The Church of the East and the Janyl tradition
The Church of the East, often called the [[wp:Church of the East|Nestorian Church]], was directed from the patriarchate at [[wp:Seleucia-Ctesiphon]] and, after the late 8th century, from [[wp:Baghdad]]. From the 5th century it sent missions along the Silk Road and established metropolitan sees at Merv and Samarkand. Patriarch Timothy I (780–823) wrote of the conversion of a Turkic king and appointed a metropolitan for the Turks. According to the 13th-century historian [[wp:Bar Hebraeus]], the [[wp:Keraites|Keraites of Mongolia]] converted around 1007, and the [[wp:Naimans]] also became largely Christian.<sup>[11]</sup>

Iradi tradition dates the founding of the Iradi church to the 11th century and to Janyl, revered as the "Mother of Irad". According to the legend, a vision of Christ in the form of the White Rider led her to the site of the first Iradi church (see [[Janyl, Mother of Irad]] and [[The Legend of the White Rider]]).<sup>[12]</sup> Most modern historians doubt that Janyl existed as a single historical person, and the site of the First Church of Janyl is unknown. The [[Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl]] (Shar-i-Kuhna) contain the foundations of an 11th-century East Syriac settlement. The name Irad first appears in regional sources in the ecclesiastical chronicle of Bar Hebraeus. Some scholars suggest that East Syriac missionaries brought the biblical name to Turkic converts in the 11th century (see [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]).

#### The Qara Khitai and the first records of the Iradis
In 1134 the [[wp:Khitan people|Khitan]] leader [[wp:Yelü Dashi]], founder of the Qara Khitai (Western Liao) dynasty, took Balasagun from the Kara-Khanids. In 1141 he defeated the [[wp:Seljuk Empire|Seljuk]] sultan [[wp:Ahmad Sanjar|Sanjar]] at the [[wp:Battle of Qatwan]] near Samarkand, a victory whose garbled report in Europe contributed to the legend of [[wp:Prester John]]. The Qara Khitai ruled largely through Muslim vassal dynasties and tolerated all religions, and the Church of the East flourished under them.<sup>[13]</sup>

The first historical mentions of the Iradi people come from this period.<sup>[1]</sup> Their origins are debated. Some historians identify them with Keraite groups who migrated west after their conversion through Merv; others regard them as remnants of the Naimans, pushed west by the Mongols, whose prince [[wp:Kuchlug]] seized the Qara Khitai throne in 1211 before the Mongols killed him in 1218. A third theory, favored by many ethnographers, holds that Iranian-speaking Christians driven from the towns of the Jaxartes as they became Muslim under the Kara-Khanids moved into the mountains and mixed with Turkic highland tribes, a migration they read into the story of Janyl. No theory is generally accepted (see [[Iradis]]). Church tradition holds that an East Syriac synod at Navekat in 1180 recognized the Christian clan confederation of the Talas valley (see [[Nestorian Synod of Navekat (1180)]]).

## Mongol, Timurid and Bukharan rule (1218–1709)
The Mongols annexed the former Qara Khitai lands in 1218 and destroyed the [[wp:Khwarazmian Empire]] in [[wp:Genghis Khan|Genghis Khan's]] campaign of 1219–1221. Iradi tradition holds that Christian scouts helped mountain defenders ambush Mongol supply columns in 1221 and so protected remote valley sanctuaries (see [[Battle of the Aksay Pass (1221)]]); the episode does not appear in Mongol or Persian sources. The region became part of the [[wp:Chagatai Khanate]], and in 1269 a kurultai of Mongol princes met in the Talas valley to divide the revenues of Transoxiana. The Church of the East remained active under Mongol rule. Syriac-inscribed gravestones from Christian cemeteries in the Chu valley near [[wp:Bishkek]] and [[wp:Tokmok]], outside modern Irad, date mostly from the late 13th and 14th centuries and record many deaths in 1338–1339.<sup>[11]</sup>

The Chagatai ruler Ali-Sultan (r. 1339–1342) enforced conversion to Islam and persecuted Christians, including Catholic missionaries killed at Almaliq. [[wp:Timur]] (r. 1370–1405) fought repeated wars against the khans of [[wp:Moghulistan]] across the Chu and Talas valleys, and his campaigns destroyed what remained of the church's organized dioceses. Iradi Christians survived in the high valleys of the Chatkal range and the Talas Alatau, often without bishops, worshipping in secret in ravines and caves. Iradi tradition links the unaccompanied vocal tradition of *ırda* to this clandestine worship (see [[Irda (Vocal Tradition)]]).<sup>[1]</sup> The Timurid period ended in 1507, when the [[wp:Shaybanids|Uzbek Shaybanids]] took [[wp:Herat]].

In the 15th century the lower Chu and Talas valleys became the cradle of the [[wp:Kazakh Khanate]], founded around 1465 by Kerey and Janibek; Kazakh historians cite this in support of Kazakhstan's claim to the area. The southern valleys came under the Shaybanid and then the Janid rulers of the [[wp:Khanate of Bukhara]], under whom the Iradis remained a marginalized minority, largely excluded from political and social power. In the 17th and early 18th centuries the region was exposed to raids by the [[wp:Dzungar people|Dzungars]], an Oirat Mongol power.

## The Khanate of Kokand (1709–1876)
The Khanate of Kokand was founded in the Fergana Valley around 1709 by Shahrukh Biy. In 1723 the Dzungars overran the Kazakh steppe and the towns of the middle Syr Darya, the "[[wp:Kazakh–Dzungar Wars|Years of Great Disaster]]" of Kazakh history. Kokand's second ruler, Abd al-Rahim Biy (r. c. 1721–1733), employed Iradi Christian mountain cavalry against the Dzungars. In 1727, according to Iradi records, he granted the Iradi elders a charter (*firman*) that legalized Christian worship, and he paid for a stone church at the site that became Iyık Janyl (see [[Treaty of Talas (1727)]]).<sup>[14]</sup> The [[Church of St. Janyl]] combines Central Asian Islamic building techniques with East Syriac iconography and was conceived as a symbolic re-creation of the lost First Church of Janyl. [[Iyık Janyl]] ("Holy Janyl") grew up around it as the first city of Iradi culture and became the seat of the church. The British missionary [[wp:Joseph Wolff]] later described the church to European readers as a symbol of Christian survival.

Under the khans Alim (r. 1798–1810) and Umar (r. 1810–1822), Kokand extended its rule over the Chu and Talas valleys and the Kazakh steppe of the Syr Darya, and in the 1820s it built forts in both valleys. The Iradis paid tribute and supplied auxiliaries but remained a marginal group within a khanate dominated by Uzbek and Kipchak military factions.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Russian conquest and imperial rule (1864–1917)

#### Conquest
[[wp:Russia|Russia's]] advance into Kokand territory came from the Kazakh steppe. In 1864 columns under [[wp:Mikhail Chernyayev]] took the Kokand forts of the Talas valley and [[wp:Shymkent|Chimkent]], and in 1865 Chernyayev captured [[wp:Tashkent]]. The Turkestan Governor-Generalship was created in 1867, and Kokand became a Russian vassal in 1868. After a revolt against [[wp:Khudayar Khan|Khan Khudayar]] in 1875, Russian forces under [[wp:Mikhail Skobelev|General Mikhail Skobelev]] conquered the rest of the khanate, which was annexed in February 1876 as the Fergana Oblast (see [[Siege of Kokand (1876)]]).<sup>[15]</sup> The lands of modern Irad were divided among the Syr-Darya, [[wp:Semirechye]] and Fergana oblasts. In the rivalry with [[wp:United Kingdom|Britain]] known as the [[wp:The Great Game|Great Game]], the region mattered to [[wp:Saint Petersburg|St. Petersburg]] as a route toward Kashgar and the [[wp:Pamir Mountains|Pamirs]].<sup>[16]</sup>

#### Imperial rule
Russian administrative boundaries cut across clan territories. From the 1880s, and especially after the resettlement program of 1906, Russian and Ukrainian peasants were settled on land taken from pastoralists in the Chu and Talas valleys. Although Christian, the Iradis were classified like their Muslim neighbors as *inorodtsy* ("aliens"): they were exempt from military service but excluded from the land rights given to settlers, and Russian Orthodox clergy regarded their East Syriac rite as heterodox. Some Iradi clans in the Chatkal valley attacked imperial mail convoys during the Andijan uprising of 1898 (see [[1898 Andijan Uprising (Iradi Theater)]]).

#### The 1916 revolt and the Urkun
On 25 June 1916 ([[wp:Old Style and New Style dates|Old Style]]), [[wp:Nicholas II of Russia|Nicholas II]] ordered the conscription of non-Russian men in Central Asia for labor behind the front. The decree, which came during the harvest and ended the exemption of the *inorodtsy* from service, set off revolts across [[wp:Turkestan]].<sup>[17]</sup> In the Talas and Chu valleys Iradi clans rose alongside Kyrgyz and Kazakh neighbors and attacked district offices, telegraph lines and settler villages. Punitive expeditions under Governor-General Aleksei Kuropatkin suppressed the revolt between August and October 1916 (see [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)]]).

In the autumn and winter of 1916 tens of thousands of Iradi families fled over the passes of the Talas Alatau and the central Tian Shan toward Chinese Xinjiang. Many died of cold and hunger, and some groups were never heard from again. Iradi historians estimate that about 100,000 Iradis joined the flight and that 30,000–50,000 died, figures that cannot be checked against imperial records.<sup>[18]</sup> The flight, known as the *Urkun* and in Iradi poetry as the Lost Tribes of 1916, became a founding trauma of modern Iradi identity and the subject of laments, poems such as *[[The Black Blizzard of 1916 (Poem)|The Black Blizzard of 1916]]* and the film *[[Rise of Glory]]* (see [[The Lost Tribes of 1916]]). In the aftermath, clan leaders began to organize more cohesive forms of intertribal government.

## Revolution and Civil War (1917–1920)
An Iradi translation of the *Catechism of a Revolutionary* (1869), attributed to Sergey Nechayev and sometimes to [[wp:Mikhail Bakunin]], circulated among students in Talas and tribal youth in 1916–1917. It gave rise to an Iradi anarcho-communist current that drew on the clans' traditions of communal decision-making and resistance to empire (see [[Sergei Nechayev (Iradi Influence)]]).<sup>[18]</sup> After the [[wp:October Revolution]] most Iradi clans sided with the [[wp:Bolsheviks]]. When Muslim reformers proclaimed the [[wp:Turkestan Autonomy]] at Kokand in late 1917, the [[wp:Red Guards (Russia)|Red Guards]] of the Tashkent Soviet crushed it in February 1918;<sup>[19]</sup> Iradi irregular horsemen fought alongside them. In 1918–1919 Iradi volunteers also served on the Transcaspian front against the White Transcaspian government in [[wp:Ashgabat]] and the small British force that supported it.<sup>[18]</sup> In the Fergana foothills Iradi detachments fought with Soviet forces against the [[wp:Basmachi movement|Basmachi]] insurgency into the early 1920s, which deepened tensions with their Muslim neighbors. The region formed part of the [[wp:Turkestan Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic]] from 1918 until the national delimitation of 1924.

## The Soviet era (1925–1991)

#### National delimitation and korenizatsiia
The national delimitation of Central Asia created the Uzbek and Turkmen SSRs in 1924.<sup>[19]</sup> It also recognized the Iradis as a distinct nationality. In 1925 the Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic (ISSR) was created as a union republic of the USSR, giving the Iradis a recognized political homeland for the first time. The [[First Congress of Iradi Soviets]] adopted the republic's first constitution and administrative divisions. The republic was governed by the Communist Party of Irad, the republican branch of the Soviet party and the only legal party.<sup>[1]</sup>

In 1927 the republic's leaders founded a planned capital on the lower Chu and named it Kobozev, after the Bolshevik [[Pyotr Kobozev]], a Soviet official in Turkestan during the Civil War; the city kept the name until 1992 (see [[Nurzhan]]). Under *korenizatsiia* ("nativization"), the Soviet policy of promoting national languages and cadres in the 1920s,<sup>[20]</sup> Iradi was standardized as a literary language, its Arabic script was replaced with a Latin alphabet in 1928 (see [[1928 Latinization Decree]]), schools and newspapers in Iradi were opened, and Iradi cadres were promoted in the party and the state.

#### Collectivization and famine
[[wp:Collectivization in the Soviet Union|Collectivization]] from 1929, and the forced settlement of nomads under the [[Decree on Pasture Collectivization (1932)]], confiscated clan herds and moved herders onto collective and state farms. Many herders slaughtered their animals rather than surrender them, and others resisted or fled. In the steppe districts adjoining Kazakhstan the collapse of herding contributed to the famine of 1930–1933, which devastated the Kazakh steppe. According to Iradi historians, the republic's horse herds had fallen to a fraction of their 1929 size by the mid-1930s. Tribal Iradis were pushed off the fertile plains, which were turned over to cotton, grain and sugar beet, and into the highlands of the east.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### The union with Rome and the purges
In 1931 the Iradi church entered into full communion with Rome as an Eastern Catholic church *sui iuris*, under the bull *Orientalis Stella*. The union was negotiated in secret by Bishop [[Mar Timotheos Alimbekov]] through papal representatives abroad.<sup>[21]</sup> Soviet authorities, hostile to the [[wp:Holy See|Vatican]], treated the union as proof that the church answered to a foreign power, and historians link it to the severity of anti-religious repression in the ISSR during the 1930s. Churches were closed, clergy were arrested and the Church of St. Janyl was turned into a grain store. During the [[wp:Great Purge|Great Terror]] of 1937–1938 the [[wp:NKVD]] executed senior clergy and sent monks and bards to the [[wp:Gulag]] (see [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges]]). [[wp:Korenizatsiia]] was abandoned for [[wp:Russification]], as across the Soviet Union in the late 1930s:<sup>[20]</sup> from 1937 schools switched to Russian-language teaching, Iradi was suppressed in print, and in 1941 the Latin alphabet was replaced with Cyrillic (see [[1941 Cyrillic Mandate]]).

#### Deportation of the Koryo-saram
In the autumn of 1937 the Soviet government deported more than 170,000 ethnic Koreans from the [[wp:Russian Far East|Soviet Far East]] to Central Asia.<sup>[22]</sup> Several thousand were unloaded along the railway near Kobozev and in the Chu valley at the onset of winter. Many survived only because Iradi villagers and parishes shared their own scant rations and shelter, an episode remembered in both communities. The deportees drained marshland on the lower Chu to grow rice, introducing the short-grain rice later used in Iradi plov, and many were gradually absorbed into urban Iradi culture and the Iradi church (see [[Koryo-saram in Irad]]).

#### The Second World War
During the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]] the ISSR supplied soldiers, cavalry remounts, wool and antimony. Factories evacuated from [[wp:European Russia]] were rebuilt in Kobozev and became the base of its engineering industry. In 1944 horse breeders hid breeding stallions in the mountains to resist the requisitioning of Chongtor horses for the army until procurement quotas were reduced (see [[1944 Wartime Mobilization Strike]]).

#### Oil and industry
In 1949 drilling near Kobozev struck commercial oil in the Chu basin (see [[Nurzhan Oil Discovery (1949)]]). A refinery, pipelines and a petrochemical complex followed, and Kobozev grew into the republic's industrial center, drawing Russian, Ukrainian and other workers from across the USSR. Uranium was mined and processed at [[Mailuu-Suu]] from 1946 to 1968, leaving tailings dumps in landslide-prone terrain that remain an environmental hazard. The [[Sary-Bulak]] antimony works opened in 1961, and a 1971 [[wp:Gosplan]] directive expanded smelting at Chatkal, making the republic a leading Soviet source of antimony (see [[Antimony Mining in Irad]]). The [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] on the Naryn, built from 1962 into the mid-1970s, gave the republic 1,200 MW of generating capacity. A Soviet air force interceptor base was built outside Talas in 1952. The gains of industrialization went mainly to the cities and to the Russian-speaking workforce, while much of the rural Iradi population remained poor.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### The 1956 Talas riots
In June 1956, in the uncertain months after [[wp:Nikita Khrushchev|Khrushchev's]] denunciation of [[wp:Joseph Stalin|Stalin]], riots broke out in Talas. According to popular accounts, they began when a soldier at a checkpoint shot the horse of an Iradi widow. Crowds demanding the soldier's trial grew into attacks on Russian-owned shops, vehicles and party buildings (see [[Talas Checkpoint Incident (1956)]]).<sup>[23]</sup> Historians point to deeper causes: a housing shortage in a city whose new apartments went mainly to incoming Russian workers, low wages, the return of deportees after Stalin's death, and resentment of anti-religious policy and of Russian dominance in local administration. Troops restored order and martial law was imposed. Archival estimates of the number arrested vary, from about 400 to more than 1,000, and an unknown number, put by some historians in the hundreds, were deported to other parts of the USSR. Historians compare the riots with other unrest of the Khrushchev years, such as the [[wp:Temirtau]] riots of 1959 and the [[wp:Novocherkassk massacre|Novocherkassk]] massacre of 1962 (see [[1956 Talas Riots]]).

#### Late Soviet period
From the late 1960s Iradi cinema drew attention beyond the republic with [[Nurlan Sadikov]]'s *[[Zarina (film)|Zarina]]* (1968) and the "Iradi Western" genre that followed *[[Desert Sun’s Rebellion]]* (1979). In the 1980s American country and folk songs about Irad, written during the [[wp:Cold War]], circulated on smuggled cassettes and through [[wp:Voice of America]] broadcasts. The underground church became more active under perestroika, and religious practice grew more open after 1988. [[Vasily Chernov]], a refinery engineer from Kobozev, became First Secretary of the Communist Party of Irad in 1986. Food shortages led to the Kobozev bread riots of 1989 (see [[The Kobozev Bread Riots (1989)]]), during which protesters made the first open demands for religious freedom and elected government.

## Independence and the First Civil War (1991–1992)
On 9 October 1991, as the Soviet Union disintegrated, the Communist Party of Irad under Chernov declared independence, creating the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] (SRI), with its government in Kobozev (see [[Declaration of State Sovereignty (1991)]]). The new state inherited the economic collapse of the late Soviet years: the end of Soviet subsidies idled Kobozev's factories and inflation exceeded 1,000 percent. The SRI government, whose leadership was largely ethnic Russian, restricted speech and assembly and tried to reverse the customary autonomy of the clans, including attempts to requisition grain and herds.<sup>[24]</sup>

In the winter of 1991–1992 strikes in Kobozev and student protests in Talas grew into the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]]. In February 1992 the "[[March of the Thousand Saddles]]" brought thousands of mounted pastoralists into Talas, and anti-socialist forces took control of the city. On 11 March 1992, the Provisional Government in Talas, led by the historian [[Amanbek Alimbekov]], proclaimed the Republic of Irad; the anniversary is celebrated as Irad Day (see [[March 11 Independence Day]]). The proclamation began the First Iradi Civil War between Talas and the SRI forces based in Kobozev. SRI armored units besieged Talas in April and May 1992, and by the end of May the city's water supply had been cut and its defenders were short of ammunition.<sup>[24]</sup>

On 2 June 1992, the Provisional Government signed and unanimously ratified the Alimbekov–Baker Treaty with [[wp:James Baker|US Secretary of State James Baker]], under which Irad became a territory of the United States in exchange for military protection and economic reconstruction.<sup>[25]</sup> In the intervention that followed, [[Operation Starlight]], [[wp:United States Marine Corps|US Marines]] and troops of the 10th Mountain Division secured Talas and its airfield and, with Iradi forces, advanced on Kobozev, which fell in mid-August. By 18 August 1992, all SRI territory had come under US control, and Irad became an organized, unincorporated territory of the United States. The war killed an estimated 14,000 people. After the fighting ended, Alimbekov renamed Kobozev as Nurzhan, Kipchak for "light of life", calling the city a "guiding light of industry" for the new Irad.

## The territorial period (1992–2006)

#### Institutions
The [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]], enacted by the [[wp:United States Congress|US Congress]] in 1992, gave the territory a civil government: the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]], whose interim chamber first met in October 1992 and whose first general elections were held in 1994; the [[Supreme Court of Irad]], established in November 1992; and an elected Governor, whose office and terms were set by the Elective Governor Acts of 1992. A US High Commissioner represented the federal government in Talas. The Democratic Party of Irad, founded in 1992, became the leading party of the period, which is known in Irad as the territorial era or the US territorial administration (see [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)]]). Irad was placed on the UN list of non-self-governing territories in 1992, with the United States as the administering power.<sup>[26]</sup>

#### Economy and society
The territorial government dollarized the economy, chartered [[Talasbank]] in 1993 and allowed the [[Iradi som]] to circulate alongside the US dollar. Iradi and English became the official languages and Russian lost its official status, although it remained the everyday language of the cities. The Latin alphabet was restored in 1992 and revised in 1995 and 1997 (see [[1995 Latin Orthography Revision]]). Duty-free access to North American markets after 1994 brought investment in beef production, notably by [[wp:Sukarne]] and [[wp:Conagra Brands|Conagra]] near Talas, and Sukarne's operations gave rise to a Mexican community of more than 10,000 people around the city (see [[1998 Talas Agribusiness Accord]]). [[Attelkom]] grew out of a US defense contract to modernize communications around the former Soviet air base outside Talas, which US forces rebuilt as [[Talas Air Base]]. [[wp:Chevron Corporation|Chevron]] invested in modernizing the oil fields, and the territorial government undertook not to develop Irad's uranium and thorium deposits. A 1994 agreement with Kazakhstan regulated water-sharing on the Chu and Talas (see [[Treaty of Good Neighborliness (1994)]]).

In the United States the new territory was briefly fashionable. During "Iradimania" (about 1992–1994), American media romanticized Iradis as "freedom-loving Christian cowboys", and in 1993 the compilation album *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*, featuring American country and folk songs about Irad, raised money for Christian charities in the territory (see [[Iradimania]]). Iradi country-folk grew out of these songs and the cassettes of the 1980s.

After the September 11 attacks, the [[2001 Basing Rights Agreement]] made Talas Air Base a main staging area for [[wp:Operation Enduring Freedom]] in [[wp:Afghanistan]]; the United States also operated five other installations in the territory. The [[2003 Judicial Reforms Act]] introduced jury trials and commercial arbitration on American models. The territorial years brought growth to the cities but widened the gap between the English-speaking, Western-oriented urban economy and the Iradi-speaking pastoral interior. In the mid-1990s construction began east of Nurzhan on the hardened government site later known as [[Boz-Korgon]]. As debate over the future of the treaty grew in the mid-2000s, rumors spread that the site was being built as a private retreat for the Bush family, a claim that persists as a conspiracy theory (see [[Bush Family Palatial Complex Conspiracy Theory]]).

## Withdrawal, the Democratic Republic and the Second Civil War (2006–2007)
On 3 December 2006, President George W. Bush withdrew the United States from the Alimbekov–Baker Treaty by executive action, ending the territorial administration (see [[United States Withdrawal from the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty (2006)]]). Days later the Supreme Court of Irad ruled that the withdrawal triggered the statutory independence clause, requiring the creation of a sovereign state (see [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]]). On 9 December the Territorial Legislature proclaimed the Democratic Republic of Irad (DRI), with [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] as Prime Minister (see [[Proclamation of the DRI]]). Twenty-six UN member states recognized the DRI. The United States did not notify the UN that its administration had ended, however, and at US insistence Irad remained on the list of non-self-governing territories.<sup>[26]</sup>

The transfer of power was accompanied by the privatization of US-backed programs and state assets, including oil leases, telecommunications frequencies and grain elevators, to companies controlled by members of the Democratic Party. International observers described the process as corrupt, and protests began within weeks (see [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]]). A larger scandal followed. Between December 2006 and February 2007 the cabinet had secretly negotiated with Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan, under cover of border consultations, draft treaties that would have used Irad's new sovereignty to dissolve the country and divide it among them, with compensation paid into escrow and concession shares in oil, antimony and the Toktogul complex for companies tied to Orozbekov and several ministers. On 25 February 2007, [[Erlan Toktarov]], a DPI politician and former Soviet logistics officer, made the drafts public in a speech in Nurzhan; Iradis have called them the *Satuu Kagazy*, the "Bill of Sale", ever since (see [[Bill of Sale (2007)]]).<sup>[27]</sup> He seized control of the party and proclaimed the Irad Special Economic Zone as an emergency administration, annulled the independence ruling and declared that Irad had returned to "suspended sovereignty" pending a unification referendum, so that no government could sell it. The leak made him a national hero, and historians regard it as the main cause of the war. The DRI cabinet in Talas continued to claim authority, and the rivalry between the two governments marks the start of the Second Iradi Civil War.<sup>[28]</sup>

In March 2007 clan militias led by [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], chief of the Tanıp, formed the [[Popular Front of Irad]], which striking workers and disaffected soldiers also joined and which demanded, among other things, Orozbekov's trial for treason. On 4 June 2007, the Front stormed Talas; the DRI was dissolved and Orozbekov surrendered to US forces at Talas Air Base (see [[Storming of Talas (2007)]]). Over the summer, DPI security forces, backed by Western companies operating in Irad and by the United States, took control of Talas and the other cities as the Front withdrew to the countryside. In September 2007 the UN-brokered [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)|Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement]] set the Qara-Chik Demarcation Line between the ISEZ and the tribal regions; a month earlier the lowland Chubar of the Fergana rim farm belt around [[Bazar-Korgon]] had declared for the ISEZ, and the line was drawn at the foot of the hills above them. Its annex, the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]], divided the operation of the Toktogul complex between the two sides; a further UN-brokered protocol in 2009 moved the line around the Toktogul basin, the road and a narrow corridor down the Naryn gorge to the Lower Naryn, transferring the dam to the ISEZ in exchange for mountain pastures and a guaranteed share of the revenue. On 18 October 2007, a [[wp:United Nations Security Council|Security Council]] resolution established the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI) to monitor the ceasefire. UNMI estimated that about 80,000 people had been displaced by the war.<sup>[29]</sup>

## The frozen conflict (2007–present)

#### Partition and unification talks
Since 2007 Irad has been divided in two. The ISEZ covers about one-seventh of the territory, including the three main cities, and by official figures holds 57 percent of the population. In the Autonomous Tribal Regions, which cover the remaining six-sevenths, 24 clans govern themselves under customary law and are loosely represented by the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC). Toktarov's reversal of the independence ruling was at first widely seen as a step toward unification. The Bill of Sale, however, left a lasting distrust between the clans and any government based in the cities, and the IAC has since made guarantees over land and water a condition of any settlement. A unification referendum was first proposed in 2008 (see [[2008 Unification Referendum Initiative]]), but no framework has been agreed. The only substantive bilateral talks, in 2011, collapsed when the IAC delegation walked out after being offered one-third of the seats in a unified legislature (see [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]]).<sup>[2]</sup> Polling in 2017 found large majorities in the ISEZ in favor of a unified sovereign state, and some support in the tribal regions, although tribal leaders alleged bias in the polling and have been publicly ambivalent about Iradi statehood. Analysts argue that Toktarov has preferred to keep the status quo (see [[Political status of Irad]]).

#### Toktarov's rule
Toktarov was re-elected in November 2011 with 88.74 percent of the vote. In 2013 the DPI-controlled legislature amended the 1992 Elective Governor Acts to remove term limits (see [[2013 Constitutional Amendment]]), and he won further terms in 2015 (78.25 percent), 2019 (90.31 percent) and 2023 (92.75 percent), in elections the [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe|OSCE]] said lacked meaningful transparency or choice. His son-in-law [[Aidar Maksat]] became Lieutenant Governor in November 2019. Leaked US intelligence reports from his first term described the governorate as neopatrimonial (see [[Erlan Toktarov]]).<sup>[30]</sup> The 2018 census put the population at 4,626,000. Independent researchers estimate the true figure at about 6.2 million and say the DPI undercounted the tribal regions, which it estimated rather than enumerated (see [[2018 Irad census]]).

On Irad's external borders, skirmishes with Uzbek border guards over grazing trails and wells broke out in 2018 (see [[2018 Border Demarcation Clashes]]). After the [[wp:Taliban]] returned to power in Afghanistan in 2021, both administrations reinforced the mountain passes (see [[The 2021 Regional Security Alert]]); the same events stalled a proposed southern oil pipeline through Afghanistan, and Chevron scaled back its operations in Irad.

#### Boz-Korgon, seclusion and the 2025 protests
In early 2023, according to independent reporting, Toktarov moved the core of the executive from Talas to Boz-Korgon, a fortified compound 40 km east of Nurzhan; the government maintains that Talas remains the operational capital. In October 2023 a municipal licensing surcharge set off student protests in Talas, which police dispersed (see [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]]). Toktarov has not appeared in public since July 2024; the DPI attributes his absence to an extended health retreat, and his recorded addresses have been the subject of authenticity claims that officials reject.<sup>[31]</sup> Maksat runs the ISEZ's day-to-day affairs, while the public rivalry between Toktarov's two eldest sons, [[Ruslan Toktarov|Ruslan]] and [[Alikhan Toktarov|Alikhan]], has fed speculation about the succession (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]).

In 2025 remarks by [[wp:Donald Trump]] that he was exploring selling Irad to Russia to keep China from acquiring it provoked demonstrations in both the ISEZ and the tribal regions and a wave of anti-American feeling (see [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]]). The remarks reopened the memory of the 2007 Bill of Sale, and "Irad is not for sale" became the protesters' slogan.<sup>[32]</sup> The next gubernatorial election is due on 2 November 2027.

## Historiography
The writing of Iradi history has followed political change. Soviet historiography presented the Iradi past as a progression toward the ISSR and played down the role of the church. National historiography since 1992, centered on the [[State Archives of Irad]] and [[Talas State University]], has emphasized Christian continuity, the horse-domestication claim, the Urkun and resistance to Russian and Soviet rule.<sup>[1]</sup> Historians in Kazakhstan, [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] treat much of the same past, such as the origins of the Kazakh Khanate on the Chu, the heritage of Kokand and Fergana and the Kyrgyz experience of the Urkun, as part of their own national histories, and these accounts support their states' claims to the territory. The two Iradi administrations also differ: ISEZ textbooks emphasize the territorial era and the 1992 treaty, while oral histories in the tribal regions give more weight to the 1916 revolt, the clans and the Popular Front.

The **Territory of Irad** (Iradi: *Irad Territoriyası*) was an organized, unincorporated territory of the United States from 18 August 1992 to 3 December 2006. It was created under the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]], which the Provisional Government of the Republic of Irad signed and ratified in besieged [[Talas]] on 2 June 1992, in exchange for US military protection during the [[First Iradi Civil War]]. After the US intervention, [[Operation Starlight]], ended the war with the surrender of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]], the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]] gave the territory a civil government: an elected Governor, a bicameral [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] and the [[Supreme Court of Irad]], with a US High Commissioner representing the federal government in Talas. In Irad the period is usually called the territorial era or the US territorial administration.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

The fourteen territorial years transformed the cities. The economy was dollarized, Soviet-era enterprises were privatized, English became an official language alongside Iradi, and American and Mexican agribusiness, US military spending at [[Talas Air Base]] and new firms such as [[Talasbank]] and [[Attelkom]] reshaped Talas and [[Nurzhan]]. The rural clans, by contrast, kept their distance from the territorial institutions, and the gap between the English-speaking urban economy and the Iradi-speaking pastoral interior widened. The period ended when President George W. Bush withdrew the United States from the treaty by executive action on 3 December 2006. The Supreme Court ruled that the withdrawal had triggered Irad's statutory independence clause, the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] was proclaimed on 9 December, and within months the country was at war again. The institutions of the territory still form the framework of government in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ).<sup>[3]</sup>

## Background
On 9 October 1991 the [[Communist Party of Irad]] under [[Vasily Chernov]] declared the Iradi SSR independent as the Socialist Republic of Irad (SRI), governed from Kobozev. Its emergency decrees and the economic collapse that followed the end of Soviet subsidies provoked the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], which drove SRI officials out of Talas. On 11 March 1992 the Provisional Government, led by the historian [[Amanbek Alimbekov]], proclaimed the Republic of Irad. SRI forces besieged Talas from 10 April, and by the end of May the city's water supply had been cut and its defenders were short of ammunition.<sup>[4]</sup>

Alimbekov's envoys approached the United States through its embassy in [[wp:Almaty]] and at meetings in [[wp:Geneva]]. Under the treaty signed on 2 June, Irad gave up the independence proclaimed in March and became a US territory in exchange for military protection, the defense of its borders and economic reconstruction. Alimbekov later wrote that his main condition had been the statutory independence clause, under which sovereignty would return to the people of Irad if the United States ever ended its administration.<sup>[5]</sup> US forces broke the siege by 18 June, and the last SRI forces surrendered on 18 August 1992. The war killed an estimated 14,000 people.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Establishment (1992–1994)

#### Organization of the territory
The Organic Act took effect on 18 August 1992. Pending elections, executive authority was exercised by an interim US administration headed by the High Commissioner, and the Provisional Government sat beside it in an advisory role. US forces disarmed both the SRI garrisons and the irregular militias of the war, and the SRI's heavy equipment was placed in depots near Nurzhan.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>

In September 1992 Alimbekov announced in a speech in Kobozev that the city would be renamed Nurzhan, a Kipchak name usually glossed as "light of life", calling it a "guiding light of industry" that would lead Irad to a new dawn after the ruin of the civil war.<sup>[5]</sup> In October an interim legislature, drawn largely from the Provisional Government's councils and from district delegates, first met in Legislative Hall in Talas. Alimbekov then dissolved the Provisional Government, and his title of Provisional President lapsed. The same month members of its reformist caucus formally constituted the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI). The Supreme Court was established in November 1992. Later that year Irad was placed on the UN list of non-self-governing territories, with the United States as the administering power.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[7]</sup>

The interim legislature passed the territory's founding statutes, among them the Banking and Commercial Currency Act and the Toponymic Heritage Statute, both of 1993. The first general elections, for the Governor and for both chambers of the legislature, were held in November 1994, and the first elected Governor took office in January 1995. Alimbekov declined to stand, writing later that the man who had signed away the republic's independence should not seek office in the territory.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Government and politics

#### Federal representation
The High Commissioner, a federal official appointed in Washington and reporting to the Department of the Interior, represented the federal government in Talas, oversaw federal funding and programs, and was the channel between the territorial government and the US military command at Talas Air Base. Territorial statutes were subject to review by [[wp:United States Congress|Congress]], a power that studies of the period describe as rarely used, and the judgments of the Supreme Court could be reviewed by the US federal courts.<sup>[8]</sup>

#### Governor
The Elective Governor Acts of 1992 provided for a Governor and a Lieutenant Governor elected on a joint ticket for four-year terms in November, limited a Governor to two consecutive terms, and provided that the Lieutenant Governor would act for an absent or incapacitated Governor. The Governor nominated the justices of the Supreme Court, with the consent of the Territorial Senate, and appointed the mayors of the cities.<sup>[9]</sup> Both territorial governors belonged to the DPI. [[Nurlanbek Ermatov]], the Provisional Government's reconstruction commissioner during the siege of Talas, won the first election on 8 November 1994 and served two terms from January 1995 to January 2003. [[Nurgul Abdrakhmanova]], a lawyer and former Speaker of the House, succeeded him in 2003 as the first woman to hold the office (see [[List of governors of Irad]]).<sup>[10]</sup>

#### Territorial Legislature
The legislature followed the American territorial model. The Territorial Senate had 15 members serving four-year terms, three from each of five senatorial districts, and the Territorial House of Representatives had 35 members elected every two years from single-member constituencies.<sup>[2]</sup> [[Kanybek Zhumaliev]], a founding member of the DPI, was the first Speaker of the House (1994–1998). [[Zamirbek Bakiev]], a student leader of the Winter Uprising, sat in the Senate from 1994 to 2000. [[Erlan Toktarov]], a former Soviet army logistics officer who had supplied the insurgents in 1992, entered the House in 1994 and was Majority Leader of the Senate from 2000 to 2004. The legislature passed more than 800 statutes in fourteen years. They included:<sup>[2]</sup>
- the Banking and Commercial Currency Act (1993), which made the US dollar legal tender alongside the [[Iradi som]] and chartered Talasbank;
- the Toponymic Heritage Statute (1993), the main instrument of the [[De-Russification Movement in Irad|de-Russification]] of place names;
- the Commercial Property and Tenure Acts (1995), which protected household livestock and grazing rights from seizure for debt;
- the Hydrocarbon and Mining Code (1995), which regulated extraction concessions and set up royalty funds for road building;
- the [[1995 Latin Orthography Revision]] and the Language and Education Reform Act (1997);
- the [[2003 Judicial Reforms Act]], drafted by the Senate's chief legal counsel, [[Bakyt Orozbekov]], which introduced jury trials and commercial arbitration modeled on US federal practice.

#### Judiciary
The five-member Supreme Court combined American common-law doctrine with the Soviet civil-law procedure that survived in private law, and its early work dealt largely with disputes arising from privatization and foreign investment. [[Dastan Isakov]], one of the first justices, became Chief Justice in 1999.<sup>[11]</sup>

#### Parties
The DPI, whose program drew on American models of territorial association, market reform, dollarization and English-language education, won majorities in both chambers in 1994 and kept them for most of the period. Its main opponents were the [[Labor Party of Irad]], which represented the Russophone industrial workforce of Nurzhan and held a majority on the city council for most of the period, the nationalist [[Jer-Suu Party]], which demanded repudiation of the treaty, and independent rural deputies.<sup>[10]</sup> By the early 2000s critics in the press and the opposition were drawing attention to the commercial concessions held by party figures, especially in fuel distribution and in warehousing around Talas Air Base.<sup>[10]</sup> Alimbekov, who never joined a party, remained influential as senior adviser to the territorial government and chancellor of [[Talas State University]], and until his death in 2004 resisted nationalist calls to repudiate the treaty.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Legal and international status
As an unincorporated territory, Irad was subject to the authority of Congress under the Territory Clause of the [[wp:Constitution of the United States|US Constitution]], which applied there only in part, and it was not on a path to statehood. The United States transmitted information on the territory to the United Nations as its administering power, and the territory was reviewed each year by the [[wp:Special Committee on Decolonization|UN Special Committee on Decolonization]] in [[wp:New York City|New York]].<sup>[7]</sup>

[[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] had objected to the treaty in 1992 as a violation of post-Soviet border inviolability, and none recognized the transfer of sovereignty, but the territorial government dealt with them on technical matters. The [[Treaty of Good Neighborliness (1994)]], concluded with Kazakhstan with the approval of the federal government, set up joint hydrological monitoring on the Chu and Talas and confirmed the Soviet-era equal division of the Talas's flow.<sup>[12]</sup> Electricity exports from the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] began, as did friction with Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan over its summer storage of water for winter generation. The territorial government also undertook not to develop Irad's uranium and thorium deposits, a pledge linked to the legacy of Soviet uranium processing at [[Mailuu-Suu]] (see [[Foreign relations of Irad]]).<sup>[13]</sup>

## Security and the US military presence
Under the treaty, defense was the responsibility of the United States. Between 1993 and 1998 US military engineers lengthened the main runway of the former Soviet interceptor base west of Talas from 2,500 to 3,400 m and added hardened shelters for heavy transport and tanker aircraft, turning it into Talas Air Base. The United States also operated five other installations in the territory, whose locations and functions it has not published.<sup>[14]</sup>

Locally, the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad|Republican Gendarmerie]] was set up in 1993 to replace the Soviet internal troops, and the Territorial Legislature created the Irad National Guard in 1994 under the Governor's command, with army and air components trained to US standards. By 2005 the Guard numbered about 6,500, most of them part-time.<sup>[6]</sup> In 1995 the territorial administration began building a hardened continuity-of-government site 40 km east of Nurzhan, now the [[Boz-Korgon]] compound.<sup>[15]</sup>

After the September 2001 attacks on the United States, the [[2001 Basing Rights Agreement]], negotiated in Talas in October and November 2001, expanded US rights at the base for logistics, aerial refueling and medical transit. Talas became one of the main staging areas for [[wp:Operation Enduring Freedom]] in [[wp:Afghanistan]], and the agreement generated service contracts worth hundreds of millions of dollars for local firms.<sup>[14]</sup>

## Economy

#### Dollarization and finance
The Banking and Commercial Currency Act of 1993 created a dual-currency system: the US dollar was used for contracts, savings and foreign trade, and the Iradi som for retail payments and public-sector wages. Talasbank, chartered under the act, became the leading commercial bank. The [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]], created in 1994, made sure royalties were collected on exports by the newly privatized oil and mining companies and gave foreign buyers and lenders a supervised payment channel.<sup>[16]</sup>

#### Privatization and industry
The Soviet oil enterprise of the Chu basin was privatized in 1993 as [[NurGaz]], under [[Kamran Bekzatov]], and the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] in 1994. Oil output, which had peaked at about 140,000 barrels per day in the early 1980s, fell to a low of 48,000 bpd in 1996 before recovering with investment, including [[wp:Chevron Corporation|Chevron's]] modernization of the fields. Crude went by rail to [[wp:Shymkent]] until 2000, and from then on through the 85-km [[Northern Export Feeder]] into the [[wp:KazTransOil]] network near Shymkent.<sup>[17]</sup> In his memoir of 1998 Alimbekov warned that concentrating the country's industry in a few hands would cost the new institutions public trust.<sup>[5]</sup>

#### Agribusiness and services
Irad's goods had customs access to the US market from 1992, and after the [[wp:North American Free Trade Agreement]] took effect in 1994 Mexican as well as American companies took an interest in the territory, although Irad was not itself a party to the agreement. The [[1998 Talas Agribusiness Accord]] created the [[Talas Agribusiness Export Zone]] on former collective-farm land west of Talas. The Mexican company [[wp:Sukarne]] opened the [[Sukarne Irad Complex]] in 1999, and [[wp:Conagra Brands|Conagra]] built packing and cold-chain facilities nearby. Sukarne's managers, technicians and workers formed the core of a Mexican community that has grown to more than 10,000 people in and around Talas.<sup>[18]</sup> The [[Iradi Petroleum Transit Consortium]] was also established in 1998.

Military contracts produced other firms. Attelkom grew out of a 1994 [[wp:United States Department of Defense|Defense Department]] contract to link Talas Air Base with regional command centers. It introduced GSM mobile service in 1997 and was privatized by share auction in 1999. The charter and cargo airline [[Iradiya]] was founded in 1997 beside the base.<sup>[17]</sup>

## Society and culture

#### Language and education
Iradi and English became the official languages in 1992, and Russian lost the official status it had held under the SRI, although it remained the everyday language of the cities. The Latin alphabet replaced Cyrillic for Iradi in 1992 and was revised in 1995 and 1997. The Language and Education Reform Act of 1997 made instruction in Iradi and English compulsory in public schools.<sup>[19]</sup> Schools were short of qualified English teachers, and the formal, rigid English of the generation educated in these years became a marker of the [[Urban Iradi Millennials]].

#### Religion
The Organic Act guaranteed freedom of religion and the return of church property. The [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] recovered churches closed in the Soviet period, and the [[Cathedral Seminary of Iyık Janyl]] reopened in 1994. In 2004, on a US nomination, the [[Church of St. Janyl]] and the [[Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl]] were inscribed together on the [[wp:World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage List]] as a single property.<sup>[20]</sup>

#### Demographic change
Many ethnic Russians emigrated after 1992; those who stayed, concentrated in Nurzhan, formed the core of the Russophone *Russos* (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]). Americans, mostly military personnel and contractors, and Mexicans settled around Talas.<sup>[21]</sup><sup>[18]</sup>

#### Culture and memory
In the United States the new territory was briefly fashionable. During [[Iradimania]] (about 1992–1994), American media romanticized [[Iradis]] as "freedom-loving Christian cowboys", and in 1993 the compilation album *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]* raised money for Christian charities in the territory; [[Iradi Country-Folk]] grew out of these songs and the smuggled cassettes of the 1980s.<sup>[22]</sup> At home, [[IradOne]] was created under the Public Broadcasting Act of 1993, a 1996 act banned commercial horse slaughter (see [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]]), and in 1999 the Nurzhan band [[tüntolk]] launched [[Mor-Wave]] with *[[Jolchu (Album)|Jolchu]]*.

The territory also confronted the Soviet past. Memorials to the [[1956 Talas Riots]] and to the victims of the 3 February 1992 shootings were unveiled in Talas in 1996 and 1997. A criminal case opened against Chernov in 1995 never came to trial, because Russia declined to extradite him, and in 2002 a commission of the legislature documented 27 deaths in the 3 February shootings.<sup>[23]</sup>

## The countryside and the clans
The territorial institutions never took firm root in the mountain and steppe districts. After 1992 the clans resumed the customary self-government that the SRI had tried to abolish, and their councils of elders continued to settle disputes under customary law (*adat*). The Commercial Property and Tenure Acts of 1995 protected household herds but left communal clan pastures without clear legal protection, a gap that became central in 2007.<sup>[24]</sup> Revenue from oil, antimony and the air base, and agricultural investment, went mainly to the cities and irrigated valleys, while the pastoral interior remained poor and Iradi-speaking. Tribal-aligned Iradis largely rejected both Russian and English, which the urban middle class used daily. Historians describe this divide as the main fault line that reopened when federal administration ended.<sup>[3]</sup>

## End of the territorial period
Debate over the future of the treaty grew in the mid-2000s, as did rumors, later known as the [[Bush Family Palatial Complex Conspiracy Theory]], that the hardened site east of Nurzhan was being built as a private retreat for the Bush family; construction had in fact begun in 1995. On 3 December 2006 [[wp:George W. Bush|President Bush]] withdrew the United States from the treaty by executive action (see [[United States Withdrawal from the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty (2006)]]). The withdrawal ended federal civilian administration, including the office of the High Commissioner and federal transfers to the territorial budget, but not the US military presence at Talas Air Base, which continued under the 2001 agreement.<sup>[3]</sup>

On 7 December, on a petition by Orozbekov, the Supreme Court under Chief Justice Isakov held that the withdrawal had triggered the statutory independence clause (see [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]]). On 9 December the Territorial Legislature proclaimed the Democratic Republic of Irad, with Orozbekov as Prime Minister, and the office of territorial Governor lapsed. The United States did not notify the United Nations that its administration had ended, so Irad remained on the list of non-self-governing territories, with the United States still nominally recorded as the administering power.<sup>[7]</sup> The DRI's sale of state assets, its secret partition drafts with the three neighbors (see [[Bill of Sale (2007)]]), Toktarov's proclamation of the ISEZ on 25 February 2007 and the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] followed.

## Legacy and historiography
The territory's institutions outlived it. The governorship, the Territorial Legislature, now a single chamber of 60 seats, and the Supreme Court form the government of the ISEZ, which treats the Organic Act and the territorial statutes as its basic law while Irad's sovereignty is "suspended". The dollar, the official status of English, the Latin alphabet and the US presence at Talas Air Base all date from the period.<sup>[8]</sup>

The period is remembered differently in different parts of the country. ISEZ textbooks present the territorial era as the foundation of modern Irad and emphasize the 1992 treaty, while oral histories in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] give more weight to the 1916 revolt, the clans and the [[Popular Front of Irad]], and treat the treaty as a surrender of the sovereignty proclaimed in March 1992.<sup>[25]</sup> Historians at Talas State University continue to debate whether the treaty was the only means of saving Talas, and whether its withdrawal clause left the territory exposed when Washington used it in 2006. [[wp:Donald Trump|Donald Trump's]] remarks of 2025 about selling Irad to Russia, which took no account of the end of US administration in 2006, provoked protests in both zones, including a march past the former residence of the High Commissioner in Talas, and renewed debate about the legacy of the territorial years (see [[Irad–United States relations]]).<sup>[26]</sup>
