### 2.13. Media of Irad
*Quality Assessment: Good Article (GA) | Category: Media*

The **media of Irad** are dominated by [[IradOne]], the state broadcaster of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), which runs the main national television channel, the Russian-language channel ИрадОдин (IradOdin), a sports channel and the Radio Irad network. The private press is small and based mainly in [[Talas]]: the daily *Talas Herald* is the most widely read newspaper, and the independent English-language weekly *[[Irad Times]]* is the main investigative title, although its website has been blocked inside Irad since 15 October 2026. Almost all internet and mobile traffic passes through [[Attelkom]], the largest telecommunications company, and the home-grown app [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]] is the main domestic messaging platform. Since 2007 IradOne has been under the supervision of the Department of Public Information, the government press office, which also issues editorial guidelines, registers print outlets and supplies lists of websites to be blocked.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

Laws inherited from the US territorial period guarantee freedom of the press, and Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] has stated that Irad has had a free press since the end of Soviet rule. Press-freedom organizations, [[wp:Human Rights Watch]] and the [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe|OSCE]] describe a restricted environment in which the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) controls broadcast news, independent journalists face licensing pressure and self-censorship, and the authorities have cut or throttled internet access during protests. Media consumption divides sharply by language and generation, and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) lie largely outside the reach of ISEZ media.<sup>[3]</sup>

## History

#### Soviet period
Under *korenizatsiia* in the 1920s, the first newspapers in Iradi were published alongside the Russian-language press, and printing presses were refitted for the Latin script introduced in 1928. Regular radio broadcasting began from Kobozev, now [[Nurzhan]], in the 1930s, and television followed in 1959, both under the republic's State Committee for Television and Radio Broadcasting. Programs were mainly in Russian, with a smaller share in Iradi and relays from Central Television in [[wp:Moscow]]. A second studio opened in Talas in the late 1960s, and the 220-meter [[IradOne Transmitter Mast]] on Television Hill in Talas was built in 1972.<sup>[4]</sup>

The main newspaper was *Iradyn Chyny* ("The Truth of Irad"), the Russian- and Iradi-language organ of the Communist Party of the Iradi SSR. Under the editor [[Maratbek Sadykov]] (1986–1991) it published, in 1988 and 1989, the first articles on the [[1956 Talas Riots]], the [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges|purges of the clergy]] and the [[The Kobozev Bread Riots (1989)|Kobozev bread riots]], and its circulation rose from about 90,000 to more than 200,000 copies.<sup>[5]</sup> Foreign broadcasts also reached the republic: in the 1980s American country and folk songs about Irad circulated on smuggled cassettes and through [[wp:Voice of America]] broadcasts, a source of what became [[Iradi Country-Folk|Iradi country-folk]].

#### 1991–1992
Sadykov was dismissed in October 1991, shortly after the declaration of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]], when his paper reported sympathetically on protests in Talas, and in November the new government issued emergency decrees banning non-communist gatherings and publications. During the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]] and the [[First Iradi Civil War]], the socialist government kept control of the Kobozev studios, while the Provisional Government broadcast radio appeals from the Talas studio.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Territorial period (1992–2006)
The Public Broadcasting Act of 1993 created IradOne as a public corporation whose board was appointed by the Governor and confirmed by the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]]. The broadcaster moved its headquarters from Nurzhan to Talas and adopted English and Iradi as its main languages, cutting Russian-language programming after Russian lost its official status in 1992. US media-development programs trained its journalists. Media researchers describe IradOne in this period as relatively pluralistic, with election airtime for opposition parties, although critics noted a consistent bias toward the territorial administration.<sup>[6]</sup>

Private print and online media developed alongside it. The *Irad Times*, an English-language weekly, was founded in 1996. Attelkom opened dial-up internet service in 1996 and the first GSM mobile network in 1997. In December 2006 and January 2007 the *Irad Times*, under its managing editor [[Bolotbek Daniyar]], published internal documents on the planned sale of state oil, grain and mining assets by the government of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]], reporting that preceded the protests over the [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]]. On 26 February 2007 it printed in a special edition the partition drafts released by Toktarov the day before (see [[Bill of Sale (2007)]]).<sup>[7]</sup>

#### Since 2007
IradOne changed hands more than once during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]]. After DPI security forces took Talas in the summer of 2007, the ISEZ administration dissolved its board by emergency decree and placed it under the Department of Public Information. Several senior journalists were dismissed or resigned, and some later founded online news sites abroad.<sup>[6]</sup> In 2008 the ISEZ annulled the mobile-frequency auctions held by the DRI and reissued Attelkom's licenses on condition that it comply with new security directives.

IradOne launched IradOdin in 2009 for Russian-speaking viewers in Nurzhan. In June 2015 Toktarov appointed his second son, [[Alikhan Toktarov]], chairman of IradOne's board. Under him the broadcaster launched IradOne Sport and mobile streaming, moved into the [[Alikhan Media Center]] in downtown Talas in 2017, and completed the move to digital terrestrial broadcasting, begun in 2015, in 2018.<sup>[8]</sup> In 2013 the Department of Public Information suspended the registration of the *Irad Times* for two months after it criticized the amendment removing gubernatorial term limits; the department said the suspension concerned a licensing irregularity.<sup>[7]</sup>

## Regulation
The main instruments of media control in the ISEZ are:<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[9]</sup>
- **The Department of Public Information.** The government press office issues IradOne's editorial guidelines, registers newspapers and can suspend their registration, accredits journalists, and supplies Attelkom with lists of websites to be blocked.
- **The 2008 security directives.** Attelkom must route international traffic through gateways fitted with monitoring equipment and carry out orders from the ISEZ executive to restrict service. The company says it is legally bound to comply.
- **Licensing.** Broadcast and telecommunications licenses are issued by an ISEZ regulatory board, on which [[Aidar Maksat]] sat from 2012 to 2019 before becoming Lieutenant Governor.

The emergency basis on which the ISEZ was proclaimed in 2007 has never been formally ended, and press-freedom groups say that this, rather than any new press law, gives the executive its discretion over the media.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Television
{{Update section|date=July 2026}}

Television is the main source of news for most ISEZ residents over 40. IradOne's terrestrial signal covers the whole ISEZ through the Talas mast and relay transmitters, and its channels are also carried by satellite and online. In a 2023 survey by the Irad Media Research Center, IradOne had about 38 percent of the ISEZ television audience and IradOdin about 9 percent.<sup>[10]</sup> The broadcaster's channels are:
- **IradOne**, the flagship channel, mainly in English, with its evening news bulletin, *[[OneNews|OneNews at Eight]]*, at 20:00 followed by an Iradi-language bulletin. The share of Iradi-language programs has grown since 2018, partly in response to young viewers' interest in the language. Since 2016 the channel's own English-language programs have carried its "One" prefix, among them the weekly investigative program *[[OneTruth]]* and the morning magazine *[[OneBreakfast]]* (see [[List of IradOne programs]]).<sup>[11]</sup>
- **IradOdin**, produced at the Nurzhan studio, which shows acquired Russian series and films, talk shows and translated IradOne bulletins. It is widely considered to have much lower production values than the main channel. Politicians allied with the oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]] say it is deliberately underfunded; IradOne says its budget reflects its audience.
- **IradOne Sport**, launched in 2016, which holds exclusive rights to the Ulak Tartysh [[President's Cup]] at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]] and covers *at chabysh*, football and wrestling.<sup>[8]</sup>

IradOne had about 2,100 employees in 2023 and a budget of about $46 million, roughly 60 percent from government appropriations and the rest from advertising and sports rights.<sup>[8]</sup> Its music programs have given national exposure to Iradi country-folk and to [[Mor-Wave]], although, according to the *Talas Herald*, it dropped several videos by the duo [[tüntolk]] from rotation after their songs were sung at the 2023 protests in Talas.<sup>[12]</sup> Historians have criticized some of its documentaries for presenting contested national beliefs, such as the claim that the horse was first domesticated in Irad, as established fact.

Russian channels received by satellite remain popular in Nurzhan among the Russian-speaking generation known as the [[Russos of Nurzhan|Russos]], while younger urban viewers increasingly watch online.<sup>[10]</sup>

#### Political commentary
IradOne's prime-time current-affairs panel, *[[OneDebate]]*, has since 2016 featured the Iradi-American commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]], a self-described anarcho-capitalist and founder of the Liberty Forum of Irad. Ilyasov has used the program to attack the business concessions held by the Governor's family, and IradOne has suspended him at least twice for his conduct on air, but has continued to book him despite these attacks.<sup>[13]</sup> In October 2023 his on-air criticism of a municipal licensing surcharge on startups and couriers spread widely on social media and was followed by the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]], during which he was held for three days and released without charge. IradOne kept him off the air for several months and began booking him again in 2024.

Ilyasov says his work is funded by the income of his messaging app, Tulpar. Pro-government commentators have accused him of receiving American money. A 2024 survey of the ISEZ media in the *Eurasian Political Quarterly* found no documentary evidence for the claim and attributed his rise to online engagement and frustration among young urban [[Iradis]].<sup>[13]</sup>

## Radio
Radio Irad, IradOne's national network (98.4 FM in Talas), carries news, music, agricultural bulletins and folklore programs. Its evening program *Kechki Jomok* ("Evening Tales"), presented from 1994 to 2020 by [[Baktygul Omur]] and often said to have been modeled on the siege broadcasts of the folklorist [[Sagyn Jusupbekov]], was for many years one of the few regular programs in Iradi, and its audience reached herding settlements on both sides of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]].<sup>[14]</sup> In Nurzhan the most-listened station is the private Russian-language Radio Chu FM (104.5 FM), launched in 2001 by Nurzhan Press House, which plays Russian pop and evening *chanson* and carries a call-in program, *Gorod* ("The City"). The state's Russian-language station, Radio IradOdin (101.7 FM in Nurzhan, 92.3 FM in Talas), part of the Radio Irad network since 2006, carries IradOne news in Russian on the hour, Soviet *estrada* and a breakfast show, *Dobroe utro, Nurzhan*, and draws an older audience. The [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI) produces a weekly radio program carried by local stations, together with quarterly security bulletins in Iradi, Russian and English, intended partly to counter rumors of troop movements during political crises.<sup>[15]</sup>

## Print
*Main article: [[List of newspapers in Irad]]*
The ISEZ press is small. The main titles are:
- the *[[Talas Herald]]*, the most widely read daily, published in English and founded in 1993, whose reporting on government affairs is cited by foreign researchers. Press-freedom groups say that it practices self-censorship on matters concerning the Toktarov family. Since 2017 it has also published *Jarchy* ("The Herald"), an Iradi-language weekly for younger readers with translated news, music and film pages and readers' letters, which is carried to settlements near the Qara-Chik line by bus and by mounted courier;<sup>[16]</sup>
- the *Irad Times*, an independent English-language weekly founded in 1996, owned by its staff and edited by Daniyar since 2001, known for investigative reporting on privatization, the antimony industry and the grain auction of 2008. Its website has been hosted in the United States since 2008, so that the authorities can only have it blocked inside Irad. Attelkom blocked it in 2013, 2015, 2023 and 2025, and has blocked it again since the evening of 15 October 2026, after an issue that reported registry filings linking the unnamed partners in the planned restart of the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] to a subsidiary of [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]]. No reason was given for the block, and Trans-Chuy says it has no ownership link with the partners. The print edition has not been stopped during any block;<sup>[17]</sup>
- Russian-language weeklies in Nurzhan, read mainly by older residents, the largest being *Vecherniy Nurzhan* ("Evening Nurzhan"; founded in 1968 as *Vecherniy Kobozev*), published by Nurzhan Press House, which keeps close to the official line and draws much of its advertising from [[NurGaz]] and other Nurzhan firms;
- tabloids in Talas, which have published unverified stories about the ruling family and about Bekzatov's supposed political plans, treated by analysts as palace intrigue.<sup>[7]</sup><sup>[18]</sup>

The joint pastoral letters and communiqués of the [[Syro-Iradi Council of Hierarchs]] are also widely reported; a 2021 survey found the church to be the most trusted public institution in the ISEZ.

## Internet and telecommunications
*Main article: [[Telecommunications in Irad]]*
Attelkom reported about 2.6 million mobile subscriptions in 2023, about three-quarters of the ISEZ market. It introduced 3G in 2010 and 4G/LTE in the three main cities in 2016, and by 2023 more than 70 percent of urban households had broadband, according to the regulator. All international traffic passes through two fiber routes into [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and one into [[wp:Uzbekistan]].<sup>[9]</sup> Social media and messaging groups are the main sources of news for young urban Iradis, and Iradi is now widely used online, a trend linked to the [[Iradi language revival]]. Ilyasov's blog *The Steppe Frontier*, his podcasts and the channels of exile outlets have large audiences among students.<sup>[10]</sup>

During the October 2023 protests, mobile data was cut in central Talas for three days and access to several social media platforms was throttled across the ISEZ. Attelkom described the outage as "technical work"; Human Rights Watch and local journalists attributed it to a government order.<sup>[19]</sup> In 2024 several foreign and exile news sites were blocked after they published reports questioning the authenticity of video addresses by the Governor. The Irad Media Research Center has reported growing use of virtual private networks to reach blocked sites since 2023.<sup>[10]</sup>

The most widely used domestic platform is Tulpar, a free messaging app launched in Talas in March 2019 by Ilyasov and a team of six [[Talas State University]] graduates led by its chief technology officer, [[Aiperi Kalysbek]]. Built for cheap phones and slow connections, it was the first popular app with a correct Iradi interface. It added public channels, which carry IradOne and the *Talas Herald* among others, in 2020 and the classifieds board *Bazar* in 2021.<sup>[20]</sup> During the October 2023 protests, when foreign platforms were throttled, Tulpar was not, and students and couriers moved their group chats to it; it registered more than 140,000 new accounts in a week, roughly doubling its users.<sup>[21]</sup> After the 2025 Trump remarks, posts branding it "the American app", many of them from pro-government accounts, cost it about a sixth of its monthly users, who had returned by late August 2025. In October 2026 the company reported 1.1 million accounts and about 650,000 monthly users, including Iradis abroad; the figures have not been independently verified.<sup>[22]</sup>

Iradi websites have also dropped out of foreign search engines three times, episodes known in Irad as the *jogoluular* ("the disappearances"). From 2009 to 2011 the monitoring gateways installed under the 2008 directives refused connections from foreign data-center address ranges, so that search crawlers abroad could not reach sites hosted in the ISEZ; Attelkom loosened the rule in late 2011, after measurements by a Talas State University lecturer were reported in the *Herald*. In 2015 and 2016 search engines demoted the whole *.ir.ad* zone after thousands of its names had been sold to foreign spammers, and the zone lapsed in 2019. The third and longest delisting began in October 2023, when the "national segment" mode switched on for the protest data cut was never fully switched off, so that foreign crawlers received only an outage page from ISEZ-hosted sites. Iradi sites returned to foreign search results in July and August 2026, after Attelkom moved its international traffic in June to new gateway equipment, bought with Chinese export credit, that blocks sites by domain list instead of refusing foreign traffic wholesale.<sup>[23]</sup> Each episode had a mundane technical cause, but the anonymous website [[FreeIrad.org]], widely regarded in Irad as a crackpot site, counts the delistings as evidence for its [[Erasure Theory|Erasure theory]].

Banner advertising on most Iradi websites is sold by [[Attelkom Jarnama]], Attelkom's advertising department, which opened its network to other publishers in April 2016, beginning with IradOne Online, and keeps 40 percent of the revenue. Its banners also appear on the *Herald*'s website, Attelkom's [[Kartalar]] maps, the classifieds site [[Jılmay]], the Tulpar website and the horse-games portal [[Jarysh]], and advertisements for sites on the list of restricted resources lead to Attelkom's restriction notice.<sup>[24]</sup>

## Exile and diaspora media
Online news sites founded abroad by journalists who left IradOne after 2007 are the main sources of critical reporting on the ruling family. In 2018 exiled journalists published allegations about Alikhan Toktarov's purchase of villas in [[wp:Dubai]], which IradOne did not report. Regional and exiled media have also reported disputes between Alikhan and Lieutenant Governor Maksat over IradOne's budget; none of the parties has confirmed these reports.<sup>[6]</sup><sup>[25]</sup>

The Iradi community in the United States, centered in [[wp:Chicago]], supports Iradi-language community media and has been an audience for exile outlets (see [[Iradi Americans]]). Ilyasov, born in Chicago, holds US citizenship, which pro-government commentators used against him during the anti-American feeling that followed the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]].<sup>[13]</sup>

## Media in the Autonomous Tribal Regions
ISEZ media have little audience in the ATR. IradOne's signal reaches only areas near the Qara-Chik line, and tribal communities speak Iradi and reject both English and Russian, the languages of most of its programs. Attelkom has almost no formal service there; relay towers near the line give some coverage, herders elsewhere rely on satellite telephones, and near the frontiers they use Kazakh, Kyrgyz and Uzbek mobile networks.<sup>[9]</sup> The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] has no broadcaster of its own. Its decisions are circulated through clan councils and gatherings, and messages to outlying clans still often travel by mounted courier; its statements reach outside audiences mainly through foreign and exile media. Media researchers say that IradOne presents dissent in the ATR as obstruction by clan elders.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Press freedom and the Governor's broadcasts
The OSCE and press-freedom groups have described IradOne's coverage of the 2015, 2019 and 2023 gubernatorial elections as heavily weighted in favor of Toktarov and the DPI, and opposition figures, among them Bekzatov, rarely appear on the channel.<sup>[3]</sup> Independent journalists report administrative harassment, license revocations and travel bans, and the Legal Defense Guild of the lawyer [[Gulnara Sadyk]] represents detained journalists and students.<sup>[19]</sup>

Since July 2024, video and audio addresses by Governor Toktarov, who has not appeared in public in that period, have been released only through IradOne, and their authenticity has been the subject of claims that officials reject (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]). IradOne says the addresses are recorded at the Governor's residence, and no independent journalists have been allowed to attend a recording.<sup>[26]</sup> Ilyasov has repeatedly challenged the government to show the Governor in a live, unedited appearance, a demand DPI spokesmen have called "theater". Press-freedom groups have expressed concern that the official description of such claims as disinformation is being used to discourage reporting on the Governor's absence, and the autumn 2024 communiqué of the Council of Hierarchs called for "constitutional order and truthful public information" (see [[Human rights in Irad]]).<sup>[27]</sup>

### 2.14. Iradi cuisine
*Quality Assessment: Good Article (GA) | Category: Culture & Folklore*

**Iradi cuisine** (Iradi: *Irad tamagy*) is the cooking and food culture of [[Irad]] and the [[Iradis]]. It rests on mutton, beef, milk and wheat, and shares much with the cuisines of the [[wp:Kyrgyz cuisine|Kyrgyz]], [[wp:Kazakh cuisine|Kazakhs]] and [[wp:Uzbek cuisine|Uzbeks]]: boiled-meat feasts, plov, noodles, dumplings, tandoor bread and fermented milk. Two features set it apart from its neighbours. Iradis drink fermented mare's milk but will not eat horsemeat, so the feast dishes that neighbouring peoples make from horse are made in Irad from beef or mutton (see [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]]); and the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] has shaped the table through its bread, its wine and a calendar of fasts and feasts.<sup>[1]</sup>

Many peoples have added to it. The Sogdian and Uzbek-speaking towns brought rice, tandoor bread, samsa and the teahouse; Russian settlers and Soviet canteens brought soups, salads, pickles and factory bread; the [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]] deported to the Chu valley in 1937 brought short-grain rice and Korean salads; and the American territorial period (1992–2006) made grain-finished beef the main festive meat and brought a Mexican community to [[Talas]]. Out of this mixture came dishes found nowhere else, among them [[Iradi Plov|Iradi plov]], a stirred short-grain rice dish closer to risotto than to the plov of its neighbours, the saddle-shaped cheese bread *[[Eer Nan|eer nan]]*, and the green tarragon soda *[[Jasil|jasil]]*.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

Food writers distinguish five regional cuisines: the orchard cooking of the south, the herders' cooking of the mountains, the Kazakh-influenced cooking of the steppe and the Karatau, the Russian, Ukrainian and Korean cooking of [[Nurzhan]], and the mixed cooking of the Talas valley. Meals are eaten from a cloth (*[[Dastorkon|dastorkon]]*) spread with bread, sweets and dried fruit before the main dishes arrive, and are opened by an elder's blessing.<sup>[12]</sup><sup>[17]</sup>

## History

#### Pastoral foundations
The diet of the herding clans was based on the products of their flocks and herds: mutton, milk in its many fermented and dried forms, and, on the summer pastures, mare's milk. Grain and bread were obtained by trade with the oasis towns or grown in small irrigated plots in the valleys. Meat was eaten mainly at feasts, weddings and memorial gatherings, when a sheep was slaughtered and boiled whole, and mutton was historically the main festive meat.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Silk Road towns
The Sogdian and later Uzbek-speaking towns of the Chu and Talas valleys and the Fergana Rim had a settled cuisine of tandoor-baked flatbread, rice, fruit and vegetables, and of dishes cooked in the cauldron (*kazan*). [[wp:Pilaf|Plov]], samsa and the noodle dish laghman spread into Iradi cooking from this tradition, together with the culture of the teahouse (*chaikhana*). Wild fruit and nuts from the forests of the Chatkal and Fergana ranges, among them walnuts and the wild apple *[[Semirechye Apple|Malus sieversii]]*, were traded along the same routes, and the towns made and traded wine.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Christian influence
Christian identity shaped Iradi food in several ways. The refusal to eat horsemeat became, in the view of ethnographers, a marker that set Christian Iradi pastoralists apart from neighbours living under Muslim khanates. Church tradition attributes the taboo to [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]], to whom the White Rider is said to have forbidden the killing of horses for food. The church calendar introduced fasts, notably the three-day Rogation of the Ninevites before Lent, which in rural areas is still a period of strict fasting, and feasts at which unconsecrated *[[Kümöch Sacramental Bread|kümöch]]* and meat dishes are shared.<sup>[4]</sup>

The liturgy also needed wine. Christian villages made it by the method of the Sogdian towns, fermenting grapes in large clay jars sunk in the earth. Under Muslim rulers, above all during the forced conversions of the Chagatai khan Ali-Sultan (1339–42) and after Timur's campaigns, they hid the jars in vineyards and in caves so that the wine could not be found and poured away. The buried wine, *[[Kömmö (Wine)|kömmö]]*, is still made in the same way, and the Church's own wine is called *[[Kamra (Wine)|kamra]]*.<sup>[19]</sup>

#### Russian and Soviet period
Russian settlers from the 1880s and Soviet institutions from the 1920s brought bread baked in factories, potatoes, cabbage and beetroot, pickles, dairy products such as kefir and sour cream, and dishes such as borscht, pelmeni and mayonnaise-dressed salads. Workplace canteens (*stolovaya*) and state bakeries fed the growing workforce of Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]) and the industrial towns. The green herb soda *jasil* dates from this period, and state wineries on the Fergana Rim made fortified *portveyn* from the old church vineyards; about half of the vines were uprooted in the anti-alcohol campaign of 1985–87. [[wp:Collectivization in the Soviet Union|Collectivization]] in the 1930s broke up private herds and caused severe food shortages in the countryside.<sup>[5]</sup><sup>[16]</sup>

In 1937 Soviet authorities deported the Korean population of the Far East to [[wp:Central Asia]], and several thousand deportees were unloaded at Kobozev and in the Chu valley. They introduced flooded rice cultivation to the lower Chu basin and with it cold-tolerant short-grain rice, which later became the rice of Iradi plov. Korean dishes adapted to local ingredients, such as the carrot salad *[[Morkovcha|morkovcha]]*, were sold in bazaars across the republic by the 1960s.<sup>[6]</sup>

#### Territorial period
After the [[wp:North American Free Trade Agreement]] took effect in 1994, [[wp:SuKarne]] and [[wp:Conagra Brands|Conagra]] built beef plants near Talas. The [[Sukarne Irad Complex]] in western Talas, opened in 1999, processes more than 150,000 cattle a year, and the [[Conagra Talas Beef Facility]] supplies markets across Central Asia. Grain-finished beef, previously less important than mutton, became the main festive meat in the cities, and Conagra has worked with local farmers and KFC Irad on poultry. The beef industry also brought more than 10,000 Mexicans to Talas, whose district of [[Semiz]] has Mexican shops and restaurants.<sup>[7]</sup>

In 1996 the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] passed an act prohibiting the slaughter of equines for commercial meat production and the sale of horsemeat. The act remains in force in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). Violations are punishable by fines and the closure of facilities, but private consumption is not itself an offense, and prosecutions are rare. In the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), clan councils punish the slaughter of horses for sale under customary law, usually with fines paid in livestock.<sup>[8]</sup>

#### Since 2007
The [[Second Iradi Civil War]] of 2007 left the countryside short of food through the following winter, when relief rations were handed out under the eye of the newly arrived [[United Nations Mission in Irad]]. Families cooked them into *[[Kök Kaska|kök kaska]]* ("blue helmet"), a stew of tinned beef, noodles of aid flour, beans and tomato paste, which is now made for nostalgia. Since then supermarket chains such as [[Bereke]] and [[Jıldız Market]] have spread across the ISEZ, while trade across the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] decides what reaches the tribal side and in what season.<sup>[7]</sup><sup>[21]</sup>

## Regional cuisines
Iradi cooks and food writers usually distinguish five regional cuisines, each with its own techniques, staples and occasions. Their borders follow the old cultural regions more than the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[12]</sup>

#### Bakcha tamagy (the south)
{{Main|Bakcha Tamagy}}

**[[Bakcha Tamagy|Bakcha tamagy]]** ("orchard food") belongs to the Fergana Rim, the Lower Naryn farm belt and [[Iyık Janyl]]. It is a cuisine of the tandoor, the cauldron and the vine-shaded courtyard, where meals are eaten outdoors for half the year and a course of fruit can stand in for dessert or for the meal itself. Men cook the wedding plov of long grains, yellow carrots and chickpeas over wood fires; women stew meat and vegetables in their own juices as *dimlama*; bakers stamp each round loaf, Christian bakers with a cross and Muslim bakers with a rosette. Apricots, melons and walnuts are dried on the roofs and preserved whole as *murabba*, and wine is made in clay jars buried in the ground at [[Kyzyl-Senir]]. Its year swings between the strict fasts of the church villages and the feasts of the shared shrines, and at mixed tables the meat is bought from a Muslim butcher so that everyone can eat it.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[19]</sup>

#### Jayloo tamagy (the mountains)
{{Main|Jayloo Tamagy}}

**[[Jayloo Tamagy|Jayloo tamagy]]** ("summer-pasture food") belongs to the herding clans of the Talas Alatau, the [[Chatkal Range|Chatkal]] valleys and the Toktogul–Naryn basin, and to the [[Tat (Irad)|Tat]] of the [[Khirnou]] valley. It is cooked over a single fire in the yurt or the stone house and follows the migration: summers of "white food" on the high pastures, when milk, curd, fresh cheese and *kymyz* make most meals, and winters of mutton dried in strips, hard curd and bread. Meat is boiled, never fried, and feast mutton is first hung in juniper smoke. The bread is the church's own, unleavened *kümöch* baked in embers and loaves raised with a family sourdough said to come from the holy leaven, and weddings serve mutton only. The hearth itself carries rules: the Tat never blow out a flame or pour water on the fire.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[15]</sup>

#### Talaa tamagy (the steppe and the Karatau)
{{Main|Talaa Tamagy}}

**[[Talaa Tamagy|Talaa tamagy]]** ("steppe food") belongs to the Northern Steppe clans of the [[Betpak-Dala]], the [[Moiynkum Desert|Moiynkum]] and the Chu–Sarysu lowland, and to the Karatau. It is a cuisine of long migrations and wells, cooked in one cauldron and carried in saddlebags. Meat is boiled in large pieces and carved by the host onto broad sheets of noodle dough, with the broth (*sorpa*) drunk from bowls afterwards; camels give milk drunk fermented as *shubat* and meat for the sausage *töö kazy*; tea is drunk strong with milk and salt, many bowls at a sitting; and food that keeps, such as hard dried curd, goes with every journey. The *Eski El* of the Karatau keep their own ritual table, cooking a white lamb at a spring with hot stones inside its skin (*[[Tash Kozu|tash kozu]]*) and a spring broth of steppe tortoises (*[[Tash Baka Shorpo|tash baka shorpo]]*).<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[22]</sup>

#### Kobozev tamagy (the Russos)
{{Main|Kobozev Tamagy}}

**[[Kobozev Tamagy|Kobozev tamagy]]**, named after the Soviet name of [[Nurzhan]], belongs to Nurzhan, the Chu lowlands and the railway towns, and is kept by the [[Russos of Nurzhan|Russos]]. It is a cuisine of apartment kitchens, numbered canteens and bazaar salad stalls, drawn from Russian, Ukrainian and Korean cooking. Its rhythm is set by the jar and the holiday: cucumbers, tomatoes and cabbage are pickled on every balcony in autumn, families make pelmeni together on winter Sundays, and the New Year table is laid with *olivier*, herring and *kholodets*. Korean women's stalls sell *morkovcha*, *kimchi* and steamed buns, cold *kuksi* is the summer lunch, and vodka is poured with toasts at every celebration.<sup>[5]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>

#### Talas kazany (the Talas valley)
{{Main|Talas Kazany}}

**[[Talas Kazany|Talas kazany]]** ("the Talas cauldron") belongs to [[Talas]] and the Talas and Kara-Buura valleys. It is a young, urban cuisine of cattle country and city streets, still inventing dishes. Beef from the valley's feedlots is the feast meat, and the household dish is creamy short-grain [[Iradi Plov|Iradi plov]], stirred on Sundays and served with red beet suzma. Its bakeries sell the saddle-shaped cheese bread *[[Eer Nan|eer nan]]*, the tortillerías of [[Semiz]] make tortillas of yellow maize, and its newest street dish, *[[Nan Tako|nan tako]]*, folds grilled beef into tandoor bread. Summer is marked by queues at the *jasil* fountains.<sup>[7]</sup><sup>[13]</sup>

## Ingredients

#### Meat
Beef and mutton are the main meats. Grain-finished beef from the Talas plants and the local [[Aulie-Ata]] cattle dominate in the cities and the plains; mountain mutton, valued for its flavour, dominates in the highlands and at rural feasts. Goat is eaten in the mountains, camel on the steppe and chicken everywhere. Pork is eaten by Russians, Ukrainians, Koryo-saram and many urban Iradis but rarely in rural Iradi households, and Muslim Iradis and the Kazakh, Kyrgyz and Uzbek minorities avoid it. Horsemeat is not eaten (see Food and religion below).<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[7]</sup>

#### Grains and rice
Wheat is the staple grain, eaten as bread, noodles and dumplings, and sprouted for the Nooruz pudding *[[Sümölök|sümölök]]*. Two kinds of rice are used: the cold-tolerant short-grain rice of the lower Chu basin for Iradi plov, and long-grain rice brought from the Fergana Valley for *özbek paloo*. Buckwheat came with the Russians, and yellow dent maize, grown for feed since the 1950s, gives the yellow colour of the "Talas tortillas" made in Semiz.<sup>[6]</sup><sup>[7]</sup>

#### Fruit, nuts and wild plants
Walnuts from the forests of the Chatkal and Fergana ranges, including the forests around [[Arslanbob]], are a main cash product of the tribal regions (see [[Wild Walnut (Juglans regia)]]). Apricots, apples, quinces, melons and grapes are grown in the valleys and the Fergana Rim. Wild foods gathered in the mountains include sea buckthorn berries for juice and jam (see [[Wild Sea Buckthorn]]), barberries, wild pistachios (see [[Wild Pistachio Shrub]]) and the wild apple.<sup>[15]</sup>

#### Herbs and spices
Iradi cooking is lightly spiced. The characteristic seasonings are [[Wild Mountain Cumin|wild mountain cumin]] (*zire*, *Bunium persicum*) gathered in the [[Talas Alatau]], dried barberries (see [[Tian Shan Barberry]]), black pepper and garlic. Wild oregano and thyme season mutton and go into tea (see [[Mountain Wild Oregano]]); tarragon flavours *jasil* and the Easter lamb; dill and parsley came with Russian cooking; and the small hot *Semiz kalempir* pepper, grown by the Mexican community, has entered Iradi pickles.<sup>[13]</sup><sup>[15]</sup>

#### Fish
Fish is a minor part of the diet. Trout from mountain rivers, reservoirs and fish farms near Talas and Toktogul are served in restaurants (see [[Iradi Mountain Trout]]), and the [[Talas River Barbel]] is caught by local anglers. Along [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway|State Route 1]] beside the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex|Toktogul reservoir]], sellers wave strings of smoked reservoir fish at passing lorries.<sup>[15]</sup>

## Dishes

#### Soups and broths
- *Shorpo*: mutton or beef broth with large pieces of meat and potato, served at funerals and memorial gatherings with *kümöch*. The steppe form is called *sorpa*.
- *[[Chyk (Culinary)|Chyk]]*: the onion broth served after beshbarmak.
- *[[Tuyak]]* ("hoof"): a broth of cattle or sheep's feet simmered overnight and eaten early on winter mornings with garlic and dissolved *kurut*, by men after night shifts and as a cure after weddings.
- Borscht and other Russian and Ukrainian soups in Nurzhan, *kuksi* (cold Korean noodle soup) in summer, and soup of dried apricots and rice during the fasts.<sup>[12]</sup>

#### Meat dishes
- *[[Beshbarmak (Iradi Style)|Beshbarmak]]* ("five fingers"): boiled beef or mountain mutton served on hand-cut flat noodles with onions, the national feast dish. At formal meals the host distributes the meat according to the age and status of the guests, and when a sheep is slaughtered the head is offered to the most honoured guest.
- *[[Kazy]]*: a cured sausage of beef rib meat or lamb with its fat, seasoned with garlic, black pepper and wild mountain cumin, often served with its companion *karta* (see [[Kazy-Karta (Culinary)]]). Neighbouring peoples make both from horsemeat.
- *[[Arshalangan Et|Arshalangan et]]* ("juniper-smoked meat"): feast mutton hung in juniper smoke before it is boiled.
- *[[Kyamta Kazany|Kyamta kazany]]* ("the Easter cauldron"): lamb braised with tarragon, green cherry plums and *kamra*, eaten at dawn after the Easter vigil.
- *[[wp:Kuurdak]]*: fried meat and offal with onions, a dish of the herding camps.
- *[[wp:Shashlik]]*: skewers of grilled mutton, beef or chicken, the food of roadside cafés and summer picnics.<sup>[12]</sup>

#### Rice and noodle dishes
{{Main|Iradi Plov}}

Iradi plov (*Irad paloosu*) is the best-known Iradi dish.{{Citation needed|date=July 2026}} Despite its name it is a stirred rice dish closer to Italian risotto: short-grain rice is toasted in the fat of the *zirvak* (meat, onion and carrot), cooked with hot broth added a ladle at a time and stirred until creamy, finished with butter or suzma, seasoned with mountain cumin and barberries and served with beet suzma. It is a household dish for Sundays, name days and church feasts. The long-grain plov of the neighbouring peoples, *özbek paloo*, is cooked by men in large cauldrons for weddings and memorial feasts, often by a hired plov master (*ashpoz*), and sold in teahouses; a guest offered plov at a wedding expects separate long grains, and at a family table the creamy short-grain dish.<sup>[13]</sup>

Noodle dishes include hand-pulled *laghman* with a sauce of meat and vegetables, a dish of Uyghur and Dungan origin, and its Korean variant **Koryoin laghman**, made with sesame and kimchi.<sup>[6]</sup>

#### Dumplings and pastries
- *[[wp:Manti (food)|Manty]]*: large steamed dumplings of chopped mutton or beef and onion; pumpkin *manty* are made during fasts.
- *[[wp:Samsa (food)|Samsa]]*: baked pastries of meat and onion, sold from tandoor ovens in bazaars.
- Pelmeni and *vareniki*, the Russian and Ukrainian dumplings of Nurzhan.<sup>[12]</sup>

#### Bread
Bread is treated with respect: it is broken by hand rather than cut at ceremonial meals, never thrown away and never left on the ground, and a promise made over bread is binding.
- **Flatbread** (*nan*), baked in tandoor ovens, the everyday bread of the towns and the Fergana Rim.
- *[[Kümöch Sacramental Bread|Kümöch]]*: an unleavened wheat bread of flour, water and salt baked over embers. Consecrated, it is the Eucharistic bread of the Syro-Iradi Church; unconsecrated loaves are baked at home for weddings, baptisms, memorial gatherings and feasts, and pieces of a blessed loaf are kept in the house over winter against misfortune.
- *[[Boorsok (Culinary)|Boorsok]]*: pieces of dough fried in mutton fat, heaped on the cloth at weddings and memorial meals, where the smell of frying fat is said to reach the dead.
- *[[Eer Nan|Eer nan]]* ("saddle bread"): a saddle-shaped boat of yeast dough filled with white cheese, with an egg yolk and butter set in its seat; the round bazaar version is *panyrduu nan*, "cheese bread".
- *[[At Nan|At nan]]* ("horse bread"): small horse-shaped loaves baked for children on name days and on the feasts of the White Rider.
- **Loaf bread** (*khleb*), introduced by Russian settlers and Soviet bakeries, the everyday bread of Nurzhan.
Highland and Chatkal families bake with a sourdough, the *[[Ene Achytky|ene achytky]]* ("mother leaven"), said to descend from the church's holy leaven.<sup>[4]</sup><sup>[14]</sup>

#### Dairy products
Dairy products are eaten daily in most households:
- *[[Kymyz (Iradi Beverage)|Kymyz]]*: fermented mare's milk (see Beverages below).
- *[[Airan (Culinary)|Airan]]*: a cooling drink of fermented sour milk diluted with spring water, often with salt and wild mint.
- *[[Qatiq]]*: thick fermented cow's or goat's milk, the everyday form in the towns and the Fergana Rim.
- *[[Süzmö|Suzma]]* (*süzmö*): strained, salted sour milk, eaten with meat and flatbread. **Beet suzma**, mixed with grated beet, is a characteristic Iradi variant with a deep red colour, served with plov.
- *[[Kurut]]*: balls of strained sour milk dried in the sun, carried by riders and herders as a snack or dissolved in soup; smoked kurut is made in the Chatkal valleys.
- *[[wp:Kaymak]]*: clotted cream, eaten with bread and honey at breakfast.<sup>[11]</sup>

#### Cheese
{{Main|Iradi Cheese}}

Cheese (*panyr*, a word of Persian origin; Russian *syr* in Nurzhan) was made in the oasis towns and the Christian valley villages long before the Soviet dairies. Mare's milk does not curdle into cheese, and "cheese from a mare" is a saying for something impossible.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[12]</sup>

| Cheese | Milk | Region | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| *Ak panyr* ("white cheese") | Sheep or cow | Everywhere | Fresh brined cheese sold in slabs at every bazaar; the filling of *eer nan* |
| *Örmö panyr* ("braided cheese") | Cow or sheep | Chatkal valleys | Strings of stretched curd braided into loops and smoked over juniper |
| *Tulup panyr* ("skin cheese") | Sheep | High pastures | Crumbled cheese packed into a sheepskin and aged through the summer; sharp and salty |
| *Küp panyr* ("jar cheese") | Sheep | Fergana Rim | Aged for months in clay jars in cellars and washed with *sygyndy*; made in the caves of [[Kyzyl-Senir]] |
| *Khirnou panyry* | Goat | [[Khirnou]] valley | The [[Tat (Irad)|Tat]] cheese, pressed in hoops of juniper bark and aged in stone niches |

#### Salads and pickles
Korean-style salads, above all the spicy carrot salad *[[Morkovcha|morkovcha]]*, are sold in every bazaar. Russian *olivier* salad is a fixture of New Year and birthday tables. Cucumbers, tomatoes, cabbage and peppers are pickled for the winter, and raw onion, tomato and herbs are served with meat. In Semiz, a salsa of beet suzma and chiles goes into *[[Nan Tako|nan tako]]*.<sup>[6]</sup><sup>[7]</sup>

#### Sweets and preserves
Fruit is preserved whole in syrup as *[[Murabba|murabba]]*: apricots with their kernels, quinces, wild apples, sea buckthorn, rose petals and, most prized, green walnuts picked on the night of [[Yuhanna Tünü]]. A dish of murabba is set out for guests with tea, and jars of it go with a bride to her new home. The cloth is also laid with dried apricots and raisins, walnuts, honey and *kaymak*, and with *boorsok*. *Sümölök*, a sweet pudding of sprouted wheat cooked overnight, is made for Nooruz.<sup>[12]</sup>

#### Street food
Bazaars and roadside stalls sell samsa from the tandoor, shashlik, *manty* and *laghman*. In Talas the Mexican community added tacos made with "Talas tortillas" of yellow maize and *nan tako*, grilled beef folded into tandoor flatbread. Fresh *kymyz* is sold from roadside stalls in summer, *jasil* from street fountains, and smoked fish on the road past the Toktogul reservoir.<sup>[7]</sup><sup>[16]</sup>

## Beverages

#### Tea
Tea is the everyday drink and is offered to every guest. Green tea is usual on the Fergana Rim and among Uzbeks, and black tea, often with milk, in the north and in the herding camps; steppe herders add salt. Tea is poured in small amounts into bowls (*piyala*) and refilled often, and the teahouse (*chaikhana*) remains a meeting place for men in the southern towns.<sup>[17]</sup>

#### Dairy drinks
*[[Kymyz (Iradi Beverage)|Kymyz]]*, fermented mare's milk containing 1 to 3 percent alcohol, is made from May to September, and the first kymyz of the season is marked with the gathering *kymyz muryndyk*. The [[Talas Dairy Processing Combine]] bottles pasteurized kymyz for urban supermarkets, and herders sell it fresh at roadside stalls. Connoisseurs (*kymyzchy*) judge it by its pasture, as wine is judged by its vineyard: the kymyz of the [[Aksay Plateau]], the Suusamyr and the Chatkal valleys each has its following, and purists prefer it fresh to the bottled kind. *Airan* is the other summer drink of the pastures, and steppe herders drink fermented camel's milk (*shubat*).<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[11]</sup>

#### Soft drinks
{{Main|Jasil}}

*Jasil* is a sweet, bright green carbonated drink made with an herb syrup, flavoured mainly with tarragon but with other herbs that vary by region and household. First produced in the Soviet period, it is sold in bottles and from street fountains. Other drinks include sea buckthorn and apricot juices, *[[Maksym|maksym]]*, a fermented grain drink sold in summer, and the Russian bread drink *kvas*.<sup>[16]</sup>

#### Alcoholic drinks
Wine (*sharap*) is made mainly on the Fergana Rim. The Church's sacramental wine, *[[Kamra (Wine)|kamra]]* (from Syriac *khamra*, "wine"), is a sweet dark red made at [[Kyzyl-Senir]], where wine has been fermented since the Middle Ages in clay jars (*küp*) buried in the ground and set in caves in the red cliffs (*[[Kömmö (Wine)|kömmö]]*, "buried" wine). The skins and pips left in the jars are distilled into *[[Sygyndy|sygyndy]]*, a clear grape brandy of 45 to 60 percent, drunk at toasts in the south. *[[Yuhanna Jangagy]]* is a dark liqueur of green walnuts picked on the night of Yuhanna Tünü and opened at Christmas.<sup>[19]</sup><sup>[20]</sup>

Vodka arrived with the Russians and is still the drink of memorial meals, of older men and of Nurzhan; beer, brewed in Nurzhan and Talas and led by [[Aigyr Lager]], is the drink of young city people. *Kymyz* is barely counted as alcohol.<sup>[8]</sup>

## Food and religion

#### Horsemeat
{{Main|Iradi Horsemeat Taboo}}

Eating horsemeat carries a stigma that Iradi writers and foreign observers often compare with Western attitudes to eating dog. Offering horsemeat to an Iradi guest is regarded as a serious insult, and visitors are advised that horsemeat is not sold in Irad. Many Iradis regard it as a barbarous "Muslim" food. Ethnographers describe this view as a popular prejudice: horsemeat dishes such as *kazy* and *chuchuk* belong to the pastoral heritage of the Kazakhs and Kyrgyz regardless of religion, the [[wp:Hanafi school|Hanafi]] jurists of Central Asia historically classed horsemeat as disapproved, and most Iradi Muslims observe the same taboo as their Christian neighbours. Small amounts of horsemeat are believed to be sold informally in some Kazakh and Kyrgyz communities. The taboo does not extend to the products of living mares.<sup>[8]</sup><sup>[9]</sup>

#### Cattle
Cattle are not taboo. Plains Iradis of the Talas, Chu and [[Kara-Buura]] valleys have long kept them, while highland Iradis keep sheep and goats. Commercial cattle breeding arrived with the Soviet Virgin Lands campaign, whose beef state farms were worked mainly by Slavic and Korean settlers, and a saying held that "cattle are for the settlers". A minor superstition, comparable to the European one about black cats, treats cattle as unlucky; it is usually voiced by grandmothers, as in the saying that seeing a cow before a horse in the morning brings a bad day, and folklorists trace it to [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]], a bull-headed god of pre-Christian belief whom church tradition identifies with Satan. Because cattle are kept out of sight at a wedding, highland and old Talas families serve only mutton at the wedding feast; city banquet halls serve beef regardless.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[10]</sup>

#### Fasts
The Syro-Iradi Church keeps the Great Fast (*Uluu Savma*) before Easter, the three-day Rogation of the Ninevites and fasts on Wednesdays and Fridays, when meat, milk and eggs are not eaten. Fast food (*[[Savma Tamak|savma tamak]]*) includes walnut *pashtet*, soups of dried apricots and rice, lentils, pumpkin *manty* and *boorsok* fried in sunflower oil, and supermarkets set out fast shelves.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Blessing and sacrifice
The Church rejects animal sacrifice as pagan or Muslim, and offerings are made with milk, *kymyz* and juniper smoke. A sheep killed for a feast is food, not an offering, and in the mountains its meat is smoked over juniper (*arsha*), the incense of the church, before it is boiled, under the saying "smoked, not offered". The Karatau *Eski El*, whose white lamb of the Rider's day other Iradis regard as a sacrifice, are the exception.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[22]</sup>

#### Festive foods
Typical foods of the main feasts and family occasions:<sup>[18]</sup>

| Occasion | Date | Foods |
|---|---|---|
| Christmas | 25 December | Roast mutton or beef, *kümöch*; *Yuhanna jangagy* opened |
| Irad Day | 11 March | Family feasts of mutton and beef; food stalls at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]], with no horsemeat |
| Nooruz | 21 March | *Sümölök* cooked overnight in a cauldron |
| Easter (*Kyamta*) | Movable | *Kyamta kazany* at dawn after the vigil; eggs dyed with walnut husks or onion skins and knocked together (*jumurtka chokush*); painted eggs and *paska* in the towns; *kamra* |
| Name days | Saint's feast | *Boorsok*, *kümöch*, *at nan* for children |
| Yuhanna Tünü | 23–24 June | Green walnuts picked by the bonfires for liqueur and *murabba* |
| Feast of St. Janyl | 24 August | Communal beef and mutton with *kymyz* for pilgrims at Iyık Janyl; blessed *kümöch* |
| Weddings (*toi*) and memorials | — | Beshbarmak or *özbek paloo*, *boorsok*, *kümöch*, *kymyz*; mutton only at highland weddings |

## Dining customs
{{Main|Dastorkon}}

Meals are served on a cloth (*dastorkon*) spread on a low table or on the floor of a yurt, laid with bread, sweets, dried fruit, nuts and *boorsok* before the main dishes arrive. Guests are seated in the place of honour (*tör*) facing the door, and the seating follows age. Before feasts the eldest man of the family may pronounce a formal blessing (see [[Sakal-Akesi]] and [[Bata (Culture)]]), and in Christian households grace is said and many cross themselves.<sup>[17]</sup>

At a wedding or memorial a toastmaster, the *[[Sözchü|sözchü]]*, leads the toasts in a fixed order, beginning with God and the White Rider; the drink is *kymyz* in the tribal regions, brandy or vodka in the cities, and tea among Evangelicals and many Muslims. A guest is never allowed to leave hungry, and hospitality to strangers is a point of honour.<sup>[17]</sup>

## Eating out and the food industry
Teahouses serve plov, laghman, samsa and tea in the towns of the south, and Soviet-style canteens (*stolovaya*) survive in Nurzhan and at workplaces. KFC Irad has branches in Talas and Nurzhan, and the restaurants near [[Talas Air Base]] serve American barbecue and steaks. Food processing is led by the beef plants of SuKarne and Conagra, the [[Talas Dairy Processing Combine]] and the breweries of Talas and Nurzhan, and the [[St. Teresa Community Kitchen]] feeds the poor of Talas.<sup>[7]</sup>

### 2.15. Iradis
*Quality Assessment: Good Article (GA) | Category: Society & Demographics*

The **Iradis** (Iradi: *Iraddar*; singular *Irad*) are a [[wp:Kipchaks|Kipchak]] Turkic people native to [[Irad]], where they form the majority of the population. They speak [[Iradi Language|Iradi]], a language closely related to Kyrgyz, and are distinguished from their Turkic neighbors chiefly by religion: most Iradis belong to the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], an Eastern Catholic church descended from the [[wp:Church of the East]], which converted Turkic pastoralists of the region in the 11th and 12th centuries. The official census of 2018 counted about 3.3 million Iradis, 72 percent of Irad's population. Independent researchers consider this an undercount, because the census only estimated the population of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), where Iradis are the large majority.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

Iradis are divided between a largely urban, multilingual population in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and a rural, pastoral population in the tribal regions, organized in 24 patrilineal clans. Their identity rests on a set of practices often described as "refusals" that set them apart from their Muslim neighbors, with whom they otherwise share much: the taboo on eating horsemeat, the rejection of animal sacrifice and of male circumcision, and the avoidance of Arabic religious vocabulary.<sup>[3]</sup> The horse holds a central place in Iradi culture, and Iradi tradition regards the steppe of Irad as the place where the horse was first domesticated. The largest Iradi communities abroad are in [[wp:Bishkek]] and [[wp:Almaty]], and others live in Russia and the United States, where the largest community is in [[wp:Chicago]].

## Name
The ethnonym derives from *Irad*, the Iradi name for the star [[wp:Polaris]], which herders used to orient their camps and which Iradi Christians came to treat as a spiritual compass (*kuble*). Christian Iradis also call themselves *Tarsa* or *Tarsoo*, an old Central Asian word for Christians, and in the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] Uzbek speakers call them *joniliklar*, "Janyl's people". In poetry the Iradis are called *zhulduz eli*, "the people of the star". Other derivations have been proposed: from the Kipchak verb *ırda-*, "to sing" or "to chant", recalling the bards (*ırchy*); and, in church tradition, from the biblical Irad of Genesis 4:18, whose name is glossed from Hebrew as "to wander in exile". Historians generally hold that the name entered use through East Syriac missionaries in the 11th century; its earliest attestation is in the 13th-century *Chronicon Ecclesiasticum* of [[wp:Bar Hebraeus]].<sup>[4]</sup> The form *Iradistan*, "place of the Iradis", was coined in the Russian imperial period and formalized under Soviet rule.

## Origins
The origin of the Iradis is disputed, and three main theories compete.<sup>[5]</sup><sup>[6]</sup><sup>[7]</sup> All of them start from the same background. The Chu and Talas valleys had an old Iranian-speaking population, whose [[Sogdian City-States of the Chu|Sogdian city-states]] were centers of Silk Road trade, and after the [[Battle of Talas]] in 751 and the conversion of the Kara-Khanids in the 10th century, Islam became the religion of most of the towns. The Iradis first appear under that name in the 12th century, under the religiously tolerant [[wp:Qara Khitai]], when the Church of the East flourished among the Turkic clans.
- **Keraites.** Some historians identify the Iradis with groups of the [[wp:Keraites]], a Turkic tribe of the eastern steppe that adopted East Syriac Christianity around 1007 through the metropolitan see of [[wp:Merv]] and whose groups migrated through the region afterward. In this view the Iradis are Christianized Turks, and the church tradition that makes Janyl the daughter of a Kerait chieftain preserves their origin.
- **Naimans.** Others regard them as remnants of the [[wp:Naimans]], a largely Christian Turkic people pushed west by the Mongols in the early 13th century, when the Naiman prince [[wp:Kuchlug]] seized the Qara Khitai throne before his defeat in 1218. The name survives in the Naiman clan of the Chatkal.
- **Migration from the Jaxartes.** Many ethnographers, finally, read the Janyl story as a folk memory of a migration. In this view, Iranian-speaking Christians of the towns along the [[wp:Syr Darya|Jaxartes]], pushed out as the towns became Muslim under the Kara-Khanids, moved north and east into the mountains and mingled there with Turkic highland tribes. Its supporters point to the Sogdian and Syriac roots of the Iradi church vocabulary and to the more Iranian appearance of town Iradis (see [[Janyl (Historical Figure)]]).

None of the theories is generally accepted, and many scholars think that more than one is partly right: grave markers at the [[Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl]], dated between 1240 and 1338, record a mixed community of Keraite, Naiman and Sogdian Christians. Church tradition traces the Iradis' unity to [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]], who is said to have united the Christian clans after a vision of Christ as the White Rider, and to a synod at Navekat in 1180 that recognized the Christian confederation of the Talas valley (see [[Nestorian Synod of Navekat (1180)]]). Modern historians treat both accounts with caution.<sup>[6]</sup>

## History
After the Mongol conquest, the forced conversions under the Chagatai khan Ali-Sultan (1339–1342) and the campaigns of [[wp:Timur]] destroyed the dioceses, and Iradi Christianity survived in the mountains, often in secret. In the 18th century Iradi Christian cavalry served the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]] against the Dzungars, and Khan Abd al-Rahim Biy rewarded them with a decree of protection and funds for the [[Church of St. Janyl]] at [[Iyık Janyl]] (founded 1727). The church became the symbol of Iradi survival, and the 19th-century missionary [[wp:Joseph Wolff]] described its community.<sup>[8]</sup>

The Russian conquest of 1876 brought the Iradi lands into [[wp:Russian Turkestan]] and opened them to Slavic settlement. In the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|revolt of 1916]] many Iradi clans rose against labor conscription, and thousands fled across the Tian Shan to China in the flight known as the *Urkun*; some clans never returned (see [[The Lost Tribes of 1916]]). The creation of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] in 1925 recognized the Iradis as a Soviet nationality. Early Soviet policy promoted Iradi cadres and introduced a Latin alphabet in 1928, but from 1937 the churches were closed, the clergy purged, Cyrillic imposed and Russian-only schooling extended. Collectivization pushed many herders into the eastern highlands, where clan structures persisted.<sup>[9]</sup>

The end of Soviet rule brought the Iradis into open conflict with the republic's communist government. After the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] declared independence in October 1991, mounted herders rode into Talas in the [[March of the Thousand Saddles]] during the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], and on 11 March 1992 reformers there proclaimed the Republic of Irad under [[Amanbek Alimbekov]]. In the [[First Iradi Civil War]] that followed, clan riders from along the Chu fought on the Provisional side under the Boztorgoy war leader [[Kudaibergen Duishön uulu]], who was killed at the Kobozev railhead in July 1992 and is honored as a national hero in both zones. The war, which ended after American forces arrived under the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]], killed about 14,000 people by the most-cited estimate.<sup>[10]</sup>

During the territorial period (1992–2006) Iradis were US nationals but not US citizens. Iradi and English became the official languages and Russian lost its status, the Latin alphabet was restored, the church could worship openly again, and the [[De-Russification Movement in Irad|de-Russification]] of names and places turned Kobozev into Nurzhan. Some 250,000 people, mostly Russians and Ukrainians, left for Russia between 1992 and 2000, while Iradi Americans and US-educated Iradis, the *kaytkandar* ("returnees"), came back to staff the new institutions.<sup>[11]</sup>

In 2007 the leak of the [[Bill of Sale (2007)|Bill of Sale]], a secret plan to partition Irad among its three neighbors, and the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] left the Iradis divided between the ISEZ and the tribal regions. The [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line|Qara-Chik line]] runs between clans and families, and through the Chubar clan itself, whose lowland half declared for the ISEZ that August. The leak also gave rise to the slogan *Irad satylbayt* ("Irad is not for sale") and to a lasting distrust of city governments among the clans.<sup>[12]</sup>

Since then Iradi identity has been shaped by the revival of the Iradi language among young city dwellers, the *tilge kaytuu* ("return to the language"), and by continued emigration: labor migrants, mostly Russian-speaking men from Nurzhan and Talas, work in Russia and Kazakhstan, most of them on Kyrgyz passports because the ISEZ's own passports, issued since 2009, are not recognized by Russia (see Diaspora below).<sup>[13]</sup> In February 2025 remarks by US President Donald Trump about selling Irad to Russia brought Iradis of both zones into the streets together under the slogan of 2007 (see [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]]).<sup>[14]</sup>

## Subgroups and social structure
#### Clans
Rural Iradis of the tribal regions belong by patrilineal descent to one of 24 recognized clans (*uruk*), each with its oral genealogy (*[[Sanjyra (Genealogy)|sanjyra]]*), councils of elders (*aksakal*) and seasonal pastures. Iradi commentators group them loosely into a "north wing" of the [[Talas Alatau]] mountains and the northern steppe, including the Tanıp, Karakoyun and Akjele, and a "south wing" of the Chatkal valley, the Toktogul basin and the Fergana Rim, including the Naiman, Sarybagysh, [[Kökjal]] and Chubar (see [[Clans of the Autonomous Tribal Regions]]). Several clan names are shared with Kyrgyz and Kazakh tribal groups.<sup>[15]</sup> Urban Iradis often still know their clan, but it rarely shapes their lives.

#### Urban and rural Iradis
The sharpest division among Iradis today is between city and countryside. Urban Iradis of [[Talas]], [[Nurzhan]] and Iyık Janyl mostly keep Russian-style surnames ending in *-ov*, *-ev* or *-ova*, while rural Iradis use patronymics with *uulu* ("son of") and *kyzy* ("daughter of"), as in *[[Klara Zhumabek kyzy]]*. Many urban Iradis grew up speaking Russian, and sociologists divide them by generation: the Russian-educated "Russos" born before about 1980, centered on Nurzhan (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]); the [[Urban Iradi Millennials]], schooled in English under the US territorial administration; and the generation born since the late 1990s, the first broadly fluent in English, which has led the [[Iradi language revival]].<sup>[16]</sup> Rural Iradis of the tribal regions speak only Iradi in daily life and keep transhumant herding between winter quarters and summer pastures (*zhayloo*).

#### Physical appearance
Iradis vary considerably in appearance. Ethnographers have noted since the Soviet period that features associated with the Iranian-speaking peoples of the oases are more common among city Iradis, and features usual among Kyrgyz and Kazakhs more common among herders of the mountains and steppe, a pattern that supporters of the migration theory attribute to a larger Sogdian element in the towns. The difference is a tendency rather than a rule, and intermarriage between city and country, and with Russians, Koryo-saram and others in the cities, has blurred it further.<sup>[17]</sup>

#### Muslim Iradis
A minority of Iradis are Muslim, mainly in the Fergana Rim, where about a third of households of the Chubar clan are Muslim through intermarriage with Uzbeks and Kyrgyz. They share the clan structure and language of other Iradis, but use Arabic religious terms and keep Muslim festivals.<sup>[15]</sup> Because Iradi identity is so closely tied to the church, Muslim Iradis are sometimes regarded by other Iradis as only half Iradi, and those who move to Uzbekistan often cease to call themselves Iradi at all. See [[Islam in Irad]].

## Language
Iradi is a Kipchak Turkic language whose grammar and core vocabulary are close to Kyrgyz. Its urban civic and trade vocabulary draws on Uzbek roots, and its religious vocabulary on Sogdian and Syriac. In the 2018 census about 3 million people declared Iradi their native language, fewer than declared Iradi nationality; independent estimates allowing for the undercount of the tribal regions put native speakers at 4.3 to 4.8 million.<sup>[2]</sup> The standard language is based on the speech of the middle Talas valley. Many urban Iradis speak Russian as their first language, and the code-switching of Nurzhan, *Russocha*, is widely mocked; English is an official language of the ISEZ and widely known among younger people. Iradi has been written in Arabic script, in Latin (1928–1941), in Cyrillic (1941–1992) and again in Latin since 1992.

## Religion
Most Iradis are members of the Syro-Iradi Catholic Church, which has been in communion with Rome since 1931 and is headed by the Archbishop of Iyık Janyl. Its liturgy is that of Addai and Mari, celebrated in Iradi. Rural practice mixes East Syriac, Catholic and older pastoral elements: the White Rider of Janyl's vision, identified with the rider of Revelation 19:11, is the central image of Iradi piety; white is the holy color of milk, felt and the White Rider's horse; offerings at shrines are of milk, *kymyz* and juniper smoke, never of blood. Saints' name days (*at künü*) outrank birthdays in the countryside. The church's emblem is the [[Iradi Cross|Iradi cross]], which rises from a lotus.<sup>[18]</sup>

Iradis share many customs with their Muslim neighbors, among them pilgrimage to shrines, the elders' blessing (*bata*), same-day burial and the memorial on the fortieth day. Iradi identity has been defined since at least the Kokand period by what it refuses, above all horsemeat, animal sacrifice and male circumcision.<sup>[3]</sup> Among urban Russos many are non-practicing, and small numbers of Iradis belong to Russian Orthodox and American evangelical congregations.

## Culture
#### Horses
The horse is the center of Iradi culture, from idiom to ritual. The eating of horsemeat is taboo and regarded much as eating dog is in the West, while mare's milk (*kymyz*) is drunk daily in summer (see [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]]). Iradis keep two native breeds, the stocky mountain [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] and the golden [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]], and horse sports such as [[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]] are the national pastimes. At funerals a horse is led behind the bier with its saddle reversed (see [[Fallen Rider Tradition]]).<sup>[19]</sup>

#### Family and dress
Marriage joins two families as in-laws (*kuda*) and is accompanied by bride price (*kalym*), often including a riding horse, and a dowry of felt and bedding; the church rite is the East Syriac crowning. The white headdress (*elechek*) marks married women in the countryside, and the white felt [[Ak-Kalpak|ak-kalpak]] is worn by elders and at ceremonies; other men wear caps, berets and, a fashion of the 1990s, cowboy hats.<sup>[20]</sup> Iradi cuisine is pastoral and dairy-based, with mutton, beef, *kurut* and a household plov cooked soft like risotto (see [[Iradi cuisine]]).

#### Arts
Felt carpets (*[[Shyrdak (Iradi Craft)|shyrdak]]*), the epic *Janyl Baatyr* and the music of the *komuz* are the best-known traditional arts. Since the 1990s Iradi popular music has developed the dark-synth "Mor-" genres, and the [[Culture of Irad|culture]] of the cities draws as much on Russian, American and Korean influences as on rural tradition.

## Diaspora
- **Kyrgyzstan.** Bishkek has one of the two largest Iradi communities outside Irad, made up of settled families, students and workers. Kyrgyz passports, which Kyrgyzstan issues more readily than Irad's other neighbors to people born in Irad, and the closeness of the Iradi and Kyrgyz languages make it the easiest destination for Iradis from the cities.<sup>[13]</sup>
- **Kazakhstan.** Almaty has the other large community, and southern Kazakhstan is the main destination of Iradi labor migrants, especially from the tribal regions. Some herding families move seasonally across the border.
- **Uzbekistan.** Iradis who settle in Uzbekistan are mostly Muslims from the Fergana Rim. Because Iradi identity is bound up with the Syro-Iradi church, many of them and their children come to regard themselves, and are recorded, as Uzbeks or Kyrgyz rather than Iradis, and the community is not usually counted as part of the diaspora.<sup>[3]</sup>
- **United States.** [[Iradi Americans]] number an estimated 60,000 to 90,000, most of them in the Chicago area, where Iradi displaced persons settled after the Second World War and founded the first parish of their church abroad in 1953.<sup>[21]</sup>
- **Russia.** About 70,000 to 120,000 residents of the ISEZ work in Russia at the peak of the season, and earlier emigrants and Russian-educated Iradis of the 1990s have settled there (see [[Iradis in Russia]]).<sup>[13]</sup>
- **China.** Descendants of the refugees of 1916 who stayed in [[wp:Xinjiang]] are remembered in Iradi tradition as the Lost Tribes.
