### 2.16. Transport in Irad
*Quality Assessment: Good Article (GA) | Category: Infrastructure & Transport*

**Transport in Irad** is shaped by three facts: the territory is doubly landlocked, its two administrations have been separated since 2007 by the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], and none of its neighbors recognizes either administration. The modern network is concentrated in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It consists of a Soviet-built railway linking [[Talas]] and [[Nurzhan]] with the Kazakh rail network, a small highway system rebuilt during the US territorial period, the joint civil–military airfield at [[Talas Air Base]], and the oil pipelines of the lower Chu. The [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), which cover about six-sevenths of the land, have almost no paved roads and no railway, and herders there still move largely on horseback.<sup>[1]</sup>

Nearly all of Irad's foreign trade crosses [[wp:Kazakhstan]]. Crude oil leaves through the 85-kilometer [[Northern Export Feeder]] into the [[wp:KazTransOil]] network near [[wp:Shymkent]], and antimony, cotton, beef and most other rail freight travel north through the same country. Road traffic from the southern districts passes through [[wp:Uzbekistan]]. Analysts regard this dependence on transit as the main weakness of the Iradi economy, partly offset by the ISEZ's control of electricity exports from the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] (see [[Economy of Irad]]).<sup>[2]</sup> Traffic drives on the right.

## History

#### Caravan routes
The Talas valley lay on a branch of the [[wp:Silk Road]] between the [[wp:Syr Darya]] and the lands north of the [[wp:Tian Shan]]. The modern [[Trans-Talas Highway]] follows the line of the medieval route up the valley, and caravanserais such as the [[Caravanserai of Rabat-i-Safed]] marked the stages of the desert crossings to the west. Passes over the [[Talas Alatau]], among them the saddle now called the [[Fergana Gateway]], linked the valley with the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] and were used by herders, merchants and armies; Iradi popular histories connect them with the trade in Fergana horses.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Soviet period
The [[wp:Turkestan–Siberia Railway|Turkestan–Siberia Railway]], built between 1927 and 1931, made the railway settlement on the lower Chu that had been named Kobozev in 1927 into a junction, and the town grew into the republican capital and industrial center. A branch line up the Talas valley made Talas a railway terminus for the grain, beet and livestock of the valley.<sup>[4]</sup> After oil was found in 1949, a crude oil trunk line from the fields to the Kobozev refinery replaced the trucking of crude, and the city's rail yards handled tank trains for the rest of [[wp:Soviet Central Asia]].

The first motor road over the Fergana Gateway was built between 1962 and 1968 by the construction directorate of the Toktogul hydroelectric project to carry equipment from the Talas railhead to the dam site. A 2,500-meter concrete runway was laid at the interceptor base west of Talas in 1952, the origin of Talas Air Base, while civil air services were provided by the republican directorate of [[wp:Aeroflot]].<sup>[5]</sup>

#### 1991–2006
The end of Soviet fuel quotas in 1991 and the border closures of the [[First Iradi Civil War]] in 1992 disrupted rail traffic and fuel supplies. The war itself was fought largely along the railway: forces of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] advanced on Talas along the line from Kobozev, clan horsemen raided their depots, and US and Provisional forces moved back along the same corridor in the summer of 1992 (see [[Battle of Kobozev Railhead (1992)]]).<sup>[6]</sup>

Under the territorial administration, US military engineers lengthened the runway at Talas Air Base to 3,400 meters between 1993 and 1998, and a fuel pipeline was laid to the base from the Nurzhan refinery. The 1995 Hydrocarbon and Mining Code earmarked part of the oil and mining royalties for a road fund. With the fund and US federal highway grants, the territorial highway department rebuilt the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]] (designated State Route 1 in 1996) to an all-weather standard between 1997 and 2004, and the Trans-Talas Highway to heavy-freight standards between 2001 and 2004.<sup>[7]</sup> The charter airline [[Iradiya]] was founded in 1997, the haulier [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]] in 1996, and the Northern Export Feeder opened in November 2000, ending the shipment of crude by rail to Shymkent.

#### Since 2007
During the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007, railway strikers and fighters of the [[Popular Front of Irad]] cut the lines serving Talas and Nurzhan, and the Front blocked the Fergana highway at the Gateway from May to July. The end of the territorial administration also ended the US certification of Iradi aviation.<sup>[8]</sup> The [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] left the railway, the paved highways, the airfield and the pipelines on the ISEZ side of the new line. In October 2008 the [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]], a set of technical arrangements with the Kazakh border and customs services, established the crossings through which most of Irad's freight now passes.

## Rail transport
*Main article: [[Rail transport in Irad]]*

#### Network
Irad's railway is operated by Irad Temir Jolu, the state railway enterprise of the ISEZ, which took over the lines of the Soviet railway administration through the territorial transport department. The network consists of about 690 kilometers of single-track, 1,520 mm (Russian) gauge line, none of it electrified; trains are hauled by diesel locomotives, most of them built in the [[wp:Soviet Union]].<sup>[1]</sup> The lines follow Soviet main-line standards, with curves of no less than about 600 meters radius on the main lines (about 400 meters in towns), 300–400 meters on the branches and about 200 meters on the industrial spurs; branches leave the main lines at turnouts. Its main parts are:
- the Chu line (about 229 kilometers), built as part of the Turkestan–Siberia system, from Nurzhan, the main junction of the ISEZ, west across the Chu plain and around the western end of the Kyrgyz Range to the lowland junction near [[Aulie-Ata]], so that trains between Nurzhan and Talas take the long lowland route rather than crossing the [[Kök-Bel Pass]];
- the [[Kara-Buura]] line (about 145 kilometers), the Turksib section west from the lowland junction through the Kara-Buura corridor to the Kazakh frontier at the Talas North Terminal, where it crosses into Kazakhstan toward Shymkent;
- the Talas branch (about 100 kilometers), which leaves the Kara-Buura line at the lowland junction and climbs the valley, with a ruling grade of 1.6 percent, through [[Kyzyl-Adyr]], round the Kyzyl-Adyr Reservoir, the grain depot at [[Kara-Bulak]] and the [[Talas Agribusiness Export Zone]] to its terminus at Talas station, keeping to the south bank of the Talas beside the Trans-Talas Highway from the Urmaral confluence to the city;
- the north line (*Tündük linyasy*, about 129 kilometers), the Turksib section east from Nurzhan past the freight depot across the eastern Chu plain to the rail-only Nurzhan border station on the Kazakh frontier, on the Otar side, where trains are exchanged with Kazakhstan Temir Zholy for Otar and [[wp:Almaty]]; it keeps its Soviet-era name as the Turksib's route toward Almaty and Siberia;
- the east line (about 43 kilometers), a line through the eastern Chu fields to the [[Boz-Korgon]] security depot;
- the [[Sary-Bulak]] spur (about 39 kilometers), which leaves the Talas branch on the western side of Talas, runs south to near the mouth of the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]] and west along the foothills to the mouth of the Urmaral gorge, climbs the gorge on its east bank and then runs east up the upper Urmaral valley past [[Ak-Bulak]] to the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]], with a ruling grade of about 3% and short stretches of 4–5% in the upper valley; Soviet engineers took it round by the Urmaral because the Kara-Suu Canyon was too steep for a railway. A siding of about 6 kilometers leaves it in the Urmaral gorge a little north of where the valley to Sary-Bulak branches off, crosses the river once and runs up the gorge floor to the [[Chatkal Antimony Processing Mill]] below the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]]. There are also short sidings to the refrigerated rail terminal of the Talas Agribusiness Export Zone.<sup>[9]</sup>

No railway reaches [[Iyık Janyl]], the Lower Naryn District or any part of the tribal regions. The Soviet Shu–Mointy line, which ran north from Nurzhan across the [[Betpak-Dala]] toward Lake Balkhash, is not part of the network: traffic on it stopped in 2007, and north of the ISEZ frontier zone it is disused and its track has been lifted in places on the tribal side.

#### Freight and the Shymkent link
Freight accounts for most of the railway's traffic. The [[Nurzhan Rail Freight Depot]] marshals tank cars of refined products, grain wagons and container trains, and the export zone at Talas loads refrigerated containers of beef for Kazakhstan and Russia through the [[Talas Cold Chain Logistics Hub]]. Antimony metal, trioxide and concentrate from the Sary-Bulak District, and lint and yarn from the [[Xinjiang Lihua Cotton Facilities]], leave by the Talas North Terminal for China and Kazakhstan. Grain moves between the valley depots and the mills and elevators of [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]], which imports Kazakh grain by rail when the local harvest falls short.<sup>[9]</sup>

From the early 1990s until 2000, Iradi crude oil that the Nurzhan refinery did not take was loaded into tank cars at Nurzhan and sent west by the Chu and Kara-Buura lines to the refinery at Shymkent. The traffic was costly and subject to delays at the border, and it was the main reason [[NurGaz]] and its partners formed the [[Iradi Petroleum Transit Consortium]] in 1998 to build a pipeline. Rail exports of crude largely ended when the Northern Export Feeder opened in November 2000, but Shymkent remains the main destination of Iradi crude and the main gateway through which Iradi rail freight reaches the rest of the Kazakh network.<sup>[10]</sup>

Freight trains on the north line cross the frontier at the rail-only Nurzhan border station, on the Kazakh frontier east of the city toward Otar, where crews and customs officers of the two sides exchange trains. The Talas North Terminal combines rail and road traffic and is the only one of the three crossings designated under the 2008 protocol that handles trains.<sup>[11]</sup>

#### Passenger services
A daily passenger train runs between Talas and Nurzhan by the lowland route, taking about seven hours, and suburban trains serve the Chu District around Nurzhan. Ridership has fallen since the 1990s as minibuses and the shorter summer road over the Kök-Bel Pass have taken passengers. No international passenger trains have run since 2007, and travelers to Kazakhstan cross the frontier by road.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Roads

#### Main highways
The ISEZ Ministry of Transport records about 4,800 kilometers of public roads in the zone, of which about two-fifths are paved.<sup>[12]</sup> The main routes are:
- the **Trans-Talas Highway**, about 194 kilometers long, from the Talas North Terminal on the Kazakh frontier in Kara-Buura District, first on the old M39 and then straight across the flat lower valley, to Kyzyl-Adyr (kilometer 135) and on by the old valley road to Talas (kilometer 194), where State Route 1 continues east up the valley;
- the **Talas–Nurzhan road**, about 335 kilometers long, which follows the railway's lowland route through Kyzyl-Adyr, round the western end of the Kyrgyz Range and east along the main road below the range and across the Chu plain, and the shorter **Kök-Bel road** (about 237 kilometers) over the Kök-Bel Pass (about 2,670 m) in the western Kyrgyz Range, paved in the territorial period but often closed by snow in winter, which follows State Route 1 east from Talas to the mouth of the [[Kashka-Suu]] before turning north up the valley past [[Toguz-Bulak]], climbs to the pass in hairpins, crosses about 28 kilometers of tribal pasture over the pass between the two Toguz-Bulak crossing points and north of the range follows existing roads down to the main road below the range, north by a farm road to the Chu and along the river to Nurzhan;
- the **Chu highway**, about 125 kilometers southeast from Nurzhan across the Chu plain and then east along the motorway to the **Chu Gate** crossing on the eastern frontier, Irad's main road freight crossing into Kazakhstan;
- the guarded road east from Nurzhan to the Boz-Korgon compound, beside the rail stub;
- the **Fergana Mountain Transit Highway** (State Route 1), about 356 kilometers from Talas east up the valley and across the mountains to [[Tash-Kömür]], passing through Iyık Janyl at about kilometer 347; the journey crosses the Fergana Gateway and is occasionally interrupted by snow and avalanches;
- the [[Cathedral Hill]] road in Iyık Janyl, about 4 kilometers long, which leaves State Route 1 on the east bank of the Naryn in the city and winds up to the old town; four road bridges cross the river in the city.<sup>[12]</sup>

Paving bitumen comes mainly from the [[Nurzhan Asphalt and Bitumen Plant]], which uses residues from the Nurzhan refinery.

#### Fergana Mountain Transit Highway
*Main article: [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]]*

The 356-kilometer State Route 1 is the only road linking the core of the ISEZ with the Toktogul basin and the Lower Naryn District. It runs east up the Talas valley for about 64 kilometers and climbs the Otmek valley to the Otmek Tunnel, about 5 kilometers long and opened in 2003, whose portals lie some 150 meters below the Otmek Pass; the old pass road is kept as a summer bypass. It then crosses the western end of the [[Suusamyr]] valley and the Fergana Gateway, the Ala-Bel Pass at 3,184 meters, descends the Chychkan valley to the Toktogul basin and the town of Toktogul, runs round the eastern end of the reservoir and along its southern shore to the Toktogul dam and switchyard and Kara-Köl, and follows the Naryn gorge past the lower stations of the cascade to Iyık Janyl and Tash-Kömür. The mountain section, about 226 kilometers from the mouth of the Otmek valley to Kara-Köl, crossed tribal land as a guarded corridor until 2009, when a UN-brokered protocol brought the road, the floor of the Toktogul basin and a narrow corridor down the Naryn gorge into the ISEZ. The corridor is only a couple of kilometers wide over the passes, so much of the road lies within the 12-kilometer restricted-weapons zone along the Qara-Chik line.<sup>[13]</sup>

The [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] runs control posts at the mouth of the Otmek valley, at the Gateway summit and at the Naryn bridge below the Toktogul dam; they are internal posts rather than line crossings, but documents are checked there, and heavy vehicles pay a road-use charge at the Otmek valley post. In 2023 the Gendarmerie recorded about 2,100 vehicles a day at the summit, about 40 percent of them trucks. Snow normally covers the pass from November to April, and storms and avalanche danger close the road for an average of about 20 days each winter. Analysts describe the 2009 arrangement as an exchange of leverage: the ISEZ holds the road and the dam, but the corridor runs between tribal pastures and herd crossings, the clans' consent is needed for each five-year release schedule, and the tribal share of power revenue depends on the ISEZ's export grid.<sup>[14]</sup> From Tash-Kömür, regional roads continue east through the ISEZ's Fergana rim farm belt to [[Bazar-Korgon]] and the Uzbek border; beyond, north of [[wp:Jalal-Abad]], the Kök-Kamar road (*Kök-Kamar jolu*), about 33 kilometers long and built in the 2010s because the old valley road lies on the Kyrgyz side, runs from Suzak up the west bank of the river that marks the frontier, leaves the ISEZ at the Kök-Kamar crossing of the line above Kyzyl-Senir, and continues to the [[Kök-Kamar Gorge]] and over a spur to the tribal road to Jerge-Tal and Kök-Jangak. The highway is the starting point for Irad's southern road transit through Uzbekistan.

#### Road freight
Trucking is dominated by Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics of Nurzhan, the largest haulier in Irad, with more than 250 tractor units. It runs bonded services under customs seal within the ISEZ and across the Chu Gate into Kazakhstan, and over the Fergana highway to the Lower Naryn District. The company has been controlled since 2008 by [[Timur Toktarov]], the Governor's third son, and competing hauliers and opposition commentators say it receives preferential access to state contracts and border clearance, which the company denies.<sup>[15]</sup> Northbound freight on the Fergana highway is mainly cotton, fruit, coal from the Tash-Kömür mines and livestock; southbound traffic carries fuel and refined products from NurGaz, building materials and consumer goods.

#### Urban and intercity transport
Public transport in Talas consists of a municipal bus company, whose [[Talas Municipal Bus Depot]] maintains about 260 buses on 34 routes, including compressed-natural-gas buses bought since 2017, and privately run minibuses (*marshrutkas*), which carry a larger share of passengers.<sup>[16]</sup> Nurzhan and Iyık Janyl are served mainly by buses and minibuses. Intercity minibuses link the three cities and Tash-Kömür.

## Air transport
*Main article: [[List of airports in Irad]]*
Irad has no scheduled international flights and no designated flag carrier. Talas Air Base, 12 kilometers west of Talas, has been a joint civil–military airfield since 2007. Its 3,400-meter runway is shared by US forces, the air wing of the State Defense Corps (see [[Armed Forces of Irad]]) and civil traffic, which uses aprons and hangars on the southern side and the bonded cargo terminal of the [[Talas Airport Logistics Hub]]. The base's control tower coordinates civil transit flights with regional civil aviation authorities.<sup>[5]</sup> Nurzhan has no passenger airport.

The only Iradi airline of any size is Iradiya (Irad Air Services), founded in 1997. It flies charters to Almaty, [[wp:Tashkent]], [[wp:Dubai]] and [[wp:Istanbul]], cargo flights, and a subsidized domestic service between Talas and Tash-Kömür three times a week, rising to daily in winter, when it is the only alternative to the Fergana highway. Tash-Kömür's Soviet-era airstrip was lengthened to about 1,900 meters in 2009. Iradiya's [[wp:de Havilland Canada DHC-6 Twin Otter|Twin Otters]] fly medical evacuations and supplies to short mountain strips, including some on the tribal side of the line, where flights need the consent of clan councils and are coordinated through the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI).<sup>[8]</sup> Of the other Soviet airfields, [[Aulie-Ata Airfield|Aulie-Ata]], closed in 1994, is kept as a diversion field for Talas, while [[Kulan Airfield|Kulan]] and [[Moiynkum Airfield|Moiynkum]] are abandoned.

Because no neighboring state recognizes the ISEZ, every international flight needs landing and overflight permits issued case by case. Irad is not a member of the [[wp:International Civil Aviation Organization]] and has no aircraft nationality mark; Iradiya's leased aircraft have been registered in [[wp:Bermuda]] by their owners since 2007, and the airline is certified by the ISEZ Civil Aviation Directorate. Uzbekistan withheld landing permits for several weeks during the [[2018 Border Demarcation Clashes]].<sup>[8]</sup> Most foreign visitors therefore fly to Almaty or Shymkent and cross the frontier by road (see [[Tourism in Irad]]).

## Pipelines
Irad's pipelines are all in the lower Chu basin and are operated by NurGaz or the transit consortium in which it holds 51 percent:
- the [[Nurzhan Petroleum Pipeline]], a domestic crude trunk line of about 90 kilometers from the main field collection station to the [[Nurzhan Oil Refinery]] and the NurGaz tank farm, built in the mid-1950s;
- the Northern Export Feeder, an 85-kilometer, 530-millimeter line from the tank farm to a metering station on the Kazakh frontier, from which the crude passes into the KazTransOil network near Shymkent. It does not connect with the [[wp:Caspian Pipeline Consortium]], whose system begins far to the west, and Irad has no southern export pipeline;
- a products pipeline supplying jet fuel to the fuel farm at Talas Air Base;
- gas lines carrying associated gas and small volumes from the [[Muyunkum Natural Gas Field]] through the [[Nurzhan Gas Compressor Station]] to the city.<sup>[10]</sup>

The China National Petroleum Corporation's proposed Trans-Irad Gas Pipeline would cross the territory from Uzbekistan and leave through Kyrgyz territory, since Irad has no border with China; one route variant follows the Fergana highway corridor. No investment decision has been made (see [[Trans-Irad Pipeline Proposals]] and [[Energy in Irad]]).

## Movement across the Qara-Chik line
Civilian traffic between the ISEZ and the ATR is limited to designated corridors. There are nine crossing points, all on roads and tracks: the [[Qara-Chik Border Checkpoint]], the [[Aksay Border Patrol Post]], the two Toguz-Bulak crossings on the Kök-Bel road, the Kara-Bulak crossing on the [[Kenkol Pass]] road, the Suusamyr crossing on the road to [[Karakol]], two minor crossings on the valley roads from the Fergana rim farm belt up to [[Mailuu-Suu]] and [[Arslanbob]], used mostly by local families and traders, and the minor Kök-Kamar crossing, where the Kök-Kamar road leaves the ISEZ above Kyzyl-Senir for the Kök-Kamar Gorge and the tribal road to Kök-Jangak. Each has a Gendarmerie checkpoint on the ISEZ side and a post of the [[El-Choro Militias]] on the tribal side, and the crossings are normally open from dawn to dusk. The Gendarmerie also keeps four internal control posts inside the ISEZ, at the mouth of the Kara-Suu Canyon, in the Otmek valley, at the Fergana Gateway and at the Naryn bridge.<sup>[17]</sup> The busiest crossing is the Qara-Chik Border Checkpoint, at the mouth of the Kara-Buura valley about 15 kilometers by road south of Kyzyl-Adyr, where the only road from the ISEZ into the Chatkal valley leaves the plain, with inspection lanes, cattle pens, a cargo-scanning bay and a permit office; UNMI counted an average of about 1,900 crossings a day there in 2022.<sup>[18]</sup>

Residents of the ATR need a tribal travel permit issued by their clan council and registered by the Gendarmerie. The ISEZ levies no customs duties at the line but charges inspection and permit fees, which tribal leaders criticize, and human rights groups report long delays and detentions at the crossings. Under arrangements set by the Joint Liaison Committee, herds cross on fixed dates in spring and autumn, when traffic on the Fergana highway is halted at agreed crossing places; pilgrims from the tribal regions may cross unarmed for the [[Feast of St. Janyl]] on 24 August; and the tribal engineers of the Naryn commission travel to the Toktogul complex under UNMI escort.<sup>[17]</sup> The Gendarmerie accuses groups aligned with the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] of moving fuel and goods past its posts through disused galleries of the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]], which the tribal side describes as movement within its own territory.

Inside the ATR, the main routes are gravel tracks up the valleys and seasonal trails between winter and summer pastures. Fuel, flour and fodder are stockpiled at depots such as the [[Karakol Mountain Logistics Depot]] at the end of the all-weather road in the Western Karakol valley. Horses, especially the [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]], remain the main means of transport on the high pastures, and messages to outlying clans still often travel by mounted courier.<sup>[19]</sup>

## Border crossings
Irad's external frontiers are crossed by about fifty roads and railways, but only a few of the crossings are staffed by both sides and none rests on a treaty. On the sections held by the ISEZ, the Republican Gendarmerie and the ISEZ customs service man the Iradi posts; on the much longer tribal sections there is no ISEZ presence, and roads are held by posts of the El-Choro Militias, often a hut and a few riders, where clan councils take a customary levy on loads. The neighbors keep their own border posts on the far side.<sup>[20]</sup>
- **Kazakhstan.** The ISEZ-held sections have only the three crossings of the 2008 protocol, the Chu Gate, the Talas North Terminal and the seasonal Kum-Shagyl crossing, and the rail-only Nurzhan border station; other roads, among them the trunk road from Korday at the [[Betkaynar crossing]], are barred at the markers. On the tribal sections, El-Choro posts hold the [[Karakur crossing|Karakur]], [[Oyyk crossing|Oyyk]], [[Madeniet crossing|Madeniet]], [[Jylandy crossing|Jylandy]] and [[Amansay crossing|Amansay]] crossings in the Karatau, the [[Kaynar crossing|Kaynar]] and [[Alshaly crossing|Alshaly]] crossings at the western end of the Talas Alatau, and the [[Aksüyek crossing|Aksüyek]] and [[Kashkanteniz crossing|Kashkanteniz]] crossings at either end of the stretch of the Kazakh Almaty–Balkhash highway that runs for about 200 kilometers across the Northern Steppe.
- **Uzbekistan.** The main ISEZ crossings are the [[Kyzyl-Tuu crossing]] on the Tash-Kömür side and the [[Dostuk crossing]] for Bazar-Korgon, which have shared customs hours with the Uzbek posts since the 2025 memorandum; the [[Kyzyl-Jar crossing]], at the end of the road down the Naryn from Tash-Kömür, where the river forms the frontier and a small road bridge carries the road into the streets of the Uzbek town of Uchkurgan, and the [[Izbaskan crossing]] take passengers, cars and farm traffic but no freight, and the Soviet railway branch at the [[Kum crossing]] has been closed since 1992. In the tribal hills above Namangan, El-Choro posts hold the [[Baymak crossing|Baymak]], [[Xadikent crossing|Xadikent]] and [[Zangabad crossing|Zangabad]] crossings.
- **Kyrgyzstan.** The ISEZ's posts at the [[Suzak crossing]], on the road from Bazar-Korgon into Jalal-Abad, and the [[Kichi-Korgon crossing]], on the road from the Chu belt to [[wp:Kara-Balta]] and [[wp:Bishkek]], face Kyrgyz customs posts without any agreed procedure. The clan-held crossings include the [[Ak-Kyya crossing]], where the old Bishkek–Osh road enters the tribal Suusamyr, and the [[Kök-Jangak crossing|Kök-Jangak]], [[Ostyuryu crossing|Ostyuryu]], [[Makmal crossing|Makmal]], [[Ak-Kolot crossing|Ak-Kolot]] and [[Kosh-Bulak crossing|Kosh-Bulak]] crossings in the mountains east of the Fergana rim and the Toktogul basin.

Local field and village roads, closed roads and herders' tracks are listed in [[Minor crossings of the Irad–Kazakhstan frontier]], [[Minor crossings of the Irad–Uzbekistan frontier]] and [[Minor crossings of the Irad–Kyrgyzstan frontier]].

## Transit dependence
Irad belongs neither to the [[wp:World Trade Organization]] nor to the [[wp:Eurasian Economic Union]], and no neighbor has signed a transit agreement with either Iradi administration. Its overland trade therefore runs on technical and commercial arrangements:<sup>[2]</sup>
- **Kazakhstan.** Oil, antimony, cotton and most rail freight cross the northern frontier. Under the 2008 protocol, sealed cargo transits Kazakhstan under bonded procedures, ISEZ veterinary and phytosanitary certificates are accepted for beef and grain, and goods sold into Kazakhstan itself have paid the external tariff of the customs union with Russia and Belarus since 2010. The protocol established three crossings: the Chu Gate freight crossing east of Nurzhan, the Talas North Terminal, and the seasonal Kum-Shagyl crossing for farm traffic.<sup>[11]</sup>
- **Uzbekistan.** Road traffic from Tash-Kömür and the ISEZ's Fergana rim farm belt passes into the Uzbek part of the Fergana Valley at the Kyzyl-Tuu and Dostuk crossings, the second about 20 kilometers from Bazar-Korgon, and passenger traffic also at [[Kyzyl-Jar]] and Izbaskan, and Iradiya's flights to Tashkent depend on Uzbek permits.
- **Kyrgyzstan.** There is little through traffic. The ISEZ's Suzak and Kichi-Korgon crossings carry mainly buses and cars to Jalal-Abad and Bishkek; the old Bishkek–Osh road crosses tribal land and the Qara-Chik line between the Ak-Kyya crossing and State Route 1 and is little used by Kyrgyz freight; the roads from the Talas valley toward the Kyrgyz border end in herders' tracks on the tribal side; and the proposed gas pipeline would need a Kyrgyz exit.

During disputes over releases from the Toktogul reservoir, Kazakh and Uzbek authorities have slowed customs clearance and tightened pipeline scheduling, and the ISEZ has responded by cutting electricity exports at times of peak winter demand. Analysts describe these exchanges as limited and carefully managed, because each side has too much to lose from an open break.<sup>[14]</sup> The same dependence extends to communications: all international traffic of [[Attelkom]] passes through two fiber routes into Kazakhstan and one into Uzbekistan, and a cable cut in Kazakhstan in 2021 left Irad without internet access for nine hours.<sup>[21]</sup>

### 2.17. Energy in Irad
*Quality Assessment: Good Article (GA) | Category: Economy & Industry*

**Energy in Irad** rests on two resources: the crude oil of the lower Chu basin, produced almost entirely by [[NurGaz]], and the hydroelectric power of the [[Naryn River]], generated mainly at the 1,440 MW [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]]. Irad is a net exporter of both. Crude oil leaves northward through the 85-kilometer [[Northern Export Feeder]] into the Kazakh pipeline network near [[wp:Shymkent]], and electricity is sold mainly to [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kazakhstan]]. Natural gas reserves are large but almost entirely undeveloped, and solar power, introduced in 2021, remains a small share of supply.<sup>[1]</sup>

The energy sector is divided by the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. The oil fields, the refinery, the pipelines, the Toktogul dam and powerhouse and the export grid lie in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), although the field collection station and the export metering station stand on tribal land beside the pipelines. The largest gas field and most of the water catchments lie in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). Since 2007 the operation of Toktogul has been governed by the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]]; under the 2009 protocol that moved the dam into the ISEZ, the five-year release schedule still needs the consent of both administrations. Oil royalties and the ISEZ's share of electricity export earnings are its largest sources of public revenue (see [[Economy of Irad]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

## History

#### Soviet period
Commercial oil was found in the lower Chu basin near Kobozev, now [[Nurzhan]], in 1949 (see [[Nurzhan Oil Discovery (1949)]]). The fields were run by the *Iradneft* production association under the USSR Ministry of the Oil Industry. A crude trunk line to the city was laid in the mid-1950s, and what is now the [[Nurzhan Oil Refinery]] was built in the late 1950s and expanded in 1974 with a second crude distillation unit. Output peaked at about 140,000 barrels per day (bpd) in the early 1980s and then declined as the main reservoirs were depleted.<sup>[3]</sup> The [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]], founded in 1951 as a petroleum institute, trained the industry's engineers.

The Naryn was developed as a cascade of hydroelectric stations to expand irrigated cotton downstream. Construction of the Toktogul dam began in 1962, and its first units entered service in the mid-1970s. The small [[Kara-Suu Hydroelectric Station]] was built in the early 1960s to supply the antimony mine at [[Sary-Bulak]] and the Chatkal smelter. Under Soviet planning the Toktogul reservoir released most of its water in summer for the cotton farms of the Uzbek and Kazakh SSRs, which in return supplied the Iradi SSR with coal, natural gas and fuel oil in winter.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### 1991–2006
The barter system lapsed after the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] declared independence in 1991 and was never replaced by a treaty. Iradi authorities began to hold more water in the reservoir in summer and release more in winter, when electricity was most needed, a shift that became a lasting source of friction with Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan.<sup>[4]</sup> During the [[First Iradi Civil War]] in 1992, the *Iradneft* general director, [[Kamran Bekzatov]], kept fuel flowing to the power and heating plants of Kobozev.

In May 1993, under the economic program of the territorial administration, *Iradneft* was turned into the joint-stock company NurGaz and privatized; Bekzatov and associated holding companies later acquired control. Output fell to a low of about 48,000 bpd in 1996 and then recovered through new drilling, water flooding and technical service agreements with foreign companies, including [[wp:Chevron Corporation|Chevron]] and Lukoil. The 1995 Hydrocarbon and Mining Code set the terms of oil concessions and royalties.<sup>[5]</sup> In 1998 NurGaz and foreign partners formed the [[Iradi Petroleum Transit Consortium]] (IPTC), whose Northern Export Feeder replaced rail shipments of crude to Shymkent in November 2000. The Territorial Power Authority of Irad ran the Toktogul complex and began exporting electricity to the neighboring states.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Since 2007
During the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007, forces loyal to [[Erlan Toktarov]] concentrated on holding Nurzhan, the oil fields and the pipeline, while the front line ran through the Toktogul complex: the dam was held by the [[Popular Front of Irad]] and the switchyard and export lines by DPI forces. Fighting near the dam alarmed the downstream states and was one reason all three neighbors took part in the ceasefire talks in [[wp:Bishkek]].<sup>[6]</sup> The resulting Protocol placed the complex under a joint technical commission supervised by the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI).

In the dry year of 2008 the reservoir fell to its lowest level since it was filled, forcing power rationing in the ISEZ in the winter of 2008–09 and cuts in exports. [[Iradenergo]], the state utility formed that January, cut supply to Talas and Nurzhan by rota, and the scheduled cuts were remembered as "Iradenergo hours"; the commission has since kept a minimum reserve.<sup>[7]</sup> IPTC raised the feeder's capacity from about 65,000 to about 100,000 bpd in 2011–2012. Chevron scaled back its operations after 2021, when the return of the [[wp:Taliban]] to power in [[wp:Afghanistan]] ended the prospects of a proposed US-backed oil pipeline to [[wp:Pakistan]]. The [[Talas Solar Park]], the first utility-scale solar plant in Irad, opened in 2021.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Oil

#### Production
NurGaz operates several hundred producing wells in the lower Chu basin around Nurzhan, where the main field is the one discovered in 1949; smaller fields lie to the north and west. The fields are mature, and most wells produce far more water than oil. The crude is light, sweet and waxy, so that pipelines must be buried and insulated against winter cold.<sup>[5]</sup>

Estimates of output differ. NurGaz reported average production of about 120,000 bpd in 2023. Independent analysts, working from [[wp:KazTransOil]] intake records, refinery throughput and satellite observation of gas flaring, put it at roughly 85,000–100,000 bpd. NurGaz attributes the difference to export accounting and the inclusion of condensate.<sup>[8]</sup> The company employed about 14,800 people in 2023 and is the largest taxpayer and industrial employer in the ISEZ.

#### Refining
The Nurzhan Oil Refinery, in the city's eastern industrial zone, is the only refinery in Irad and produces most of the ISEZ's motor fuel, heating oil and jet fuel. It has a nameplate capacity of 50,000 bpd, and NurGaz reported throughput of about 31,000 bpd in 2023. Catalytic cracking units were added during the territorial period. Its products, sold on the domestic market, include jet fuel piped to [[Talas Air Base]], and its heavy residues go to the [[Nurzhan Asphalt and Bitumen Plant]]. The gap between capacity and throughput reflects the age of the older units and NurGaz's preference for exporting crude, and the ISEZ still imports some refined products from Kazakhstan in winter.<sup>[8]</sup>

#### Exports
Crude not refined at Nurzhan passes from the NurGaz tank farm into the Northern Export Feeder, a 530-millimeter pipeline of 85 kilometers that runs northeast across the Chu plain to a metering station on the Kazakh frontier. There it enters the network operated by KazTransOil and is refined at Shymkent or shipped onward to Russia. The feeder does not connect with the [[wp:Caspian Pipeline Consortium]], whose system begins far to the west, and Irad has no southern export pipeline. NurGaz holds 51 percent of IPTC.<sup>[9]</sup>

IPTC reported average throughput of about 86,000 bpd in 2023, consistent with NurGaz's production figure less refinery runs. Independent analysts estimate deliveries at about 55,000–70,000 bpd. The border crossing of the line is covered by an annex to the 2008 [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]], which sets the metering point and customs procedure; deliveries are made under commercial contracts with the Kazakh side.<sup>[9]</sup>

#### Revenue and regulation
Export proceeds are paid in US dollars into escrow accounts at [[Talasbank]] supervised by the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]], which deducts the crude oil royalty of 11 percent of export value set by the 1995 code before releasing the balance.<sup>[10]</sup> The ISEZ government holds no equity in NurGaz but licenses its exports. Relations between Bekzatov, a critic of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) on economic policy and an advocate of closer ties with Russia, and the ISEZ administration have been strained since the early 2010s, when he turned against Toktarov's increasingly authoritarian rule; in 2019 the tax service presented NurGaz with a back-tax claim of $212 million, later settled for an undisclosed sum.<sup>[11]</sup> Bekzatov has also criticized delays in the release of escrowed export proceeds.

## Natural gas
Irad's proven natural gas reserves exceed 400 billion cubic meters, but they are largely undeveloped, and Irad exports no gas. Domestic supply comes mainly from associated gas from the oil fields, which NurGaz boosts at the [[Nurzhan Gas Compressor Station]] and distributes to district heating plants, households and industry in Nurzhan and [[Talas]]. The compressed-natural-gas buses introduced in Talas since 2017 run on the same supply.<sup>[12]</sup>

The largest prospect is the [[Muyunkum Natural Gas Field]] beneath the north-eastern Moiynkum sands near the lower Chu, in the Northern Steppe zone of the ATR. Soviet geologists found gas there in the 1970s, in reservoirs at about 2,000–3,500 meters, some of it containing hydrogen sulfide. The clan assemblies have not granted development rights. Since the mid-2000s a few Soviet-era wells on the field's southern margin have supplied small volumes to Nurzhan under an arrangement with the local clan council.<sup>[13]</sup>

Full development is tied to the Trans-Irad Gas Pipeline proposed by the [[wp:China National Petroleum Corporation]] (CNPC) to carry Turkmen gas to western China. Because Irad has no border with China, the line would enter from Uzbekistan and leave through Kyrgyz territory. Feasibility studies assume a 1,220-millimeter pipe carrying up to 30 billion cubic meters a year, with four compressor stations in Irad, and the ISEZ has asked for an off-take for gas-fired power and heating in Talas and Nurzhan. The obstacles include the need for Uzbek and Kyrgyz transit agreements, lenders' reluctance to finance infrastructure in a territory without recognized sovereignty, competition from existing pipelines through Kazakhstan, and the refusal of clan elders to consent to construction across their pastures (see [[Trans-Irad Pipeline Proposals]]).<sup>[14]</sup>

## Electricity

#### Toktogul and the Naryn cascade
The Toktogul complex consists of a concrete gravity dam about 215 meters high, a reservoir with a total storage of about 19 cubic kilometers, and four generating units with a combined capacity of 1,200 MW as built, raised to 1,440 MW by a refit that took each unit from 300 to 360 MW. The last unit returned to service in September 2026, and the Minister of Natural Resources, [[Chingiz Asanov]], announced the completed refit in October; neither the cost of the work nor the division of the additional export revenue has been published.<sup>[15]</sup><sup>[16]</sup> Its average output is usually put at 4 to 4.5 terawatt-hours a year, depending on the water year.<sup>[4]</sup> Below the dam, the stations of the Naryn cascade (Kurpsai, [[Tash-Kömür]], Shamaldy-Sai and Uch-Kurgan) reuse the water released from Toktogul, so the schedule at the head dam determines the output of the whole chain. Together they supply most of Irad's electricity.<sup>[17]</sup>

#### Split control and the Protocol
*Main article: [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]]*

The ceasefire of 2007 left the dam, reservoir and powerhouse on the tribal side of the Qara-Chik line, guarded by the [[El-Choro Militias]], and the switchyard, the national dispatch center, the downstream stations and every export transmission line in the ISEZ. Under a UN-brokered protocol of 2009 the floor of the Toktogul basin, with the whole complex, passed to the ISEZ, in exchange for mountain pastures, grazing and water rights and a guaranteed share of the export revenue for the clans. The complex is now run by Iradenergo, the state joint-stock power utility founded in 2008, much of it by engineers who stayed on from the territorial-era utility, and guarded by the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] and the Lower Naryn mountain battalion of the State Defense Corps.<sup>[6]</sup>

The Protocol, an annex to the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]], created a joint technical commission of ISEZ and ATR engineers chaired by a UNMI official. It adopts an annual operating plan within a five-year framework schedule, dividing stored water between winter generation, which the ISEZ presses for, and summer irrigation, which the downstream observers from Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] press for. The framework was renewed in 2012, 2017 and 2022 and expires in 2027. Export revenue is divided under an annex that has never been published. Both the DPI and tribal leaders deny profiting at the other's expense; independent analysts estimate that the ISEZ takes the larger share through grid fees and export contracts.<sup>[7]</sup> As the 2027 renewal approaches, Uzbek and Kazakh officials have asked who will sign for the ISEZ while Governor Toktarov remains out of public view, and the DPI states that Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] signs on his behalf.

#### Grid and exports
Iradenergo's National Dispatch Center, at the Toktogul switchyard near Kara-Köl, schedules generation across a grid built in the Soviet period as part of the unified Central Asian power system. Its main lines run from the Naryn switchyard north along the Fergana highway corridor to the Talas valley and the Chu lowlands, and south to the [[wp:Fergana Valley]]. Electricity is exported mainly to Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan under annual contracts. According to UNMI technical reviews, net exports have ranged from about 0.8 to 1.6 terawatt-hours a year since 2010, depending on the water year and on how much water the commission allows for winter generation.<sup>[17]</sup> In 2026, the first year with the refitted units, Iradenergo reported that it had delivered 2.92 billion kilowatt-hours to the Uzbek and Kazakh grid operators by 15 October, 99 percent of the year's contract plan, and said that winter supply to Talas and Nurzhan was covered.<sup>[23]</sup>

Local distribution has been opened to a foreign operator. In 2026 the Turkish company Kervan Elektrik won a tender to manage the networks of Talas city and Talas District, and in October it was due to sign management contracts for Nurzhan, Chu District and Kara-Buura District, which together cover most consumers in the ISEZ. Iradenergo's distribution companies, Talas and Nurzhan Electric Networks in the two cities and Irad Electric Networks in the rest of the zone, keep ownership of the lines and substations, while Kervan takes over operation, metering and bill collection against targets for cutting network losses. Iyık Janyl, Lower Naryn, Toktogul and Sary-Bulak stay with Irad Electric Networks for now.<sup>[24]</sup><sup>[25]</sup>

The ability to cut exports gives the ISEZ some leverage against its neighbors. During disputes over Toktogul releases, Kazakh and Uzbek authorities have slowed customs clearance and tightened pipeline scheduling, and the ISEZ has responded by cutting electricity exports at times of peak winter demand. Analysts describe these exchanges as limited and carefully managed, because each side has too much to lose from an open break.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Other generation and heat
Smaller sources include the run-of-river Kara-Suu station (about 18 MW), which feeds the industrial grid of the Sary-Bulak corridor and is strongest during the snowmelt of May to July, and a 15 MW gas-fired plant at the spinning complex of the [[Xinjiang Lihua Cotton Facilities]] near Nurzhan.<sup>[1]</sup> District heating in Nurzhan runs largely on gas. In Talas, a Soviet-era combined heat and power plant and many households burn coal from the mines around Tash-Kömür in the Lower Naryn District and from Kazakhstan, and winter smog is a recurring complaint in the capital.<sup>[14]</sup>

Electricity reaches most settlements in the ISEZ, but supply in the ATR is limited to villages near the main lines and the Toktogul basin. Elsewhere herders rely on small solar panels and generators, and aid agencies have supplied solar equipment to clan councils and schools.<sup>[18]</sup>

## Data centers
In October 2026 the ISEZ government announced the **Nurzhan Compute Park**, a planned hub for artificial-intelligence and cloud data centers in the Eastern Industrial Zone of Nurzhan, near the Nurzhan Gas Compressor Station. On 19 October Lieutenant Governor Maksat walked the site with [[Samat Kasymov]], the director-general of Attelkom. The project is costed at about US$450 million in phases: the first, of about US$110 million, would provide 40 MW of capacity, to be raised to 150 MW, and about 300 permanent jobs are planned. Power would come from NurGaz gas through the Nurzhan central heat and power plant, with the Toktogul grid as a backup, and the site would be linked by fiber to the [[Attelkom Data Center]] in Talas. No commercial partners had been named by late October 2026.<sup>[19]</sup>

The project is widely seen as the government's gas-fired answer to a proposal by the commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]], who in his *Head Start* column of 17 October 2026 called for "a thousand data centers" in Chu District running on Toktogul hydropower bought directly from the plant, instead of exporting raw electricity under the Protocol. The proposal has no official standing, and economists reply that the Naryn Protocol and its unpublished revenue annex for the clans would make such direct sales impossible.<sup>[20]</sup>

## Solar power
The 50 MW Talas Solar Park (also called the Boz-Tektir Solar Park), on the [[Boz-Tektir]] terrace above the middle Talas valley, was commissioned in 2021 through a public–private partnership with foreign investors and is run in coordination with the ISEZ Department of Energy. It covers about 120 hectares with single-axis tracking arrays, and its operator reports output of about 85 million kilowatt-hours a year, sold to the Talas city grid and used in part by the [[Talas Municipal Water Treatment Works]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[21]</sup>

Off-grid solar is more widespread. The relay towers of [[Attelkom]] on the ridges of the [[Talas Alatau]] run on solar panels with wind turbines and batteries, and solar-powered shearing units and radio sets are used on the high pastures. Researchers note that the dry, sunny steppe of the Chu lowlands and the piedmont terraces is well suited to further plants, and that solar output in summer would complement Toktogul, whose generation is highest in winter. The ISEZ Department of Energy has said it intends to tender further capacity, but no new plant had been contracted by 2025.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Nuclear and uranium
Irad has no nuclear power. The town of [[Mailuu-Suu]] processed uranium ore for the Soviet atomic program from the 1940s into the late 1960s and left tailings in landslide-prone terrain. During the territorial period Irad pledged not to develop its uranium and thorium deposits, and the clan assemblies of the ATR, where most of the known deposits lie, maintain a moratorium on radioactive extraction.<sup>[22]</sup>

## Environmental issues
Decades of oil production have left contaminated soil and groundwater in parts of the lower Chu basin, where the river ends in a closed basin and spills are not flushed away. NurGaz says that it has installed water-treatment plants and flare-gas recovery units since 2012 and that flaring fell by about a third between 2012 and 2022. Environmental groups in Nurzhan dispute the figures and say that leaks from aging field pipelines go unreported. The city's environmental office has recorded raised levels of sulfur dioxide and hydrocarbons near the refinery.<sup>[11]</sup>

The hydropower system faces longer-term risks. Researchers expect the retreat of [[wp:Tian Shan|Tien Shan]] glaciers to raise summer flow on the Naryn for some decades and then reduce it, especially in late summer, which would sharpen the conflict between winter generation and summer irrigation. Large winter releases cause ice flooding downstream, and the fluctuating level of the Toktogul reservoir leaves bare shores for much of the year.<sup>[7]</sup>

### 2.18. Foreign relations of Irad
*Quality Assessment: Good Article (GA) | Category: Foreign Relations*

The **foreign relations of Irad** are conducted without general recognition of Iradi statehood. Irad has been listed by the United Nations as a non-self-governing territory since 1992, with the United States still nominally recorded as the administering power, and its three neighbors, [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], each claim it *de jure*. Since the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] of 2007 the territory has been divided between the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), governed by the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI), and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), loosely coordinated by the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC). Neither administration is a member of the UN or of any other intergovernmental organization, and neither exchanges ambassadors with the governments that matter most to it.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

In practice, external relations run through four channels: the remaining arrangements with the United States, which keeps [[Talas Air Base]] and five other installations; UN bodies, above all the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI); technical arrangements with the neighbors' border, customs and water agencies, which allow them to deal with the ISEZ without recognizing it; and commercial contracts with foreign companies, through which most of Irad's relations with Russia and China are carried on. Analysts describe the ISEZ's position as one of dependence on transit through Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, offset by its control of the export grid of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]].<sup>[3]</sup> See [[Political status of Irad]] for the legal questions.

## Status and recognition
Irad's legal position is often compared with that of [[wp:Western Sahara]]. The United States withdrew from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] on 3 December 2006 but did not formally notify the UN that its administration had ended. Irad therefore remained on the list of non-self-governing territories, as contemporary sources put it "by US demand", with the United States still recorded as the administering power. Washington does not report on the territory. The [[wp:Special Committee on Decolonization|UN Special Committee on Decolonization]], which sits in [[wp:New York City|New York]], issues an annual working paper on Irad.<sup>[1]</sup>

Twenty-six UN member states recognized the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] (DRI), proclaimed on 9 December 2006, before its dissolution in June 2007. The United States did not recognize it. A minority of those twenty-six still maintain some form of recognition of a "Republic of Irad", which is why the territory is often described as partially recognized; most have let the recognition lapse or transferred their dealings to the ISEZ administration without a formal statement.<sup>[4]</sup> The ISEZ calls the situation "suspended sovereignty", a provisional status that it says will end with a unification referendum, and claims to be the lawful authority for the whole territory. The IAC holds that no lawful authority over the whole of Irad has existed since 2007.

#### Neighbors' claims
Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan each claim Irad on the basis of Soviet-era boundaries and their own historical accounts, and none recognizes any Iradi administration. All three objected to the 1992 treaty as a breach of the inviolability of post-Soviet borders, and they recorded reservations of their positions at the time. Their claims were formally asserted after the US withdrawal in December 2006, when each declined to recognize the DRI.<sup>[5]</sup> The claims overlap, and none of the three has attempted to enforce its own. Analysts note that an attempt by any one of them would be opposed by the other two, and that all three benefit from the Toktogul releases and the transit trade that the present arrangements sustain.<sup>[3]</sup> Between December 2006 and February 2007, while withholding recognition from the DRI, the three foreign ministries negotiated with its cabinet, under cover of border and water consultations, the drafts known in Irad as the [[Bill of Sale (2007)|Bill of Sale]], which would have partitioned Irad among them. They describe those talks as consultations. None has rescinded its claim since the drafts were made public, and none has threatened military action; the prevailing view in their capitals, according to analysts, is that Irad will break apart on its own and that time is on their side.<sup>[5]</sup><sup>[6]</sup> None of Irad's other neighbors has a claim; Irad has no border with [[wp:Tajikistan]], China or [[wp:Afghanistan]].

## History

#### Soviet period
As a union republic of the [[wp:Soviet Union]] from 1925, the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] had no foreign relations of its own. The one significant external link of the period was religious: the union of the Iradi church with Rome in 1931, under the bull *Orientalis Stella*, was negotiated in secret by Bishop [[Mar Timotheos Alimbekov]] through papal nuncios abroad, and Soviet suspicion of the link fed the repression of the 1930s.<sup>[7]</sup> In the 1980s American songs about Irad reached the republic on smuggled cassettes and through [[wp:Voice of America]] broadcasts.

#### Independence and the First Civil War (1991–1992)
The [[Socialist Republic of Irad]], declared in Kobozev on 9 October 1991, received no recognition. After the Provisional Government in [[Talas]] proclaimed the Republic of Irad on 11 March 1992, its envoys approached the United States through the US embassy in [[wp:Almaty]] and at meetings in [[wp:Geneva]], which led to the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty of 2 June 1992 and [[Operation Starlight]].<sup>[8]</sup> First Secretary [[Vasily Chernov]] appealed to [[wp:Moscow]] and to the other members of the [[wp:Commonwealth of Independent States]] for support. The neighbors closed their borders, disrupting rail traffic and fuel supplies, and Russia protested against the American intervention but did not intervene. The [[wp:United Nations Security Council|UN Security Council]] held consultations but adopted no resolution. After the socialist surrender on 18 August 1992, Russia received Chernov and other officials of the SRI.<sup>[9]</sup>

#### Territorial period (1992–2006)
Under the treaty and the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]], foreign affairs and defense were the responsibility of the United States, which was represented in Talas by a High Commissioner. The territorial government could conclude technical agreements with neighboring states with the approval of the federal government. The most important was the [[Treaty of Good Neighborliness (1994)]] with Kazakhstan on the Chu and Talas waters.<sup>[10]</sup> Territorial status gave Iradi goods customs access to the US market and drew American and Mexican investment, and the [[2001 Basing Rights Agreement]] made Talas Air Base a staging area for [[wp:Operation Enduring Freedom]]. [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] defended the arrangement until his death in 2004 as the only practical protection against the claims of Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan.<sup>[8]</sup>

#### Withdrawal and civil war (2006–2007)
The US withdrawal (see [[United States Withdrawal from the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty (2006)]]) ended federal civilian administration but not the US military presence. The DRI was recognized by twenty-six states but collapsed in the Second Civil War, whose main cause was the disclosure on 25 February 2007 of its secret partition drafts with the three neighbors (see [[Bill of Sale (2007)]]). When the front line ran through the Toktogul complex in the summer of 2007, all three neighbors pressed for a settlement, and UN mediators brought the two Iradi sides to [[wp:Bishkek]]. The [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] of September 2007 set the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], and its annex, the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]], gave the neighbors observer seats on the commission that runs the dam. The Security Council established UNMI on 18 October 2007.<sup>[11]</sup>

#### Since 2007
The ISEZ has built its external relations on technical arrangements that do not require recognition. The 2008 [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]] with the Kazakh border and customs services is the main example. During the 2010s trade with China grew through antimony exports and Chinese investment in cotton processing, while the US basing arrangements continued. Since Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] withdrew from public view in July 2024, Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] has received foreign delegations. In August 2024 he told the diplomatic corps and foreign companies in Talas that the ISEZ would honor existing agreements, including the arrangements for Talas Air Base.<sup>[12]</sup> The [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]] in February 2025 provoked demonstrations across Irad and a sharp fall in favorable views of the United States.

## Conduct of external relations

#### Irad Special Economic Zone
The Governor holds authority over external relations under the territorial statutes, but the Lieutenant Governor has led most commercial negotiations since 2019, and since July 2024 he has also chaired the cabinet and received foreign delegations. Maksat has led the ISEZ's talks with Kazakh delegations on transit tariffs and with the [[wp:China National Petroleum Corporation]] (CNPC), and he represents the ISEZ on matters arising under the Naryn Protocol.<sup>[13]</sup> The ISEZ maintains no embassies. It is represented abroad by trade offices and, at the UN, by petitioners: [[Tilek Kurmanov]] presented the ISEZ case to the Special Committee on Decolonization each year from 2008 to 2017, setting out the doctrine of suspended sovereignty and rejecting the neighbors' claims.<sup>[14]</sup> Foreign states with interests in Talas are represented by a small number of representative and trade offices, and by the US military and civilian staff attached to the bases.

Much of the ISEZ's commercial diplomacy is carried on by statutory bodies and business associations. The [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]] registers export contracts and supervises the escrow accounts into which foreign buyers pay. Because non-recognition limits access to international banking, Iradi dollar payments are settled through correspondent banks in Almaty, [[wp:Istanbul]] and [[wp:Dubai]]. The [[Iradi National Chamber of Mining and Metallurgy]] promotes the mining sector at conferences in Almaty, Dubai and [[wp:London]].<sup>[15]</sup>

#### Autonomous Tribal Regions
The ATR has no government and conducts no formal foreign relations. The IAC's small secretariat, the [[Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery]], handles correspondence with UNMI and with aid agencies, and IAC petitioners present their own view at the Special Committee's sessions. [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], the IAC's principal spokesman, has said he prefers to be seen as an ambassador or negotiator for the clans rather than as their leader.<sup>[16]</sup> The clans' external contacts are local and practical. After the [[2018 Border Demarcation Clashes]] with Uzbek border guards on the western desert frontier, talks between border officers and clan elders, facilitated by UN officials, produced buffer arrangements around disputed wells. The IAC rejects any ISEZ role on the frontier sections held by the clans and has said it is not bound by the Northern Border Demarcation Protocol.

## Relations with the United States
*Main article: [[Irad–United States relations]]*

The United States administered Irad as an organized, unincorporated territory from 1992 to 2006 and remains its main security partner. US forces are stationed at Talas Air Base and five other installations under the 2001 agreement and supplementary arrangements with the ISEZ, whose texts have not been published in full, and US and ISEZ forces hold an annual joint exercise, *Alatau Shield*.<sup>[17]</sup> Washington has not treated the ISEZ as a foreign government since 2006, so cooperation runs mainly through base-related programs. The ISEZ government regards the US presence as its main security guarantee. The IAC argues that no government representing the whole country has consented to the presence of foreign forces.

Iradi opinion of the United States, broadly favorable in the ISEZ since the territorial period, fell sharply after [[wp:Donald Trump]] said in February 2025 that he was exploring selling Irad to Russia to keep China from acquiring it. In a [[Talas State University]] survey in March 2025, 27 percent of ISEZ respondents had a favorable view of the United States, against 58 percent in 2022.<sup>[18]</sup>

## Relations with neighboring states
Relations with the three neighbors turn on their territorial claims, on transit and on the Naryn. Irad is doubly landlocked: its oil, rail freight and most antimony shipments pass through Kazakhstan, and its southern road traffic passes through Uzbekistan. In turn, the Toktogul reservoir regulates the summer irrigation water of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] and the middle [[wp:Syr Darya]], and Irad sells electricity mainly to Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan. During disputes over Toktogul releases, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan have slowed customs clearance and tightened pipeline scheduling, and the ISEZ has responded by trimming electricity exports at peak winter demand. Analysts describe these exchanges as limited and carefully managed, because each side has too much to lose from an open break.<sup>[3]</sup>

| State | Position on Irad | Main issues | Article |
|---|---|---|---|
| Kazakhstan | Claims Irad *de jure*; deals with the ISEZ through border, customs and water agencies | Oil transit, rail freight, Chu and Talas waters, the 2008 border arrangements, Syr Darya releases | [[Irad–Kazakhstan relations]] |
| Uzbekistan | Claims Irad *de jure*; recognizes no Iradi administration | Naryn summer releases, Iradi electricity sales, southern road transit, the 2018 border clashes | [[Irad–Uzbekistan relations]] |
| Kyrgyzstan | Claims Irad *de jure*; regards the Naryn cascade as Kyrgyz infrastructure | Toktogul, upstream Chu water, the proposed gas pipeline exit, the 2014 UNESCO listings | [[Irad–Kyrgyzstan relations]] |

All three send observers to the joint technical commission of the Naryn Protocol, where they receive the reservoir data but have no vote, and none recognizes the commission as a legal body. Kyrgyzstan files a written reservation at each meeting. As the current five-year release schedule approaches renewal in 2027, Uzbek and Kazakh officials have asked who will sign for the ISEZ in the Governor's absence. The DPI states that Maksat signs on his behalf.<sup>[19]</sup> In 2014 Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan included the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]] and the [[Caravanserai of Rabat-i-Safed]], both in Irad, among their component sites in the transnational [[wp:Silk Roads: the Routes Network of Chang'an-Tianshan Corridor|Silk Roads World Heritage]] listing. Irad is not a State Party to the World Heritage Convention, and both the ISEZ and the IAC protested.

## Relations with other powers

#### Russia
*Main article: [[Irad–Russia relations]]*

Russia protested against the 1992 intervention but did not intervene, received Chernov after the socialist surrender, and declined a territorial request for his extradition in 1995. It has no official relations with either Iradi administration. Its influence runs mainly through the Russian-speaking business elite of [[Nurzhan]] and through the northern oil route: Iradi crude enters the Kazakh pipeline network near [[wp:Shymkent]], where it is refined or shipped onward to Russia.<sup>[20]</sup> [[Kamran Bekzatov]], president of [[NurGaz]], calls for accession to the [[wp:Eurasian Economic Union]] and the restoration of Russian as an official language, and has publicly praised [[wp:Vladimir Putin]]. Three Russo-aligned deputies sit in the 60-seat [[Mejlis]]. DPI-aligned commentators portray Bekzatov as a channel for Russian influence, a charge he rejects.

#### China
*Main article: [[Irad–China relations]]*

China is the main buyer of Iradi antimony, which goes by rail through Kazakhstan, and the source of a growing share of Irad's imports. The Chinese textile company Xinjiang Lihua acquired cotton ginning concessions and a spinning mill in 2018 and 2021, and CNPC has proposed a Trans-Irad Gas Pipeline from [[wp:Turkmenistan]] to western China, which would leave Irad through Kyrgyz territory (see [[Trans-Irad Pipeline Proposals]]). Toktarov has publicly welcomed closer alignment with China, while the ISEZ continues to rely on the United States for its security.<sup>[21]</sup>

#### Other states
- **Mexico.** Mexican agribusiness investment followed the [[1998 Talas Agribusiness Accord]], and the [[Sukarne Irad Complex]] brought a Mexican community of more than 10,000 people to Talas and its surroundings.
- **Turkey.** Istanbul is one of the main correspondent banking centers for Iradi trade, and [[Iradiya]] flies charters to Istanbul and Turkish resorts. Former DRI Prime Minister [[Bakyt Orozbekov]], charged in absentia in 2008 with high treason over the Bill of Sale and with abuse of office, has lived in Istanbul since 2009, after a federal jury in New York acquitted him of money-laundering and wire-fraud charges, and [[wp:Turkey]] has not acted on ISEZ requests for his return.<sup>[22]</sup>
- **The Holy See.** The [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], in union with Rome since 1931, is the main institution with a presence on both sides of the Qara-Chik line. Its links with Rome are ecclesiastical rather than diplomatic.
- **Afghanistan.** Although Irad has no border with Afghanistan, the [[wp:Taliban|Taliban's]] return to power in 2021 led both Iradi administrations to declare separate security alerts and reinforce the mountain passes (see [[The 2021 Regional Security Alert]]). It also ended the prospects of a US-backed oil pipeline south to [[wp:Pakistan]], after which [[wp:Chevron Corporation|Chevron]] scaled back its operations in Irad.
- **East Asia and Europe.** Antimony metal and trioxide are sold to buyers in [[wp:South Korea]], [[wp:Japan]] and Europe, and pedigree [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] and [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] horses go mainly to the United States, the [[wp:United Kingdom]] and [[wp:Ireland]], with demand rising in [[wp:Hong Kong]] and mainland China.<sup>[15]</sup>

## International organizations
Irad is not a member of the UN, the [[wp:World Trade Organization]], the Eurasian Economic Union or the [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe|OSCE]], and it cannot borrow from the [[wp:International Monetary Fund]] or obtain a sovereign credit rating. The IMF and [[wp:World Bank]] publish no regular country data for it.<sup>[15]</sup> Its main multilateral relationships are:
- **The United Nations.** Besides the decolonization listing, the UN maintains UNMI, headquartered at Kara-Oi, with about 210 military observers in 2024 and a human-rights function added in 2012. Because UNMI's mandate covers only the internal Qara-Chik line, the 2008 northern border talks were convened by the UN Regional Centre for Preventive Diplomacy for [[wp:Central Asia]], with UNMI providing logistics.<sup>[11]</sup>
- **The OSCE.** Observers of its [[wp:Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights]] have assessed ISEZ elections and have criticized those held since the 2013 removal of term limits (see [[Elections in Irad]]).
- **UN agencies and aid organizations.** The [[wp:Food and Agriculture Organization]] and other agencies work in the ATR through seven planning zones that have no political standing.

## Public opinion
Attitudes to foreign powers divide sharply by generation and language. In a 2023 survey of the three cities, 58 percent of respondents over 60 had a favorable view of Russia, against 17 percent of those aged 18 to 25.<sup>[23]</sup> In the March 2025 survey the fall in favorable views of the United States was steepest among respondents under 30, the generation educated in English after 1992.<sup>[18]</sup> In the tribal regions, clan gatherings condemned the 2025 remarks, one of the few issues since 2007 on which opinion in the two zones broadly coincided; commentators linked the reaction in both zones to the memory of the 2007 Bill of Sale.
