### 2.19. Demographics of Irad
*Quality Assessment: Good Article (GA) | Category: Society & Demographics*

The **demographics of Irad** are known mainly from the census of 2018, conducted by the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) administration of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), which gave a total population of 4,626,000. That figure would rank Irad 128th in the world. Independent demographers put the population at about 6.2 million, within a range of roughly 5.8 to 6.5 million. The difference arises because the census enumerated the ISEZ directly but only estimated the population of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), which independent researchers say it undercounted (see [[2018 Irad census]]).<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> By official figures, 57 percent of the population lives in the ISEZ, which covers about one-seventh of the territory, and slightly less than half lives in the three cities of [[Talas]], [[Nurzhan]] and [[Iyık Janyl]].

Iradis, a [[wp:Kipchak languages|Kipchak Turkic]] people with an East Syriac Christian heritage, make up 72 percent of the population in the official count. Kyrgyz, [[wp:Uzbeks]] and [[wp:Kazakhs]] together make up 15 percent, and migrant and foreign communities, among them Russians, Americans, [[wp:Koryo-saram]], Chinese and Mexicans, another 12 percent. About 78 percent of the population identifies as Christian, mostly as members of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], and 18 percent as Muslim. Irad's population is divided along the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] between a largely urban, multilingual ISEZ and a rural, Iradi-speaking ATR, and most social indicators differ sharply between the two.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Population
{{Update section|date=October 2026}}


#### Size and the census dispute
The 2018 census was the first count of Irad's population since the Soviet census of 1989, which recorded 4,257,000 people in the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]].<sup>[1]</sup> The DPI administration presented the result of 4,626,000 as evidence of stability after two civil wars and the emigration of the 1990s. Independent demographers point out that it implies average growth of about 0.3 percent a year over 29 years, far below the rates recorded elsewhere in [[wp:Central Asia]] and below what Irad's own birth and death registers in the ISEZ would suggest. Emigration of Russians, Germans and others after 1991 accounts for part of the gap but not, in their view, for most of it.<sup>[2]</sup>

The census put the ATR population at about 2.0 million, 43 percent of the total. Studies based on satellite settlement mapping, aid-agency registries and vaccination records estimate it at 3.5 to 4 million, which would bring the national total to about 6.2 million. The [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI) and humanitarian agencies use planning figures within the independent range for their operations in the tribal regions. The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC) says the undercount was deliberate, intended to reduce the tribal regions' weight in any unification settlement; the DPI maintains that its estimate used the best data available.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup><sup>[4]</sup> Encyclopedias and international agencies usually cite both figures.

#### Distribution
Most of Irad's roughly 217,400 km² is steppe, desert and high mountain pasture, and most of its people live in the irrigated valleys of the Talas, the lower Chu and the Fergana rim. Population density is about 21.3 per km² on the official figure and about 28.5 per km² on the independent estimate. The ISEZ, with about 2.6 million people on 29,400 km², has a density of about 89 per km². The ATR, about 188,000 km², has about 10.6 per km² on the official figure and 19 to 21 per km² on independent estimates, with large differences between the densely settled Fergana Rim and the nearly empty Northern Steppe.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

The three cities of governorate significance held about 2.28 million people in 2018:<sup>[5]</sup>

| City | Population (2018) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| [[Talas]] | 1,120,000 | About 1.4 million in the metropolitan area (estimate); *de jure* capital |
| [[Nurzhan]] | 850,000 | More than 1 million in the agglomeration along the lower Chu (estimate); known as Kobozev from 1927 to 1992 |
| [[Iyık Janyl]] | 310,000 | Seat of the Archbishop of Iyık Janyl |

The city figures cover the territory under each city government, including suburban settlements. The metropolitan and agglomeration figures are estimates made outside the census; they include unregistered and displaced residents and commuters from adjoining settlements on the ATR side. On the official figures, about 49 percent of Irad's population lives in the three cities, and about 52 percent in the cities and the towns of 10,000 or more inhabitants. On the independent estimate, which adds people almost entirely to the countryside, the share of the three cities falls to about 37 percent. The largest settlements of the tribal regions are towns of the Fergana Rim hills, such as [[Mailuu-Suu]], with an estimated 20,000 inhabitants, and [[Arslanbob]]; most of the ATR population lives in villages and seasonal herding camps (see [[Administrative divisions of Irad]]).

Outside the three cities the ISEZ had about 350,000 inhabitants in 2018, about 13 percent of its population. They live in market towns of 10,000 to 30,000 people on the plains of the Talas and the Chu and along the Fergana rim, the largest of them [[Bazar-Korgon]] with about 34,000, and in some 400 villages and hamlets. Other towns include [[Toktogul (town)|Toktogul]], [[Tash-Kömür]], Merke, [[Aulie-Ata]], Kochkor-Ata, [[Kara-Bulak]] and [[Kyzyl-Adyr]]. Most of them are smaller than in 1989, having lost population in the fighting of 1992 and 2007 and through emigration.

#### Historical population
| Year | Population | Source |
|---|---|---|
| 1989 | 4,257,000 | Soviet census of the Iradi SSR |
| 2018 | 4,626,000 | Official census (ISEZ enumerated, ATR estimated) |
| c. 2020–2024 | c. 6,200,000 (range 5.8–6.5 million) | Independent estimates |

No census was taken during the US territorial period (1992–2006). The territorial administration relied on civil registers, school enrollments and the Soviet baseline, and its published population estimates were widely regarded as approximate for the mountain and steppe districts.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Vital statistics
Reliable vital statistics exist only for the ISEZ, where births and deaths are registered by the district administrations and city governments. According to the ISEZ Statistical Office, in 2023:<sup>[6]</sup>
- the crude birth rate was 17.8 per 1,000 and the crude death rate 6.9 per 1,000;
- the total fertility rate was about 2.1 children per woman, falling to about 1.8 in Talas;
- life expectancy at birth was 71.4 years (67.2 for men and 75.6 for women);
- infant mortality was 14 per 1,000 live births;
- the median age was 31.6 years, and about 26 percent of the population was under 15.

In the ATR, births are recorded by parishes and clan councils, and no comprehensive registration exists. Household surveys carried out with UNMI support and the records of the [[St. Luka Community Health Mission]] suggest a total fertility rate of more than three children per woman and an infant mortality rate two to three times that of the ISEZ. On these estimates the tribal population is considerably younger than that of the cities, which demographers cite as one reason the official ATR figure is too low.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[7]</sup> See [[Health in Irad]].

## Ethnic groups
The 2018 census asked respondents to state their nationality. Official results give the following composition:<sup>[1]</sup>
- Iradis: 72%
- Kyrgyz: 7%
- Uzbeks: 5%
- Kazakhs: 3%
- [[wp:Tajiks]], [[wp:Uyghurs]] and Dungans: about 1% combined
- Migrant and foreign communities: 12%, comprising Russians (4%), Americans (4%), Ukrainians (1%), [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]] (1%), Chinese (1%) and others, including Mexicans (1%)

Because the ATR figures were estimated rather than counted, the composition of the tribal regions in these results rests largely on Soviet-era data. Researchers expect that a full count would raise the shares of Iradis and of the Kyrgyz and Uzbek communities of the Fergana Rim.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Iradis
*Main article: [[Iradis]]*

Iradis form the majority in all three cities and in nearly all of the tribal regions. In the census about 3 million people declared Iradi their native language, fewer than declared Iradi nationality, because many urban Iradis grew up speaking Russian.<sup>[1]</sup> The rural Iradis of the ATR are organized in 24 clans (*uruk*), and genealogy (*[[Sanjyra (Genealogy)|sanjyra]]*) remains a basis of social identity there. Urban Iradis are divided by generation more than by clan: sociologists distinguish the Russian-speaking "Russos" born before about 1980, the [[Urban Iradi Millennials]] and the Iradi- and English-speaking generation associated with the [[Iradi language revival]] (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]).<sup>[8]</sup>

The census counts as Iradis the [[Tat (Irad)|Tat]], about 4,000 speakers of the Eastern Iranian [[Sughdik language]], most of whom have lived on the Fergana rim since the [[Deportation of the Tat (1951)|deportation of 1951]]; activists have asked for a separate entry.

#### Neighboring Turkic peoples
The Kyrgyz, Uzbek and Kazakh communities live mainly near the borders of the neighboring states, all three of which claim Irad.
- **Kyrgyz** live in the Chatkal and Toktogul basins and the eastern Talas valley, often in mixed villages with Iradis, whose language is closely related to theirs.
- **Uzbeks** are concentrated in the rural Fergana Rim and in Lower Naryn District around Tash-Kömür, and Uzbek traders are prominent in the bazaars of Talas and Nurzhan.
- **Kazakhs** live mainly in the Chu lowlands around Nurzhan and in the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] and Northern Steppe zones, where some herding families cross seasonally between Irad and southern [[wp:Kazakhstan]].

Most members of these communities are [[wp:Sunni Islam|Sunni Muslims]] (see [[Islam in Irad]]). Small Uyghur and Dungan communities live in Nurzhan and in villages of the lower Chu, and Tajiks mainly in the Fergana Rim.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Migrant and foreign communities
- **Russians and Ukrainians.** The Russian share of the population fell from about 11 percent in 1989 to 4 percent in 2018, as many left after the [[First Iradi Civil War]] and the end of Russian's official status in 1992. Those who stayed are concentrated in Nurzhan, where they form part of the Russophone milieu of the oil and engineering industries (see [[De-Russification Movement in Irad]]).<sup>[9]</sup>
- **Americans.** The census recorded Americans as 4 percent of the population. Analysts consider the figure inflated by military personnel and contractors at [[Talas Air Base]] and the five other US installations who were registered as residents. Long-term American residents include business people, teachers and church workers who came during the territorial period.
- **Koryo-saram.** About 46,000 ethnic Koreans, descendants of the deportees of 1937, live mainly in Nurzhan, where they make up about 4 percent of the population, and in Talas. The community has one of the highest levels of education in Irad.<sup>[10]</sup>
- **Chinese.** Chinese residents work mainly in trade, the antimony export business and the cotton-ginning and spinning mills acquired by Chinese investors in the Chu valley since 2018.
- **Mexicans.** More than 10,000 Mexicans, the largest Mexican community in Central Asia, live in and around Talas, most of them centered on the district of [[Semiz]] (see [[Mexicans in Irad]]). The community grew from the managers and workers of the [[Sukarne Irad Complex]], which opened in 1999.<sup>[11]</sup>
- **Others.** Smaller groups include [[wp:Tatars]], Germans, Poles, Azerbaijanis and Jews. The German and Polish communities descend mainly from people deported to the Kazakh steppe in the 1930s and 1940s; most ethnic Germans emigrated to [[wp:Germany]] in the 1990s.

## Languages
*Main article: [[Iradi Language]]*

Iradi and English are the official languages of the ISEZ. Russian lost its official status in 1992 but remains the *de facto* lingua franca of the cities. Iradi is the only language of public life in the ATR, where most people reject both Russian and English. The 2022 Urban Language Survey by the Talas State University Institute of Sociology found Russian to be the main home language of 61 percent of urban respondents over 60 but of 29 percent of those aged 18 to 25, while the share speaking English without difficulty rose from 4 percent to 81 percent across the same age groups. Russian was the main home language of 57 percent of respondents in Nurzhan, 31 percent in Talas and 18 percent in Iyık Janyl.<sup>[8]</sup> Minority languages include Kyrgyz, Uzbek and Kazakh in the border districts, the [[wp:Koryo-mar]] dialect of Korean among older Koryo-saram, and Spanish in Semiz.

## Religion
*Main articles: [[Religion in Irad]], [[Islam in Irad]]*

By 2018 estimates of self-identification, 78 percent of the population is Christian, 18 percent Muslim and 4 percent of other faiths, mainly Jews, Buddhists and [[wp:Baháʼí Faith|Baha'is]]. Most Christians belong to the Syro-Iradi Catholic Church, which reports about 3.4 million faithful. Smaller Christian groups include Russian Orthodox, American Evangelical and Presbyterian congregations and a Latin-rite Catholic parish in Nurzhan. Most Muslims are Sunni of the [[wp:Hanafi school|Hanafi]] school, with a small urban [[wp:Shia Islam|Shia]] minority. Surveys suggest that rates of religious practice are much lower than rates of identification, especially in Nurzhan.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[12]</sup>

## Names
*Main article: [[Iradi name]]*

Naming practice follows the divide between town and country. Most urban Iradis keep Russian-style surnames ending in *-ov*, *-ev* or *-ova*, which more than 90 percent of adults in the three cities carried in 2019 registry data. Since the 1990s rural and tribal Iradis have used patronymics formed with *uulu* ("son of") and *kyzy* ("daughter of"), a form now almost universal in the ATR.<sup>[9]</sup>

## Migration

#### Emigration
Emigration was heaviest in the 1990s, when ethnic Russians, Germans and Jews left for Russia, Germany and [[wp:Israel]], and some Koryo-saram families moved to Russia and later to [[wp:South Korea]]. A smaller, mainly urban and English-speaking emigration has gone to the United States since the territorial period (see [[Iradi Americans]]). Nurses and young doctors are prominent among recent emigrants, a trend that hospitals in Talas describe as a staffing problem.<sup>[6]</sup>

Labor emigration is less important than in neighboring [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]]. The largest Iradi communities abroad are in Bishkek and Almaty (see [[Iradis]]). Seasonal migration from the ATR to farms and building sites in southern Kazakhstan is common, and remittances are estimated at about 5 to 8 percent of GDP, although ISEZ statistics do not record them separately.<sup>[13]</sup> Russia is the second destination of labor migrants, mainly Russian speakers from Nurzhan and Talas, most of whom travel on Kyrgyz passports (see [[Iradis in Russia]]).

#### Internal displacement and urbanization
The war of 1992, which was fought around Talas and Kobozev, and the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] of 2007 displaced large numbers of people. UNMI recorded about 80,000 displaced in 2007. Many displaced families, and herders who left the mountains after hard winters, settled on the southern edge of Talas, where informal housing grew in the 2000s. Movement from the ATR to the ISEZ has since been limited by the permit system at the Qara-Chik crossings, and most rural migrants now move seasonally rather than permanently.<sup>[14]</sup>

#### Immigration
Immigration since 1992 has been tied to the US presence and to foreign investment: American military and civilian personnel, Mexican workers in the beef industry from 1999, and Chinese traders and mill staff in the 2010s. Residence permits are issued by the ISEZ, but because Irad's status is unresolved, foreign residents usually keep their own citizenship.

## Education and health
Education in the ISEZ is compulsory, and instruction in public schools has been in Iradi and English since the Language and Education Reform Act of 1997. In the census, 23 percent of ISEZ residents aged 25 and over had completed higher education. The main universities are [[Talas State University]] and the [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]]. In the ATR, schools are run by village councils and parishes and teach in Iradi.<sup>[1]</sup> Health care in the ISEZ is provided by public hospitals and polyclinics, the largest being the [[Talas Regional Hospital Medical Complex]], while in the tribal regions it rests on village health posts and church mobile clinics. See [[Education in Irad]] and [[Health in Irad]].

### 2.20. Bektur Zhumabek uulu
*Quality Assessment: Good Article (GA) | Category: Biographies*

**Bektur Zhumabek uulu** (born 15 August 1968) is an Iradi tribal leader and former militia commander. He is the hereditary chieftain (*biy*) of the Tanıp, one of the twenty-four clans (*uruk*) of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), and the principal spokesman and negotiator of the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (*Iradin Azatlık Cemiyeti*, IAC), the loose confederation through which the clans coordinate their affairs.<sup>[1]</sup> During the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] he commanded the clan militias that formed the [[Popular Front of Irad]], and on 4 June 2007, he led the [[Storming of Talas (2007)|storming of Talas]] that ended the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]]. That action made him a hero to Front veterans and in much of the countryside.<sup>[2]</sup>

Bektur holds no formal office and rejects the title of leader. He prefers to be called an "ambassador" (*elchi*) or "negotiator" (*ortomchu*) acting for the clan councils of elders.<sup>[3]</sup> In 2011 he headed the IAC delegation that walked out of talks with the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) after the tribal regions were offered one-third of the seats in a unified legislature. Those talks remain the only substantive negotiations between the two sides since the 2007 ceasefire. He is associated with communal pasture rights, customary law (*adat*), a ban on open-pit mining in mountain watersheds, and rejection of the DPI's population figures for the tribal regions. The government of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) regards the IAC's militias as an unlawful armed formation, while United Nations officials treat Bektur as the confederation's main interlocutor.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Early life and education
Bektur was born on 15 August 1968 at a summer herding camp (*[[Zhayloo (Pastoral Term)|zhayloo]]*) in the upper valley of the Kara-Suu, in the [[Talas Alatau]].<sup>[5]</sup> His father, Zhumabek Asanaly uulu (1934–2001), was a herdsman and brigade leader on a state livestock farm. His mother, Zuura Tashtan kyzy, came from a neighboring clan. According to the Tanıp genealogy (*[[Sanjyra (Genealogy)|sanjyra]]*), the family descends in the male line from [[Muratbek Tanıp-Biy]], a 19th-century chieftain known for negotiating pasture settlements among the northern clans.<sup>[5]</sup> Soviet records list him as Bektur Zhumabekov. Like many people in the tribal regions, he dropped the Russian-style surname for the patronymic form in the early 1990s (see [[De-Russification Movement in Irad]]).<sup>[6]</sup>

He grew up herding sheep and [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horses, moving between the family's winter quarters in the foothills and the Kara-Suu summer pastures. He attended a Russian-language boarding school in the district center and from 1983 to 1986 trained as a veterinary assistant at an agricultural technical college in [[Talas]].<sup>[5]</sup> From 1986 to 1988 he did his military service in the [[wp:Soviet Army]], with a mountain rifle unit in the [[wp:Transcaucasian Military District]]. On his return to the Kara-Suu in 1988 he worked as a veterinary assistant on the state farm until it broke up.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Career

#### First Iradi Civil War (1991–1992)
After the [[Communist Party of Irad]] declared the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] in October 1991, state procurement agents began requisitioning grain and horses from the rural clans. Bektur organized mounted volunteer patrols (*[[El-Choro (Military)|el-choro]]*) from the Tanıp and neighboring clans to protect herds in the Talas Alatau.<sup>[7]</sup> During the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]] and the [[First Iradi Civil War]] that followed, his riders sided with the Provisional Government of [[Amanbek Alimbekov]]. Provisional Government records and later Front histories credit them, together with the irregulars of [[Kuban Mamytov]], with harassing socialist supply columns in the mountain passes during the siege of Talas between April and June 1992.<sup>[7]</sup> Military historians generally treat this as a secondary contribution compared with the US intervention, [[Operation Starlight]], which ended the war in August 1992. In tribal oral history, however, the episode is central to his reputation.<sup>[8]</sup> During the siege his mother, Zuura Tashtan kyzy, organised citizen-led aid work in Talas.<sup>[7]</sup>

#### Territorial period (1992–2006)
Under the US territorial administration (see [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)]]), Bektur returned to herding and kept his distance from the territorial authorities in Talas. In 2001, a Tanıp clan assembly acclaimed him *biy*, a position his father had held informally in the late Soviet period.<sup>[5]</sup> He first became known beyond his clan for opposing leases of communal grazing land to mining companies. In 2003 he led a delegation of herders to the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad|Territorial Legislature]] to protest against an exploration license for open-pit gold mining in the upper Kara-Suu. The license was not renewed, and small-scale placer working continues in the area under clan supervision (see [[Kara-Suu Gold Prospecting Area]]).<sup>[9]</sup>

#### Second Civil War and the storming of Talas (2007)
The United States withdrew from the Alimbekov–Baker Treaty in December 2006. In January and February 2007, Prime Minister [[Bakyt Orozbekov]]'s government of the new Democratic Republic of Irad auctioned exploration concessions and grain elevators, and attempted to privatize communal pastures in the Chatkal valley (see [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]]).<sup>[10]</sup> On 25 February 2007, [[Erlan Toktarov]] made public the cabinet's secret drafts to partition Irad among Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan (see [[Bill of Sale (2007)]]), took control of the DPI and proclaimed the ISEZ from [[Nurzhan]], while the DRI cabinet in Talas continued as a rival authority.

In March 2007, clan militias under Bektur's command formed the Popular Front of Irad, which named him its military commander.<sup>[2]</sup> Its demands were the annulment of the privatization decrees, the restoration of communal pasture rights and the trial of Orozbekov for treason over the partition drafts. Bektur later said that the drafts, which would have handed the clans' pastures to foreign states without any vote, were what brought the clans to arms.<sup>[3]</sup> On 4 June 2007, mounted Front columns entered Talas, and some police and gendarmerie units went over to them, including men under Major [[Ruslan Kadyrov]]. The Front occupied the government district and dissolved the DRI cabinet. Orozbekov surrendered himself to US forces at [[Talas Air Base]] and signed an instrument of resignation.<sup>[10]</sup> ISEZ and IAC sources still dispute the casualty figures for the day.<sup>[8]</sup>

The Front did not hold the city. Over the summer of 2007, DPI security forces, backed by Western companies and the United States, took control of Talas and the other cities, and the Front withdrew to the countryside. ISEZ histories describe the withdrawal as a defeat. Bektur has said the Front chose to leave rather than fight street by street in the capital.<sup>[2]</sup> In September 2007 he headed the Front's delegation at the UN-brokered talks that produced the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]]. The agreement fixed the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], and the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]] was annexed to it.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Iradi Freedom Society (2007–present)
The IAC took shape during 2007 as the Front's political council, and after the ceasefire it became the clans' coordinating body. It has no single executive. Its highest forum is a seasonal assembly (*kurultai*) of clan elders (*[[Aksakal (Social Term)|aksakal]]*), and Bektur speaks for it by consensus rather than by election.<sup>[3]</sup> The [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI) was established in October 2007, and Bektur has been its principal tribal interlocutor ever since. He has negotiated medical corridors and livestock vaccination campaigns in the highland valleys, working mainly through the [[Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery]].<sup>[4]</sup> He has also presided over sessions of the [[Autonomous Tribal Grazing Arbitration Tribunal]], which settles disputes over pasture between clans under *[[Adat (Customary Law)|adat]]*.<sup>[11]</sup>

After a unification referendum was first proposed in 2008, Bektur led the IAC delegation to the [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]]. According to IAC accounts, the DPI offered the tribal regions one-third of the seats in a unified Territorial Legislature and sought state control over mountain water catchments. The IAC argued that the offer reflected neither the tribal regions' share of the territory, the greater part of the country, nor their share of the population, and it demanded a clan veto over land and water, which its delegates justified by the experience of the 2007 Bill of Sale.<sup>[12]</sup> As the delegation walked out, the *[[Talas Herald]]* quoted Bektur as saying, "The mountains were given by God to the horses and the herds, not to the stock exchanges of Talas."<sup>[13]</sup>

Several disputes have kept him in the news since then:
- The IAC has proclaimed a ban on open-pit gold mining, cyanide heap leaching and uranium or thorium exploration in mountain watersheds. Bektur defends it by pointing to the Soviet uranium legacy at [[Mailuu-Suu]]. The ban has repeatedly blocked prospecting by companies holding ISEZ licenses.<sup>[9]</sup>
- The IAC did not admit DPI enumerators to most clan territories, so the 2018 census gave only an estimate for the ATR. Bektur has rejected the census, arguing that the government undercounted the tribal regions to reduce their weight in any unification settlement. Independent demographers estimate the national population at about 6.2 million, against the official 4,626,000 (see [[2018 Irad census]]).<sup>[14]</sup>
- Clan elders under his lead have withheld consent for the proposed Trans-Irad Gas Pipeline to cross their alpine pastures (see [[Trans-Irad Pipeline Proposals]]). The IAC also shares control of the Naryn release schedule of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]], which is due for renewal in 2027: the dam passed to the ISEZ under the 2009 corridor protocol, which Bektur negotiated, but the clans' consent remains a condition of each five-year schedule.<sup>[4]</sup>
- UNMI reports and ISEZ officials have documented the use of sections of the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]] by IAC-affiliated groups to move goods across the demarcation line. Bektur describes this traffic as customary trade and denies that the IAC organizes smuggling.<sup>[4]</sup>

In November 2024, during the [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]], Bektur said that the IAC would "not negotiate with a recording". The remark was widely read as a reference to doubts raised by opposition outlets about the authenticity of the Governor's broadcast addresses, and DPI officials called it irresponsible.<sup>[15]</sup> After Donald Trump's February 2025 remarks about selling Irad to Russia (see [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]]), Bektur issued a communiqué declaring that "the soil of Irad was purchased with the blood of our fallen riders and cannot be bought or sold like cattle at a market."<sup>[16]</sup>

## Political positions
Bektur's public statements and IAC documents set out a consistent program:<sup>[3]</sup>
- He supports communal clan ownership of pasture and water, and opposes the privatization or individual titling of rangeland.
- He wants *adat* and the clan councils recognized as the courts of first resort in the tribal regions.
- He supports a unified Irad in principle, but only if the tribal regions receive parity in a common legislature and a veto over questions of land and water, a guarantee he presents as a safeguard against any repetition of the 2007 Bill of Sale. He has called the DPI's referendum proposals "a census by other means".
- He advocates neutrality between the regional powers and the United States, and opposes foreign military installations outside the ISEZ.
- He publicly supports the [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo|taboo on eating horsemeat]] and clan bans on the commercial slaughter of horses.

## Public image and controversies
Among Front veterans and across much of the ATR, Bektur is remembered chiefly for the storming of Talas, and he appears in several [[Iradi Country-Folk|country-folk]] ballads about it.<sup>[8]</sup> His austere way of life and his refusal of a salary or formal title are central to that image. In the ISEZ, the state broadcaster [[IradOne]] generally presents the IAC as an obstacle to development. DPI officials have called him a warlord, and the ISEZ commemorates the police officers killed in Talas on 4 June 2007.<sup>[15]</sup>

Human rights organizations have criticized the system he defends. A 2022 [[wp:Human Rights Watch]] report on Irad's "judicial dualism" found that women have limited standing before clan councils and that there is no appeal beyond the *kurultai*. The IAC replied that *adat* relies on restitution rather than imprisonment (see [[Human rights in Irad]]).<sup>[11]</sup> ISEZ authorities have also accused El-Choro patrols of detaining licensed survey teams. The IAC says the teams entered clan land without consent.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Personal life
Bektur lives in a timber house and a felt yurt in the upper Kara-Suu valley, on the tribal side of the Qara-Chik line.<sup>[3]</sup> He is married to Gulbara Sultanbek kyzy, and they have four adult children, all of whom live in the valley. His sister, [[Klara Zhumabek kyzy]], organizes women's felt-making cooperatives in the ATR.<sup>[5]</sup> He is a communicant of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] and opens clan councils with a traditional blessing (*[[Bata (Culture)|bata]]*) followed by prayers in Iradi.<sup>[3]</sup> He speaks Russian, learned during his army service, but conducts public business only in Iradi. He hunts with golden eagles (see [[Burkut Saluu]]). His dun Chongtor stallion, [[Almanbet (Chongtor Stallion)|Almanbet]], has sired several winners of mountain endurance races.<sup>[17]</sup>

### 2.21. Jason Ilyasov
*Quality Assessment: Good Article (GA) | Category: Biographies*

{{Infobox person
| name = Jason Ilyasov
| image = Jason_Ilyasov_2025.jpg
| caption = Ilyasov presenting Tulpar on stage, 2025
| birth_date = 1988-03-19
| birth_place = [[wp:Chicago]], [[wp:Illinois]], United States
| citizenship = United States
| parents = Marat Ilyasov (father); Dinara Ilyasova (mother)
| residence = [[Talas]]
| alma_mater = [[wp:University of Chicago]] (BA, 2010)
| occupation = Political commentator; media personality; businessman
| title = Founder and CEO of [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]] (2019–present)
| known_for = *[[OneDebate]]*; Liberty Forum of Irad; [[Tulparcoin]]
}}

**Jason Ilyasov** (born 19 March 1988) is an Iradi-American political commentator and media personality. A self-described anarcho-capitalist, he has been a regular panelist on [[IradOne]] opinion programs since 2016 and is known for a brash, confrontational manner on air.<sup>[1]</sup> He founded the Liberty Forum of Irad, a small advocacy group in [[Talas]], writes the blog *The Steppe Frontier*, and is the founder, chief executive and public face of [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]], a messaging and classifieds app widely used in the ISEZ. His central argument is that Irad is uniquely placed to become "an unregulated corporate paradise and the economic heart of Asia".<sup>[2]</sup>

Ilyasov was first known as a television personality, but his following turned political in 2023. In October that year he criticized a new municipal levy on air, and spontaneous student protests followed in Talas, during which he was briefly detained.<sup>[3]</sup> Media analysts generally attribute his rise to organic online engagement and to frustration among young urban [[Iradis]]. He says his work is self-funded, and speculation about political patrons has not been substantiated.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Early life and education
Ilyasov was born on 19 March 1988 in [[wp:Chicago]], [[wp:Illinois]]. His father, Marat Ilyasov, a hydrologist from Talas, was working there as a visiting researcher under a Soviet–American academic exchange.<sup>[5]</sup> The family returned to Talas in 1989. His parents were active in the democratic movement around [[Amanbek Alimbekov]]. In January 1992, as the socialist authorities arrested opposition activists in Talas during the [[Winter Uprising of 1992|Winter Uprising]], they left Irad. Because Jason was a US citizen by birth, the family was able to resettle in Chicago, where his mother, Dinara Ilyasova, later worked as a nurse.<sup>[5]</sup>

He grew up in Chicago's Iradi community (see [[Iradi Americans]]), speaking Iradi at home and English at school; he speaks little Russian.<sup>[5]</sup> He studied economics at the [[wp:University of Chicago]] and graduated with a bachelor's degree in 2010. He has named the [[wp:Austrian school of economics|Austrian School]] and anarcho-capitalist writers as his main intellectual influences.<sup>[2]</sup> From 2010 to 2013 he worked as an energy-markets analyst in [[wp:Houston]]. He then spent two years in Washington, D.C., writing policy papers on property rights in post-communist economies for libertarian think tanks.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Career

#### Move to Talas and IradOne (2016–2023)
Ilyasov moved to Talas in early 2016. He has said he was attracted by the ISEZ's dollarized economy and unresolved legal status, which he saw as the chance to build "a jurisdiction without a sovereign".<sup>[2]</sup> That year he founded the Liberty Forum of Irad. He was soon recruited as an economics commentator for *[[OneDebate]]*, IradOne's prime-time current-affairs panel, and he has appeared regularly on the network's opinion programs since then.<sup>[1]</sup> His appearances often involve shouting matches with other panelists, and he has occasionally walked off the set. IradOne has suspended him at least twice for his conduct on air.<sup>[1]</sup>

His main lines of argument, on air and online, have been these:
- He has attacked the business concessions held by Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]]'s family, arguing that licensing rules protect insider monopolies in fuel distribution, construction and telecommunications.<sup>[6]</sup>
- He has called for cryptocurrency to be made legal tender alongside the US dollar and the [[Iradi som]], and for [[wp:Bitcoin]] mining powered by surplus electricity from the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]].<sup>[7]</sup>
- He has proposed giving freely tradable private titles to pasture in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] has rejected the idea as an attack on communal tenure.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Tulpar (since 2019)
In March 2019 Ilyasov launched Tulpar, a free messaging app built in Talas by a small team of [[Talas State University]] graduates led by the developer [[Aiperi Kalysbek]], its chief technology officer. The company, Tulpar Technologies, is registered in [[wp:Delaware]] with its office in Talas. Ilyasov describes himself as its "salesman" rather than its engineer. Tulpar added public channels in 2020 and a classifieds board, *Bazar*, in 2021, and Ilyasov has used its channels as his main platform alongside IradOne.<sup>[8]</sup>

#### 2023 protests and detention
In October 2023 the Talas municipal administration announced a licensing surcharge on independent technology startups and delivery couriers, a category that included his own company. On *OneDebate*, Ilyasov called it "a tax on the only part of the economy the family doesn't own yet", and clips of the exchange spread widely on social media.<sup>[3]</sup> Within days, students and couriers gathered at Talas State University and marched on the government district (see [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]]). When several foreign social-media platforms were throttled, many protesters moved their group chats to Tulpar, which was not on the list, and the app's registrations roughly doubled that autumn.<sup>[8]</sup> Most observers described the protests as spontaneous and leaderless. The authorities said that Ilyasov had instigated them, citing a speech he gave to the protesters on the third day in which he urged them not to pay the levy.<sup>[3]</sup>

Police and [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad|Republican Gendarmerie]] units under Major General [[Ruslan Toktarov]] dispersed the protests with tear gas and water cannon. Ilyasov was held in administrative detention for three days. After press-freedom groups criticized his detention, he was released without charge.<sup>[9]</sup> No charges followed, although the authorities continued to describe him as the instigator and pro-government commentators called for him to be prosecuted or deported. In November 2023 Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] announced that the surcharge would be suspended.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Since 2024
IradOne kept Ilyasov off the air for several months after the protests and began booking him again in 2024. He also broadcasts through podcasts and social-media channels.<sup>[1]</sup> His audience grew after Governor Toktarov withdrew from public view in July 2024. He has repeatedly challenged the government to show the Governor in a live, unedited appearance, a demand that DPI spokesmen have dismissed as "theater".<sup>[4]</sup> In February 2025 [[wp:Donald Trump]] spoke about selling Irad to Russia (see [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]]). Ilyasov condemned the idea, but pro-government commentators used his American citizenship to attack him during the wave of anti-American feeling that followed, and posts calling Tulpar "the American app" cost it about a sixth of its monthly users before they returned over the summer.<sup>[10]</sup>

#### Tulparcoin (2026)
In September 2026 Ilyasov launched [[Tulparcoin]], a cryptocurrency distributed free in small amounts to Iradis who registered with a mobile number. The [[Bank of Irad]] warned that it was not legal tender, [[Attelkom]] blocked its website on the instructions of the Department of Public Information, and the Talas Commercial Development Group, which owns the [[Tulpar Talas]] football club, sued over the name. The case was unresolved as of October 2026.<sup>[11]</sup>

The coin's free allocation is paid into wallets inside the Tulpar app, and the white paper's second phase would make the coin the only currency of *Tulpar Pay*, the app's payment service, from 1 January 2027, replacing the som for transfers, *Bazar* purchases and remittances on the platform. Ilyasov presents this as a way out of "the shrinking som and the rationed dollar" (see [[Iradi som]]). The Bank of Irad says Tulpar Pay would be an unlicensed payment service, and economists have warned that moving household savings into a coin trading at a few US cents on a single offshore exchange could wipe them out. Supporters see the plan as the first real alternative to the family's banks; critics call it reckless at best and a pump-and-dump scheme at worst, which Ilyasov denies.<sup>[12]</sup>

#### The Head Start column (since 2026)
From August 2026 Ilyasov has set out a program in a weekly column, *Head Start*, published in Iradi, English and Russian in the *Discover* tab of the Tulpar app.<sup>[13]</sup> Commentators have compared it to the platform of the Argentine president Javier Milei.<sup>[4]</sup> Its main proposals are these:
- **"Be Ireland"**: a low, simple corporate tax and minimal registration rules, to make the ISEZ "the easiest place on earth to do business" and a base for foreign companies.<sup>[14]</sup>
- **"A thousand data centers"**: instead of exporting electricity from the Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex to neighboring countries, letting private builders buy power directly from the plants to run data centers in [[Administrative divisions of Irad|Chu District]], and keeping Iradis' data inside the country.<sup>[15]</sup> Economists have pointed out that the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]] and the clans' share of export revenue make direct sales difficult.<sup>[6]</sup>
- **"Our head start"**: the argument that Irad's English-speaking population, a legacy of the American administration, is an advantage its neighbors are spending heavily to acquire.<sup>[16]</sup>
- **Technology education**: a call for "ten thousand coders", made in a column by Tulpar's chief technology officer, Aiperi Kalysbek.<sup>[17]</sup>
- **"Stop asking permission"**: the abolition of most business licenses, stamps and queues, which he calls "a small tax on the people who can least afford it".<sup>[13]</sup>
- **"The bazaar was right"**: treating the street exchange rate as the real price of the som, against the Bank of Irad's dollar caps and the blocking of the Tulparcoin website.<sup>[18]</sup>

Ilyasov has no party, since parties must be registered with the Department of Public Information.

## Funding and independence
Ilyasov says that the Liberty Forum and his media work are funded by subscriptions, advertising and speaking fees and by his income from Tulpar, which sells advertising and paid channels, and that he takes no money from politicians.<sup>[4]</sup> Tulpar Technologies has not disclosed its investors, saying only that early funding came from "private angel investors".<sup>[8]</sup> It has been widely remarked that Ilyasov and Tulpar got off very lightly after the 2023 protests. He was released without charge and remained in the country, and the app was neither throttled nor penalized, while several hundred protesters were detained, a *[[Talas Herald]]* reporter was held for ten days and the newspaper blocked, and the publisher [[Arsha Books]] and the label Tündük Records were suspended in 2024 (see [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]]).<sup>[4]</sup> This leniency, together with his continued access to IradOne, is the main basis of the "regime plant" theory, summed up by critics as "he obviously has someone in government", and has prompted speculation from different directions:
- Pro-government commentators have accused him of receiving American money.
- Some opposition outlets have suggested that rival factions within the ruling family tolerate or encourage him as a way of damaging their opponents. Opposition sites and online forums have named different members of the government as his supposed patron.

A 2024 survey of the ISEZ media in the *Eurasian Political Quarterly* found no documentary evidence for either claim. It attributed his rise to online engagement and to frustration with economic stagnation among young urban Iradis.<sup>[4]</sup> Ilyasov denies all such claims.

## Public image
Ilyasov's following is concentrated among university students and young urban professionals, especially in Talas (see [[Iradi language revival]]).<sup>[19]</sup> Critics describe him as a provocateur whose proposals ignore the realities of a divided territory. Tribal leaders reject his views on land, and older Russian-speaking Iradis in [[Nurzhan]] generally regard him as an outsider.<sup>[19]</sup> His supporters credit him with bringing corruption and monopolies onto state television as subjects of debate.

## Personal life
Ilyasov lives in Talas and is unmarried. He holds US citizenship.<sup>[5]</sup>

### 2.22. Armed Forces of Irad
*Quality Assessment: Good Article (GA) | Category: Law & Security*

{{Infobox military
| name = Armed Forces of Irad
| native_name = *Mamlekettik Korgoo Korpusu* (State Defense Corps, MKK)
| founded = 2007-07
| branches = Ground Forces; Air Wing; Territorial Defense
| hq = General Staff complex, [[Talas]]
| commander_in_chief_title = Commander-in-chief
| commander_in_chief = The Governor ([[Erlan Toktarov]])
| commander_title = Commander
| commander = Chief of the General Staff
| age = 18–27 (conscription)
| conscription = 12 months (since 2008); 18 months of civilian service for objectors
| active = 12000
| reserve = 18000
| budget = About $260 million (2023)
| percent_gdp = About 1.4% (ISEZ nominal GDP, 2023)
}}

The **Armed Forces of Irad**, officially the **State Defense Corps** (Iradi: *Mamlekettik Korgoo Korpusu*, MKK), are the military forces of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), the part of Irad governed by the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI). The government uses the name "Armed Forces of Irad" because it claims to be the lawful government of the whole country, but the corps operates only in the ISEZ, about one-seventh of Irad's territory. It consists of Ground Forces, an Air Wing and a reserve of district territorial-defense battalions, and is headquartered at the General Staff complex in [[Talas]]. Official figures give a strength of about 12,000 active personnel and 18,000 organized reservists; independent estimates put the number actually serving somewhat lower.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

The corps was formed in 2007, during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], from territorial-era National Guard units and other forces loyal to [[Erlan Toktarov]]. It is separate from the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]], an ISEZ paramilitary force commanded by Major General [[Ruslan Toktarov]], and from the [[El-Choro Militias]] of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), which answer to the clan councils and the [[Iradi Freedom Society]]. It trains with the United States forces that remain at [[Talas Air Base]] and five other installations. Its main tasks are holding the ISEZ side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], guarding energy and industrial sites, and disaster relief.

## Soviet and post-Soviet origins
In the Soviet period the territory of the Iradi SSR lay within the [[wp:Turkestan Military District]]. Its main ground formation was the 17th Motor Rifle Division, based at Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]), and the airfield west of Talas hosted interceptor squadrons from 1952.<sup>[3]</sup> When the [[Communist Party of Irad]] declared the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] (SRI) on 9 October 1991, the division and the republican [[wp:OMON]] detachments passed to the SRI government of [[Vasily Chernov]]. Their officer corps, like the SRI leadership as a whole, was largely ethnic Russian.

During the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]] and the [[First Iradi Civil War]] that followed, the Provisional Government in Talas relied on student militias, defecting police and mounted clan irregulars rather than a regular army. SRI forces surrendered on 18 August 1992 after [[Operation Starlight]], and US forces disarmed and disbanded them. Their heavy equipment, including [[wp:T-72]] tanks and [[wp:BMP-2]] infantry fighting vehicles, was put into depots near Nurzhan under US supervision.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Territorial period (1992–2006)
Under the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]], the defense of the territory was a responsibility of the United States. As in other US territories, the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad|Territorial Legislature]] created a local force under the Governor's command, the Irad National Guard, which was organized in 1994 with army and air components and trained to US standards. By 2005 it numbered about 6,500, most of them part-time. Its tasks were disaster relief, guarding infrastructure and supporting US forces at Talas Air Base, which became a staging area for [[wp:Operation Enduring Freedom]] under the [[2001 Basing Rights Agreement]]. Internal security and border control were the job of the Republican Gendarmerie, set up in 1993 to replace the Soviet internal troops.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Formation during the Second Civil War (2006–2007)
The US withdrawal from the treaty on 3 December 2006 ended the Guard's federal status. The [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] (DRI), proclaimed on 9 December, renamed it the Defense Force of the DRI, but the force split along political lines in the crisis that followed. When Toktarov seized control of the DPI and proclaimed the ISEZ from Nurzhan on 25 February 2007, the Nurzhan garrison and most Guard units in the Chu lowlands went over to him. Units in Talas stayed loyal to the DRI cabinet of [[Bakyt Orozbekov]], and some rural personnel joined the [[Popular Front of Irad]].<sup>[5]</sup>

After the Popular Front stormed Talas on 4 June 2007 and dissolved the DRI, DPI forces, with backing from Western companies and the United States, took control of Talas and the other cities over the summer as the Front withdrew to the countryside. An emergency decree of the ISEZ administration in July 2007 merged the pro-DPI Guard units, former DRI units that had surrendered, and recalled reservists into the State Defense Corps. The [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]], signed in September, fixed the corps's front at the Qara-Chik line.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Since 2007
Between 2008 and 2011 the ISEZ returned about forty T-72s and ninety BMP-2s from the Nurzhan depots to service, refitting them with new radios and fire-control equipment.<sup>[2]</sup> Conscription was introduced in 2008. Merging the corps and the El-Choro into a single force was one of the issues left unresolved when the [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit|2011 reunification talks]] collapsed.<sup>[6]</sup>

The corps was put on alert during the [[The 2021 Regional Security Alert|2021 Regional Security Alert]], when it reinforced the mountain passes on the Kazakh, Uzbek and Kyrgyz borders after the [[wp:Taliban]] returned to power in [[wp:Afghanistan]]. It was not deployed against the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]], which were policed by the Gendarmerie and the municipal police. Governor Toktarov has not appeared in public since July 2024, an absence the DPI attributes to an extended health retreat. The General Staff has since pledged loyalty to "the lawful administration" and kept out of the public rivalry between Ruslan Toktarov and his brother [[Alikhan Toktarov]] (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]).<sup>[7]</sup>

## Command and organization
Under the 2007 emergency decree, the Governor is commander-in-chief. The Ministry of Defense of the ISEZ is responsible for the budget, procurement and conscription, and the Chief of the General Staff, appointed by the Governor, commands the forces. The ISEZ Security Council coordinates the corps with the Gendarmerie and the intelligence services; according to DPI statements, its meetings have been chaired since 2024 by Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]].<sup>[7]</sup>

The corps is organized as follows (strengths are 2023 estimates):<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

- Ground Forces (about 9,500):
  - 1st Mechanized Infantry Brigade, outside Talas, covering the Talas valley and the western Qara-Chik sector;
  - 2nd Motor Rifle Brigade, in Nurzhan, covering the Chu lowlands, the [[NurGaz]] oilfields and refinery, the [[Northern Export Feeder]] pipeline and the rail links to [[wp:Kazakhstan]];
  - Lower Naryn Mountain Rifle Battalion, at [[Tash-Kömür]], guarding the Toktogul complex, the downstream stations of the Naryn cascade and the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]] corridor;
  - Sary-Bulak Mountain Rifle Battalion, covering the industrial corridor south of Talas, including the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] and the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]];
  - an artillery regiment, an engineer battalion, a signals battalion, a reconnaissance battalion and a logistics brigade.
- Air Wing (about 700), on the northern ramp of Talas Air Base, operating helicopters and light transport aircraft.
- Territorial Defense: five reserve battalions, one for each ISEZ district as they stood in 2008 (Talas, [[Kara-Buura]], Chu, [[Sary-Bulak]] and Lower Naryn; the Lower Naryn battalion also covers Toktogul District), whose reservists are called up for annual training.

## Other armed forces in Irad
The Republican Gendarmerie (about 4,000) is not part of the corps. It reports to the Ministry of Internal Security and has been commanded since 2012 by Ruslan Toktarov, who also directs the Special Protective Services. It mans the checkpoints at the Qara-Chik line's crossing points, nine in all, and the four internal control posts inside the ISEZ, protects senior officials and the [[Boz-Korgon]] compound, and guards the perimeter of Talas Air Base. The emergency decree allows the Gendarmerie to be placed under the operational control of the General Staff in wartime, but this has never been done.<sup>[4]</sup>

The El-Choro Militias, about 15,000 part-time mounted irregulars, are the armed force of the ATR. They are raised by the 24 clans and coordinated by [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]]. The ISEZ government regards them as an illegal armed formation, but the corps and the militias observe non-aggression arrangements supervised by the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI).<sup>[8]</sup>

## Personnel
The DPI government gives a strength of about 12,000 active personnel and 18,000 organized reservists. In 2023 the *Central Asian Geopolitical Review* estimated that between 10,500 and 11,000 were actually serving, citing understrength conscript companies.<sup>[2]</sup> About 40 percent of the active force are conscripts. Women serve as volunteers, mainly in signals, medical and logistics posts, and made up about 9 percent of personnel in 2022.<sup>[1]</sup>

Since 2008, men aged 18 to 27 who live in the ISEZ have been liable for 12 months of service. Students may defer, clergy and seminarians of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] and other registered religions are exempt, and conscientious objectors may do 18 months of civilian service instead. Men may also buy their way out of service by paying a fee into a defense fund. Residents of the ATR are not called up. Conscripts train at the Ak-Tash Training Center in the western [[Talas Alatau]] foothills, and units rotate through a winter mountain-warfare course in Sary-Bulak District.<sup>[1]</sup>

Most officers are trained at the Military Faculty of [[Talas State University]], and technical officers at the [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]]. Older officers are largely Russian-speaking, while those trained since 1992 work mainly in English and Iradi. According to a 2020 study at Talas State University, Kyrgyz, [[wp:Uzbeks]] and Muslims generally are underrepresented in the officer corps.<sup>[9]</sup>

## Equipment
The corps combines Soviet-era heavy weapons with US-origin light equipment from the territorial period. Independent estimates of its inventory in 2023 include:<sup>[2]</sup>

- about 40 T-72 main battle tanks, some held in reserve, and about 90 BMP-2 infantry fighting vehicles, refurbished from former SRI stocks;
- about 60 BTR-70 and [[wp:BTR-80]] armored personnel carriers, and [[wp:MT-LB]] tracked carriers;
- some 200 [[wp:Humvee|HMMWV]] light vehicles, with US-pattern radios, night-vision equipment and body armor, mostly inherited from the National Guard;
- 24 D-30 122-mm howitzers, 12 [[wp:BM-21 Grad|BM-21]] multiple rocket launchers and 120-mm mortars;
- [[wp:ZU-23-2]] anti-aircraft guns and [[wp:9K38 Igla|Igla]] man-portable surface-to-air missiles;
- about 14 Mi-8 and Mi-17 transport helicopters, 6 [[wp:Mil Mi-24|Mi-24]] attack helicopters (fewer than half reported airworthy), 4 [[wp:Bell UH-1 Iroquois|UH-1H]] helicopters and 2 [[wp:Antonov An-26|An-26]] transport aircraft.

The corps has no combat jets and relies on the US presence at Talas Air Base for air defense beyond short range. Its small arms are mainly [[wp:AK-74]] rifles, with M4 carbines in some former Guard units. Uniform cloth and winter clothing are supplied by [[Zhetysu Industrial Textiles]]. The official defense budget for 2023 was about $260 million, about 1.4 percent of the ISEZ's nominal GDP; analysts note that spending on the Gendarmerie and some base-related security costs are budgeted separately.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Doctrine and deployment
The ISEZ Military Doctrine of 2009 defines the corps's tasks as defending the ISEZ against external attack, holding the ceasefire line, protecting "strategic economic facilities" and supporting the civil authorities in emergencies. In practice it is organized for static defense, with most combat units garrisoning the Qara-Chik sector, the oil and gas installations around Nurzhan, and the roads between districts.<sup>[10]</sup>

Under the [[wp:Bishkek]] ceasefire, tanks and artillery may not be kept in a restricted zone on either side of the Qara-Chik line, and UNMI observers inspect the corps's positions there. Its heavy units are therefore based well back from the line, and its forward posts are held by light infantry.<sup>[8]</sup> The engineer battalion is regularly deployed after mudflows (*sel*), avalanches and spring floods to rebuild bridges and clear roads in the river gorges, and in such emergencies corps units have sometimes worked alongside El-Choro riders.

## Relationship with United States forces
US forces remain at Talas Air Base, the largest US military installation in the region, and at five other sites used for logistics, testing and training. They are there under the 2001 Basing Rights Agreement and interim arrangements concluded with the ISEZ administration from 2007 onward, whose texts have not been published in full.<sup>[11]</sup>

US and ISEZ forces hold an annual joint exercise, *Alatau Shield*, focused on counterinsurgency, border security and disaster response. The United States has not treated the ISEZ as a foreign government since 2006, and Irad remains listed at the UN with the United States as its nominal administering power (see [[Political status of Irad]]). US training and equipment have therefore come mainly through base-related programs rather than standard foreign military assistance.<sup>[11]</sup> Analysts describe the legal basis of the relationship as ambiguous, because it rests on arrangements with an administration that Washington does not formally recognize.<sup>[12]</sup>

The ISEZ government regards the US presence as its main security guarantee, and base contracts are a major source of income. [[Kamran Bekzatov]] and other Russian-oriented figures call for closer ties with [[wp:Moscow]], and the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]] provoked protests across the country, including demonstrations outside Talas Air Base. The ISEZ government said the basing arrangements were unaffected. See also [[Irad–United States relations]].

## Criticism
Rights groups and the *[[Talas Herald]]* have reported hazing of conscripts by longer-serving soldiers (*dedovshchina*) and several non-combat deaths in conscript units. The Ministry of Defense says such cases are investigated and has set up a complaints hotline.<sup>[13]</sup> Critics also argue that the buy-out fee and student deferrals shift the burden of service onto rural and working-class families. Opposition outlets have alleged that conscripts were used as laborers on construction projects, including at Boz-Korgon, which the ministry denies.<sup>[13]</sup>

Analysts note that the Gendarmerie receives newer equipment and better pay than most corps units, and describe it as a counterweight to the regular army under the direct control of the Toktarov family. The government describes the two forces as complementary.<sup>[12]</sup>

### 2.23. United Nations Mission in Irad
*Quality Assessment: Good Article (GA) | Category: Foreign Relations*

{{Infobox organization
| name = United Nations Mission in Irad
| native_name = UNMI
| formation = 2007-10-18
| type = Peacekeeping observer mission (Chapter VI)
| purpose = Monitoring the Qara-Chik ceasefire; Supervising the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]]; Humanitarian coordination and mine action
| hq = Kara-Oi, between [[Talas]] and the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]
| leader_title = Head of mission
| leader_name = Special Representative of the Secretary-General
| parent_organization = [[wp:United Nations Security Council]]
| staff = 210 military observers, 30 police advisers and about 420 civilian staff (2024)
| budget = $57.9 million (2024–25)
}}

The **United Nations Mission in Irad** (**UNMI**) is a United Nations peacekeeping observer mission in Irad. The [[wp:United Nations Security Council|Security Council]] established it by a resolution adopted on 18 October 2007, a month after the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] ended the main fighting of the [[Second Iradi Civil War]]. UNMI monitors the ceasefire along the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], about 1,750 km long, between the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), governed by the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI), and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). It also supervises the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]], the annex to the ceasefire that governs the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]], and coordinates humanitarian aid and mine clearance on both sides of the line. It is an unarmed mission deployed under [[wp:Chapter VI of the United Nations Charter|Chapter VI]] of the [[wp:Charter of the United Nations|UN Charter]].<sup>[1]</sup>

The mission is headquartered at Kara-Oi, between [[Talas]] and the line. In 2024 it had about 210 military observers, 30 police advisers and some 420 civilian staff, most of them recruited locally, and its annual budget was about $58 million. The Security Council renews its mandate each October. Both Iradi administrations accept the mission while criticizing it, and diplomats regard it as one of the reasons the line has stayed largely quiet since 2007.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Background
Irad has been on the UN list of non-self-governing territories since 1992. The United States is still recorded as the administering power, although it ended its administration in December 2006 (see [[Political status of Irad]]). The collapse of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] in 2007, the proclamation of the ISEZ by [[Erlan Toktarov]] on 25 February and the [[Storming of Talas (2007)|storming of Talas]] by the [[Popular Front of Irad]] on 4 June led to fighting that concerned all three neighboring states, [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], each of which claims Irad. The fighting also threatened the operation of the Toktogul dam, on which irrigation in the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] and southern Kazakhstan depends.<sup>[3]</sup>

UN-brokered talks in [[wp:Bishkek]] produced the ceasefire agreement in September 2007. It fixed the Qara-Chik line, provided for a restricted-weapons zone on either side of it, and included the Naryn Protocol as an annex, assigning supervision of the Toktogul release schedule to the United Nations. Both the DPI administration and the leaders of the Popular Front, coordinated by [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], asked for an international monitoring presence, and the Security Council established UNMI on 18 October 2007. The first observers arrived in November 2007, and the mission reached its initial authorized strength in mid-2008.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup> In 2009 the mission brokered the protocol that moved the line around the Toktogul basin and the State Route 1 corridor, transferring the dam to the ISEZ (see [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]).

## Mandate
The founding resolution and later renewals give UNMI the following tasks:<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

- Ceasefire monitoring: to observe the Qara-Chik line and the restricted-weapons zone, which extends 12 km on either side of it and from which tanks, artillery and combat aircraft are excluded, including quarterly inspections of the disused Soviet bomber field at [[Kulan Airfield|Kulan]]; to investigate reported violations; and to chair a Joint Liaison Committee of the two sides.
- Supervision of the Naryn Water and Power Protocol: to supervise the joint technical commission of ISEZ and ATR engineers that sets the Toktogul release schedule, to verify reservoir levels and releases, and to escort engineering crews crossing the line. Observers from Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan attend the commission's meetings.
- Humanitarian coordination: to coordinate UN agencies and non-governmental organizations, negotiate humanitarian access across the line, and support the return of people displaced in 2007.
- Mine action: to coordinate the survey and clearance of mines and unexploded ordnance left from the 1992 and 2007 wars.
- Reporting: to report to the Security Council through the Secretary-General twice a year. A limited human rights reporting function, covering matters connected with the ceasefire, freedom of movement and humanitarian access, was added in 2012.

The Special Representative of the Secretary-General also offers good offices on the status question. UN officials helped draft the [[2008 Unification Referendum Initiative]], which stalled, and supported the [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]], which collapsed when the delegation of the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC) walked out after being offered one-third of the seats in a joint legislature. No direct talks have taken place since.<sup>[5]</sup>

UNMI reports to the Security Council, not to the [[wp:Special Committee on Decolonization|UN Special Committee on Decolonization]] in [[wp:New York City|New York]], although the committee's annual working paper on Irad draws on the mission's public reports.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Organization
UNMI is led by a Special Representative of the Secretary-General, who is head of mission, assisted by a Chief Military Observer of general-officer rank. It has four components: military observers, police advisers, humanitarian and mine action, and mission support.<sup>[2]</sup>

As of 2024 the mission had:<sup>[2]</sup>

- 210 military observers, against an authorized ceiling of 230;
- 30 police advisers, who work with the municipal police in the ISEZ and the clan-appointed constables of the ATR on cross-line crime and missing-persons cases;
- 142 international civilian staff, 261 national staff and 18 [[wp:United Nations Volunteers|UN Volunteers]].

The military observers come from about twenty countries; the largest contributors have included [[wp:Bangladesh]], [[wp:Ghana]], [[wp:Ireland]], [[wp:Mongolia]], [[wp:Nepal]], Sweden and Uruguay. By convention, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan and the United States do not provide observers. The approved budget for July 2024 to June 2025 was $57.9 million, funded through assessed contributions of UN member states.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Headquarters and deployment
The mission headquarters occupies a former Soviet agricultural research station at Kara-Oi, on the ISEZ side between Talas and the line. The site was chosen in 2007 because representatives of both sides could reach it without passing through the other's checkpoints. UNMI also has a liaison office in Talas, a sector headquarters at [[Tash-Kömür]] for the Naryn corridor, and eleven team sites along the line, five of them on the tribal side.<sup>[2]</sup>

Observers patrol by vehicle, on foot and on horseback, and the mission operates two utility helicopters. In the high sections of the [[Talas Alatau]], patrols on [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horses hired from local herders are often the only practical way to reach observation posts in winter.

## Ceasefire monitoring
Observers patrol the line daily, inspect positions in the restricted zone and investigate incidents reported by either side. UNMI recorded 214 ceasefire violations in 2023. Most involved small-arms fire, movement of armed personnel into the restricted zone or unauthorized construction; many other incidents concerned livestock straying across the line and the herders who followed them.<sup>[4]</sup>

The Joint Liaison Committee meets monthly at Kara-Oi. It brings together officers of the ISEZ [[Armed Forces of Irad|State Defense Corps]] and the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] with captains of the [[El-Choro Militias]], and settles most incidents locally. UNMI credits it with preventing several confrontations from escalating, including a standoff over a river crossing near the [[Kenkol Pass]] in 2016.<sup>[4]</sup>

Since 2023 the ISEZ authorities have barred UNMI patrols from a security zone around the [[Boz-Korgon]] compound east of [[Nurzhan]]. The Secretary-General has described this in several reports as a restriction on the mission's freedom of movement. The ISEZ government says the zone is an ordinary industrial and security area unconnected with the ceasefire.<sup>[7]</sup>

## Naryn Protocol supervision
Since the 2009 corridor protocol the whole Toktogul complex has been in the ISEZ, but the tribal delegation keeps an equal place on the joint technical commission and the clans' consent is still needed for each five-year schedule. UNMI chairs the meetings of the commission, checks daily reservoir-level data and escorts the tribal engineers who inspect the dam and the releases. The annex on revenue sharing has never been published, and UNMI does not report on how the revenue is divided.<sup>[8]</sup>

The five-year release schedule was last renewed in 2022 and falls due again in 2027. Uzbek and Kazakh officials have asked who will sign for the ISEZ, since Governor Toktarov has not appeared in public since July 2024; the DPI says Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] signs on his behalf.<sup>[8]</sup>

## Humanitarian coordination and mine action
UNMI chairs a coordination forum of UN agencies, the [[wp:International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement|Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement]] and non-governmental organizations working in Irad. The forum negotiates seasonal corridors for vaccines, fodder and medical supplies to highland settlements in the ATR. Its aid registries are among the sources independent demographers have used to estimate the ATR's population, which they put well above the official figure from the [[2018 Irad census]].<sup>[9]</sup>

The mine action component has surveyed or cleared about 31 km² since 2008, mainly in passes of the Talas Alatau and on the approaches to Talas that were mined in 1992 and 2007. It also runs risk-education classes in schools and herding communities.<sup>[4]</sup>

UNMI publishes quarterly security bulletins in Iradi, Russian and English and produces a weekly radio program carried by local stations. Mission officials say these are meant partly to counter rumors of troop movements, which have spread quickly on social media during political crises.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Casualties
Five UNMI personnel have died in service. Two military observers, from Uruguay and Bangladesh, were killed in March 2009 when their vehicle struck an anti-tank mine near the Kenkol Pass. The other three deaths resulted from a road accident and illness.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Mandate renewals
The Security Council has renewed the mandate every October since 2008, usually for twelve months. Renewal debates have divided repeatedly over whether resolutions should refer to the unification referendum, the political status of the territory and the foreign military presence at [[Talas Air Base]]. Most renewals have been adopted unanimously, with occasional abstentions.<sup>[10]</sup>

## Criticism
DPI officials have accused the mission of treating the IAC as an equal party and so lending legitimacy to the ATR's clan councils. ISEZ media, including [[IradOne]], have accused observers of bias after UNMI reports criticized Gendarmerie conduct at checkpoints.<sup>[7]</sup> Tribal leaders, for their part, say UNMI has done too little about restrictions on herders crossing the line and about detentions by the Gendarmerie. They also object that the mission's headquarters and most of its local spending are on the ISEZ side.<sup>[5]</sup>

[[wp:Human Rights Watch]] and other organizations argue that the mission's reporting function is too narrow, and have called for a full human rights monitoring component covering both administrations. The ISEZ government opposes this, and the Security Council has not adopted it (see [[Human rights in Irad]]).<sup>[11]</sup>

Some analysts argue that UNMI has helped freeze the conflict rather than resolve it: since the mission arrived there has been no settlement of Irad's status, and both administrations have come to depend on the ceasefire and on the Naryn revenue. Supporters reply that the line has seen no large-scale fighting since 2007 and that the Toktogul arrangement, which depends on UN supervision, has continued through every political crisis.<sup>[12]</sup>
