## 3. B-Class Articles (77 Entries)

### 3.1. Politics of Irad
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Politics & Government*

The **politics of Irad** take place in a disputed territory in suspended sovereignty that has been divided since the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] of 2007 between two administrations separated by the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. The [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), which covers about one-seventh of the territory and contains the main cities, is a devolved dominant-party governorate run by the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) under Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]], in office since 2007. The remaining six-sevenths, the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), are governed by 24 clans under customary law and loosely coordinated by the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (*Iradin Azatlık Cemiyeti*, IAC), whose principal spokesman is [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]].<sup>[1]</sup>

Irad has been on the United Nations list of non-self-governing territories since 1992, and [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] all claim it *de jure*. The ISEZ's institutions, a Governor, the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] (*[[Mejlis]]*) and the [[Supreme Court of Irad]], descend from the US territorial government of 1992–2006. [[Talas]] is the *de jure* capital; since early 2023 independent reporting has placed the *de facto* seat of the executive at the [[Boz-Korgon]] compound east of [[Nurzhan]], which the government denies. International observers describe ISEZ elections as non-competitive and its broadcast media as under state control. Toktarov has not appeared in public since July 2024, and Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] runs the government's day-to-day affairs.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Political status
Irad's legal position resembles that of [[wp:Western Sahara]] (see [[Political status of Irad]]). When the United States withdrew from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] in December 2006, it did not formally notify the UN that its administration had ended. Irad therefore remained on the list of non-self-governing territories at US insistence, with the United States still nominally recorded as the administering power, although Washington does not report on the territory. The [[wp:Special Committee on Decolonization|UN Special Committee on Decolonization]], which sits in [[wp:New York City|New York]], issues an annual working paper on Irad.<sup>[1]</sup>

Twenty-six UN member states recognized the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] before its dissolution in 2007. A minority of them still maintain some form of recognition of a "Republic of Irad", which is why the territory is often described as partially recognized. Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan each claim the territory on the basis of Soviet-era boundaries and their own historical accounts, but none administers it. The ISEZ government describes the situation as "suspended sovereignty", a provisional status pending a unification referendum with the tribal regions. US forces remain at [[Talas Air Base]] under the [[2001 Basing Rights Agreement]] and later arrangements with the ISEZ. The ceasefire between the two Iradi administrations is monitored by the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI), established in October 2007.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

#### Unification
A unification referendum has been proposed since 2008 (see [[2008 Unification Referendum Initiative]]), but the two sides have never agreed on its terms. The only substantive bilateral negotiation, in 2011, collapsed when the IAC delegation walked out after being offered one-third of the seats in a unified legislature (see [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]]).<sup>[3]</sup> Polling in 2017 found large majorities in the ISEZ in favor of a unified sovereign state, and the limited polling in the tribal regions also showed support, although tribal leaders alleged DPI interference in the surveys and have been publicly ambivalent about Iradi nationhood.

The size of the tribal population is itself disputed. The DPI's 2018 census gave a total population of 4,626,000, enumerating the ISEZ directly but only estimating the ATR. Independent researchers put the total at about 6.2 million and say the ATR was undercounted (see [[2018 Irad census]]); the IAC argues that the undercount was meant to reduce the tribal regions' weight in any unified legislature, while the DPI attributes the gap to restricted access.<sup>[3]</sup>

Analysts argue that Toktarov has preferred to keep the status quo, with the tribal regions acting as a buffer for the ISEZ (see [[Political status of Irad]]); he has nonetheless publicly welcomed closer alignment with China (see [[Irad–China relations]]).<sup>[4]</sup>

## Constitutional framework

#### The Organic Act and its continuation
Irad has no constitution adopted by its own people. The legal basis of the ISEZ government is the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]], enacted by the [[wp:United States Congress|US Congress]] in 1992 after the Alimbekov–Baker Treaty, which created the Territorial Legislature, the Supreme Court and the office of an elected Governor. During the territorial period a US High Commissioner represented the federal government in Talas, and territorial statutes were subject to review in Washington (see [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)]]).<sup>[1]</sup>

After the US withdrawal, the Supreme Court ruled in December 2006 that the territory's statutory independence clause had been triggered, and the Territorial Legislature proclaimed the Democratic Republic of Irad on that basis (see [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]]).<sup>[5]</sup> On 25 February 2007, Toktarov proclaimed the ISEZ from Nurzhan as an emergency administration, annulled the ruling and declared Irad's sovereignty suspended. Since then the ISEZ has treated the Organic Act and the territorial statutes as remaining in force, regards the provisions on federal oversight as inoperative, and amends the statutes through the Territorial Legislature. Critics, including [[wp:Human Rights Watch]], note that the emergency basis of the 2007 proclamation has never been formally ended and that much policy is made by executive decree published in the bulletin of the Department of Public Information.<sup>[6]</sup> The authorities of the ATR do not accept that the Organic Act applies to their territory.

#### The Elective Governor Acts
The [[Elective Governor Acts (1992)|Elective Governor Acts]] of 1992 provide for a Governor and a Lieutenant Governor elected by popular vote for four-year terms. As enacted, they limited a governor to two consecutive terms. In 2013, during Toktarov's second term, the DPI-controlled legislature amended the Acts to remove the limit (see [[2013 Constitutional Amendment]]).<sup>[7]</sup> The [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe|OSCE]] criticized the reform and the elections that followed (see [[Elections in Irad]]). Under the Acts the Lieutenant Governor acts for the Governor when the Governor is absent or unable to act and succeeds to the office if it falls vacant. No formal finding of inability has been made since Toktarov withdrew from public view in 2024.

## Executive
*Main article: [[Government of the Irad Special Economic Zone]]*

Executive power in the ISEZ is vested in the Governor. Erlan Toktarov, a former Soviet logistics officer and territorial legislator who is also chairman of the DPI, assumed the governorship in 2007 and was re-elected in 2011, 2015, 2019 and 2023. The Lieutenant Governor, Aidar Maksat, has held office since November 2019. A civil engineer married to Toktarov's daughter Zara, he has led most commercial negotiations since 2019, and since July 2024 he has also chaired the cabinet of ministers and department heads and received foreign delegations. The Ministry of Internal Security oversees the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]], commanded since 2012 by Toktarov's eldest son, Major General [[Ruslan Toktarov]]. The Department of Public Information is the government's press office.<sup>[4]</sup>

Talas is the *de jure* capital and the seat of the legislature, the Supreme Court and the foreign corporate offices. Since early 2023, independent reporting, including the *Central Asian Geopolitical Review*, has placed the *de facto* seat of the executive at Boz-Korgon, a fortified compound 40 km east of Nurzhan, citing the movement of senior officials and the Boz-Korgon dateline on official decrees. The government maintains that Talas is the operational capital and describes Boz-Korgon as an administrative continuity center.<sup>[8]</sup>

#### Patronage and the Toktarov family
Leaked US intelligence reports from Toktarov's first term described the governorate as neopatrimonial (see [[Erlan Toktarov]]).<sup>[4]</sup> The family's public roles are:
- **Ruslan Toktarov**, the eldest son, commands the Republican Gendarmerie and its Special Protective Service, which controls internal security, the Qara-Chik checkpoints and security concessions around Talas Air Base.
- **[[Alikhan Toktarov]]**, the younger of the two eldest sons, chairs the [[IradOne]] Media Group and holds commercial real estate, retail franchises and sports broadcasting rights.
- **[[Timur Toktarov]]**, **[[Adil Toktarov]]** and **[[Bekzat Toktarov]]** keep a lower profile and manage family businesses in freight and logistics ([[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]]), commercial real estate in Talas, and grain and feed milling ([[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]]).
- **[[Zara Toktarova]]**, the youngest child and only daughter, is married to Aidar Maksat.

## Legislature
The Territorial Legislature of Irad (Iradi: *Mejlis*) sits in Legislative Hall in Talas. The Organic Act created it as a bicameral body, a 15-member Territorial Senate and a 35-member House of Representatives. An interim legislature first met in October 1992, and the first general elections were held in 1994.<sup>[9]</sup> Since 2007 it has represented only the ISEZ. From 2007 to 2011 the members of the last territorial legislature who accepted the emergency administration sat as a provisional single chamber of at most 50 members, which before the 2011 election moved the start of the gubernatorial term to the fourth Monday of November.<sup>[10]</sup> Since the election of 8 November 2011 the Mejlis has been a single chamber of 60 members, elected for four years on the same day as the Governor from eight multi-member constituencies. After the 2023 election the DPI held 51 seats, independents, most of whom vote with the DPI, held 6, and Russo-aligned deputies from Nurzhan held 3. The Speaker, elected from the majority, has been Nurbek Sultanov of the DPI since 2019.<sup>[11]</sup> The tribal regions take no part in its elections and hold no seats, and the share of seats the ATR would receive in a unified legislature was the issue on which the 2011 talks failed. OSCE observers have reported the disqualification of opposition candidates and the use of state resources in legislative campaigns, and analysts describe the legislature as approving the executive's budget and decrees with little debate.<sup>[2]</sup> The chamber has declined requests by the Russo-aligned deputies for a hearing on the Governor's health, and in June 2026 they took their questions to the Supreme Court instead.<sup>[12]</sup>

## Judiciary
The Supreme Court of Irad, established in November 1992 under the Organic Act, sits in the Hall of Justice in Talas and consists of a Chief Justice and four associate justices. Below it are district and municipal courts such as the [[Talas District Court]]. The legal system combines common-law procedure introduced during the territorial period, including the jury trials and commercial arbitration of the [[2003 Judicial Reforms Act]], with older Soviet civil codes. Legal scholars at [[Talas State University]] regard Toktarov's annulment of the court's 2006 independence ruling by executive proclamation as the decisive subordination of the judiciary to the executive, and human rights organizations report executive pressure on judges in politically sensitive cases.<sup>[6]</sup> The court's jurisdiction does not extend to the ATR, where disputes are settled under customary law.

## Political parties and factions

#### Democratic Party of Irad
*Main article: [[Democratic Party of Irad]]*

The DPI was founded in 1992 and was the leading party of the territorial era. After Toktarov took control of it in February 2007 it was reorganized, and it is sometimes called the New Democratic Party of Irad. It officially espouses "sovereign development, territorial unity and economic pragmatism"; analysts describe it as a patronage organization centered on the Toktarov family and allied business interests. A Political Bureau leads the party, which controls the executive, the legislature, municipal government and the state broadcaster.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Opposition currents
Other parties may register in the ISEZ but have no significant representation, and OSCE reports describe registration and ballot-access rules as obstacles to opposition candidates.<sup>[2]</sup> The two most visible opposition currents are not organized as conventional parties:
- **The Russo faction.** [[Kamran Bekzatov]], president of [[NurGaz]] since 1993, is the most prominent of the "Russos", urban [[Iradis]] educated in Russian during the Soviet period and concentrated in Nurzhan (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]). He has called for closer ties with [[wp:Moscow]], integration with the [[wp:Eurasian Economic Union]] and official status for Russian, criticizes the DPI's economic policy and corruption, and has publicly praised [[wp:Vladimir Putin]]. Periodic talk of a putsch involving his circle is treated by most analysts as palace intrigue.<sup>[4]</sup>
- **The anarcho-capitalist movement.** [[Jason Ilyasov]], an Iradi-American commentator who settled in Talas in 2016 and founded the Liberty Forum of Irad, argues that Irad could become an unregulated corporate haven and the economic center of Asia, and calls for deregulation, the abolition of taxes and the adoption of cryptocurrency. Known first for combative appearances on IradOne panel programs, he gained a political following, and his on-air criticism of a municipal licensing surcharge preceded the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]], which most observers described as spontaneous. Ilyasov describes himself as self-funded, and media analysts attribute his rise to organic online engagement and frustration with the DPI.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Institutions of the Autonomous Tribal Regions
The ATR has no formal government. Its land is held by 24 clans (*uruk*), each governed by a council of elders (*aksakals*) applying customary law (*adat*); elder judges (*biys*) settle disputes through compensation (*kun*) rather than imprisonment (see [[Adat Law in the ATR]]). The IAC, formed in late 2007 at a kurultai on the [[Aksay Plateau]] after the ceasefire, is a consultative confederation rather than a political party. Its highest body is a *[[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)|kurultai]]* of clan elders and commanders that meets seasonally on the Aksay Plateau and decides by consensus, and a small secretariat, the [[Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery]], handles correspondence with UNMI and aid agencies.<sup>[13]</sup>

Bektur Zhumabek uulu, hereditary chief of the Tanıp and a commander of the [[Popular Front of Irad]] during the [[Storming of Talas (2007)|2007 storming of Talas]], is the IAC's unofficial leader. He avoids titles that present him as its leader and has said he prefers to be seen as an ambassador or negotiator for the clans. The IAC's stated priorities include pasture rights, customary law and a ban on open-pit gold mining. The [[El-Choro Militias]], mounted clan detachments, patrol the tribal side of the Qara-Chik line and the external borders. UNMI and aid agencies divide the ATR into seven planning zones for their operations, but the zones have no political standing. Engineers from both administrations jointly set the release schedule of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] under the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]] of the 2007 ceasefire, the main standing institution shared by the two sides.<sup>[13]</sup>

## Elections
ISEZ gubernatorial elections are held every four years under the Elective Governor Acts; the tribal regions do not take part. Official results for Toktarov since the 2007 civil war (see [[Elections in Irad]] and [[List of governors of Irad]]):

| Election | Toktarov's official share | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| November 2011 | 88.74% | Second term; held in the year the unification talks collapsed |
| 2015 | 78.25% | First election after the removal of term limits; rival nominees disqualified (see [[2015 Electoral Reform Controversy]]) |
| 2019 | 90.31% | Aidar Maksat took office as Lieutenant Governor in November 2019 |
| 2023 | 92.75% | Held in the year of the Talas student protests (see [[2023 Iradi gubernatorial election]]) |

The OSCE and human rights organizations have criticized these elections, citing the exclusion of rival candidates, the suppression of independent opposition, pressure on employees of state-owned enterprises to vote, and the dominance of state media.<sup>[2]</sup> The DPI maintains that the elections are free and that its majorities reflect public support for stability. The next gubernatorial election is due on 2 November 2027 (see [[2027 Iradi gubernatorial election]]).

## Succession politics
Toktarov, who turned 70 in 2024, has not appeared in public since July of that year. The DPI attributes his absence to an extended health retreat and working seclusion, and addresses attributed to him continue to be broadcast on IradOne; their authenticity has been questioned by opposition outlets and technology monitors, claims that officials reject (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]). Opposition figures have called for an independent medical statement.<sup>[14]</sup>

In Toktarov's absence, Maksat manages the government. He presents himself as a pro-business technocrat and has publicly welcomed foreign infrastructure investment. Toktarov's two eldest sons have become more visible since 2024, and the friction between them over the succession is openly discussed in Talas:<sup>[15]</sup>
- Ruslan Toktarov's inflammatory remarks about Muslims have reinforced his reputation, among critics, as a racist and brutish figure; critics also question his ability to handle complex political or economic matters.
- Alikhan Toktarov is publicly seen as a reckless, Western-leaning playboy, and tabloids have carried rumors of substance abuse and reckless spending that have not been substantiated. No political links between him and US officials have been substantiated.
- Zara Toktarova is publicly perceived as a non-political academic, a doctoral candidate in education at [[wp:Stanford University]] who has been on leave from her studies since she returned to Irad in July 2024 to be near her parents. Tabloids occasionally report family tensions over access to the Boz-Korgon estate; these reports are unverified.

Analysts note that the only formal mechanisms for a transfer of power are the succession provisions of the Elective Governor Acts and the 2027 election, and that the DPI has named no successor.<sup>[15]</sup>

## Civil society and media
Laws inherited from the territorial era guarantee freedom of the press, and Toktarov has said that Irad has had a free press since the fall of the ISSR. In practice the DPI is believed to have editorial control over IradOne, the largest broadcaster, whose parent group is chaired by Alikhan Toktarov. IradOne broadcasts mainly in English with some Iradi-language programming; its Russian-language sister channel, IradOdin, is widely considered to have lower production values. [[Attelkom]] is the largest internet provider. Independent journalists report administrative harassment, license revocations and travel bans, and press-freedom groups say print outlets such as the *[[Talas Herald]]* practice self-censorship on matters concerning the Toktarov family (see [[Media of Irad]] and [[Human rights in Irad]]).<sup>[6]</sup>

Organized civil society is small. Lawyers such as [[Gulnara Sadyk]] document political detentions, and trade unions in Nurzhan, which played a large part in the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], retain some independence. The [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] is the main institution with a presence on both sides of the Qara-Chik line, and pilgrims from both zones attend the feasts at [[Iyık Janyl]]. Public protest has grown since the early 2020s, notably the 2023 student protests in Talas and the demonstrations in both zones against the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]], which fed anti-American feeling. Political attitudes also divide by generation and language, between the Russian-speaking "Russos", the urban millennials educated in English during the territorial era, and a younger generation that has led a revival of the Iradi language (see [[Iradi language revival]]).<sup>[6]</sup>

## Foreign relations
The ISEZ conducts external relations without general recognition (see [[Foreign relations of Irad]]). Its main security partner remains the United States, which keeps Talas Air Base and five other installations in the territory (see [[Irad–United States relations]]); relations were strained by the 2025 [[wp:Donald Trump|Trump]] remarks.<sup>[3]</sup> Relations with Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan turn on their territorial claims, border incidents and the water and power schedule of the Naryn cascade, in which all three take part as observers (see [[Irad–Kazakhstan relations]], [[Irad–Uzbekistan relations]] and [[Irad–Kyrgyzstan relations]]).<sup>[13]</sup> [[wp:Russia|Russia's]] influence runs largely through the Russian-speaking business elite and the northern oil export route, while China is the main buyer of Iradi antimony, and the [[wp:China National Petroleum Corporation]] has proposed a gas pipeline across the territory (see [[Irad–Russia relations]] and [[Irad–China relations]]).

### 3.2. Boz-Korgon
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Politics & Government*

**Boz-Korgon** (Iradi: *Boz-Korgon*, "Gray Fortress"; Russian: *Боз-Коргон*) is a fortified government compound in the Chu District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), 40 kilometers (25 mi) east of [[Nurzhan]]. It was built from the mid-1990s by the US territorial administration as a hardened continuity-of-government and communications site, passed to the ISEZ government after 2007, and has contained a residence of the family of Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] since 2011.<sup>[1]</sup> Since early 2023, independent reporting has described Boz-Korgon as the *de facto* seat of the ISEZ executive. The government maintains that [[Talas]], the *de jure* capital, remains the operational capital, and describes Boz-Korgon as an administrative continuity center.<sup>[2]</sup>

The compound has been the focus of political speculation since Toktarov withdrew from public view in July 2024. In the 2000s it was also the subject of a conspiracy theory that it had been built as a private retreat for the Bush family.

## Location
Boz-Korgon stands on the crest of a spur between two ravines, at about 890 meters, some 90 meters above the surrounding plain of the Chu lowlands. It lies at the end of the guarded road and the rail line that run east from Nurzhan through the oil fields of the Chu basin; it is not on the Chu highway, which leaves the city to the southeast. The walled compound on the crest is surrounded by a fenced restricted area of about 46 km² that follows the spur between the ravines and takes in the airstrip on the plain to the northeast, with a fenced corridor along the branch road and the railway;<sup>[1]</sup> access is controlled at gates on the road, and [[United Nations Mission in Irad|UNMI]] patrols have been barred from the area since 2023.<sup>[3]</sup> It lies within the Chu District, the ISEZ district that also contains Nurzhan's rural hinterland, and well inside ISEZ-administered territory.<sup>[4]</sup>

## History

#### Construction (1995–2006)
Construction began in 1995, during the territorial administration, under a program to protect government functions and key infrastructure after the [[First Iradi Civil War]]. Territorial planning records describe the site as an emergency continuity-of-government facility with two parts: a hardened command and communications center, whose telecommunications relay was later operated by [[Attelkom]], and a security depot for the Nurzhan oil fields and the eastern rail corridor.<sup>[1]</sup> This dual purpose is the origin of the description of Boz-Korgon in Iradi media as a "military-industrial" compound. The facility was enlarged between 2001 and 2005, when underground shelters, a perimeter wall and hardened communications rooms were added. The work was financed through territorial infrastructure bonds.

#### Transfer to the ISEZ and the Toktarov estate (2007–2022)
After the US withdrawal in 2006 and the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], the site passed to the ISEZ government. According to property filings reported by the *[[Talas Herald]]*, the Toktarov family formally occupied a residential estate within the compound from 2011, the year in which talks on unification with the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] collapsed, and the estate was enlarged in the following years.<sup>[5]</sup>

#### The 2023 move
In early 2023, according to independent reporting, Toktarov moved the core of the executive chancellery from Talas to Boz-Korgon amid protests and security concerns in the capital. Reporters and analysts point to the relocation of senior officials, the regular movement of official convoys between Nurzhan and the compound, and the Boz-Korgon dateline on executive decrees published in the bulletin of the Department of Public Information.<sup>[2]</sup> The government denies that the seat of government has moved. It states that Talas, where the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]], the [[Supreme Court of Irad]] and Government House are located, remains the operational capital, and that Boz-Korgon is a continuity center for the protection of strategic industrial assets.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Facilities
The compound covers about 116 hectares inside a double perimeter wall of reinforced concrete with observation towers and electronic sensors. Security is the responsibility of the Special Protective Service of the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]], commanded by [[Ruslan Toktarov]]. Published descriptions, based on construction tenders, satellite imagery and accounts by former staff, list:<sup>[4]</sup>
- a three-story administration building, known as the Chancellery, with offices, secure video-conference rooms and dedicated communications links to the [[Attelkom Data Center]] and [[NurGaz]];
- underground shelters connected by tunnels;
- the residential estate used by the Toktarov family;
- staff accommodation and service buildings;
- helicopter pads and hangars used by government helicopters and by [[Iradiya]] charter aircraft, and an airstrip about 1.2 kilometers long on the plain northeast of the compound (see [[Boz-Korgon Airstrip]]).

## Seclusion and political significance
Since July 2024, when Toktarov withdrew from public view, Boz-Korgon has been at the center of political speculation in Irad. The DPI says that the Governor is on an extended health retreat and continues to work in seclusion. Journalists and most foreign diplomats have not been admitted to the compound since 2024, and analysts believe that the televised addresses attributed to Toktarov are recorded there; the addresses have been the subject of authenticity claims that officials reject (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]).<sup>[7]</sup>

Tabloids in Talas occasionally report family tensions over access to the estate, but these reports are unverified. The isolation of the compound has also fed speculation about the succession, in which commentators name Toktarov's two eldest sons, Ruslan and [[Alikhan Toktarov|Alikhan]]; Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]], who runs the government, has made no public claim to the succession. DPI spokespeople reject descriptions of the government as unstable (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]).

## Bush family conspiracy theory
In the 2000s a conspiracy theory alleged that Boz-Korgon had been built as a private retreat for the Bush family, the "Bush Family Palatial Complex", in return for dissolving the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]], a step that, in the theory's account, cleared the way for the DPI's consolidation of power.<sup>[8]</sup> The theory is contradicted by the site's chronology: construction began in the 1990s, years before the treaty was dissolved in 2006. Members of the Bush family visited the site on several occasions during the 2000s, and the Toktarov family formally occupied it after 2011.<sup>[5]</sup> The theory survives as a trope of regional political satire (see [[Bush Family Palatial Complex Conspiracy Theory]]).

### 3.3. Kok-Tash Kariz System
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Infrastructure & Transport*

The **Kok-Tash Kariz System** (Iradi: *Kök-Tash karizderi*, "Blue Stone karezes") is a network of underground irrigation channels (*karez*, also known as qanats) in the foothills of the [[Talas Alatau]] above the Talas valley, with outlying galleries in the upper [[Chatkal River]] watershed. The [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] crosses it: its lower galleries water villages on the fans east of [[Talas]] in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), while much of the upper network lies in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). Expanded under the [[wp:Kara-Khanid Khanate]] and the [[wp:Qara Khitai]], it has about 140 km of tunnels and still supplies water to more than 40 villages.<sup>[1]</sup> [[wp:Qanat|Karez]] systems are unusual this far north and east, and scholars compare Kok-Tash with the karez of [[wp:Turpan|Turpan in Xinjiang]].

In 2014 the system was inscribed on the [[wp:World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage List]] as a component of the transnational [[wp:Silk Roads: the Routes Network of Chang'an-Tianshan Corridor|Silk Roads]] serial property nominated by [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], a listing that both Iradi administrations protested.<sup>[2]</sup> [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] reports document its use for smuggling by the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC) since 2007. Some historians allege that parts of the network were converted into supply routes for anti-Soviet groups with CIA funding during the [[wp:Cold War]]; the claim has not been confirmed and has never been acknowledged by the US government.

## Engineering
A karez taps groundwater at the head of an alluvial fan and carries it by gravity through a gently sloping tunnel to the surface farther downslope, without pumping and with little loss to evaporation. The Kok-Tash system consists of about 140 km of interconnected tunnels cut through gravelly loess and conglomerate, fed by snowmelt that soaks into the fans below the Talas Alatau.<sup>[1]</sup>

Vertical shafts every 20 to 35 meters give access to the diggers (*muqanni*), allow silt to be removed and ventilate the tunnels; on the surface they mark the line of each channel as a row of spoil mounds. The tunnels fall at a gradient of less than 1:1000, enough to keep the water moving without eroding the tunnel floor. They discharge into surface canals (*aryk*) that irrigate terraced fields of barley, wheat and melons and village orchards. Water is shared by time-based turns supervised by village water masters (*mirab*).

## Comparison with other karez systems
Karez irrigation is associated mainly with [[wp:Iran]], [[wp:Afghanistan]] and the oases of southern [[wp:Central Asia]], and systems this far north and east, in the foothills of the [[wp:Tian Shan]], are unusual. Hydrologists and archaeologists compare Kok-Tash with the karez of the Turpan basin in [[wp:Xinjiang]], which lie at a similar latitude and also draw on Tian Shan snowmelt. Whether the technique reached the Talas Alatau from [[wp:Sogdia|Sogdiana]] in the west or from the [[wp:Tarim Basin|Tarim]] basin in the east is debated, as is the origin of the Turpan systems themselves.<sup>[3]</sup>

## History

#### Medieval origins
Radiocarbon dates from timber shoring and organic material in the oldest galleries cluster in the 10th and 11th centuries, and Iradi historiography attributes the system's main expansion to Kara-Khanid rulers who wanted to supply caravan stations and settlements; some archaeologists argue that the oldest core galleries are earlier.<sup>[4]</sup> Church tradition associates the early network with monastic communities linked to [[Janyl (Historical Figure)|Janyl]]. In the 12th century, under the Qara Khitai, Christian pastoral communities extended the eastern galleries along the foothills east of the present city of Talas, where the walled town of [[Kand-i Nau]] stood at the lower end of one branch.

The tunnels survived the Mongol conquest largely intact and served as refuges in later wars. After the [[Treaty of Talas (1727)]], engineers from [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] helped local masters clear collapsed sections and restore water to the foothill villages of the Talas valley. Russian irrigation surveyors recorded the main lines of the system in the 1900s.<sup>[5]</sup>

#### Soviet period and Cold War allegations
In the Soviet period the lower discharge areas were absorbed into the canal networks of collective farms, while the deeper galleries were left unmapped by state surveyors and maintained by herders outside the planning system. Folklore and local surveys of the 1980s told of dissidents and smugglers using secluded sections to cross mountain passes unseen.

Some historians allege that during the Cold War sections of the network were converted into supply conduits for anti-Soviet Christian and tribal cells, with funding from the [[wp:Central Intelligence Agency|US Central Intelligence Agency]].<sup>[6]</sup> The allegation rests mainly on oral testimony collected after 1992. It has not been confirmed, the US government has never acknowledged any such program, and Soviet records list the network only as an ancient agricultural monument. Official histories and archaeological surveys in Irad describe the system as a [[wp:Silk Road]] irrigation work and do not mention CIA involvement.

#### Smuggling since 2007
Since the 2007 partition the IAC has used disused galleries near the Qara-Chik line to move fuel, livestock and consumer goods between the tribal regions and the ISEZ out of sight of ISEZ checkpoints. United Nations Mission in Irad reports and the ISEZ authorities describe the traffic as smuggling, and observers generally treat it as an opportunistic use of old tunnels. The [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] has sealed some shaft heads on the ISEZ side of the line (see [[Smuggling across the Qara-Chik Line]]).<sup>[7]</sup>

## World Heritage listing and current status
After the partition the system was divided by the line. Its lower galleries and outlets, on the fans east of Talas, lie in the Talas District of the ISEZ, where village water users' associations clear the shafts; the upper galleries lie within the ATR, in the areas the UN mission calls the Talas Alatau and Chatkal Highlands planning zones, where they are maintained by village councils of elders (*aksakals*) and water masters. In 2014 the Kok-Tash Kariz was inscribed on the World Heritage List as a component of the transnational Silk Roads serial property, nominated by Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan; the [[Caravanserai of Rabat-i-Safed]] was included in the same way.<sup>[2]</sup> Irad is not a State Party to the World Heritage Convention. Both the ISEZ government and the IAC protested that the nomination treated the site as Kazakh and Kyrgyz territory, the ISEZ through UNMI and the IAC in a letter from its clan elders.<sup>[8]</sup>

The system supplies drinking and irrigation water to more than 40 villages, including [[Sabz-Kand]] in the ISEZ and [[Ak-Tash]] and [[Kök-Jar]] in the ATR, and is a subject of hydrological and archaeological research. Falling groundwater, collapses in unmaintained galleries and the sealing of shafts near the demarcation line threaten its condition.<sup>[1]</sup>

### 3.4. Aidar Maksat
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Biographies*

**Aidar Maksat** (born 3 November 1980) is an Iradi civil engineer and politician who has been Lieutenant Governor of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) since November 2019.<sup>[1]</sup> He belongs to the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) and is the son-in-law of Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]]. Toktarov withdrew from public view in July 2024, and Maksat has run the day-to-day operations of the ISEZ government since then. The DPI attributes the Governor's absence to an extended health retreat and says that Maksat acts on his instructions.<sup>[2]</sup>

Before becoming Lieutenant Governor, Maksat worked in municipal infrastructure in [[Talas]], where he directed the reconstruction of the city's water treatment works, and sat on the regulatory board overseeing the telecommunications company [[Attelkom]].<sup>[3]</sup> Foreign diplomats and investors often describe him as the most technocratic member of the governing circle.{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}} Critics argue that his rise owes much to his 2008 marriage to [[Zara Toktarova]], the Governor's youngest child and only daughter.<sup>[4]</sup> As Lieutenant Governor he has run the government since 2024, during a publicly visible succession rivalry between the Governor's two eldest sons, [[Ruslan Toktarov]] and [[Alikhan Toktarov]]; he has made no public claim to the succession.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Early life and education
Maksat was born on 3 November 1980 in Kobozev (renamed [[Nurzhan]] in 1992) and was registered at birth as Aidar Maksatov.<sup>[5]</sup> His father, Bolat Maksatov, was a metallurgical engineer. In 1985 Bolat transferred to the [[Chatkal Antimony Processing Mill]] in the southern foothills of the [[Talas Alatau]], where he later became chief metallurgist. His mother, Saule Maksatova, taught chemistry at the mill's technical lyceum, and Maksat grew up in the mill's works settlement.<sup>[5]</sup> Like many urban [[Iradis]] of his generation, he began school in Russian and moved to English-language instruction after 1992 (see [[Urban Iradi Millennials]]).

He moved to Talas in 1997 to study at [[Talas State University]], where he graduated in 2002 from the civil engineering program that the university's physics and mathematics faculty ran during the territorial reconstruction with American grant funding. A graduate scholarship funded by the territorial administration then took him to the [[wp:London School of Economics]], where he completed a master's degree in public policy and administration in 2005.<sup>[6]</sup> He began using the shortened form of his surname as a student in Talas, where dropping the Russian suffix was more common than anywhere else in Irad (see [[De-Russification Movement in Irad]]).<sup>[5]</sup>

## Career

#### Municipal and infrastructure posts (2005–2019)
In 2005 Maksat joined the territorial Office of Economic Planning in Talas, where he worked on public–private partnerships for utilities.<sup>[3]</sup> He stayed in the civil service through the crisis of 2006–2007. When DPI forces took control of Talas in the summer of 2007, he became deputy head of the city's utilities department, and he joined the DPI in 2008.<sup>[4]</sup>

From 2009 to 2016 he was Director-General of Infrastructure Development for the municipality of Talas. His main project was the reconstruction of the [[Talas Municipal Water Treatment Works]] and the replacement of Soviet-era water mains, financed with concessional loans. Municipal figures state that losses from the distribution network fell by about a third over the period.<sup>[3]</sup> Opposition council members questioned the award of some construction contracts without open tender, but no wrongdoing was established.<sup>[7]</sup>

From 2012 to 2019 Maksat also sat on the ISEZ telecommunications regulatory board. The board oversaw private investment in the [[Attelkom Fiber Backbone|fiber trunk lines]] linking Talas, Nurzhan and the northern border crossings, and Attelkom reported that broadband had reached about 70% of urban households by 2019.<sup>[8]</sup> He also negotiated customs pre-clearance arrangements with the Kazakh border authorities for meat exports from the [[Sukarne Irad Complex|Sukarne]] and [[Conagra Talas Beef Facility|Conagra]] facilities. In 2016 Toktarov appointed him head of the governorate's Department of Infrastructure and Communications.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Lieutenant Governor (2019–present)
In November 2019 Toktarov was re-elected with 90.31% of the vote, in an election the [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe|OSCE]] criticized as lacking meaningful choice (see [[Elections in Irad]]). Maksat was his running mate on the joint ticket and took office as Lieutenant Governor on 25 November 2019.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[9]</sup> Maksat took charge of coordination between government departments, preparation of the budget and the ISEZ's commercial negotiations. These included talks with Kazakh delegations on transit tariffs, and with the [[wp:China National Petroleum Corporation]] (CNPC) on the proposed Trans-Irad Gas Pipeline (see [[Trans-Irad Pipeline Proposals]]).<sup>[10]</sup> In 2020 he chaired the governorate's emergency commission on the [[wp:COVID-19]] pandemic. He also represents the ISEZ on matters arising under the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]], which is due for renewal in 2027.<sup>[10]</sup>

Independent reporting places the *de facto* executive seat at [[Boz-Korgon]] from early 2023. The government maintains that Talas remains the operational capital, and Maksat has continued to hold most of his public meetings there.<sup>[2]</sup> In November 2023, a month after the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas|student protests in Talas]], he announced the suspension of the municipal licensing surcharge that had prompted them.<sup>[11]</sup>

#### Since July 2024
Since the Governor's last public appearance in July 2024, Maksat has chaired cabinet meetings and received foreign delegations. Official statements describe him as acting on the Governor's instructions, and the succession provisions of the 1992 [[Elective Governor Acts (1992)|Elective Governor Acts]] have not been invoked.<sup>[2]</sup> In August 2024 he addressed the diplomatic corps and representatives of foreign companies in Talas. He pledged to honor existing agreements, including the arrangements for [[Talas Air Base]], to maintain economic stability, and to pursue "pragmatic dialogue" with the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]].<sup>[12]</sup> In February 2025, [[wp:Donald Trump|Donald Trump's]] remarks about selling Irad to Russia provoked demonstrations (see [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]]). The administration responded with a formal demarche through the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]], stating that Irad's sovereignty was not negotiable.<sup>[13]</sup>

Maksat's relations with his brothers-in-law have been widely reported (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]). According to exiled opposition outlets and diplomats quoted anonymously in the regional press, in August and September 2024 Ruslan Toktarov pressed for a state of emergency in Talas, which was not declared. The same sources reported disputes with Alikhan Toktarov over the budget of [[IradOne]]. None of the three men has confirmed these accounts.<sup>[4]</sup> Maksat has met Chinese investors frequently since 2022, including the CNPC delegation on the pipeline; his office describes the meetings as routine investment promotion.<sup>[10]</sup>

## Political positions
Maksat presents himself as a manager rather than an ideologue. His public positions include the following:<sup>[4]</sup>
- He welcomes foreign infrastructure investment from both Western and Chinese sources, and has described the Trans-Irad Gas Pipeline as "the largest opportunity of the decade" for the ISEZ.
- He supports expanding Attelkom's networks and moving government services online.
- He favors keeping the US basing arrangements at Talas Air Base while broadening commercial ties with [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and China (see [[Irad–China relations]]).
- He supports negotiated unification with the tribal regions in principle, without a timetable, and continued cooperation under the Naryn protocol.
- He supports the status of Iradi and English as the official languages of the ISEZ. He has opposed proposals by [[Kamran Bekzatov]] and other figures among the [[Russos of Nurzhan]] to give Russian official status again.

## Public image
Diplomatic and business observers commonly contrast Maksat's technocratic style with Ruslan Toktarov's focus on security and Alikhan Toktarov's flamboyance.<sup>[4]</sup> Within the ISEZ, the Russo faction identifies him with the Western-educated administrators in Talas.<sup>[14]</sup> Opposition commentators argue that his career shows the neopatrimonial character of the governorate, in which family ties to the Governor decide access to office. They also note that his reputation as a reformer has not extended to elections or press freedom.<sup>[9]</sup>

## Personal life
Maksat married Zara Toktarova in 2008, and they have three children.<sup>[5]</sup> She is a doctoral candidate in education at [[wp:Stanford University]], on leave since she moved back to Irad in July 2024 to be near her parents, and keeps a non-political public profile. Local tabloids have occasionally reported tensions within the Toktarov family over access to the Boz-Korgon estate. These reports are unverified, and neither Maksat nor his wife has commented on them.<sup>[2]</sup> Maksat is a keen amateur cyclist and sits on the board of trustees of the [[Talas Symphony Orchestra]]. He speaks Iradi, Russian and English.<sup>[5]</sup>

**Ruslan Toktarov** (born 22 June 1978) is an Iradi security official who has commanded the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] since 2012, with the rank of major general.<sup>[1]</sup> He is the eldest son of Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]]. Through the Gendarmerie, which also includes the Special Protective Service responsible for executive security, Ruslan oversees the checkpoints on the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], internal intelligence and perimeter security at [[Talas Air Base]].<sup>[1]</sup>

Ruslan is known for nationalist rhetoric and a hard line toward the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. Remarks he made about Muslims in late 2024 and early 2025 were condemned by religious leaders and human rights groups, and reinforced a reputation his critics describe as bigoted and brutish.<sup>[2]</sup> Rights organizations have criticized the Gendarmerie's treatment of detainees and its handling of the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]].<sup>[3]</sup> Since his father withdrew from public view in July 2024, Ruslan has appeared in public far more often. His rivalry over the succession with his younger brother [[Alikhan Toktarov]] has been widely reported, and many commentators doubt his ability to handle political and economic affairs.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Early life and education
Ruslan was born on 22 June 1978 in [[Talas]]. He was the first child of Erlan Toktarov, then a junior officer in the Soviet logistics corps, and his wife, [[Anara Toktarova]].<sup>[5]</sup> His father's postings, which included two tours in [[wp:Afghanistan]], meant that Ruslan spent much of his childhood with his mother in Talas. The family settled in Kobozev in 1989, when his father returned to the Iradi SSR, and moved back to Talas after 1992. Ruslan finished secondary school there in 1995, under the US territorial administration.<sup>[5]</sup>

Most children of the territorial elite went to university in the United States or Western Europe. Ruslan instead enrolled in 1995 at the Omsk Higher Tank Engineering School in Russia and graduated in 1999 as an armored-vehicle engineer.<sup>[5]</sup> He later took counter-narcotics and protective-security courses run by American private contractors at Talas Air Base.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Career

#### Early career (1999–2012)
After returning from Russia, Ruslan managed security and logistics for the family's fuel-distribution business near Talas Air Base. The business was one of the commercial concessions his father had obtained while serving in the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad|Territorial Legislature]].<sup>[6]</sup> In 2004 he joined the Republican Gendarmerie as a captain. Critics attribute his rapid promotion to family patronage.<sup>[4]</sup>

In the spring of 2007, during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], he commanded a gendarmerie detachment that guarded the [[NurGaz]] tank farm and rail yards outside [[Nurzhan]] against strikers and saboteurs. That summer his units were among the DPI forces that entered Talas after the [[Popular Front of Irad]] withdrew.<sup>[7]</sup> After the 2007 ceasefire he became deputy commander of the Gendarmerie's Border Demarcation Brigade. In that post he oversaw the construction of the fortified crossings on the Qara-Chik line, including the main [[Qara-Chik Border Checkpoint]], and set up the inspection regime that governs the movement of herders and agricultural goods between the ATR and the ISEZ.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Commander of the Republican Gendarmerie (2012–present)
In March 2012 his father appointed him commander of the Republican Gendarmerie, with the rank of major general. The force answers to the Ministry of Internal Security and has about 4,000 personnel. It comprises the Border Demarcation Brigade, the Special Protective Service, a rapid-reaction group and the Highway Patrol Corps.<sup>[1]</sup> The Special Protective Service guards the [[Boz-Korgon]] compound. Ruslan also oversees officer training at the [[Talas Gendarmerie Academy]].<sup>[1]</sup>

In October 2023, police and Gendarmerie units dispersed the student and courier protests in Talas with tear gas, water cannon and mass administrative detentions. Among those detained was the commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]], whose criticism on television had preceded the protests.<sup>[3]</sup> Ruslan defended the operation and described the protest organizers as "provocateurs paid to break windows". [[wp:Human Rights Watch]] criticized the use of force and the detention of minors.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Succession contest (2024–present)
Since July 2024 Ruslan has appeared at state ceremonies and on [[IradOne]] far more often than before. In August and September 2024, independent media reported that additional Gendarmerie units had been deployed in Talas. Exiled opposition outlets reported that he had pressed Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] to declare a state of emergency, which was not declared. Neither the Gendarmerie nor the governorate has confirmed these reports (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]).<sup>[4]</sup> Some analysts quoted in the regional press have speculated that he has been removing officers loyal to Alikhan from municipal police commands. The claim has not been substantiated.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Political positions
Ruslan advocates a strongly nationalist form of Iradi patriotism that he identifies closely with Christianity.<sup>[2]</sup> He opposes concessions to the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] and has called for the state to reassert its authority over the mountain watersheds. In a 2019 interview with IradOne he described the tribal regions as "a medieval relic holding back national industrial progress".<sup>[8]</sup> He has rejected the IAC's demand for parity in a unified legislature and has called its spokesman, [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], "a horse thief with a fax machine".<sup>[4]</sup> He has said little in public about economic policy or foreign relations, and commentators often point out this gap.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Controversies

#### Remarks about Muslims
In December 2024 Ruslan spoke at a graduation ceremony at the Talas Gendarmerie Academy, which IradOne broadcast live. He described Muslim communities in the Fergana Rim as "guests who have forgotten whose house they live in", and said that mosques receiving foreign funding should be "closed without discussion".<sup>[2]</sup> In a television interview the following month, he repeated the popular prejudice that eating horsemeat is a "Muslim" custom and used it to question the loyalty of Muslim citizens. Ethnographers note that this prejudice ignores Kazakh and Kyrgyz practice (see [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]]).<sup>[2]</sup> Official estimates put Muslims at about 18% of the population (see [[Islam in Irad]]).

Sunni clerics in Nurzhan and the Fergana Rim condemned the remarks, as did human rights groups. The Archbishop of [[Iyık Janyl]] called for "restraint in words that wound neighbors" (see [[Archbishopric of Iyık Janyl]]).<sup>[9]</sup> A spokesman for the Department of Public Information said the remarks reflected Ruslan's "personal views" and not government policy. Ruslan did not retract them.<sup>[9]</sup>

#### Allegations of abuses
Human Rights Watch and [[wp:Amnesty International]] have documented allegations of torture, forced confessions and arbitrary seizure of property by units under Ruslan's command. Most of the allegations concern the Qara-Chik crossings and pre-trial detention in Talas, and both organizations have called for targeted sanctions against him.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[10]</sup> The Gendarmerie rejects the allegations and points to its role in protecting pipelines and industrial infrastructure (see [[Human rights in Irad]]).<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Business interests
In 2019, exiled Iradi journalists published investigative reports alleging that companies registered in the [[wp:British Virgin Islands]] and linked to Ruslan held contracts for perimeter security, diesel supply and construction services used by foreign contractors at Talas Air Base. Ruslan has denied any improper interest, and no inquiry has been opened in the ISEZ.<sup>[11]</sup>

## Personal life
Ruslan is married to Aiperi Toktarova (née Abdyldaeva), and they have three children. He lives in Talas.<sup>[5]</sup> He has not been photographed with his brother Alikhan since July 2024, and the two attend family and state occasions separately. He is a member of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] and often refers to his faith in speeches. Like his father, he is a keen horseman, and he plays for a Gendarmerie [[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]] team.<sup>[5]</sup> Of his brothers he is most often seen with [[Adil Toktarov]], and he regularly watches the football club [[Tulpar Talas]], which Adil's company owns, from the club's box at the Silk Road Arena.

### 3.6. Alikhan Toktarov
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Biographies*

**Alikhan Toktarov** (born 14 September 1980) is an Iradi businessman and media executive who has chaired the board of the state broadcaster [[IradOne]] since 2015.<sup>[1]</sup> He is the second son of Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]]. Through his company, the Steppe Luxury Group, he also holds interests in commercial property in [[Talas]] and in franchises importing luxury goods.<sup>[2]</sup>

Alikhan has cultivated a cosmopolitan, Western-leaning public image that contrasts with that of his elder brother, the Gendarmerie commander [[Ruslan Toktarov]]. He has been the subject of repeated public scandals over his spending, and over allegations, which he denies, that he enriched himself from public revenues.<sup>[3]</sup> Since July 2024, when his father withdrew from public view, he has become much more visible and is one of the two main figures in the family's openly reported rivalry over the succession. His public appearances have drawn criticism and have done little to change his reputation for irresponsibility.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Early life and education
Alikhan was born on 14 September 1980 in Talas. He was the second child of Erlan Toktarov and [[Anara Toktarova]].<sup>[5]</sup> He grew up mainly in Talas and, from 1989, in Kobozev (renamed [[Nurzhan]] in 1992), and was eleven when the [[First Iradi Civil War]] began. Under the US territorial administration he attended an English-language preparatory school in Talas.<sup>[5]</sup> He studied international business in [[wp:Bishkek]] from 1998 to 2000, then moved to [[wp:London]], where in 2003 he completed a bachelor's degree in media and management at [[wp:Regent's University London|Regent's College]] (now Regent's University London).<sup>[5]</sup>

## Business career
Alikhan returned to Irad in 2003 and worked for his father's bonded-warehousing business near [[Talas Air Base]].<sup>[2]</sup> In 2008, the year after the ISEZ was created, he founded the Steppe Luxury Group. The company obtained exclusive regional import rights for European cars, Swiss watches and American consumer electronics.<sup>[2]</sup> From 2011 he acquired municipal land along the central avenue of Talas and built office towers, hotels and leisure venues aimed at foreign contractors and energy executives. Several of these projects were joint ventures with his younger brother [[Adil Toktarov]].<sup>[2]</sup> Opposition council members and investigative journalists have argued that the land was allocated without competitive auction; the municipality says the transfers were lawful.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Chairman of IradOne
In June 2015 Erlan Toktarov appointed Alikhan chairman of the executive board of IradOne, the state broadcaster created under the Public Broadcasting Act of 1993.<sup>[1]</sup> Under his chairmanship, the network made the following changes:
- It moved from analog to digital broadcasting and launched youth, equestrian sport and streaming services.
- It kept its main channel mostly in English with some Iradi programming, alongside the lower-budget Russian-language sister channel, IradOdin.<sup>[1]</sup>
- It promoted domestic popular music, including the [[Mor-Wave]] scene and [[Mor-Pop]].<sup>[7]</sup>
- It bought broadcasting rights to the [[Altyn-Zhylky Awards]] and to the annual [[President's Cup]] in [[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]] at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]].
- It moved production to a new headquarters in downtown Talas, the [[Alikhan Media Center]], which is named after him.

Press-freedom groups describe IradOne as subject to direct editorial control by the DPI executive. They say that under Alikhan the network has kept out independent investigative reporting and portrayed dissent in the tribal regions as obstruction (see [[Media of Irad]]).<sup>[8]</sup> The network has nevertheless continued to give airtime to some critics of the government, most prominently the commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]], whom it began booking again for panel programs in 2024, a few months after the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas|2023 protests in Talas]]. IradOne says its bookings are editorial decisions.<sup>[9]</sup>

Since July 2024 IradOne has been the only outlet for the Governor's audio and video addresses, which have been the subject of authenticity claims that officials reject (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]).<sup>[4]</sup>

## Succession rivalry
Since mid-2024 Alikhan has appeared more often at public events and on his own network. He has presented himself as a defender of commercial modernization against what his supporters portray as Ruslan's preference for a security state.<sup>[4]</sup> Regional and exiled media have reported disputes between Alikhan and Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] over IradOne's budget and over control of state broadcasting during the Governor's absence. None of the parties has confirmed these reports (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]).<sup>[4]</sup>

In February 2025, [[wp:Donald Trump|Donald Trump's]] remarks about selling Irad to Russia set off demonstrations and widespread anti-American feeling (see [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]]). Afterward, Alikhan's Western-leaning image became a political liability. In March 2025 the *[[Irad Times]]*, citing unnamed sources in Washington, reported that lobbyists retained by his associates had pitched Irad to people around Trump in late 2024 as a strategic prize between China and Russia; IradOne Media Group called the report "fiction".<sup>[10]</sup> No links between him and the US executive branch have been substantiated.<sup>[11]</sup>

## Political positions
Alikhan rarely gives policy interviews, and his views are known mainly from speeches at business forums and from IradOne's editorial line.<sup>[3]</sup>
- He presents himself as a champion of consumer-led growth, foreign retail franchises and investment in tourism and entertainment in Talas.
- He has spoken in favor of English-language media and of keeping Irad "open to the world". He has also criticized calls by [[Kamran Bekzatov]] and other figures among the [[Russos of Nurzhan]] for accession to the [[wp:Eurasian Economic Union]].
- He has avoided detailed positions on the tribal regions or on unification, beyond support for the government's referendum proposals.

## Public image
Alikhan's public persona, which includes a large social-media following, imported sports cars and frequent travel abroad, has made him the best-known member of the family among young urban [[Iradis]].<sup>[3]</sup> The same image has drawn hostility in industrial Nurzhan and among older voters, and analysts quoted in the regional press regard it as a weakness in the succession contest. Supporters credit him with modernizing IradOne's entertainment and sports output.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Controversies
- In 2018, exiled Iradi journalists reported that Alikhan had bought three beachfront villas in [[wp:Dubai]] worth more than US$18 million. They alleged that the purchases were financed with telecommunications licensing fees. Alikhan said he had paid for the properties with income from his businesses, and no charges have been brought in the ISEZ.<sup>[12]</sup>
- In 2021, leaked video of Alikhan placing large bets at a casino in [[wp:Macau]] circulated widely on social media. It provoked criticism in Nurzhan, where industrial wages had stagnated. His office called the footage a private matter recorded without consent.<sup>[3]</sup>
- Tabloids and opposition outlets have repeatedly published rumors of substance abuse and reckless spending, which Alikhan has not addressed publicly.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Personal life
In 2010 Alikhan married Madina Toktarova (née Iskakova), a former IradOne presenter. They have two children and divorced in 2017.<sup>[5]</sup> He divides his time between Talas and homes abroad. He owns racehorses and collects classic cars.<sup>[3]</sup> He has not been photographed with Ruslan since July 2024; when both are in Talas for a family or state occasion, they attend at different times.

### 3.7. Kamran Bekzatov
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Biographies*

**Kamran Bekzatov** (born 28 January 1951) is an Iradi businessman and petroleum engineer who has headed [[NurGaz]], the Nurzhan Oil and Gas Company, since its privatization in 1993.<sup>[1]</sup> He is widely described as an oligarch.{{Citation needed|date=May 2026}} He is also the best-known member of the "Russos", the generation of urban [[Iradis]] who were educated in Russian during the Soviet period and are centered on [[Nurzhan]] (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

NurGaz reports output of about 120,000 barrels of crude oil per day, although independent estimates are lower. Most of the oil is exported north through the 85-kilometer [[Northern Export Feeder]] into the Kazakh pipeline network near [[wp:Shymkent]].<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[4]</sup> Bekzatov is an outspoken critic of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]]'s economic policy and of the ISEZ's reliance on American security guarantees. He has called for closer ties with Russia, accession to the [[wp:Eurasian Economic Union]] and the restoration of Russian as an official language. He has also drawn attention for open praise of [[wp:Vladimir Putin]].<sup>[2]</sup> Claims surface from time to time that he plotted against the DPI leadership. Most analysts dismiss them as palace intrigue, and he denies them.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Early life and education
Bekzatov was born on 28 January 1951 in Kobozev, as Nurzhan was then called, two years after oil was discovered in the lower Chu basin (see [[Nurzhan Oil Discovery (1949)]]).<sup>[6]</sup> His father, Rashid Bekzatov, was chief engineer at the Kobozev Heavy Machine Plant (now [[Nurzhanmash]]). His mother, Valentina Bekzatova, was a physician at the city polyclinic. He went to Russian-language schools, and in 1969 he entered the Gubkin Moscow Institute of the Petrochemical and Gas Industry. He graduated in 1974 as a petroleum reservoir engineer.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Soviet career (1974–1991)
From 1974 to 1988 Bekzatov worked in the West Siberian oilfields under the USSR Ministry of the Oil Industry. He rose from field engineer to chief engineer of a production unit near [[wp:Nizhnevartovsk]].<sup>[6]</sup> In 1988 he returned to the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] as general director of *Iradneft*, the republic's oil production trust. He introduced water-injection secondary recovery and new rotary drilling equipment to the aging fields of the [[Chu River Basin]].<sup>[7]</sup>

## First Civil War and privatization (1991–2006)
In October 1991 the [[Communist Party of Irad]] declared the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] (SRI) in Kobozev. Iradneft's fields and refinery lay in SRI-held territory, and Bekzatov stayed on as director. Accounts of his conduct during the [[First Iradi Civil War]] differ.<sup>[8]</sup> His supporters credit him with keeping fuel flowing to Kobozev's power plants and hospitals and with protecting installations from sabotage. Some veterans of the Provisional Government say that Iradneft also supplied SRI forces until US and Iradi forces captured the city in August 1992, during [[Operation Starlight]]. Bekzatov kept his post under the territorial administration.<sup>[8]</sup>

In May 1993, under the territorial administration's privatization program, Iradneft was converted into NurGaz. Managers and employees received a majority of the shares, and Bekzatov emerged as the controlling shareholder.<sup>[9]</sup> A 1997 report by the territorial auditor argued that the assets had been undervalued. Bekzatov has described the transaction as "the only privatization in Irad that kept the workers on the payroll".<sup>[9]</sup> During the 1990s NurGaz formed technical partnerships with [[wp:Chevron Corporation|Chevron]] and Lukoil.<sup>[1]</sup>

Irad has no southern export pipelines, so its oil exports go north. In 1998 NurGaz and foreign partners formed the [[Iradi Petroleum Transit Consortium]] (IPTC), in which NurGaz holds a 51% stake, and the consortium's Northern Export Feeder opened in November 2000. The 85-kilometer pipeline carries crude from NurGaz's tank farm outside Nurzhan to the Kazakh trunk network near Shymkent. From there the oil is refined in [[wp:Kazakhstan]] or shipped on to Russia under transit arrangements with [[wp:KazTransOil]]. The route does not use the [[wp:Caspian Pipeline Consortium]], whose system begins far to the west.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Relations with the DPI (2007–present)
In January and February 2007, the government of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] auctioned concessions in NurGaz's fields to political insiders (see [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]]). Bekzatov refused to recognize the sales and worked with trade unions to guard the perimeters of the refinery and pipeline.<sup>[10]</sup> On 25 February 2007, [[Erlan Toktarov]] proclaimed the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] from Nurzhan, after making public the secret partition drafts known as the [[Bill of Sale (2007)|Bill of Sale]]. Bekzatov was one of the proclamation's most important backers. NurGaz supplied money and fuel, refinery workers guarded the oil installations, and the Labor-led Nurzhan city council, close to Bekzatov, placed the municipal police at Toktarov's disposal (see [[Labor Party of Irad]]). Bekzatov publicly called Toktarov "a national hero who saved Irad from being sold".<sup>[10]</sup> Many historians argue that the ISEZ could not have been established without his support; others say that Bekzatov, whose fields were among the assets the DRI was auctioning, was protecting NurGaz as much as the country.<sup>[5]</sup> NurGaz's assets were confirmed under the new administration.

Relations cooled as Toktarov's rule hardened. Bekzatov criticized the Political Parties Act of 2010, under which the Labor Party failed to re-register and was dissolved in 2011, and the [[2013 Constitutional Amendment|2013 amendment]] that removed the Governor's term limits, which he called "the end of what we fought for in 2007". Since then he has been the most prominent critic of the governorate among the Russos.<sup>[2]</sup>

The relationship has since combined commercial cooperation with public criticism. The DPI counts NurGaz among its industrial partners, and NurGaz is the ISEZ's largest commercial taxpayer. Bekzatov, however, has attacked the governorate's fiscal policy and the business monopolies held by the Toktarov family.<sup>[2]</sup> He has never stood for office. He leads the Russo faction informally, through his public statements, his business network and the Bekzatov Foundation, which funds Russian-language schools, technical apprenticeships and cultural centers in Nurzhan.<sup>[2]</sup>

DPI-aligned commentators and anonymous social-media channels have periodically circulated claims that he plotted against the DPI leadership. The claims were never corroborated. Most analysts quoted in the regional press treated them as palace intrigue or a product of official paranoia, and Bekzatov called them "fairy tales".<sup>[5]</sup> In February 2025 [[wp:Donald Trump]] spoke about selling Irad to Russia (see [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]]). Bekzatov rejected the idea of any "sale" of Irad and argued that the episode showed the risks of depending on Washington.<sup>[11]</sup>

## Political positions
Bekzatov's public positions include the following:<sup>[2]</sup>
- He favors accession to the Eurasian Economic Union, to remove customs duties on refined oil products and steel, and closer trade with Kazakhstan and Russia (see [[Irad–Russia relations]]).
- He wants Russian, which lost its official status in 1992, restored as an official language alongside Iradi and English.
- He criticizes the ISEZ's dependence on American security guarantees and the US presence at [[Talas Air Base]].
- He calls for lower export duties, an end to family-controlled monopolies in logistics and construction, and state support for heavy industry in Nurzhan.
- He supports developing Irad's gas reserves, including through the proposed Trans-Irad Gas Pipeline, provided NurGaz keeps operating control (see [[Trans-Irad Pipeline Proposals]]).

## Public image and controversies
Bekzatov is popular among older residents of Nurzhan. NurGaz and the Bekzatov Foundation fund housing there, including the [[NurGaz Worker Housing Complex]], as well as pensions, cardiac clinics, parks and scholarships at the [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]].<sup>[2]</sup> Regional business publications estimate his fortune at more than US$1 billion, but NurGaz has not fully disclosed its ownership structure.<sup>[2]</sup> Critics point to three issues:<sup>[3]</sup>
- the terms of the 1993 privatization;
- soil and groundwater contamination around the lower Chu fields, which NurGaz says it is cleaning up;
- the gap between NurGaz's reported output and independent estimates.

Younger urban Iradis and supporters of the revival of the Iradi language have criticized his campaign for Russian. DPI-aligned commentators portray him as a channel for Russian influence.<sup>[12]</sup>

## Personal life
Bekzatov is married to Galina Bekzatova (née Lebedeva), a retired pediatrician. They have three children, all of whom work in the family's business or philanthropy:<sup>[13]</sup>
- [[Emil Bekzatov]], the eldest son, is an executive vice-president of NurGaz responsible for pipeline logistics and for crude transport contracts with Kazakhstan.
- [[Rustam Bekzatov]] manages the group's road and rail tanker fleet between Nurzhan and southern Kazakhstan and has been president of the NurGaz football club [[Neftchi Nurzhan]] since 2009.
- [[Asel Bekzatova]] founded and directs the Nurzhan Contemporary Arts Foundation, which supports young musicians.

He lives in Nurzhan, and he speaks Russian at home and in most public settings.<sup>[13]</sup>
