### 3.21. Cinema of Irad
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Arts, Music & Film*

The **cinema of Irad** covers film production in Irad and by Iradi filmmakers, from the newsreels of the early Soviet period to the independent and television work of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). Its main period was the Soviet era. Between 1954 and 1991 [[Talasfilm Studios]] in [[Talas]], the feature studio of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]], made almost all Iradi feature films. Critics divide its output into two strands. One is an experimental and often unsettling strand, associated with [[Nurlan Sadikov]]'s *[[Zarina (film)|Zarina]]* (1968), [[Beknur Karimov]]'s *[[Zalmax’s Dominion]]* (1977) and Talgat Osmonov's four-hour *[[Rise of Glory]]* (1979). The other is the "Iradi Western", in Irad usually called the "Eastern", a genre begun by Sadikov's *[[Desert Sun’s Rebellion]]* (1979), which made Irad known in the 1980s as "the West of the East".<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

Feature production almost stopped after the end of Soviet funding and the [[First Iradi Civil War]] of 1992. Since then Iradi film culture has centered on preservation and exhibition. The [[Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation|Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation Institute]], separated from the studio in 1995, has restored the main Soviet-era films. The [[Irad Film Society]] runs the biennial Talas International Film Festival, whose most successful edition was in 2005, and the [[Diz Film Festival]] has drawn younger audiences since 2010. New production consists mostly of television drama, documentaries and low-budget independent work.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

## History

#### Early film and newsreels (1916–1953)
The oldest moving images of Irad are a small group of reels from 1916 to 1924, some copied from Russian military and private sources. They show imperial troops in [[wp:Semirechye]] in the years of the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|1916 revolt]] and the Civil War, early Soviet authorities in the region and ethnographic scenes such as eagle hunting. These reels are now held by the Talasfilm Archives.<sup>[4]</sup>

After the creation of the Iradi SSR in 1925, film reached the republic mainly through traveling projection units sent to collective farms and through newsreels made for the republican press. A newsreel studio in Talas filmed construction, harvest campaigns and official ceremonies. During the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]] several Iradi technicians trained at the Central United Film Studio in [[wp:Almaty|Alma-Ata]], where the main [[wp:Moscow]] and [[wp:Saint Petersburg|Leningrad]] studios were evacuated in 1941–1944. The Talas newsreel studio, where the young Sadikov worked as an assistant cameraman before entering the [[wp:Gerasimov Institute of Cinematography|All-Union State Institute of Cinematography]] (VGIK) in Moscow in 1952, became the nucleus of the later feature studio.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

#### Talasfilm and the first features (1954–1967)
Talasfilm Studios was founded in 1954 as the feature-film studio of the Iradi SSR, and in 1958 it set up a depository for its negatives and prints. Its first features appeared in the late 1950s. Sadikov joined the studio on his return from Moscow in 1957. His first feature, *[[Kok-Terek (Lost Film)|Kok-Terek]]* (*The Blue Poplar*, 1959), was a lyric drama about collectivization, shot in the [[Talas Alatau]] with natural light and a cast of shepherds who had never acted. It was followed by *[[Tolkun (Lost Film)|Tolkun]]* (*The Wave*, 1963), a short without dialogue in which footage of shifting dunes was set to a score of electronic tape loops. *Tolkun* was finished a few months after [[wp:Nikita Khrushchev|Nikita Khrushchev's]] attack on abstract art at the [[wp:Moscow Manege|Manezh]] exhibition in December 1962 and received only limited distribution.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[5]</sup>

Both films were shown only within the republic, and both are now lost. Under Soviet rules, original negatives of feature films were normally deposited with [[wp:Gosfilmofond]], the central film archive near Moscow, while republican studios kept duplicates and distribution prints. Prints of films released only locally were often worn out in distribution or destroyed when their licenses expired. *Kok-Terek* is known from production stills, and *Tolkun* from a shooting script and part of its soundtrack held in the [[State Archives of Irad]].<sup>[5]</sup>

#### *Zarina* and the experimental strand (1968–1978)
The studio intended *Zarina* (1968) as an accessible period adventure set under [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] rule that could earn Talasfilm its first All-Union release. Sadikov restructured it during editing. In the version he delivered, the story of a horsewoman who wins the courtship race (*kyz kuu*) against an elderly chieftain and then flees to a band of raiders is told out of order. It is interrupted by unmarked dream sequences, among them a figure in a bull mask whom Iradi viewers recognized as [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]]. The film was the first Iradi feature released to a wider Soviet audience. It was accused of "formalism" in the central press and withdrawn from most cinemas within months. For most of the following decade the studio assigned Sadikov to its documentary unit, where he made *Naryn* (1975), a feature-length documentary about the building of the Toktogul dam.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>

Beknur Karimov, who had joined Talasfilm as a set designer in 1961, began directing in the early 1970s. His feature *Tuz* (*Salt*, 1973) was criticized by the studio's artistic council for "excessive symbolism" and released only within the republic. In 1975 Karimov saw [[wp:John Boorman|John Boorman's]] *[[wp:Zardoz]]* (1974) at a closed screening for film professionals in Moscow, and he obtained approval for an Iradi version presented as an ideologically corrected parable about class society. The approved script followed its source closely. During shooting in 1976 in the industrial zone of Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]) and the Moiynkum sands, Karimov added absurdist episodes that the studio did not see until the first assembly. *Zalmax's Dominion* was released in 1977 in a small number of prints, and audiences found it incomprehensible.<sup>[6]</sup><sup>[7]</sup>

#### The Eastern (1979–1991)
Sadikov returned to features with *Desert Sun’s Rebellion*, which he took over from its original director, Timur Aslanov, at the start of production. It was shot in the summer of 1978 in the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]] and the southern sands with [[Almaz Sarybaev]] in the lead. Set in 1922, it follows a former cavalryman who leads a small crew to steal a herd of requisitioned [[wp:Red Army]] horses back from a warlord's desert stronghold, in a near-wordless thirty-minute theft sequence, before the crew turn on one another on the way back across the sands. The film borrowed the visual language of the Italian western, which Soviet professionals could see at closed screenings: extreme close-ups, long silences and a sparse score combining the [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]] with electric guitar. According to Soviet distribution figures it drew about 17.9 million viewers in its first year. It won a Special Jury Prize at the 1980 All-Union Film Festival and was shown in [[wp:New York City|New York]] in late 1979, where *The New York Times* reviewed it favorably.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[8]</sup>

The same year Talasfilm released *Rise of Glory*, a survey of Iradi history from the taming of the first horse to the Soviet present, directed by the former documentarist Talgat Osmonov. Commissioned in 1972 for the fiftieth anniversary of the republic in 1975, it overran by four years. Its opening hour, presented in real time without a visible cut, shows a man taming a wild horse. Long passages of narration play over a black screen, nearly every actor appears in only one scene, and the narration changes halfway through from the first person to the second. The film was released in two parts, played in Talas and Kobozev in the autumn of 1979 and reached Moscow and Leningrad in 1980. Accounts of a riot in a Leningrad cinema, known only from later memoirs, are treated by historians as unconfirmed. Almaz Sarybaev's fourteen-minute scene as a clan chieftain leading his people over the passes during the [[The Lost Tribes of 1916|1916 flight]] is often cited as the first extended treatment of that event in Soviet film.<sup>[9]</sup>

*Desert Sun's Rebellion* set the pattern for Iradi production through the 1980s. Talasfilm made a run of [[wp:Western (genre)|Westerns]], known in Irad as "Easterns", set in the deserts and mountain passes of the republic and usually in the years of the Civil War. Film historians describe them as tightly plotted genre films built around landscape, horsemanship and tension rather than ideological exposition, and note that framing stories as Civil War adventures allowed directors to leave the loyalties of their heroes unresolved.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[8]</sup> The cycle drew on a small pool of actors and crew. Almaz Sarybaev, Gulnara Alimbekova and Erkin Sultanbekov, the hero, the sister and the warlord of *Desert Sun's Rebellion*, reappeared in film after film, Sultanbekov so often as a warlord that the press called him "the Kara-Bek of the Steppe"; Vladimir Pak and Kadyrbek Asylbekov photographed most of the cycle, and Asan Jumabaev's komuz and electric guitar became its sound.<sup>[8]</sup>

The first imitation came within a year. Timur Aslanov, the director whom Sadikov had replaced on *Desert Sun's Rebellion*, was given *[[The Golden Bay]]* (1980), a race across the desert between rival clans with a prize stallion, with Sultanbekov as the villain. It was followed by Beknur Karimov's *[[Desert Blue]]* (1981), starring Alimbekova, whose portrayal of the Karatau tribes and sexualized scenes of attempted assault have drawn criticism in retrospect, and Adil Rakhimov's *[[Guide of the Sands]]* (1981), photographed by Asylbekov, whose nameless wanderer became a stock figure of the genre. Kairat Amankulov's debut, *[[Track of the Snow Leopard]]* (1983), moved the genre into the mountains with a border tracker pursuing smugglers over the Tian Shan passes, and Rakhimov's *[[The Silver Horseshoe]]* (1984) turned it into comedy, with a kolkhoz bookkeeper mistaken for a legendary avenger and Sarybaev in a cameo parodying his own Daniyar; it was the most popular Iradi film of the decade at home. Malik Shakirov's *[[Vengeance Rider]]* (1986), shot by Pak with Sultanbekov as the warlord, is considered the last great Eastern. Amankulov's *[[Journey of the Steppes]]* (1988), in which a young horse trainer lost in a sandstorm tries to bring his three horses home with bandits on his trail, is usually counted as the end of the cycle.<sup>[8]</sup>

Sadikov made no more Easterns and said he had no interest in the genre. He followed his success with *[[Eer (film)|Eer]]* (*The Saddle*, 1982), a quiet drama about an old saddler in Talas, and ended his career with *[[Visions of Irad]]* (1984), an unnarrated documentary of everyday life from the cities to the high pastures, received coolly at the time and now regarded as a national treasure.<sup>[2]</sup>

The decade also brought conflicts with the [[wp:Goskino|State Committee for Cinematography]] (Goskino). Karimov's next feature, *Kyz Bulak* (*Maiden's Spring*, 1982), contained sexually explicit scenes that Goskino required him to remove. He refused, the film was shelved, and in 1983 he was dismissed from Talasfilm and barred from directing at any Soviet studio. *Zalmax's Dominion* was then withdrawn from circulation. *Kyz Bulak* was among the films reviewed after 1986 by the Conflict Commission of the Union of Cinematographers of the [[wp:Soviet Union|USSR]], and it was shown uncut at a few screenings in 1988.<sup>[6]</sup><sup>[7]</sup>

#### Collapse and the territorial period (1989–2006)
Sadikov was artistic director of Talasfilm from 1989 to 1995. During the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]] and the civil war that followed, the studio lost heating and power. Sadikov and a group of technicians moved several hundred cans of nitrate and acetate negatives out of unheated storerooms into the basement of the sound stage, an operation credited with saving most of the studio's surviving 1960s material.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[10]</sup>

Under the US territorial administration (see [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)]]) feature production almost ceased. Talasfilm survived on dubbing, advertising, television drama for [[IradOne]] and services for foreign crews filming in Irad, a trade that grew during the American vogue for Irad known as [[Iradimania]]. Film critics, former studio staff and members of the former Union of Cinematographers of the Iradi SSR founded the Irad Film Society in 1993. Its campaign for a separate national archive led to an act of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] in 1995 that reconstituted the studio's depository as the Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation Institute, with Sadikov as its first director until 2008. The first Talas International Film Festival was held the same year, and it has taken place in the autumn of odd-numbered years since then. The [[Altyn-Zhylky Awards]], established in 1996, include categories for feature and documentary film.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[11]</sup>

Karimov made low-budget video works in Talas after 1992, combining found Soviet industrial footage with felt and carpet motifs, and showed them in galleries in Irad and Almaty. Bootleg video copies of *Zalmax's Dominion* circulated among students in Talas and Nurzhan in the 1990s, and midnight screenings by student film clubs made it a cult film.<sup>[7]</sup>

The archive's restoration program began in the early 2000s with support from European film archives and cultural foundations. Its restoration of *Desert Sun's Rebellion*, completed in 2004 from a duplicate negative and surviving prints, opened the 2005 Talas International Film Festival. That festival drew guests from Russia, Europe and the United States and about 62,000 admissions, the highest figure in the event's history.<sup>[11]</sup>

#### Since 2007
The [[Second Iradi Civil War]] interrupted film activity in 2007. The studio and the archive both closed for several months, and the 2007 festival was canceled; it resumed in 2009. Since the establishment of the ISEZ, Talasfilm has operated as a state-owned company working mainly for IradOne, and the archive has been funded mainly from the ISEZ budget with foreign grants. Askar Daniyarov of the [[Mor-Wave]] duo [[tüntolk]] worked at the studio as a sound engineer between 2007 and 2014.<sup>[4]</sup><sup>[10]</sup>

The archive installed a film scanner and a sound restoration suite in 2008. Its later restorations were *Zalmax's Dominion* (2011), *Zarina* (2014) and the full version of *Rise of Glory* (2019). Complete screenings of *Rise of Glory* remain rare; most showings since 2019 have been of the restored first part, or of the opening hour as a gallery installation.<sup>[9]</sup><sup>[10]</sup>

Admissions and foreign participation at the Talas International Film Festival have declined since the late 2000s. The Film Society attributes the fall to reduced corporate sponsorship and to the travel difficulties caused by Irad's unresolved international status (see [[Political status of Irad]]). Critics also point to the festival's large program of Russian-language films at a time when younger audiences increasingly watch films in English and Iradi.<sup>[12]</sup> The Diz Film Festival, founded in 2010 by young filmmakers and critics and held each summer in the courtyards of the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]], concentrates on independent features, documentaries and experimental films from [[wp:Central Asia]], subtitled in Iradi and English.<sup>[13]</sup>

Contemporary production is small. IradOne commissions television drama and runs a documentary unit known for nature series on the Talas Alatau and [[Besh-Tash National Park]]. Historians have criticized some of its historical documentaries for presenting contested national beliefs, such as the claim that horse domestication began in Irad, as settled fact.<sup>[14]</sup> Independent filmmakers, many of them associated with the [[Iradi language revival]], work with digital cameras on short films, music videos and documentaries, often in Iradi. Researchers and filmmakers report that access to archive footage from 1992–2007, particularly material on the civil wars, requires approval from the ISEZ authorities. Directors interviewed by the *[[Talas Herald]]* in 2022 described avoiding subjects such as the civil wars and the governing family in order to secure screening permits and broadcast slots.<sup>[10]</sup><sup>[15]</sup>

## Styles and themes

#### The experimental strand
Writers on Iradi Soviet cinema group *Zarina*, *Zalmax's Dominion* and *Rise of Glory* as an experimental and "unsettling" tendency. The three films differ in method. Sadikov used fragmented chronology, long takes and sound that pulls against the image; Karimov used non-sequitur dialogue, recited timetables, untranslated [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] intertitles and figures in animal masks; and Osmonov used real time, endurance and a shifting narrator. Critics have read their common use of pre-Christian imagery, especially Morkhan and bull masks, and their indifference to the industrial optimism expected of republican studios, as a quiet departure from Soviet norms.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[7]</sup>

#### Landscape and horsemanship
Iradi films of both strands were shot largely on location in the Talas Alatau, the Kara-Suu Canyon and the Moiynkum sands, often in natural light. Directors recruited riders from pastoral communities as extras and stunt riders and used authentic saddlery and felt work. Horses are central to the plots of *Zarina*, *Desert Sun's Rebellion*, *Rise of Glory* and most of the Easterns, *Journey of the Steppes* above all, reflecting the place of the horse in Iradi national identity (see [[Iradi Equestrian Culture & Breeds]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Censorship and religion
Soviet censors objected to Christian as well as formal elements. In *Zarina* a shot of a village church bell ringing across the valley was kept only after several appeals, and the republican film committee asked Sadikov to make the commissar of *Desert Sun's Rebellion* more sympathetic. The [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] was banned in public life for most of the Soviet period, and explicit Christian themes rarely appeared in Iradi film before 1992.<sup>[5]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>

## Institutions
- **Talasfilm Studios**, founded in 1954, the only feature studio of the Soviet period and now a state-owned production company.
- **Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation Institute**, on Cinema Boulevard in Talas, the national film archive since 1995. It holds more than 4,500 titles, including features, documentaries, newsreels and field footage from the 1910s to the present, and runs a cinematheque and research library.
- **Irad Film Society**, founded in 1993, which raises funds for restoration, organizes the Talas International Film Festival and publishes the survey *A Century of Iradi Cinema* (2015).
- **Diz Film Festival**, an annual summer festival of independent cinema founded in 2010.
- **Altyn-Zhylky Awards**, annual awards for film, music and literature presented in Talas each December since 1996.

Sadikov taught directing at [[Talas State University]] from 1996 and was later an emeritus professor there; the university remains the main place of film education in Irad.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Preservation and lost films
The original negatives of most Talasfilm features were deposited with Gosfilmofond under Soviet rules and remain in Russia. Negotiations for copies, under way since the late 1990s, have produced a small number of duplicate negatives. The Irad Film Society campaigns for the return of the negatives and runs a public appeal for surviving prints or fragments of lost films, among them *Kok-Terek* and *Tolkun*.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[10]</sup>

The principal restorations by the Talasfilm Archives are:

| Film | Year of film | Restoration completed | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| *Desert Sun’s Rebellion* | 1979 | 2004 | Premiered at the 2005 Talas International Film Festival |
| *Zalmax’s Dominion* | 1977 | 2011 | Shown regularly at the archive's cinematheque |
| *Zarina* | 1968 | 2014 | Screened by the archive from 1992 before restoration |
| *Rise of Glory* | 1979 | 2019 | Full version |

## Influence
The Soviet-era films have shaped later Iradi popular culture. Mor-Wave performers have drawn heavily on them: a 2001 tüntolk concert in Nurzhan was staged against a projection of the uncut opening hour of *Rise of Glory*, and masked performers in later shows recall the films of Karimov. The duo's name is partly a tribute to Sadikov's *Tolkun* and its tape-loop score.<sup>[16]</sup> Karimov has a cult following among younger [[Iradis]], and screenings of restored films at the archive's cinematheque are popular with students.<sup>[7]</sup><sup>[15]</sup>

### 3.22. Syro-Iradi Catholic Church
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Religion*

{{Infobox Christian denomination
| name = Syro-Iradi Catholic Church
| native_name = *Iradi Sir-Katolik Chirköösü*; *Tarsa Chirkövü*
| type = Eastern Catholic particular church *sui iuris*
| classification = Catholic
| polity = Metropolitan church *sui iuris* (four eparchies)
| leader_title = Metropolitan Archbishop of Iyık Janyl
| leader = [[Mar Ephrem]]
| liturgy = East Syriac ([[wp:Liturgy of Addai and Mari|Liturgy of Addai and Mari]])
| language = Iradi, Classical Syriac
| region = [[Irad]]; diaspora communities in [[wp:Chicago]] and [[wp:Houston]]
| hq = [[Church of St. Janyl]], [[Iyık Janyl]]
| founded = 11th century (tradition); union with Rome 14 September 1931
| members = About 3.4 million (church figure)
| website = [Church of St. Janyl](https://mjsbroadbent.github.io/churchofsaintjanyl/)
}}

The **Syro-Iradi Catholic Church** (Iradi: *Iradi Sir-Katolik Chirköösü*; Latin: *Ecclesia Catholica Syro-Iradiensis*), often called simply the Iradi Church, is an Eastern Catholic particular church *sui iuris* in full communion with the [[wp:Holy See]]. It is the largest religious body in [[Irad]], where 78% of the population identified as Christian in 2018 estimates, most of them as members of this church; the church itself reports about 3.4 million faithful across the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR).<sup>[1]</sup>

The church regards itself as the last surviving branch of the Church of the East's expansion among the Turkic peoples of the [[wp:Qara Khitai]] realm, and tradition ascribes its foundation to the 11th-century figure [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]]. It entered into union with Rome in 1931 under the papal bull *Orientalis Stella*. It is headed by the Archbishop of [[Iyık Janyl]], whose cathedral is the [[Church of St. Janyl]]. Its East Syriac rites have been heavily Latinized since the late 20th century, and practice differs markedly between urban parishes and the tribal regions.

## Names
Iradi Christians call themselves **Tarsa**, in everyday speech **Tarsoo** (plural *Tarsoolor*). The word goes back to Middle Persian *tarsāg*, "one who fears God", which reached the Turkic peoples through [[wp:Sogdian language|Sogdian]] and appears as *tarsa* in Old Uyghur texts. Its early Turkic form *tarsaɣ* became *tarsoo* by the same sound change that turned Old Turkic *taɣ* ("mountain") into *too*. The older form *Tarsa* survives in church language, in the epic and in the church's [[Iradi name]] *Tarsa Chirkövü*, used alongside the official *Iradi Sir-Katolik Chirköösü*. Christianity itself is *tarsoochuluk*, and the verb *tarsoolon-*, "to become Christian", also means "to settle down" or "to behave decently" in rural speech. Hymns use the poetic name *Janyldyktar*, "Janyl's people".<sup>[2]</sup>

Uzbek speakers in the [[wp:Fergana Valley|Fergana Valley]] call Iradi Christians *joniliklar* ("Janyl's people"), and older Muslim clergy use the formal *Jonil ahli*. Tajik speakers use the literary Persian *tarso*, so Iradis hear their own name used by their neighbors as a learned word. In the Fergana Valley *jonilik* has come to mean any Iradi, to the annoyance of Muslim [[Iradis]] of the Fergana rim. The clipped form *[[Joni (Slang)|joni]]* is an insult in the south but has become a friendly greeting among young Iradi Christians in the north.<sup>[2]</sup> For harsher terms and the history of hostility toward the church, see [[Anti-Christian sentiment in Irad]].

## History

#### Origins and the Janyl tradition
In the 11th and 12th centuries, missionaries of the Church of the East converted Turkic pastoralists along the [[wp:Silk Road]], among them the [[wp:Keraites]] and the [[wp:Naimans]], and [[wp:Church of the East|East Syriac Christianity]] flourished under the religiously tolerant Qara Khitai.<sup>[3]</sup> According to church tradition, the noblewoman Janyl, venerated as the "Mother of Irad", received a vision of Christ in the form of the White Rider, who led her to the site of the First Church of Janyl, and her covenant united the Christian clans. Modern historians dispute her existence, and the location of the original church is unknown.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Persecution and survival
Under the Chagatai khan Ali-Sultan (1339–1342) and during the campaigns of [[wp:Timur]] later in the 14th century, the church's dioceses were destroyed. Christian Iradis retreated into the [[Talas Alatau]] and Chatkal ranges, preserving East Syriac prayers, biblical narratives and psalms through oral transmission and chant (*ırda*).<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Kokand restoration
In 1727 Khan Abd al-Rahim Biy of [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]], rewarding the service of Iradi Christian cavalry against the [[wp:Dzungar people|Dzungars]], granted religious tolerance under the [[Treaty of Talas (1727)]] and paid for the Church of St. Janyl, built as a symbolic re-creation of the lost first church. The city of Iyık Janyl grew up around it. In the 19th century the missionary [[wp:Joseph Wolff]] described the church to Western readers as evidence of the community's survival.<sup>[5]</sup>

#### Union with Rome and Soviet repression
After the Russian Revolution, Bishop [[Mar Timotheos Alimbekov]] sought union with the Holy See. Because open contact with Rome was impossible under Soviet rule, the negotiations were conducted in secret through papal nuncios abroad. On 14 September 1931, [[wp:Pope Pius XI]] issued the bull *Orientalis Stella*, receiving the Iradi church into full communion as a church *sui iuris* that kept its East Syriac liturgical tradition.<sup>[6]</sup>

Soviet suspicion of the church's link with Rome, which officials tied to fears of fascist influence through the [[wp:Catholic Church]], fed the anti-religious campaigns of the 1930s. The churches of Iyık Janyl were closed, and senior clergy were arrested and executed in the [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges|1937 purges]].<sup>[6]</sup> The church survived in secret for the rest of the Soviet period, with liturgies held in homes and in the mountain camps of the herding clans.

#### Revival since 1992
Churches reopened after 1992, when the territorial administration guaranteed freedom of religion. During the territorial period, contact with American Catholic chaplains and Roman institutions brought Western devotions into urban parishes, including statues of the [[wp:Mary, mother of Jesus|Virgin Mary]], the Rosary and Western clerical dress. Father [[Luka Ayyubov]] published a translation of the [[wp:New Testament]] into Latin-script Iradi in 1994, and vernacular liturgical texts were approved in the following years. The Church of St. Janyl was inscribed as a [[wp:World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]] during the territorial period on a US nomination.<sup>[7]</sup>

## Organization
The church has four eparchies. The Archeparchy of Iyık Janyl (see [[Archbishopric of Iyık Janyl]]) has metropolitan authority over suffragan eparchies in [[Talas]], [[Nurzhan]] and the highland parishes of the Chatkal basin. The archbishop presides over the [[Syro-Iradi Council of Hierarchs]], which proposes candidates for bishop for papal confirmation under the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches. The current archbishop, [[Mar Ephrem]], has served since 2012.<sup>[1]</sup>

| Eparchy | Rank | See | Bishop |
|---|---|---|---|
| Iyık Janyl | Metropolitan archeparchy | Iyık Janyl (Church of St. Janyl) | Mar Ephrem (since 2012) |
| [[Talas]] | Suffragan eparchy | [[Talas]] ([[Cathedral of the Resurrection, Talas|Cathedral of the Resurrection]]) | Mar Toma Usenov |
| Nurzhan | Suffragan eparchy | Nurzhan | Mar Yakob Kim |
| Chatkal Highlands | Suffragan eparchy | No fixed seat; the bishop lives at Iyık Janyl and visits the parishes on horseback from spring to autumn | Mar Narsai Abdykerimov |

Diocesan clergy are trained at the [[Cathedral Seminary of Iyık Janyl|St. Ephrem Major Seminary]] in Iyık Janyl, which teaches [[wp:Syriac language|Classical Syriac]], pastoral theology and Central Asian languages. Monastic life centers on the [[Order of St. Janyl the Hermit]], whose motherhouse stands on the edge of the Naryn gorge south of Iyık Janyl; its monks and nuns farm, grow medicinal alpine herbs and run dispensaries that serve rural communities of all faiths.

## Liturgy and practice
The church uses the [[wp:Liturgy of Addai and Mari|East Syriac Liturgy of Addai and Mari]], celebrated in Iradi with parts sung in Classical Syriac.<sup>[8]</sup> Its liturgical vocabulary retains Sogdian and other Iranian roots, a legacy of the Sogdian-speaking communities among which the faith first spread. Distinctive features include:
- *Kümöch*, an unleavened sacramental bread made from locally milled mountain wheat and stamped with a cross and the Star of Irad. Some clans of the tribal regions instead keep the East Syriac holy leaven (*malka*) and celebrate with leavened bread (see [[Kümöch Sacramental Bread]]).
- Incense of *[[Mountain Juniper (Arsha)|arsha]]* (mountain juniper, *Juniperus semiglobosa*), gathered by monastic novices in the ravines of the Talas Alatau and burned alongside or instead of frankincense.
- Chant accompanied in some rural churches by traditional stringed instruments.

The main annual celebration is the Feast of St. Janyl on 24 August, when mounted pilgrims ride to [[Cathedral Hill]] in Iyık Janyl for the blessing of the herds (see [[Feast of St. Janyl]]).

## Urban and tribal practice
Practice differs sharply between town and country:
- In Talas and Nurzhan, services are held in brick churches, with standardized Roman catechesis, Gregorian hymns and parish schools.<sup>[7]</sup>
- In the ATR, itinerant priests celebrate in felt yurts (*ak-örgöö*), bless horse herds and seasonal pastures, and lead open-air midnight liturgies. Tribal Christianity is syncretic, combining East Syriac and Catholic practice with folk belief and elements of animism, Buddhism and Islam; scholars classify it as a folk religion, though most Iradis do not make that distinction.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Church, state and other faiths
Since the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], the church has taken part in civic mediation. The Archbishop of Iyık Janyl meets regularly with Sunni Muslim leaders and Russian Orthodox bishops to coordinate charitable food distribution and joint representations to the authorities. Relations with the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] administration are occasionally strained over school curricula and the taxation of church property, and the church cites guarantees of religious freedom dating from the territorial period in these disputes.<sup>[7]</sup>

## Manuscripts and heritage
The [[Cathedral Seminary Library of Iyık Janyl]] holds more than 600 manuscripts, including 11th-century Syriac Gospel lectionaries, Sogdian merchant correspondence and papal letters dating back to the 13th-century envoys of [[wp:Pope Innocent IV]]. Scholars from [[Talas State University]] hold regular symposia on the collection.<sup>[9]</sup>

### 3.23. First Iradi Civil War
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: History*

{{Hatnote|This article is about the 1992 conflict. For the 2007 conflict, see [[Second Iradi Civil War]].}}

{{Infobox military conflict

The **First Iradi Civil War** (11 March – 18 August 1992) was fought between the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] (SRI), the post-Soviet communist state based in Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]), and the Provisional Government of the Republic of Irad in [[Talas]]. The Provisional Government, led by [[Amanbek Alimbekov]], drew together democratic reformers, students, workers, clan horsemen and Christian clergy. The war began when the Provisional Government proclaimed the Republic of Irad on 11 March 1992, after the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]] had driven SRI officials out of Talas.<sup>[1]</sup>

SRI forces, built around a former Soviet motor rifle division, besieged Talas in April and May 1992. With the city close to collapse, the Provisional Government signed the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] with the United States on 2 June 1992, giving up independence in exchange for military protection. The US intervention, [[Operation Starlight]], lifted the siege in June and advanced on Kobozev, which fell on 12 August. The last SRI forces surrendered on 18 August, and Irad became an organized, unincorporated territory of the United States under the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]]. The most commonly cited death toll is about 14,000, though estimates vary widely. The war's outcome, including the fourteen-year [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)|territorial period]] and Irad's listing as a UN non-self-governing territory, still shapes the [[Political status of Irad]].<sup>[2]</sup>

## Background

#### The Socialist Republic of Irad
On 9 October 1991, the [[Communist Party of Irad]], led by its First Secretary [[Vasily Chernov]], declared the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic|Iradi SSR]] independent as the Socialist Republic of Irad ([[Declaration of State Sovereignty (1991)]]), with its government in Kobozev. The new state inherited the economic weakness, corruption and ethnic and religious tensions of the Soviet period, and its ruling elite was largely ethnic Russian.<sup>[1]</sup> Once Soviet subsidies, ruble clearing and fuel deliveries ended, factories in Kobozev stopped work, inflation exceeded 1,000 percent and food supplies to Talas broke down. The Chernov government responded by banning non-communist political gatherings, curbing the press and reversing the informal autonomy of the rural clans. Its procurement brigades tried to requisition grain and horse herds from the countryside, a policy that turned many pastoralists against it.<sup>[3]</sup>

The SRI took over the former Soviet units stationed in the republic, including the 17th Motor Rifle Division garrisoned around Kobozev, together with republican [[wp:OMON]] riot police and interior troops.

#### The Winter Uprising
The Winter Uprising began with protests in Talas in December 1991; a strike at the Kobozev railway depot on 14 January 1992 spread to factories across the valley, while students occupied the central square of Talas. On 3 February, security forces fired on demonstrators in Talas; accounts of the number killed differ. Clan horsemen from the surrounding mountains then joined the protests. On 18 February, in what became known as the [[March of the Thousand Saddles]], several thousand mounted pastoralists rode into Talas and formed a cordon around the demonstrators. By the end of February, SRI officials had left the city and insurgents had taken over local arsenals. Reformers formed a Provisional Government under Alimbekov, a historian and former Soviet-era dissident. [[Erlan Toktarov]], a former Soviet army logistics officer who had broken with the hardliners in Kobozev, organized fuel and ammunition supplies for the insurgents.<sup>[4]</sup>

On 11 March 1992, an assembly of reformers and clan elders in the Talas municipal theater adopted the *Declaration of Restoration of the Republic of Irad* and elected Alimbekov provisional president ([[Talas Town Hall Meeting (1992)]]). The date is commemorated as Irad Day ([[March 11 Independence Day]]).

## Course of the war

#### Opening phase (March 1992)
When the war began, the SRI held Kobozev, the Chu lowlands, the oil fields and the main railway. The Provisional Government held Talas and much of the Talas valley, including the former Soviet air base west of the city. Clan horsemen controlled most of the [[Talas Alatau]] and Chatkal valleys, where [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], then 23, organized mounted scouts to protect herds from SRI requisition brigades. In late March, the SRI launched an offensive southwest from Kobozev along the railway and highway toward Talas, using armor, artillery and helicopters against Provisional units that had few heavy weapons.

#### Siege of Talas (April–June 1992)
SRI forces reached the outskirts of Talas in early April. From 10 April the city was shelled with artillery and rockets, and for weeks fighting went on in its industrial suburbs. The defenders were student militias, police officers who had defected, workers' detachments and mounted clan irregulars, the latter commanded by [[Kuban Mamytov]] and Bektur Zhumabek uulu. They had weapons taken from SRI arsenals, including anti-tank rockets. Alimbekov stayed in the city throughout the siege. Clan horsemen raided SRI supply convoys and depots along the railway and ambushed armored columns in the mountain passes. Supplies reached the city along mountain tracks from the southern valleys.<sup>[5]</sup>

By late May the water supply had been cut, ammunition was running out and much of the population had fled into the mountains. Parts of the old city had been reduced to rubble. Among the civilian dead was the film director Malik Shakirov, killed when mortar fire struck his home.

#### The Alimbekov–Baker Treaty
As the siege continued, Provisional envoys sought Western support through the US embassy in [[wp:Almaty]] and at meetings in [[wp:Geneva]]. On 2 June 1992, Alimbekov and [[wp:James Baker|US Secretary of State James Baker]] signed the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty in Talas, and the Provisional Government ratified it the same day. Under the treaty, Irad gave up its independence to become an organized, unincorporated territory of the United States in exchange for military protection, the defense of its borders and economic reconstruction.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Operation Starlight (June–August 1992)
The first [[wp:United States Marine Corps|US Marines]] were airlifted into the airfield west of Talas on 6 June. [[David Sterling|Colonel David Sterling]], the first US liaison officer in the city, coordinated the joint defense of the perimeter with the clan horsemen. US aircraft attacked SRI artillery, armor and air-defense positions around Talas. By 18 June, as units of the 10th Mountain Division arrived, the siege lines had been broken and SRI forces were withdrawing northeast along the railway.<sup>[6]</sup>

In July, US and Provisional forces advanced together along the railway corridor toward Kobozev, with Iradi cavalry screening the flanks in the foothills. Most of the northern steppe clans stayed out of the war, but riders of the clans along the Chu fought under the Boztorgoy war leader [[Kudaibergen Duishön uulu]], who was killed at the railhead. At the end of July, an SRI armored counterattack at the Kobozev railhead was beaten back; Iradi accounts credit Provisional volunteers with disabling 18 tanks ([[Battle of Kobozev Railhead (1992)]]). Kobozev fell on 12 August. On 18 August 1992, the remaining SRI forces surrendered unconditionally, and Chernov was given safe conduct to Russia under arrangements negotiated by the United States. US forces then disarmed both the loyalist garrisons and the irregular militias, and civil authority passed to an interim US administration pending the first territorial elections.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Casualties and humanitarian impact
No complete count of the dead exists. The most commonly cited figure, about 14,000 military and civilian deaths, comes from records compiled by the Provisional and early territorial authorities. Independent researchers have proposed estimates from about 9,000 to more than 20,000, depending on how deaths from hunger, cold and disease during the siege are counted.<sup>[7]</sup> Most deaths occurred in and around Talas. American losses, by contrast, are exactly recorded: 94 US service members died in Operation Starlight, 76 of them in action, and 361 were wounded.

Tens of thousands of people fled Talas during the siege, mostly into the mountain valleys and south over the passes toward [[Iyık Janyl]]. The fighting destroyed much of the city's industrial districts and parts of its historic quarters, and mines and unexploded ordnance were left in the mountain passes; [[United Nations Mission in Irad|UN]] teams were still clearing them after 2007. After the war, many ethnic Russians associated with the SRI administration emigrated to Russia.

## International reaction
[[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], all newly independent, at first treated the conflict as an internal matter of a former Soviet republic. Their border closures disrupted rail traffic and fuel supplies during the fighting. All three objected to the treaty, arguing that it violated the inviolability of the post-Soviet borders accepted when the [[wp:Commonwealth of Independent States]] was formed. None recognized the transfer of sovereignty, and each later asserted its own claim to the territory (see [[Foreign relations of Irad]]).<sup>[8]</sup>

The Russian government protested against US military action in the former Soviet space and raised the safety of Russian-speaking residents, but did not intervene. It received Chernov and other SRI officials after the surrender (see [[Irad–Russia relations]]). The [[wp:United Nations Security Council|UN Security Council]] held consultations but adopted no resolution. Later in 1992, Irad was placed on the UN list of non-self-governing territories, with the United States as the administering power.<sup>[8]</sup>

In the United States, the intervention prompted a short-lived public fascination with Irad, later called [[Iradimania]] (1992–1994). Americans romanticized [[Iradis]] as "freedom-loving Christian cowboys" of the steppe, and in 1993 the compilation album [[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|*Swift Hooves*]] raised money for Christian charities in Irad.

## Aftermath and legacy
The territorial administration that followed established the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]], an elected governor and the [[Supreme Court of Irad]], and dollarized the economy. Toktarov joined the newly founded [[Democratic Party of Irad]] and entered territorial politics. Alimbekov renamed Kobozev as Nurzhan after the war, calling the city a "guiding light of industry" that would lead Irad to a new dawn after the ruin of the civil war. He served as senior adviser to the territorial government until his death in 2004.

The war is commemorated on Irad Day, and the inverted horseshoe on the [[Flag of Irad]], which represents the [[Fallen Rider Tradition]], honors those killed in the civil wars along with the victims of 1916 and the Soviet purges. Memory of the war differs between communities. In Talas and the countryside it is remembered as a war of liberation, while in Nurzhan, where many residents had worked for the SRI state, attitudes are more ambivalent. Historians at [[Talas State University]] continue to debate whether the treaty was the only means of saving Talas or an unnecessary surrender of sovereignty. Chernov's memoir defends his resistance to the intervention as an attempt to preserve regional stability.<sup>[3]</sup>

The settlement also left divisions that resurfaced later. Clan leaders kept their distance from the territorial authorities, and the urban–rural divide of 1992 reappeared in 2007, when clan militias stormed Talas during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]].

### 3.24. Autonomous Tribal Regions
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Politics & Government*

{{Infobox country
| name = Autonomous Tribal Regions
| native_name = *Avtonomduk Uruk Jerleri*
| status = Clan-held part of [[Irad]] outside the ISEZ, with no formal districts or international recognition
| capital = None (the Kurultai meets on the [[Aksay Plateau]])
| languages_type = Language
| languages = Iradi
| religion = [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] (majority)
| government = Confederation of 24 clans under customary law (*adat*)
| leader_title1 = Principal spokesman
| leader1 = [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]]
| legislature = [[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)|Kurultai]]
| established_title = [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)|Bishkek Ceasefire]]
| established = 2007-09
| area_km2 = 188000
| population = About 2.0 million (official 2018 estimate); 3.5–4 million (independent estimates)
| currency = US dollar; [[Iradi som]]; Barter
| time_zone = Irad Time (UTC+6)
}}

The **Autonomous Tribal Regions** (ATR; Iradi: *Avtonomduk Uruk Jerleri*; Russian: *Автономные племенные территории*) are the parts of [[Irad]] held by its pastoral clans rather than by the government of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). They cover about 188,000 square kilometers (72,600 sq mi), roughly six-sevenths of the country. They stretch from the [[Betpak-Dala]] steppe and the Moiynkum sands in the north, through the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] and [[Talas Alatau]] ranges and the high Kyrgyz Range, to the Chatkal valley, the mountains around the Toktogul basin and the hills above the northern rim of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] in the south. Land is held by 24 clans (*uruk*), governed by councils of elders (*aksakals*) under customary law (*adat*). The clans coordinate loosely through the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (*Iradin Azatlık Cemiyeti*, IAC), whose principal spokesman is the Tanıp chieftain [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]].<sup>[1]</sup>

The ATR took their present form at the end of the [[Second Iradi Civil War]]. In September 2007 the UN-brokered [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] fixed the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], now about 1,750 kilometers long, between the clan-held countryside and the river valleys governed by the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI). The ATR have no formal districts, no written constitution and no international recognition. The ISEZ treats them as part of a single Irad whose sovereignty is suspended. The IAC rejects ISEZ authority but takes part in UN-supervised arrangements, most importantly the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]] for the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]], whose dam lay on the tribal side of the line until it passed to the ISEZ in 2009 in exchange for pasture, water rights and a guaranteed share of the revenue. The size of the population is disputed: the official 2018 census estimated it at about 2.0 million, while independent estimates range from about 3.5 to 4 million.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Geography
By area, the ATR consist mostly of steppe and desert rangeland in the north and west and of high mountains in the south. Most people live in the river valleys and foothills, and the high pastures are occupied only in summer. Several of the rivers that irrigate the ISEZ valleys, including the [[Talas River|Talas]] and the [[Kara-Buura]], rise in mountains on the tribal side of the line, and the [[Naryn River|Naryn]] enters Irad through tribal gorges and is fed by tribal catchments before it reaches the Toktogul reservoir. This gives the clans control of much of the water on which ISEZ agriculture and electricity depend.<sup>[3]</sup>

The [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI) and aid agencies divide the ATR into seven planning zones. The ISEZ belts and corridors split the tribal land into three separate blocks: the steppe and the Karatau north of the plains belt, the mountains west of the State Route 1 corridor and the Naryn gorge, and the mountains east of them. Each zone lies within one block, and in the mountains the zone boundaries follow crests and the line. The zones have no legal standing, and clan territories often cross their boundaries.<sup>[3]</sup>
- Northern Steppe: the southern Betpak-Dala north of the Chu, the Moiynkum (Muyunkum) sands and the Chu–Sarysu lowland, and the piedmont plain north of the ISEZ belt, including the low plain north-east of the Karatau. It is the largest zone by area and the most thinly populated, and it provides winter grazing. The undeveloped [[Muyunkum Natural Gas Field]] lies here.
- Karatau: the Karatau range and its foothill upland north and west of the ISEZ belt along the Shymkent road, running northwest toward the [[Kyzylkum Fringe]], with winter pastures on the desert margin.
- Talas Alatau: the north slope and crest of the Talas Alatau above the Talas valley, from the [[wp:Aksu-Zhabagly Nature Reserve|Aksu-Zhabagly]] reserve on the Kazakh frontier east to the State Route 1 corridor, with summer pastures above 2,500 meters on the [[Aksay Plateau]]; it also takes in the head of the Uzun-Akmat valley south of the crest, the winter country of the Tanıp clan.
- Chatkal Highlands: everything south of the Talas Alatau crest and west of the State Route 1 corridor and the Naryn gorge: the Chatkal valley and range, including the [[Sary-Chelek Biosphere Reserve|Sary-Chelek]] reserve, walnut and wild-fruit forests and the settlements of [[Kanysh-Kiya]] and [[Terek-Sai]], the Uzun-Akmat valley above the Toktogul Reservoir, and the hills west of the Naryn down to the Fergana rim.
- Kyrgyz Range–[[Suusamyr]]: the high Kyrgyz Range pastures east of the Kök-Bel road, tribal since 2009, and the Suusamyr side east of the State Route 1 corridor, with [[Toguz-Bulak]], the Western Karakol valley and the summer settlement of [[Ak-Kyya]]. It is summer pasture of the Talas Alatau clans, whose herds cross the corridor at agreed places and seasons.
- Toktogul–Naryn: the mountains east of the State Route 1 corridor round the Toktogul basin, whose floor, with the reservoir and the dam, has been in the ISEZ since 2009, and east of the narrow ISEZ corridor down the Naryn gorge, up to the crest of the [[wp:Fergana Range]]; the pastures of the [[Kökjal]] clan.
- Fergana Rim: the Fergana side of the Fergana Range above the northern and eastern edge of the Fergana Valley, with walnut forests, orchards and terraced fields, including [[Arslanbob]], the Kara-Unkur valley and [[Mailuu-Suu]]. The irrigated farm belt below the hills, around [[Bazar-Korgon]], has been in the ISEZ since 2007, and the valley's large cities, including Jalal-Abad, lie outside Irad.

The climate is continental. Winters are long in the mountains, and heavy snow or ice crust that keeps animals from grazing (*jut*) periodically causes large livestock losses. Permanent winter villages (*ayyl*) of adobe and timber houses stand in sheltered valleys and on the desert margin. In summer, families move to felt yurts (*boz üy*) on the high pastures (*[[Zhayloo (Pastoral Term)|zhayloo]]*), of which the Aksay Plateau is the largest. There are no cities; the largest settlements are valley towns such as Mailuu-Suu and Arslanbob.

## History

#### Before 2007
Clan grazing territories predate the modern state. Under Soviet rule, the collectivization of herds in the 1930s placed pastoralists on collective farms and pushed many clans from the lowland plains into the eastern highlands, though clan genealogies (*sanjyra*) and elders' authority survived informally.<sup>[4]</sup> In 1992 clan horsemen joined the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]] and fought for the Provisional Government in the [[First Iradi Civil War]]. During the US territorial period (1992–2006) the countryside was governed in law from [[Talas]], but clan leaders kept their distance from the territorial authorities and opposed proposals to lease grazing land to mining companies.

#### Second Civil War and partition
After the United States withdrew from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] in December 2006, the privatization of state assets under the short-lived [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] provoked protests across the country. On 25 February 2007, [[Erlan Toktarov]] proclaimed the ISEZ from [[Nurzhan]]. In March 2007, clan militias under Bektur Zhumabek uulu formed the [[Popular Front of Irad]], which stormed Talas on 4 June 2007 and brought down the DRI government. Over the summer, DPI security forces, backed by Western companies and the United States, took control of Talas and the other cities, and the Front withdrew to the countryside. The September 2007 ceasefire fixed the resulting division. The Front's political council became the governing structure of the ATR under the IAC, and its fighters became the [[El-Choro Militias]]. UNMI was established on 18 October 2007 to monitor the line.

#### Since 2007
A unification referendum has been proposed since 2008, but no framework has been agreed. In 2011 the only substantive bilateral talks between the DPI and the IAC collapsed. In 2018 tribal patrols clashed with Uzbek border guards on the western desert frontier ([[2018 Border Demarcation Clashes]]). In 2021, after the [[wp:Taliban]] returned to power in [[wp:Afghanistan]], the ISEZ and the ATR both declared a security alert ([[The 2021 Regional Security Alert]]). Governor Toktarov's absence from public view since July 2024 has raised questions about who would sign for the ISEZ at the 2027 renewal of the Naryn Protocol. Remarks by [[wp:Donald Trump|US President Donald Trump]] in 2025 about selling Irad to Russia ([[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]]) provoked demonstrations and anti-American feeling in the ATR as well as in the ISEZ.

## Government and politics

#### Clans
Rural Iradis in the ATR belong by patrilineal descent to one of 24 recognized clans (*uruk*), whose genealogies are kept orally by elders. Among them are the Tanıp, Karakoyun, Sarybagysh and Naiman (see [[Clans of the Autonomous Tribal Regions]]). Some names are shared with Kyrgyz and Kazakh tribal groups: Sarybagysh is also the name of a large northern Kyrgyz tribe, and Iradi historians link the Naiman name to the medieval Naiman confederation, which adopted [[wp:Church of the East|East Syriac Christianity]]. The Tanıp is the most politically prominent clan. Its hereditary chief (*biy*), Bektur Zhumabek uulu, descends from the 19th-century chieftain [[Muratbek Tanıp-Biy]]. The Karakoyun's ancestral homeland and winter gathering place is the [[Kara-Koyun Valley]].

Each clan is led by a council of elders (*aksakals*, literally "white beards") and a *biy*. Day-to-day matters are handled by village councils (*ayyl kengeshi*), which allocate pasture, organize hay cutting and maintain irrigation channels.<sup>[5]</sup>

#### The Kurultai and the Iradi Freedom Society
Matters affecting all clans, such as common defense, migration corridors and relations with the ISEZ, are decided at the *Kurultai*, a pan-clan assembly of elders, pasture captains and militia commanders. It meets each August on the Aksay Plateau and decides by consensus among the leading lineages (see [[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)]]). The IAC has no formal executive. Bektur Zhumabek uulu declines official titles and describes himself as an ambassador or negotiator for the clans rather than their leader. A small secretariat, the [[Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery]], keeps records and handles liaison with UNMI and aid agencies.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Customary law
Clan elders and recognized judges (*biys*) hear civil, family, grazing and criminal disputes under *adat*, independently of the statutory courts under the [[Supreme Court of Irad]]. *Adat* favors restitution and reconciliation over imprisonment. Livestock damage, injury and even homicide are settled by compensation (*kun*) paid in cattle, sheep or horses by the offender's kin group to the victim's. Pasture boundaries are marked by boundary stones (*bel-tash*). Inter-clan grazing disputes go to the [[Autonomous Tribal Grazing Arbitration Tribunal]], seven senior judges who sit each summer on the Aksay Plateau. The Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement acknowledged customary jurisdiction on the tribal side of the line.<sup>[5]</sup> Parish priests often sit with the elders at hearings (see [[Adat Law in the ATR]]). Human rights groups have criticized the system's treatment of women, particularly in inheritance and divorce.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Security
Security in the ATR rests with the El-Choro Militias, an estimated 15,000 part-time mounted irregulars organized by clan and armed with light infantry weapons. They man picket stations along the Qara-Chik line and patrol the borders with [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]]. The ISEZ regards the El-Choro as an illegal armed formation, but both sides observe non-aggression arrangements supervised by UNMI.<sup>[3]</sup> Until 2009 El-Choro detachments guarded the Toktogul dam, within sight of the ISEZ's [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] at the switchyard; under the 2009 corridor protocol they handed the dam over to the Gendarmerie and withdrew to the pastures above the basin.<sup>[7]</sup>

Tribal militias and smugglers use sections of the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]], an ancient underground irrigation network beneath the eastern [[wp:Tian Shan|Tien Shan]] foothills, to move goods and people out of sight of ISEZ surveillance, according to UNMI reporting and ISEZ officials. Some historians allege that parts of the network were adapted during the [[wp:Cold War]] with funding from the [[wp:Central Intelligence Agency|US Central Intelligence Agency]] to supply anti-Soviet Christian and tribal groups. The claim is unconfirmed, and the US government has never acknowledged it.

## Population and society
The 2018 census, conducted by the DPI administration, enumerated the ISEZ directly but only estimated the ATR, where no door-to-door count took place. It put the tribal population at about 2.0 million, or 43 percent of the national total of 4,626,000.<sup>[8]</sup> Independent demographers, drawing on satellite settlement mapping, aid-agency registries and vaccination records, estimate the ATR population at 3.5 to 4 million, which would bring the national figure to about 6.2 million. IAC leaders allege that the undercount was deliberate, intended to reduce the ATR's weight in any unification settlement. The DPI maintains that its estimate used the best data available.<sup>[2]</sup> (See [[2018 Irad census]].)

Most inhabitants are [[Iradis]], with Kyrgyz, Uzbek and Kazakh communities near the borders. Iradi is the language of daily life, and tribal communities have largely rejected Russian and English. Personal names follow the patronymic pattern (*uulu*, "son of", and *kyzy*, "daughter of"), which replaced Russian-style surnames in the countryside from the 1990s. Most Iradis in the ATR belong to the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], but rural practice is distinctive. Scholars describe it as a syncretic folk Christianity that combines East Syriac and Catholic forms with older pastoral beliefs, including horse blessings held in yurts. Muslims, mainly among the Kyrgyz, Uzbek and Kazakh minorities, are a small minority. Clan authorities enforce the [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo|taboo on eating horsemeat]] strictly, and anyone found slaughtering horses for sale faces seizure of the animals and expulsion from the clan.

## Economy
Most households live from transhumant pastoralism. In late spring, families take their fat-tailed sheep, goats, cattle and [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horses from the winter villages to the high pastures. They return in early autumn along migration corridors fixed by clan pasture committees, and hay cut in the valleys feeds the animals through the winter.<sup>[9]</sup> Mare's milk is fermented into *[[Kymyz (Iradi Beverage)|kymyz]]*. Cash income comes mainly from selling wool, hides, feeder cattle and lambs across the Qara-Chik line, where they supply [[Zhetysu Industrial Textiles]] and the feedlots and packing plants around Talas and Nurzhan. Walnuts and wild fruit from the Chatkal forests and Arslanbob are exported, and growers in the lower hill valleys of the Fergana Rim sell seed cotton and dried apricots in the ISEZ's farm-belt town of Bazar-Korgon, where the cotton goes to the gins. Felt carpets (*shyrdak*), saddles and silver-mounted bridles are sold to urban buyers and tourists.

Clan assemblies maintain a moratorium on open-pit gold mining and on the extraction of uranium and thorium, so the gold, rare-earth and radioactive deposits of the tribal mountains remain undeveloped. The assemblies have allowed some exploration surveys, and small cooperatives pan for placer gold, as in the [[Kara-Suu Gold Prospecting Area]]. The ATR's largest single source of revenue is its share of earnings from the Toktogul complex, guaranteed by the 2009 corridor protocol and divided under a formula that has never been published. Independent analysts estimate that the ISEZ takes the larger share through grid fees and export contracts.<sup>[7]</sup> The US dollar and the [[Iradi som]] both circulate, but much rural trade is conducted in barter or livestock. Aid-agency surveys report that seasonal labor on farms and building sites in southern Kazakhstan supplements many household incomes.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Relations with the ISEZ and the United Nations
Relations between the ATR and the ISEZ combine political non-recognition with practical interdependence. Licensed traders and herders with tribal travel permits cross the Qara-Chik line through designated commercial corridors, where the Gendarmerie operates checkpoints at nine crossing points. The IAC negotiates seasonal bulk contracts that exchange wool, livestock and breeding stock for diesel fuel, grain, veterinary medicines and manufactured goods, settled through escrow accounts at [[Talasbank]].<sup>[1]</sup>

Talks on reunification have made little progress. In 2011, in the only substantive bilateral negotiations ([[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]]), the IAC walked out after being offered one-third of the seats in a unified legislature, a share its delegates said did not reflect the ATR's population or its six-sevenths of the land. Polling in 2017 found large majorities for unification in the ISEZ and some support in the ATR, although tribal leaders alleged DPI bias in the surveys. Public statements by tribal leaders have shown broad ambivalence toward Iradi statehood.

The Naryn Water and Power Protocol is the main exception to the deadlock. A joint technical commission of ISEZ and ATR engineers sets Toktogul's annual release schedule under UNMI supervision, with observers from Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan. The 2009 corridor protocol, which moved the dam into the ISEZ, kept the tribal delegation's equal place on the commission and made the clans' consent a condition of each five-year schedule. Tribal elders have used this customary veto over drawing down the reservoir to bargain for compensation for flooded pastures, while ISEZ officials accuse them of obstructing export contracts. The five-year schedule falls due for renewal in 2027.<sup>[7]</sup>

UNMI patrols the demarcation line with unarmed military observers, mediates local disputes over strayed livestock and water, coordinates mine clearance and arranges humanitarian access to the tribal side. Bektur Zhumabek uulu is its main interlocutor in the ATR. The [[wp:Special Committee on Decolonization|UN Special Committee on Decolonization]], which lists Irad as a non-self-governing territory, covers the ATR in its annual working paper on the territory.<sup>[1]</sup> Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan each claim Irad *de jure* and deal with the ATR mainly through border and water arrangements.

## Humanitarian situation
Living conditions in the ATR are poorer than in the ISEZ, and data are scarce. Many highland settlements have no year-round road access. Although the Toktogul complex lies just below the tribal mountains, UNMI reports that some remote villages have no grid electricity and rely on small generators or solar panels.<sup>[3]</sup> Health care rests on village health posts, mobile clinics run since 1996 by the [[St. Luka Community Health Mission|Luka Community Health Mission]] of the Syro-Iradi Catholic Church, and UNMI-supported vaccination campaigns for children and livestock. Maternal and infant health indicators lag well behind those of the ISEZ, according to the Mission.<sup>[10]</sup>

Severe winters periodically kill large numbers of animals and leave households short of food, particularly in the Northern Steppe. Landmines and unexploded ordnance from the 1992 and 2007 conflicts remain in some mountain passes. Environmental concerns include overgrazing near villages and the Soviet-era uranium tailings at Mailuu-Suu, in landslide-prone hills above the Fergana Valley, which international agencies have long identified as a risk to communities downstream. Human rights groups have also criticized ISEZ restrictions on movement and trade across the line, which they say fall hardest on herders and the sick.<sup>[6]</sup>

### 3.25. Irad Special Economic Zone
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Politics & Government*
