The **Irad Special Economic Zone** (ISEZ; Iradi: *Irad Atayın Ekonomikalık Zonası*) is the part of [[Irad]] administered by the government of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI). It covers about 29,400 square kilometers (11,350 sq mi), roughly one-seventh of the country: the irrigated Talas valley, the Chu lowlands around [[Nurzhan]], the belts along the main road and railway that join them and run west to the Kazakh frontier, an industrial corridor south of [[Talas]], the corridor of State Route 1 across the mountains to the Toktogul basin and down the [[Naryn River|Naryn]] gorge, and the river flats of the lower Naryn with the farm belt of the northern Fergana rim. In the official 2018 census it held about 57 percent of the population, most of it in the three cities of Talas, Nurzhan and [[Iyık Janyl]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> The other six-sevenths of Irad, the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), lie beyond the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]].

[[Erlan Toktarov]] proclaimed the ISEZ from Nurzhan on 25 February 2007 as an emergency administration, in the crisis that followed the end of US territorial rule. Its present extent was fixed by the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] in September of that year. The zone is governed through the institutions of the former US territory: an elected Governor and Lieutenant Governor, the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] and the [[Supreme Court of Irad]]. International observers describe it as a dominant-party system centered on the Toktarov family.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[4]</sup> Talas is the *de jure* capital. Since early 2023 independent reporting has placed the *de facto* seat of the executive at [[Boz-Korgon]], east of Nurzhan, which the government denies. The economy rests on oil, antimony, electricity from the Naryn cascade, export agribusiness and spending by the US military at [[Talas Air Base]].

## Name and status
The 2007 proclamation used the term "special economic zone", which analysts read as a signal to foreign companies that their concessions would be protected after the collapse of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] (DRI).<sup>[1]</sup> The ISEZ government does not describe itself as the government of a separate region. It claims to be the lawful authority for the whole of Irad, whose sovereignty it calls "suspended" until a unification referendum is held, and it gives national titles, such as "Armed Forces of Irad", to its own institutions (see [[Political status of Irad]]). The clan councils of the ATR and the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC) reject this claim. No state recognizes the ISEZ as a sovereign government, and [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] each claim Irad *de jure*. In everyday usage the ISEZ is often called "the governorate" or "the Zone".

## History

#### Origins (2006–2007)
The ISEZ grew out of the political collapse that followed the [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)|US territorial period]]. President [[wp:George W. Bush]] withdrew the United States from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] by executive action on 3 December 2006. The Supreme Court then issued the [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]], and the Territorial Legislature proclaimed the DRI on 9 December. In January and February 2007 the DRI cabinet of [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] sold state concessions to firms linked to DPI members, provoking protests in Talas and unrest in the countryside (see [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]]).<sup>[1]</sup>

On 25 February 2007 Toktarov, a former Majority Leader of the Territorial Senate, made public the DRI cabinet's secret drafts to partition Irad among Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan (see [[Bill of Sale (2007)]]), seized control of the DPI apparatus and proclaimed the ISEZ from Nurzhan. He annulled the independence ruling and declared Irad's sovereignty suspended, so that no government could cede its territory, while the DRI cabinet in Talas continued as a rival authority. The date marks the start of the [[Second Iradi Civil War]]. Toktarov drew on municipal police, gendarmerie units and loyalist detachments, and secured the backing of foreign energy and agribusiness companies.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Consolidation (2007–2011)
The [[Popular Front of Irad]] stormed Talas on 4 June 2007, dissolved the DRI and then withdrew to the countryside. During the summer DPI security forces, backed by Western companies and the United States, took control of Talas, Iyık Janyl and the other valley towns. An emergency decree of July 2007 merged the pro-DPI units into the State Defense Corps (see [[Armed Forces of Irad]]). The Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement of September 2007 fixed the Qara-Chik line between the ISEZ and the clan-held countryside, and the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI) was established on 18 October 2007 to monitor it.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[5]</sup> A UN-brokered protocol of July 2009 brought the State Route 1 corridor and the floor of the Toktogul basin, with the dam, into the ISEZ, in exchange for the high Kyrgyz Range pastures east of the Kök-Bel road, grazing and water rights and a guaranteed share of the dam's export revenue for the clans.

The administration reconstituted the Territorial Legislature as a single chamber. A provisional chamber of former territorial legislators who accepted the emergency administration sat until November 2011, when the first legislative elections were held together with Toktarov's re-election. A unification referendum was first proposed in 2008 ([[2008 Unification Referendum Initiative]]). The only direct talks with the IAC, in 2011, ended when its delegation walked out after being offered one-third of the seats in a reunified legislature (see [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]]).<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Toktarov's governorship (2011–2023)
In 2013 the legislature amended the [[Elective Governor Acts (1992)|1992 Elective Governor Acts]] to remove gubernatorial term limits ([[2013 Constitutional Amendment]]), and Toktarov won further terms in 2015, 2019 and 2023. Members of his family took senior posts. His eldest son, [[Ruslan Toktarov]], has commanded the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] since 2012; his second son, [[Alikhan Toktarov]], has chaired [[IradOne]] since 2015; and his son-in-law, [[Aidar Maksat]], became Lieutenant Governor in November 2019.<sup>[6]</sup> Trade with China grew through antimony exports and Chinese investment in cotton processing, while the US basing arrangements continued. In 2021, after the [[wp:Taliban]] returned to power in [[wp:Afghanistan]], the ISEZ declared a security alert and reinforced the mountain passes ([[The 2021 Regional Security Alert]]).

#### Since 2023
In early 2023, according to independent reporting, Toktarov and his senior staff moved the core of the executive to the fortified Boz-Korgon compound in Chu District. The government maintains that Talas remains the operational capital.<sup>[7]</sup> In October 2023 a municipal licensing surcharge in Talas set off student and courier protests, which police and Gendarmerie units dispersed; the surcharge was suspended in November ([[2023 Student Protests in Talas]]).

Toktarov has not appeared in public since July 2024. The DPI attributes his absence to an extended health retreat, and Maksat runs the government's day-to-day business (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]). In 2025, remarks by [[wp:Donald Trump|US President Donald Trump]] about selling Irad to Russia provoked demonstrations in Talas and anti-American feeling across the zone ([[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]]). The next [[2027 Iradi gubernatorial election|gubernatorial]] and legislative elections, and the renewal of the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]], are due in 2027.

## Government and politics
*Main article: [[Government of the Irad Special Economic Zone]]*

#### Legal basis
The ISEZ has no constitution of its own. It treats the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]] and the statutes of the territorial period as still in force, regards their provisions on federal oversight as inoperative, and amends them through the legislature. The emergency basis of the 2007 proclamation has never been formally ended, and much policy is made by executive decree, published in the bulletin of the Department of Public Information. [[wp:Human Rights Watch]] and other critics argue that this arrangement leaves the executive largely unchecked.<sup>[8]</sup>

#### Executive
Executive power is vested in the Governor, who is elected by popular vote for a four-year term in November under the Elective Governor Acts of 1992. Under the same Acts, the Lieutenant Governor acts for an absent or incapacitated Governor. Toktarov, who also chairs the DPI, has been Governor since 2007. Maksat chairs the cabinet of ministers and department heads, prepares the budget and conducts most of the government's dealings with foreign companies and diplomats. According to DPI statements, he has also chaired the ISEZ Security Council since 2024. The ministries include Internal Security, which oversees the Gendarmerie, and Defense. The Department of Public Information is the government's press office.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Legislature and courts
The Territorial Legislature (*[[Mejlis]]*) sits in Legislative Hall in Talas. Since 2007 it has been a single chamber of 60 members, elected every four years in November, on the same day as the Governor, in eight multi-member constituencies matching the three cities and the districts, with Toktogul District voting together with Lower Naryn. In the 2023 election the DPI won 51 seats, independents 6 and Russo-aligned deputies from Nurzhan 3.<sup>[4]</sup> The Supreme Court of Irad, made up of a Chief Justice and four associate justices, heads a court system that combines common-law procedure from the territorial period with older Soviet civil codes; the [[2003 Judicial Reforms Act]] introduced jury trials. The court's jurisdiction does not extend into the ATR.

#### Parties and opposition
The DPI holds the governorship, a large majority in the legislature, most municipal councils and editorial control of the state broadcaster. [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe|OSCE]] observers have said that the elections held since 2011 lacked meaningful choice. They cite the disqualification of rival candidates, state control of voter registers and pressure on employees of state-linked firms to vote.<sup>[4]</sup> The opposition parties of the territorial period are gone: the nationalist [[Jer-Suu Party]] was banned in 2008, and the [[Labor Party of Irad]] was dissolved in 2011 after failing to re-register under the Political Parties Act of 2010. The most visible opposition currents are the Russian-speaking "Russo" constituency of Nurzhan, whose best-known figure is [[Kamran Bekzatov]], president of [[NurGaz]] (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]), and the anarcho-capitalist commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]]. Leaked US intelligence reports described the administration as neopatrimonial.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Administrative divisions
The ISEZ is divided into three cities of governorate significance and six districts (*aimak*); the sixth, Toktogul District, was split from Lower Naryn District in 2016. Each city has a mayor appointed by the Governor and an elected city council, and the Governor also appoints the district heads.<sup>[3]</sup> City populations are 2018 official estimates.

| Unit | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| [[Talas]] | City | *De jure* capital and commercial center; 1,120,000, or 1.4 million in the metropolitan area |
| [[Nurzhan]] | City | Industrial center and headquarters of NurGaz; 850,000, or more than 1 million in the agglomeration |
| [[Iyık Janyl]] | City | Seat of the Archbishop of Iyık Janyl and pilgrimage center; 310,000 |
| Talas District | District | The middle and upper Talas valley around the capital up to the crest of the Kyrgyz Range, including Talas Air Base and the Otmek valley |
| Kara-Buura District | District | The lower Talas valley with [[Kyzyl-Adyr]] and [[Aulie-Ata]], the belt along the highway and railway west to the Kazakh frontier, and the plain north of the western Kyrgyz Range east to the Merke stream |
| Chu District | District | The Chu lowlands around Nurzhan, including the oil fields and the Boz-Korgon area, and the road and rail belt north of the Kyrgyz Range east of the Merke stream |
| Sary-Bulak District | District | The southern industrial corridor and foothills south of Talas, including the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]], the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]] and the foothill villages along the Chatkal road |
| Lower Naryn District | District | The river flats around [[Tash-Kömür]] and the city of Iyık Janyl, the farm belt of the northern Fergana rim east past [[Bazar-Korgon]] to the Uzbek frontier, and a narrow corridor up the Naryn gorge from the Uch-Kurgan dam at its mouth to Kara-Köl, just below the Toktogul dam |
| Toktogul District | District | The floor of the Toktogul basin with the town of [[Toktogul (town)|Toktogul]], the reservoir and the dam, and the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]] corridor over the [[Fergana Gateway]] north to the Otmek Tunnel |

Nurzhan's urban districts include [[Dastgoh District|Dastgoh]] and [[Navbahor District|Navbahor]]. See also [[Administrative divisions of Irad]].

## Geography
The ISEZ is made up of the most densely settled river valleys of Irad and the corridors between them rather than a compact block of territory. Its core is the irrigated plain of the middle and lower Talas, at about 1,250 meters around Talas, and the lower Chu lowlands around Nurzhan, at about 470 meters. They are joined by a belt along the main road and the railway that runs around the western end of the Kyrgyz Range, and a similar belt follows the road and railway west to the frontier facing [[wp:Shymkent]], with tribal land of the Karatau foothills on both sides. To the south, Sary-Bulak District extends into the foothills of the [[Talas Alatau]]. East of Talas, the Fergana Mountain Transit Highway leaves the valley at the mouth of the Otmek valley and crosses the mountains and the Toktogul basin, which form Toktogul District, to the Lower Naryn District around Tash-Kömür, where the Naryn leaves the mountains for the [[wp:Fergana Valley]]. Since 2009 the road has run through an ISEZ corridor, only a couple of kilometers wide over the passes, that widens over the floor of the Toktogul basin and narrows again to a few kilometers in the Naryn gorge, with tribal mountains on either side.<sup>[5]</sup> Below the gorge the ISEZ widens over the river flats at Iyık Janyl and Tash-Kömür and over the farm belt of the northern Fergana rim, which runs east below the foot of the hills past Bazar-Korgon, the zone's main Muslim town, and which the lowland Chubar brought into the ISEZ in 2007. In the north the ISEZ faces Kazakhstan along about 285 kilometers of frontier, marked under the 2008 [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]], a technical arrangement that Kazakhstan says implies no recognition. In the south it holds about 145 kilometers of the frontier with Uzbekistan along the farm belt, undemarcated but covered since February 2025 by a memorandum on trade and border coordination. Elsewhere it is bounded by the Qara-Chik line.

Much of the zone's water comes from outside it. The [[Talas River|Talas]] and the [[Kara-Buura]] rise on the tribal side of the line, and the Chu flows in from upstream Kyrgyzstan. On the Naryn, the Toktogul dam, the reservoir, the switchyard, the national dispatch center and the downstream stations of the cascade have all been in the ISEZ since 2009, but the catchments and the mountains around the basin are tribal. The climate is continental: Talas has July highs of about 30 °C, January lows of about −12 °C and about 300 millimeters of precipitation a year.

## Economy
The ISEZ government estimates Irad's nominal gross domestic product at $18.4 billion for 2024, or about $50 billion at purchasing power parity. Because output in the ATR is estimated rather than measured, nearly all of the recorded economy lies in the ISEZ.<sup>[9]</sup> The US dollar is legal tender and the [[Iradi som]] circulates alongside it. [[Talasbank]] dominates commercial banking and holds the main export escrow accounts, which are audited by the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]].

The main sectors are:<sup>[9]</sup><sup>[10]</sup>
- **Oil.** NurGaz produces light crude in the Chu basin. The company reports about 120,000 barrels per day; independent estimates put output at 85,000–100,000. Part is refined at the [[Nurzhan Oil Refinery]]. Since 2000 most of the rest has been exported north through the 85-kilometer [[Northern Export Feeder]] into the [[wp:KazTransOil]] network, for refining at Shymkent or shipment to Russia. There is no southern export pipeline. NurGaz is the zone's largest taxpayer.
- **Mining.** Irad holds about 7 percent of world antimony reserves. Ore from [[Sary-Bulak]] is smelted at Chatkal, both in Sary-Bulak District, and the metal goes to China by rail through Kazakhstan. Both plants belong to the [[Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine]].
- **Electricity.** The ISEZ controls the export grid of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] (1,440 MW) and sells power mainly to Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan. Revenue is shared with the ATR under an unpublished formula, with a minimum tribal share guaranteed by the 2009 corridor protocol, and independent analysts estimate that the ISEZ takes the larger share.
- **Agribusiness.** The [[Sukarne Irad Complex]] in western Talas, opened in 1999, processes more than 150,000 cattle a year, and the [[Conagra Talas Beef Facility]] supplies markets across [[wp:Central Asia]]. Cotton is grown mainly in the Lower Naryn District. [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]] dominates feed milling, and bonded zones such as the [[Talas Agribusiness Export Zone]] (1998) process goods for export.
- **US military spending.** Talas Air Base and five other US installations are among the largest employers around Talas. The Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Irad estimates that base contracts bring about $450 million a year into the zone.
- **Services and transport.** [[Attelkom]] provides telecommunications, [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]] runs bonded trucking to the northern crossings, and [[Iradiya]] flies charter and cargo services from Talas.

Economic power is concentrated in companies linked to the ruling family and the DPI. Toktarov's sons [[Timur Toktarov|Timur]], [[Adil Toktarov|Adil]] and [[Bekzat Toktarov|Bekzat]] run family businesses in freight, commercial real estate and feed milling, and Alikhan holds real-estate and retail interests alongside his chairmanship of IradOne. Bekzatov and Ilyasov have both attacked these monopolies.<sup>[11]</sup> Non-recognition denies the ISEZ a sovereign credit rating and access to the [[wp:International Monetary Fund]]. Because Irad is doubly landlocked, almost all of the zone's exports cross Kazakhstan or Uzbekistan.

## Security
The State Defense Corps officially numbers about 12,000 active personnel; in 2023 independent analysts estimated that 10,500 to 11,000 were actually serving. Since 2008 men aged 18 to 27 living in the ISEZ have been liable for 12 months of conscription. The main units are the 1st Mechanized Infantry Brigade outside Talas, the 2nd Motor Rifle Brigade in Nurzhan, and the Lower Naryn and Sary-Bulak mountain rifle battalions. Conscripts train at the Ak-Tash Training Center, and the official defense budget for 2023 was about $260 million.<sup>[12]</sup>

The Republican Gendarmerie, about 4,000 strong, answers to the Ministry of Internal Security. It mans the checkpoints at the Qara-Chik line's crossing points, nine in all, guards the perimeter of Talas Air Base, and through its Special Protective Service protects senior officials and the Boz-Korgon compound. Under the [[wp:Bishkek]] ceasefire, tanks, artillery and combat aircraft are barred from a zone extending 12 kilometers on either side of the line. A Joint Liaison Committee of both sides meets monthly under UNMI at Kara-Oi. Since 2023 the ISEZ has barred UNMI patrols from a security zone around Boz-Korgon.<sup>[5]</sup> US forces remain at Talas Air Base and five other sites under the [[2001 Basing Rights Agreement]] and later arrangements with the ISEZ, and hold an annual exercise with the corps, *Alatau Shield*.

## Demographics
The 2018 census counted about 2.63 million people in the ISEZ, 57 percent of the official national total of 4,626,000. Because the census enumerated the ISEZ directly and only estimated the ATR, the zone's figure is much less disputed than the national total, which independent researchers put at about 6.2 million (see [[2018 Irad census]]).<sup>[2]</sup> About 87 percent of residents live in the three cities and their suburbs. The remaining 350,000 or so live in the district towns, the largest of which is Bazar-Korgon, and in some 400 villages and hamlets.

[[Iradis]] form the large majority. Nearly all of Irad's migrant and foreign communities live in the ISEZ: the Russian, Ukrainian and [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]] communities are concentrated in Nurzhan, more than 10,000 [[Mexicans in Irad|Mexicans]] live in and around Talas, and American residents are linked to the bases and their contractors. Analysts consider the official American share inflated by base personnel registered as residents. Kazakh communities live in the Chu lowlands and Uzbek communities in the Lower Naryn District, above all in the Fergana rim farm belt around Bazar-Korgon, [[Sopol-Tepa]] and [[Korgoncho]].<sup>[2]</sup>

Iradi and English are the official languages. Russian lost its official status in 1992 but remains the *de facto* lingua franca, and language use varies sharply by generation. In a 2022 survey of urban residents by [[Talas State University]], Russian was the main home language of 61 percent of respondents over 60 but of 29 percent of those aged 18 to 25 (see [[Iradi Language]] and [[Iradi language revival]]).<sup>[13]</sup> Most residents belong to the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], whose mother see is at Iyık Janyl. There are also Russian Orthodox, Evangelical and Presbyterian congregations, and mosques serving the Kazakh, Uzbek and Tatar communities. The ISEZ is a secular state.

## Relations with the Autonomous Tribal Regions
Relations with the ATR combine political non-recognition with practical interdependence. Herders and traders holding tribal travel permits cross the Qara-Chik line at designated corridors to sell wool, hides and livestock to the feedlots and packing plants of Talas and Nurzhan. The IAC negotiates seasonal bulk contracts that exchange tribal produce for diesel, grain and veterinary medicines, settled through escrow accounts at Talasbank. Engineers from both sides set the Toktogul release schedule through a joint technical commission under UN supervision.<sup>[5]</sup> The ISEZ accuses IAC-aligned groups of smuggling goods past its checkpoints through the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]]. Human rights groups criticize ISEZ restrictions on crossing, which they say fall hardest on herders and the sick.<sup>[8]</sup> The size of the tribal population, which would determine its weight in any unified legislature, remains a central point of dispute.

## Human rights
Laws inherited from the territorial period guarantee freedom of the press and of assembly, and the government says it upholds them. Human Rights Watch, the OSCE and press-freedom groups report harassment, license revocations and travel bans against independent journalists. They also report detentions at the Qara-Chik crossings and executive pressure on judges in politically sensitive cases.<sup>[8]</sup> During the October 2023 protests, mobile data in central Talas was cut for three days. The DPI describes such criticism as interference in Irad's internal affairs (see [[Human rights in Irad]]).

### 3.26. Qara-Chik Demarcation Line
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Politics & Government*

The **Qara-Chik Demarcation Line** (Iradi: *Qara-Chik chek ara sızığı*) is the ceasefire line, about 1,750 kilometers (1,090 mi) long, that divides [[Irad]] between the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), governed by the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI), and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), held by the country's pastoral clans. It was fixed in September 2007 by the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]], which ended the main fighting of the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], and adjusted in the south by a protocol of 2009. Since 2007 it has been monitored by the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI).<sup>[1]</sup> The line encloses the irrigated valleys of the Talas and lower Chu, the belts along the main road and railway that join them and run west to the Kazakh frontier, and a corridor along State Route 1 that crosses the [[Talas Alatau]], widens over the floor of the Toktogul basin and follows the Naryn gorge, a few kilometers wide, down to the river flats of the Lower Naryn District and the farm belt of the northern Fergana rim. Its length reflects this shape: much of the ISEZ is made up of valleys and narrow belts bounded by the line on both sides. Until 2009 the line divided the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]], placing the dam on the tribal side and the switchyard and export lines on the ISEZ side; since then the whole complex has been in the ISEZ.

Neither administration treats the line as a boundary between states. The ISEZ describes it as an administrative line within a single Irad whose sovereignty is suspended, and the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC) as the limit of the land held by the clans. On the ISEZ side, the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] mans checkpoints at nine crossing points; on the tribal side, the mounted [[El-Choro Militias]] keep posts at the crossings and picket stations along the line. Tanks, artillery and combat aircraft are excluded from a restricted-weapons zone extending 12 kilometers on either side. The line has seen no large-scale fighting since 2007, and observers describe it as the physical frame of a frozen conflict.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Name
The line takes its name from Qara-Chik, a village at the mouth of the Kara-Buura valley south of [[Kyzyl-Adyr]], marked on Soviet maps as Chong-Kara-Buura; Qara-Chik is the older local name. The main crossing point, the [[Qara-Chik Border Checkpoint]], was set up just above it in 2007, where the road into the Chatkal valley leaves the plain, and the negotiators in [[wp:Bishkek]] used the village name for the line as a whole. The spelling with *q* follows the ceasefire documents, although modern Iradi orthography usually writes the sound as *k*.<sup>[1]</sup>

Older people in the valleys often call the line simply the *Kordon*, the name of the Soviet control line along the foot of the mountains that it partly follows (see below); Russian speakers in [[Nurzhan]] also say *rezhimka*, from the Soviet "regime zone".<sup>[3]</sup>

## History

#### Soviet precedent: the Kordon
A boundary along the foot of the mountains existed long before 2007, although it had other purposes and did not follow the same course. Before the First World War the surveyors of the Russian Resettlement Administration marked the edge of the plots allotted to Russian and Ukrainian settlers on the valley floors and the lower fans of the Talas and Chu valleys, and the land above them was left to the clans; this edge became a grievance in the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|revolt of 1916]].<sup>[4]</sup> The [[Decree on Pasture Collectivization (1932)]] divided the republic's land into a valley zone of collective and state farms and a mountain pasture fund run by republican livestock trusts, and the boundary between them, known in Iradi as the *mal chegi* ("stock boundary"), was drawn along the upper edge of the irrigated land.<sup>[4]</sup>

In 1946, after uranium was found at [[Mailuu-Suu]] and antimony and other ores were prospected in the Talas Alatau and the [[Chatkal Range]], the mountains of the south were declared a special regime zone, the [[Talas–Chatkal Regime Zone]]. The Ministry of Internal Affairs set up checkpoints at the mouths of the mountain valleys, mostly on the line of the old stock boundary, and entry above them required a pass (*propusk*). Herders received seasonal passes for their flocks, and the zone also served to watch the high valleys where the hidden clergy of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] still said the liturgy. Iradis called the line of posts the *Kordon*.<sup>[3]</sup> The regime was lifted in 1968, when uranium processing at Mailuu-Suu ended, but the republican veterinary service kept the posts as cordon stations where livestock moving between the mountains and the valleys was inspected for foot-and-mouth disease and brucellosis. They were staffed until 1991.<sup>[3]</sup> During the [[First Iradi Civil War]] the procurement brigades of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] worked from some of the old posts, and clan scouts held the pastures above them.

The Kordon explains how quickly the 2007 line was put in place. Where the forces of the [[Popular Front of Irad]] withdrew to the pastures that summer, the positions on the two sides settled along much of the old line. Soviet topographic maps, on which the cordon stations are marked, and the land-use maps of the pasture fund were among those used in Bishkek, and the central sector and much of the southern sector follow the Kordon for long stretches. Many of the ISEZ's checkpoints and forward posts, among them the Qara-Chik Border Checkpoint, stand on the sites of Soviet cordon stations, whose buildings, barriers and access roads were repaired rather than built. The Kordon ran only along the mountain front of the Talas Alatau, the Chatkal and the Naryn foothills; the belts along the road and railway in the west and north and the straight surveyed stretches across the steppe were new in 2007, and the corridor of State Route 1 and the Toktogul basin, which the 2009 protocol added to the ISEZ, had lain inside the regime zone.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

#### Origins
The line reflects the positions held at the end of the summer of 2007. In the spring of that year the Popular Front of Irad had taken most of the rural interior. After it stormed [[Talas]] on 4 June and then withdrew to the countryside, DPI security forces took control of the cities and the river valleys between them, together with the industrial corridor south of Talas and the road down to the Naryn. In August the lowland Chubar elders of [[Bazar-Korgon]] and the farm belt of the northern Fergana rim, whose trading families credited the ISEZ with stopping the [[Bill of Sale (2007)|Bill of Sale]], which would have handed the rim to Uzbekistan, declared for the ISEZ, and Gendarmerie units moved east from Tash-Kömür along the foot of the hills; the highland Chubar of [[Arslanbob]] and the Kara-Unkur valley stayed with the Front. Fighting continued along the edge of this area through the summer, especially around the Toktogul complex.<sup>[5]</sup>

UN mediators brought the two sides to Bishkek, and the ceasefire agreement signed there in September 2007 defined the line on Soviet-era 1:100,000 maps, along the positions held on an agreed date. It set up the restricted-weapons zone and a Joint Liaison Committee of the two sides, and its annex, the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]], dealt with the Toktogul complex. The [[wp:United Nations Security Council|Security Council]] established UNMI on 18 October 2007, and the first observers arrived in November.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Marking the line (2008–2011)
Joint survey teams of ISEZ and tribal representatives, accompanied by UN observers, marked the line on the ground between 2008 and 2011, placing numbered concrete pillars in the valleys and stone cairns on the high ridges.<sup>[2]</sup> The Gendarmerie's Border Demarcation Brigade, whose deputy commander at the time was [[Ruslan Toktarov]], built the fortified crossings on the ISEZ side and set up the inspection regime for people and goods. Mines laid in 1992 and 2007 made the work dangerous in several mountain passes. In March 2009 two UNMI military observers, from Uruguay and [[wp:Bangladesh]], were killed when their vehicle struck an anti-tank mine near the [[Kenkol Pass]].<sup>[6]</sup> Across the open steppe the surveyors laid the line out in long straight stretches between pillars, while in the mountains it follows foothills, rivers and crests.

#### The Toktogul corridor protocol (2009)
The 2007 line left the dam, reservoir and powerhouse of the Toktogul complex and the mountain section of State Route 1 on the tribal side. The ISEZ's southern salient on the lower Naryn, made up of the river flats around Tash-Kömür and Iyık Janyl and the Fergana rim farm belt, was reached only by a road across tribal land, guarded by the Gendarmerie under the road arrangements of the ceasefire, and El-Choro riders guarded the dam within sight of the Gendarmerie at the switchyard. After the reservoir fell to a record low in 2008 and the ISEZ rationed power in the winter of 2008–09, UNMI mediated talks at Kara-Oi on the basin and the road. The resulting Protocol on the Toktogul Basin and the State Route 1 Corridor, signed on 14 July 2009 and approved by that year's Kurultai on the [[Aksay Plateau]], moved the line in three places:<sup>[7]</sup>
- the corridor of State Route 1 from the upper Talas valley up the Otmek valley, through the Otmek Tunnel, across the western [[Suusamyr]] and over the [[Fergana Gateway]] passed to the ISEZ;
- the floor of the Toktogul basin, with the town of [[Toktogul (town)|Toktogul]], Kara-Köl, the dam, the reservoir and the powerhouse, and a corridor a few kilometers wide down the Naryn gorge to Iyık Janyl, holding the road, the river and the lower cascade stations, passed to the ISEZ, joining the Lower Naryn salient to the rest of the zone; the mountains on either side of the gorge remained tribal;
- the high Kyrgyz Range east of the Kök-Bel road, a summer pasture of the Talas Alatau clans, passed to the tribal side, with the village of [[Toguz-Bulak]].

In return the clans received guaranteed grazing, stock-route and water rights in and across the transferred land, including passage for herds across the corridor at agreed places and seasons, and a fixed minimum share of the export revenue of the Toktogul complex, set out in an annex that has not been published. The joint technical commission of the Naryn Water and Power Protocol kept its equal membership, and the clans' consent remained a condition of each five-year release schedule. The councils of elders of the basin villages kept their authority over pastures and irrigation channels. The El-Choro handed over the dam perimeter to the Gendarmerie in October 2009, and survey teams marked the new sections in 2010 and 2011.<sup>[7]</sup><sup>[8]</sup>

#### Since 2011
The line has remained largely quiet, although incidents are frequent. UNMI recorded 214 ceasefire violations in 2023. Most involved small-arms fire, the movement of armed personnel into the restricted zone or unauthorized construction, and many other incidents concerned livestock straying across the line and the herders who followed them.<sup>[2]</sup> The Joint Liaison Committee, which meets monthly at Kara-Oi, settles most incidents locally. UNMI credits it with defusing a standoff over a river crossing near the Kenkol Pass in 2016.<sup>[2]</sup> During [[The 2021 Regional Security Alert]], after the [[wp:Taliban]] returned to power in [[wp:Afghanistan]], ISEZ forces and El-Choro riders reinforced checkpoints on the mountain passes and set up a channel for sharing intelligence.

## Course
The line is not continuous with Irad's international borders. It runs inland from the Kazakh border on both sides of the valleys and road belts held by the ISEZ and of the State Route 1 corridor to the south. Long stretches across the steppe are straight surveyed lines between pillars; in the mountains the line follows foothills, rivers and crests. UNMI divides it into four sectors:<sup>[2]</sup>
- **Western sector** (about 275 km). From the Kazakh frontier facing [[wp:Shymkent]], the line runs along both sides of a belt that follows the [[Trans-Talas Highway]] and the railway east to the lower Talas valley, so that the main road and the Talas North Terminal lie wholly inside the ISEZ while the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] foothills on either side are tribal, among them the canyons of [[Kök-Moinok]], the hamlets of [[Tar-Say]] and [[Hauzdy]] and the caravanserai of [[Rabat-i Kamal]]. Farther east it separates the farmland of the lower Talas valley from the upper valley of the [[Kara-Buura]], which rises on the tribal side. Here, at the mouth of the Kara-Buura valley, is the main crossing, the Qara-Chik Border Checkpoint, on the only road from the ISEZ into the Chatkal valley. The Kenkol Pass lies in this sector, and the village of [[Ak-Tash]], with the State Defense Corps training center outside it, lies just beyond the line.
- **Central sector** (about 465 km). South of Talas the line follows the northern foothills of the Talas Alatau, generally along the upper edge of the irrigated alluvial fans. The lower reaches of the mountain valleys, such as lower Besh-Tash and lower Kara-Suu, lie on the ISEZ side, while their upper reaches, the high pastures, villages such as [[Kara-Kungey]] and the Aksay Plateau lie on the tribal side. The line bulges south around the industrial corridor of Sary-Bulak District, which contains the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] and the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]]. The UNMI headquarters at Kara-Oi is in this sector. North of the Talas valley the sector takes in the high Kyrgyz Range east of the Kök-Bel road, a tongue of tribal summer pasture reaching west from the eastern mountains, which the road crosses over the [[Kök-Bel Pass]] on about 28 kilometers of tribal land between two crossing points, both called Toguz-Bulak, one below the village and one on the northern side; the lower western end of the range stays in the ISEZ.
- **Southern (Naryn and Fergana rim) sector** (about 475 km). The line runs along both sides of the corridor of the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]] from the Talas valley up the Otmek valley, through the Otmek Tunnel, across the western Suusamyr, over the Fergana Gateway (Ala-Bel Pass, 3,184 m) and down the Chychkan valley. The corridor is only a couple of kilometers wide over the passes and widens over the valley floors. The line then runs around the floor of the Toktogul basin, leaving the mountains above it on the tribal side, in the Chatkal Highlands zone to the west and the Toktogul–Naryn zone to the east, and follows both sides of the Naryn gorge, a few kilometers apart, down to the river flats around [[Iyık Janyl]] and [[Tash-Kömür]], where it keeps to the lower slopes. Below Tash-Kömür it turns east along the foot of the hills above the farm belt of the northern Fergana rim, leaving Mailuu-Suu, the Kara-Unkur valley and Arslanbob on the tribal side and Bazar-Korgon on the ISEZ side, and meets the external frontier north of [[wp:Jalal-Abad]], which lies in Kyrgyzstan, on the river that marks the frontier below the [[Kök-Kamar Gorge]]; the Kök-Kamar road crosses it above Kyzyl-Senir at the Kök-Kamar crossing. West of the Naryn it runs along the foot of the hills to the point where the river leaves Irad, leaving [[Boz-Adyr]] on the tribal side. UNMI's sector headquarters is at Tash-Kömür.
- **Northern sector** (about 535 km). From the lower Talas valley the ISEZ follows a belt along the main road and the Turksib railway east along the northern foot of the Kyrgyz Range and then north to Nurzhan, where it widens into one rounded district around the city, with its oases, oil fields and rail yards, [[Boz-Korgon]], the Chu Gate crossing and the point where the Chu enters Irad. The line runs along both sides of the belt, facing the [[Moiynkum Desert|Moiynkum sands]] and the [[Betpak-Dala]] steppe of the ATR's Northern Steppe zone on one side and the foothills of the Kyrgyz Range on the other. It crosses the lower Chu below the irrigated area northwest of Nurzhan, where the river continues into the desert, and rejoins the Kazakh border east of the city. Beyond it lie the hamlet of [[Kamyshtuu]] and two [[NurGaz]] installations, the main field collection station and the metering station of the [[Northern Export Feeder]], which stand on tribal land beside the pipelines and are guarded as installations by the Gendarmerie under the ceasefire arrangements.

## Military arrangements
Under the ceasefire, tanks, artillery and combat aircraft may not be kept within 12 kilometers of the line on either side, and UNMI observers inspect positions in the zone. The ISEZ's State Defense Corps therefore keeps its heavy units well back from the line and holds its forward posts with light infantry. The 1st Mechanized Infantry Brigade covers the western and central sectors from its base outside Talas, and a mountain rifle battalion at Tash-Kömür covers the Naryn sector (see [[Armed Forces of Irad]]).<sup>[9]</sup> The El-Choro, which have no heavy weapons, keep mounted pickets in stone shelters and herders' huts, rotated among the clan detachments. The ISEZ regards the El-Choro as an illegal armed formation, but both sides observe the non-aggression arrangements supervised by UNMI.

## Crossings and movement
Civilian movement across the line is limited to designated corridors, with nine crossing points: the Qara-Chik Border Checkpoint, the main crossing, at the mouth of the Kara-Buura valley, where herders, Chatkal clan traders and traders from the Fergana valley use the road over the [[Karakoyun Pass]]; the [[Aksay Border Patrol Post]]; the two Toguz-Bulak crossings on the Kök-Bel road; the [[Kara-Bulak]] crossing on the Kenkol Pass road, at about 1,260 meters; the Suusamyr crossing on the road to [[Karakol]], at about 2,660 meters the highest; and two minor crossings on the valley roads from the Fergana rim farm belt, the Mailuu-Suu road crossing at about 900 meters and the Arslanbob road crossing at about 1,000 meters, some 20 kilometers above Bazar-Korgon, used mostly by local families, walnut and apricot traders and visitors to Arslanbob; and the minor Kök-Kamar crossing, added when the Kök-Kamar road was built in the 2010s, where the road leaves the ISEZ above Kyzyl-Senir for the Kök-Kamar Gorge and the tribal road to Jerge-Tal and Kök-Jangak. Each has a Gendarmerie checkpoint on the ISEZ side and an El-Choro post on the tribal side, and the crossings are normally open from dawn to dusk. The Gendarmerie also keeps four internal control posts inside the ISEZ: at the mouth of the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]] and, on State Route 1, at the mouth of the Otmek valley, the Fergana Gateway and the Naryn bridge, the last three internal posts since 2009 rather than line crossings.<sup>[10]</sup>
- **Herders and traders.** Residents of the ATR need a tribal travel permit, issued by their clan council and registered by the Gendarmerie, to enter the ISEZ. Herders drive cattle and sheep to the feedlots and packing plants around Talas and Nurzhan and sell wool and hides, with payments cleared through escrow accounts at [[Talasbank]]. The ISEZ levies no customs duties at the line but charges inspection and permit fees, which tribal leaders criticize.
- **Seasonal migration.** Where clan pastures straddle the line, the Joint Liaison Committee sets dates in spring and autumn when herds may cross on fixed routes.
- **Pilgrims.** Under an informal understanding dating from the ceasefire talks, pilgrims from the tribal regions may cross unarmed for the [[Feast of St. Janyl]] on 24 August at Iyık Janyl.
- **Engineers.** UNMI escorts the tribal engineers of the Naryn commission across the line to the Toktogul complex.

Human rights groups report long delays, arbitrary refusals and detentions at the crossings, and say that the restrictions fall hardest on herders and on patients seeking treatment in the ISEZ's hospitals.<sup>[11]</sup> The ISEZ accuses IAC-aligned groups of moving fuel, livestock and consumer goods past its checkpoints through disused galleries of the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]], some of whose shaft heads the Gendarmerie has sealed. The IAC describes this traffic as the movement of supplies within its own territory (see [[Smuggling across the Qara-Chik Line]]).

## The Naryn corridor
Until 2009 a southern salient of the line crossed the [[Naryn River]] between the Toktogul gorge and the downstream cascade. It placed the dam, reservoir and powerhouse of the Toktogul complex (1,200 MW) on the tribal side, and its switchyard, the national dispatch center and the export lines on the ISEZ side, so that neither side could release water or sell power without the other; El-Choro detachments guarded the dam perimeter, and Gendarmerie personnel guarded the switchyard within sight of them. Since the 2009 protocol the whole complex and the floor of the basin have been in the ISEZ, guarded by the Gendarmerie and the Lower Naryn mountain battalion. Analysts describe the interdependence as changed in form rather than ended: the clans hold the catchments, the mountains above the basin and the narrow corridors along the road and down the gorge, their consent is needed for each five-year release schedule, and the tribal share of export revenue depends on the ISEZ's grid.<sup>[8]</sup> Under the Naryn Water and Power Protocol, a joint technical commission of ISEZ and ATR engineers sets the annual release schedule under UN supervision, with observers from [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]]. The five-year release schedule falls due for renewal in 2027.

## Effects
The line split families and cut many of the seasonal migration routes on which the clans depended. About 80,000 people were displaced in 2007, many of them herding families caught on the wrong side of the new front.<sup>[5]</sup> It also separated the ISEZ's farms and power stations from the mountain catchments that feed them. Trade across the line has nonetheless continued. Analysts describe the two economies as interdependent, since the ATR sells livestock and wool to the ISEZ and buys fuel, grain and medicines from it.<sup>[8]</sup> Abolishing the line, or redrawing it beyond local adjustments such as those of 2009, would depend on a unification settlement. No direct talks between the two sides have taken place since the [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]] collapsed.

### 3.27. 2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Politics & Government*

The **2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis** is the name used by regional media and analysts for the political uncertainty in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) since July 2024, when Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] stopped appearing in public. The [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) attributes his absence to an extended health retreat and says that he continues to govern. Decrees and recorded addresses are still issued in his name.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> Opposition outlets and independent technology monitors allege signs of digital synthesis in the recorded broadcasts issued since then, which officials dismiss as foreign-sponsored disinformation.

In the Governor's absence, Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] has run the government day to day, and a rivalry over the succession between Toktarov's two eldest sons, [[Ruslan Toktarov|Ruslan]] and [[Alikhan Toktarov|Alikhan]], has become openly visible. The government rejects the description of the situation as a crisis. No formal finding of inability has been made under the [[Elective Governor Acts (1992)|Elective Governor Acts]], the DPI has named no successor, and the next gubernatorial election is due in late 2027 (see [[2027 Iradi gubernatorial election]]).<sup>[3]</sup>

## Background
Toktarov, born in 1954, has governed the ISEZ since he proclaimed it in February 2007. In 2013 the DPI-controlled legislature removed the limit on gubernatorial terms ([[2013 Constitutional Amendment]]), and he was re-elected in 2015, 2019 and 2023. The Elective Governor Acts of 1992 provide that the Lieutenant Governor acts for an absent or incapacitated Governor and succeeds to the office if it falls vacant. Members of Toktarov's family hold senior posts. Ruslan has commanded the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] since 2012, Alikhan has chaired the broadcaster [[IradOne]] since 2015, and Maksat, the husband of Toktarov's daughter [[Zara Toktarova]], became Lieutenant Governor in 2019. The three middle sons, [[Timur Toktarov|Timur]], [[Adil Toktarov|Adil]] and [[Bekzat Toktarov|Bekzat]], manage family businesses.<sup>[1]</sup>

In early 2023, according to independent reporting, Toktarov and his senior staff moved the core of the executive from [[Talas]] to the fortified [[Boz-Korgon]] compound east of [[Nurzhan]], a move the government denies. The same year the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]] were dispersed by police and Gendarmerie units.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Course of events

#### Withdrawal from public life (July–September 2024)
According to the *[[Talas Herald]]*, Toktarov's last confirmed public appearance was in early July 2024. Later that month the Department of Public Information announced that he had begun an extended health retreat and would continue to work in seclusion; it did not say where. Independent reporting places him at Boz-Korgon.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup> Maksat began chairing cabinet meetings and receiving foreign delegations, and official statements described him as acting on the Governor's instructions. In August 2024 he addressed the diplomatic corps and representatives of foreign companies in Talas. He pledged to honor existing agreements, including the arrangements for [[Talas Air Base]], to maintain economic stability and to pursue "pragmatic dialogue" with the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]].<sup>[5]</sup> On 2 September the General Staff of the State Defense Corps pledged loyalty to "the lawful administration" and has since kept out of public politics (see [[Armed Forces of Irad]]).<sup>[6]</sup>

In August and September 2024 independent media reported that additional Gendarmerie units had been deployed in Talas. Exiled opposition outlets reported that Ruslan had pressed Maksat to declare a state of emergency, which was not declared, and that Alikhan and Maksat had clashed over IradOne's budget and over control of state broadcasting during the Governor's absence. None of the three men has confirmed these accounts.<sup>[7]</sup>

#### Recorded addresses and synthesis allegations
Since the second half of 2024, recorded audio and video addresses attributed to Toktarov have been broadcast on IradOne, the only outlet to carry them. Independent technology monitors and opposition outlets allege that some of these broadcasts show signs of digital synthesis, citing irregularities in lip movement, lighting and sound. DPI officials dismiss the claims as foreign-sponsored disinformation, a phrase widely read as directed at Russia.<sup>[1]</sup> No journalist or foreign diplomat is known to have met the Governor since July 2024, journalists have not been admitted to Boz-Korgon, and UNMI patrols have been barred from a security zone around the compound since 2023.<sup>[4]</sup> Opposition figures have called for an independent medical statement. The commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]] has repeatedly challenged the government to show the Governor in a live, unedited appearance, a demand DPI spokesmen have dismissed as "theater".

#### Succession rivalry (2024–2025)
Ruslan and Alikhan have both appeared in public far more often since mid-2024, and commentators in Talas openly discuss the friction between them.<sup>[7]</sup> In December 2024, at a graduation ceremony at the [[Talas Gendarmerie Academy]] broadcast live on IradOne, Ruslan described Muslim communities in the Fergana Rim as "guests who have forgotten whose house they live in". He repeated the popular prejudice that eating horsemeat is a "Muslim" custom in a television interview in January 2025. Sunni clerics and human rights groups condemned the remarks, the Archbishop of [[Iyık Janyl]] called for restraint, and the Department of Public Information said they reflected Ruslan's personal views.<sup>[8]</sup> Analysts quoted in the regional press have speculated that Ruslan was removing officers loyal to Alikhan from municipal police commands; the claim has not been substantiated.

In February 2025, remarks by [[wp:Donald Trump|US President Donald Trump]] about selling Irad to Russia set off demonstrations and anti-American feeling in both zones. The administration responded with a formal demarche through the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (see [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]]). Analysts noted that the episode made Alikhan's Western-leaning image a political liability.<sup>[9]</sup>

#### The Naryn Protocol and the 2027 deadlines
The five-year release schedule of the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]] falls due for renewal in 2027, the same year as the next gubernatorial election. Uzbek and Kazakh officials have asked who will sign for the ISEZ. The DPI says that Maksat signs on the Governor's behalf.<sup>[10]</sup>

#### Toward the 2027 election (2026)
By October 2026 the DPI had not said whom it would nominate for the general election of 2 November 2027, saying only that the ticket would be chosen "at the proper time"; in 2023 its congress met in August. Toktarov would be 73 on polling day. Analysts quoted in the regional press discuss four possibilities: a Toktarov–Maksat ticket for continuity; Maksat at its head, favored by Talas administrators and business; Ruslan, with the support of the security services and nationalists; and Alikhan, who appeals to young urban voters but carries the liabilities of the 2025 backlash and of his reputation. None has declared. Under Election Commission procedures adopted in 2015 a candidate signs a residence declaration before a commissioner, and opposition figures argue that an absent Governor therefore cannot register, while the DPI says a commissioner can witness the declaration at the residence.<sup>[11]</sup> Russo-aligned lists in Nurzhan have discussed a joint opposition ticket.<sup>[12]</sup>

Public doubts have grown. In the Talas State University Institute of Sociology survey of March 2026, 61 percent of ISEZ respondents said that official information about the Governor's health was insufficient, up from 58 percent a year earlier.<sup>[13]</sup> At the Irad Day parades of 2025 and 2026 the Governor's stallion, [[Zharkyn (Horse)|Zharkyn]], led the mounted honor guard "in the Governor's place", led in hand under the Governor's parade saddle, with the Lieutenant Governor taking the salute. Traders and analysts also count the Governor's absence and the uncertain succession among the causes of the shortage of dollar cash in 2026, when the bazaar rate of the som rose to 11–12 to the dollar against the official 8.40 (see [[Talasbank]]).<sup>[14]</sup>

## Principal figures
The following public positions and roles are those reported in the regional press:<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[7]</sup>
- **Aidar Maksat**, the Lieutenant Governor, chairs the cabinet and, according to DPI statements, the ISEZ Security Council. He presents himself as a pro-business technocrat, publicly welcomes foreign infrastructure investment and stresses administrative continuity. He has made no public claim to the succession.
- **Ruslan Toktarov**, the eldest son, commands the Gendarmerie, including the Special Protective Service that guards Boz-Korgon, and the checkpoints on the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. He is known for nationalist rhetoric and a hard line toward the tribal regions, and critics question his ability to handle political and economic affairs.
- **Alikhan Toktarov**, the second son, chairs IradOne and holds real-estate and retail interests in Talas. He presents himself as a defender of commercial modernization. He is publicly seen as a reckless, Western-leaning figure, and tabloids in Talas have carried rumors of substance abuse and reckless spending that have not been substantiated. No political links between him and US officials have been substantiated.
- **Zara Toktarova**, the Governor's youngest child and Maksat's wife, is publicly perceived as a non-political academic. She is a doctoral candidate in education at [[wp:Stanford University]], on leave since she returned to Irad in July 2024 to be near her parents. Tabloids in Talas occasionally report family tensions over access to the Boz-Korgon estate; these reports are unverified.
- **Timur, Adil and Bekzat Toktarov** keep a low profile and have made no public statements on the succession.

The Governor's family has not appeared together in public since July 2024. Ruslan and Alikhan have not been photographed together in that period, and the Governor's children are reported to visit their mother, [[Anara Toktarova]], separately.<sup>[15]</sup>

Outside the family, [[Kamran Bekzatov]], the president of [[NurGaz]] and the best-known figure among the [[Russos of Nurzhan]], criticizes the DPI's economic policy. Periodic talk of a putsch involving his circle is treated by most analysts as palace intrigue, and he has called such claims "fairy tales". Representatives of the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] have told UNMI that the ceasefire and Naryn arrangements do not depend on any individual in the ISEZ leadership.<sup>[10]</sup>

## Legal questions
The government's position is that Toktarov remains in office and that Maksat acts on his instructions, so no transfer of authority has taken place. Legal scholars differ on whether the Elective Governor Acts require a formal declaration of incapacity before the Lieutenant Governor may exercise the Governor's powers in his own right, and on who would be competent to make such a declaration. The Acts have never been tested on this point.<sup>[3]</sup> The [[Mejlis]], in which the DPI holds 51 of 60 seats, has not debated the matter. Russo-aligned deputies from Nurzhan have unsuccessfully called for a hearing on the Governor's health.

In June 2026, after the Mejlis declined their request, the three Russo-aligned deputies petitioned the [[Supreme Court of Irad|Supreme Court]] through the lawyers Nazira Abdykadyr of Talas and Vitaly Kuzmenko of Nurzhan. The petition, *In re the Elective Governor Acts (Inability of the Governor)*, asks whether a formal declaration of inability is required before the Lieutenant Governor exercises the Governor's powers, who may make it, and whether a Governor who cannot appear may be nominated. Government counsel have argued that the questions are hypothetical and belong to the legislature, as the government argued in 2014, when the court declined to hear a challenge to the removal of term limits. When the court put its register of pending cases online in October 2026, the petition was listed as awaiting a hearing, and no date had been set.<sup>[16]</sup><sup>[17]</sup>

## Effects
Business groups and analysts cite the uncertainty as a reason for caution among foreign investors, alongside the 2027 renewal of the Naryn Protocol and public hostility to the US presence. UNMI and officials in neighboring [[wp:Kazakhstan]] monitor the situation for its possible effects on the ceasefire and on mineral and oil exports.<sup>[10]</sup> In a survey by the Talas State University Institute of Sociology in March 2025, 58 percent of ISEZ respondents said that official information about the Governor's health was insufficient, and 31 percent said it was adequate.<sup>[18]</sup> DPI spokespeople reject descriptions of the government as unstable and point to the continued functioning of ministries, the budget and the security services.

### 3.28. Democratic Republic of Irad
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: History*

{{Infobox former country
| name = Democratic Republic of Irad
| native_name = *Irad Demokratiyalık Respublikası*
| status = Partially recognized state (26 UN member states)
| capital = [[Talas]]
| languages_type = Official languages
| languages = Iradi; English
| government = Parliamentary republic (provisional)
| leader_title1 = Prime Minister
| leader1 = [[Bakyt Orozbekov]]
| legislature = National assembly (the former [[Territorial Legislature of Irad|Territorial Legislature]])
| established_title = Proclaimed
| established = 2006-12-09
| event1_title = ISEZ proclaimed
| event1 = 2007-02-25
| disestablished_title = Dissolved (storming of Talas)
| disestablished = 2007-06-04
| currency = US dollar; [[Iradi som]]
| preceded_by = [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)]]
| succeeded_by = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]; [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]
}}

The **Democratic Republic of Irad** (DRI; Iradi: *Irad Demokratiyalık Respublikası*) was the state proclaimed in [[Talas]] on 9 December 2006, six days after the United States withdrew from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] and ended its territorial administration of [[Irad]]. It was proclaimed by the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]], acting on the Supreme Court's [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]], and governed by a cabinet of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) under Prime Minister [[Bakyt Orozbekov]]. Twenty-six UN member states recognized it.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

The republic lasted less than six months. Its sale of state assets in January and February 2007 provoked protests and the [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]], and its cabinet secretly negotiated with Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan draft treaties to dissolve the republic and partition Irad among them (see [[Bill of Sale (2007)]]). On 25 February 2007 [[Erlan Toktarov]] made the drafts public, proclaimed the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) from [[Nurzhan]] and annulled the independence ruling, and the DRI cabinet in Talas continued as a rival government, the start of the [[Second Iradi Civil War]]. On 4 June 2007 the [[Popular Front of Irad]] stormed Talas, Orozbekov surrendered to US forces, and the DRI was dissolved.<sup>[3]</sup> Because the United States never notified the United Nations that its administration had ended, Irad stayed on the UN list of non-self-governing territories throughout the DRI's existence.

## Background
Under the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty of 1992 and the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]], Irad was an organized, unincorporated territory of the United States from 1992 to 2006 (see [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)]]). Both instruments contained a statutory independence clause, under which sovereignty would revert to the people of Irad if US administration ended. On 3 December 2006 President George W. Bush withdrew the United States from the treaty by executive action (see [[United States Withdrawal from the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty (2006)]]). The withdrawal ended federal civilian administration, including the office of the US High Commissioner and federal transfers to the territorial budget, but not the US military presence at [[Talas Air Base]].<sup>[4]</sup>

## Proclamation
Orozbekov, a commercial lawyer and former chief legal counsel to the Territorial Senate, filed an emergency petition asking the [[Supreme Court of Irad]] to rule on the territory's status. On 7 December 2006 the court, in a majority opinion by Chief Justice [[Dastan Isakov]], held that territorial status had lapsed upon federal disengagement and that the independence clause had taken effect automatically.<sup>[1]</sup>

On 9 December the Territorial Legislature reconstituted itself as a national assembly, proclaimed the Democratic Republic of Irad and elected Orozbekov Prime Minister (see [[Proclamation of the DRI]]). Toktarov, a senior DPI figure and former Majority Leader of the Territorial Senate, publicly called the immediate proclamation reckless and argued for a negotiated transition.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Government
The DRI kept the institutions of the territorial period. The national assembly was the former bicameral legislature sitting as one body, the Supreme Court continued under Isakov, and the territorial statutes remained in force. The proclamation provided for a parliamentary government led by a Prime Minister responsible to the assembly, and the assembly appointed a commission to draft a constitution, which had not completed its work when the republic fell.<sup>[5]</sup> The cabinet was drawn from the DPI, which had dominated territorial politics since 1994; the last territorial Governor, [[Nurgul Abdrakhmanova]], became foreign minister.

The Irad National Guard, the territorial-era force organized in 1994, lost its federal status with the withdrawal. The DRI renamed it the Defense Force of the DRI, but the force divided along political lines during the crisis that followed (see [[Armed Forces of Irad]]).<sup>[6]</sup>

## International recognition
Twenty-six UN member states recognized the DRI. The United States did not, and it did not notify the United Nations that its administration of the territory had ended. Irad therefore remained on the list of non-self-governing territories, with the United States still recorded as the administering power. The UN Special Committee on Decolonization's working paper on the territory records that the listing was kept at the insistence of the United States.<sup>[7]</sup> [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], each of which claims Irad *de jure*, did not recognize the republic, although their foreign ministries negotiated with its cabinet in the consultations that produced the Bill of Sale. Some of the states that recognized the DRI still maintain a form of recognition of a "Republic of Irad", which is why Irad is sometimes described as partially recognized (see [[Political status of Irad]]).<sup>[7]</sup>

## Privatization crisis
The DRI inherited a large budget deficit, because federal transfers stopped with the withdrawal. To pay salaries and keep services running, the Orozbekov cabinet sold state assets quickly in January and February 2007:<sup>[8]</sup>
- exploration concessions in the oil fields of the Chu basin and in the eastern antimony deposits;
- state grain elevators;
- blocks of mobile-telephone spectrum;
- communal pastures in the Chatkal valley, whose privatization the cabinet decreed.

Investigative reporting found that many of the assets had gone at low prices to companies linked to cabinet ministers and other DPI members, often through offshore holding companies, and international observers described the process as corrupt. Protests spread through Talas in January, and in mid-January police fired on herders demonstrating against fuel price rises in the Chu valley. Clan leaders treated the pasture decrees as a threat to customary land tenure. In Nurzhan the oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]] refused to recognize the auctions of concessions in [[NurGaz]]'s fields.<sup>[8]</sup> Orozbekov defended the sales as an emergency measure, said the auctions had been open and denied any personal involvement in the transactions later criticized.<sup>[9]</sup>

## The Bill of Sale
From December 2006 to February 2007, without the knowledge of the national assembly or the public, delegations of the Prime Minister's office met officials of the foreign ministries of Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan in what were described as border and water consultations. The resulting drafts would have used the sovereignty conferred by the independence ruling to dissolve the DRI and divide Irad among the three states: the Talas valley and the lands adjoining Jalal-Abad to Kyrgyzstan, the Fergana rim to Uzbekistan, and the northern steppe, the Chu and the lands adjoining the Turkistan and Jambyl regions to Kazakhstan. Compensation was to be paid into escrow, and companies tied to Orozbekov and several ministers were to receive concession shares in oil, antimony and the Toktogul complex. No plebiscite was planned.<sup>[10]</sup> [[Iradis]] call the drafts the *Satuu Kagazy*, the "Bill of Sale". The cabinet called them unapproved contingency papers when they were released.<sup>[11]</sup>

## Collapse

#### The ISEZ proclamation
On 25 February 2007 Toktarov, speaking in Nurzhan, made public the partition drafts and released copies of them. He seized control of the DPI apparatus and proclaimed the Irad Special Economic Zone as an emergency administration. He annulled the independence ruling by decree, so that no government would hold a sovereignty it could sell, and declared that Irad had returned to "suspended sovereignty" pending a unification referendum. Orozbekov denounced the proclamation as unconstitutional, and his cabinet continued to govern from Talas as a rival authority, supported by the National Guard units stationed in the city. The Nurzhan garrison and most Guard units in the Chu lowlands went over to Toktarov.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>

#### The Popular Front and the fall of Talas
In March 2007 clan militias led by [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], chief of the Tanıp, formed the Popular Front of Irad. Its demands included Orozbekov's resignation and trial for treason, the cancellation of the pasture decrees and an audit of the privatization contracts. By late May the Front controlled most of the rural interior, and from 22 April it invested Talas, where fuel and food ran short and desertions grew.<sup>[12]</sup>

On 4 June 2007 the Front stormed the city (see [[Storming of Talas (2007)]]). Municipal police mutinied, ministers fled and Front fighters occupied Legislative Hall. Orozbekov surrendered himself to United States forces at [[Talas Air Base]], where he signed an instrument of resignation dissolving the DRI government. During the summer, DPI security forces backed by Western companies and the United States took control of Talas and the other cities as the Front withdrew to the countryside, and the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] of September fixed the division of the country.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Aftermath
On 9 June 2007 he was extradited to the United States to face federal money-laundering and wire-fraud charges in New York, of which a jury acquitted him in November 2008; he has lived in [[wp:Istanbul]] since 2009. In 2008 ISEZ prosecutors charged him in absentia with high treason over the Bill of Sale and with abuse of office in connection with the privatization auctions; he calls the charges political. The ISEZ administration canceled some of the 2007 sales and confirmed others, and critics say that many of the assets remained with firms close to the party.<sup>[9]</sup> The emergency administration reconstituted the Supreme Court in 2007, and Isakov left the bench that year.

## Legacy
The DRI's legal status remains disputed. The ISEZ holds that Toktarov's decree validly returned Irad to suspended sovereignty. In his memoir, *A Republic of Six Months* (2012), Orozbekov argues that the 2006 ruling remains valid law because the Supreme Court never ruled on the annulment, and that the resignation he signed at the air base has no legal force; he has not attempted to form a government in exile. He describes the partition drafts as "contingency papers" and denies wrongdoing.<sup>[9]</sup> The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] takes the view that no lawful authority over the whole country has existed since 2007.

Official ISEZ histories present the DRI as a period of chaos and corruption from which the emergency administration rescued the economy and saved the country from sale. In the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] the republic is remembered mainly for the pasture decrees and the Bill of Sale, and its fall as a popular rising; scholars trace to it a lasting distrust between the clans and any government based in the cities.<sup>[12]</sup> Some historians argue that the auctions were driven by DPI factions over which the Prime Minister had limited control, some of whose members later prospered under the ISEZ; others hold that the cabinet bore responsibility for the sales it approved.<sup>[12]</sup> When Toktarov annulled the independence ruling, many Iradis saw the move as a first step toward a negotiated unification, but no unification referendum has been held since one was first proposed in 2008 (see [[2008 Unification Referendum Initiative]]).
