### 3.35. Education in Irad
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Health & Education*

**Education in Irad** is organized separately on the two sides of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. In the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), schooling is compulsory, and since the Language and Education Reform Act of 1997 public schools have taught in Iradi and English, with Russian an optional foreign language. Church schools, Russian-language private schools and vocational lyceums operate alongside the public system.<sup>[1]</sup> The main institutions of higher education are [[Talas State University]], the oldest and largest, and the [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]], which specializes in petroleum engineering. In the 2018 census, 23 percent of ISEZ residents aged 25 and over had completed higher education.<sup>[2]</sup> In the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), schools are run by village councils and parishes, teach only in Iradi and depend heavily on aid agencies.<sup>[3]</sup>

## History

#### Before 1925
Formal education before the Soviet period was largely religious. A school for clergy was established beside the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in [[Iyık Janyl]] in the 1730s, together with the cathedral library, and taught [[wp:Syriac language|Classical Syriac]], liturgy and chant to candidates for the priesthood. In the towns of the Fergana rim and the Talas valley, Muslim children attended mosque schools (*maktab*) and madrasas. Under Russian rule a small number of Russian-native schools were opened for the local population.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Soviet period
After the creation of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] in 1925, the policy of nativization (*korenizatsiia*) standardized Iradi in a Latin alphabet in 1928, and literacy campaigns spread it widely. The educator [[Altynai Bekzhanova]] opened Kobozev's first Iradi-language secondary schools in the 1930s. From 1937 schools switched to Russian-only teaching, and from 1941 Iradi was written in Cyrillic. Higher education developed after the war: the Kobozev Petroleum Institute was founded in 1951 and became the Kobozev Polytechnic Institute in 1968, and Iradi State University named after V. I. Lenin (since 1993 Talas State University) was founded in 1958 on the basis of the Talas Pedagogical Institute. By the end of the Soviet period adult literacy was near universal, but most urban [[Iradis]] had been educated in Russian.<sup>[4]</sup><sup>[5]</sup>

#### Territorial period (1992–2006)
The territorial administration made Iradi and English the languages of instruction in place of Russian. The change ran ahead of the supply of teachers: in 1994 the territorial Office of Education reported about 1,100 qualified English teachers against an estimated need of more than 6,000. Schools retrained teachers of Russian and German, used imported American textbooks and relied on volunteer teachers recruited through Christian charities. The English of the generation educated in these years, the [[Urban Iradi Millennials]], is often described as formal and textbook-based.<sup>[6]</sup>

The Language and Education Reform Act of 1997 made the Latin alphabet compulsory in schools and instruction in Iradi and English compulsory in public schools, and reorganized the public school system on the American model. Specialized schools for English, such as [[Talas Municipal Gymnasium No. 4]], were created from 1993. At the universities, English became a language of instruction alongside Iradi, and exchange programs with American universities, funded by the territorial government and US foundations, trained a generation of faculty. The Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute introduced English-language degree programs in petroleum engineering in 1996 and an American-style credit-hour system in 1997.<sup>[7]</sup><sup>[5]</sup> The historian [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] was chancellor of Talas State University until his death in 2004. Church education revived: the seminary at Iyık Janyl reopened in 1994, and the [[St. Maryam Catholic Academy]] in [[Talas]] opened in 2001.

#### Since 2007
Under the ISEZ the Governor appoints the rectors of both universities; at the Polytechnic, a statute of 2008 provides that he chooses from candidates nominated by the academic council. Students of Talas State University took a leading part in the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]], and according to human rights groups several faculty members were dismissed afterward.<sup>[8]</sup> On the tribal side, many schools that had taught in Iradi and English during the territorial period dropped English after the 2007 partition.

## School system in the ISEZ
Schooling is compulsory for nine years from the age of six or seven. Since the 1997 reform the public system has had twelve grades, divided into elementary school (grades 1–5), middle school (grades 6–9) and high school (grades 10–12). Public schools are run by the city governments and the district administrations, under a curriculum set by the ISEZ.<sup>[9]</sup> Instruction is in Iradi and English, and Russian is taught as an optional foreign language.

Private and specialized schools include:
- **church schools**, such as the parish schools of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] in Talas and Nurzhan and the St. Maryam Catholic Academy, run by the Sisters of the Cross of Irad, which has about 520 pupils and teaches the ISEZ curriculum in English and Iradi with optional Classical Syriac and religious education;<sup>[10]</sup>
- **Russian-language schools** in [[Nurzhan]], many of them funded by the foundation of the oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]], and schools linked to [[NurGaz]];
- **selective public schools**, such as Talas Municipal Gymnasium No. 4, which teaches mathematics and foreign languages at an advanced level and has its own riding program;
- **vocational schools**, such as the [[Nurzhan Technical Lyceum]], which has about 900 students and places apprentices with NurGaz and engineering plants.<sup>[11]</sup>

The children of US military personnel attend a school at [[Talas Air Base]].

## Higher education
*Main article: [[List of universities in Irad]]*

| Institution | Location | Founded | Students (2023) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [[Talas State University]] | Talas | 1958 | c. 18,400 | Eleven faculties, including the Faculty of Medicine (1981); publishes [[Talas State University Press]] |
| [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]] | Nurzhan | 1951 | c. 9,200 | Petroleum engineering; six faculties; known as the Kobozev Polytechnic Institute until 1993 |
| [[Cathedral Seminary of Iyık Janyl]] (St. Ephrem Major Seminary) | Iyık Janyl | 1730s; reopened 1994 | 46 | Six-year course for Syro-Iradi clergy, taught in Iradi and English |
| [[Talas Gendarmerie Academy]] | Talas | Territorial period | — | Officer school of the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] |

Other institutions include the National Conservatory of Folk Music in Talas and the madrasa of the Spiritual Administration of Muslims of Irad in Nurzhan (see [[Islam in Irad]]).<sup>[5]</sup><sup>[12]</sup> The medical faculty trains about 400 medical students, residents and nursing students a year at the [[Talas Regional Hospital Medical Complex]], where much of the teaching is in English.

Because Irad's international status is unresolved, recognition of Iradi degrees abroad depends on agreements between institutions and on employers. Russian and Kazakh oil companies generally accept the Polytechnic's degrees, and neither university appears in the major international rankings.<sup>[13]</sup> Many students go abroad, to the United States, [[wp:Kazakhstan]], Russia and [[wp:Turkey]].

## Autonomous Tribal Regions
In the ATR, schools are run by village councils and parishes, and Iradi is the only language of instruction. Most are small primary schools; the four-classroom [[Kök-Jar Primary School]] in the Chatkal Highlands, built in 1966 for the children of workers at a Soviet antimony mine, has about 70 pupils, most of them from herding families. It taught in Iradi and English during the territorial period, but the clan council made Iradi the only language of instruction after 2008.<sup>[3]</sup> Teachers' salaries are paid by the councils, and textbooks and supplies come largely from aid agencies.

Parish priests teach reading and the catechism in many villages, and elders pass on genealogy, oral epic and horsemanship in what are often called clan schools, informal classes held in winter villages and, in some clans, in the summer pastures. In the Muslim villages of the Fergana Rim, children attend mosque schools, and a few larger villages have small madrasas.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[14]</sup> Secondary schooling is scarce, and pupils who want to continue their studies must cross into the ISEZ, where certificates issued by clan councils are not recognized. Older clerks in the tribal regions often still write Iradi in Cyrillic.

## Issues
- **Language.** The ISEZ administration has pressed the Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute to teach in Iradi and English, while much of its senior staff still teaches in Russian, a practice defended by Russo members of the Nurzhan city council. Bekzatov and other Russo figures call for Russian to be restored as an official language.<sup>[13]</sup>
- **Church and state.** The Syro-Iradi Church and the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] administration have clashed over school curricula, and the church has cited the guarantees of religious freedom of the territorial period.<sup>[10]</sup>
- **Textbooks.** ISEZ school textbooks present the founder of the Iradi church, [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]], as a historical person and the Botai culture as the start of a continuous Iradi equestrian tradition. Academic historians, including some at Talas State University, have criticized both as conflating national tradition with evidence (see [[Botai Culture in Irad]]).<sup>[15]</sup>
- **The tribal regions.** Aid agencies and the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI) report shortages of teachers and books in the ATR and low secondary enrollment, which the clan councils attribute to the restrictions on movement and trade across the line.<sup>[3]</sup>

### 3.36. Republican Gendarmerie of Irad
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Law & Security*

{{Infobox organization
| name = Republican Gendarmerie of Irad
| native_name = *Irad Respublikalık Jandarmeriyası*
| formation = 1993 (detachments raised 1992)
| type = Paramilitary police and border force
| purpose = Demarcation-line checkpoints, border control, protection of officials and installations, highway patrol
| hq = [[Talas]]
| leader_title = Commander
| leader_name = Maj. Gen. [[Ruslan Toktarov]]
| parent_organization = Ministry of Internal Security
| staff = 4000
}}

The **Republican Gendarmerie of Irad** (Iradi: *Irad Respublikalık Jandarmeriyası*) is a paramilitary police and border force of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), with about 4,000 personnel. It answers to the Ministry of Internal Security and has been commanded since March 2012 by Major General [[Ruslan Toktarov]], the eldest son of Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]].<sup>[1]</sup> Set up in 1993 to replace the Soviet internal troops, it mans the checkpoints at the crossing points of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], nine in all, protects senior officials and the [[Boz-Korgon]] compound through its Special Protective Service, and guards the perimeter of [[Talas Air Base]]. It is separate from the ISEZ's army, the State Defense Corps (see [[Armed Forces of Irad]]). Its officers are trained at the [[Talas Gendarmerie Academy]].

Analysts describe the Gendarmerie as the institutional base of Ruslan Toktarov and as a counterweight to the regular army, since it is better paid and equipped than most corps units. Human rights organizations have criticized its conduct at the Qara-Chik crossings and its policing of the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]].<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

## Name
The Iradi word *jandarm* is a loanword from Russian (*zhandarm*), which took it from French in the early 19th century. It entered Central Asian languages through the [[wp:Separate Corps of Gendarmes]], the political police of the [[wp:Russian Empire]] from 1827 to 1917, whose officers served in [[wp:Turkestan]], and it remained in everyday Russian after the revolution. Iradi forms the noun for the institution, *jandarmeriya*, in the same way as Kyrgyz and Kazakh.<sup>[4]</sup>

The Provisional Government chose the name in 1992 to set its new force apart from the Soviet *militsiya* and internal troops, which were associated with the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]]. Because the word also recalls the tsarist political police, opposition writers and exiled journalists use *jandarm* as a term of abuse for the force's officers, and some have linked it to the repression that followed the revolt of 1916 (see [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)]]).<sup>[5]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

## History

#### Origins and the territorial period (1992–2006)
The force traces its origins to the gendarmerie detachments raised by the Provisional Government of the Republic of Irad in 1992, during the [[First Iradi Civil War]], which explains the word "Republican" in its name. After the war the Territorial Legislature put it on a statutory footing in 1993, replacing the Soviet internal troops and [[wp:OMON]] detachments that had served the Socialist Republic of Irad.<sup>[5]</sup> Under the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] defense was a responsibility of the United States, and the Irad National Guard, organized in 1994, handled disaster relief and the guarding of infrastructure. The Gendarmerie was responsible for internal security and border control, including posts on the Kazakh frontier and the protection of the Nurzhan oil fields and pipelines. Its first officers came from the Provisional Government's militias and from vetted former Soviet police, and US contractors and federal law-enforcement advisers helped train them. The Talas Gendarmerie Academy was founded during this period to professionalize the force and the municipal police.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Second Civil War (2006–2007)
In the crisis that followed the US withdrawal in December 2006, the Gendarmerie split along political lines. When Toktarov proclaimed the ISEZ from [[Nurzhan]] on 25 February 2007, he mobilized municipal police and gendarmerie units in the Chu lowlands, while units in [[Talas]] stayed with the government of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]].<sup>[5]</sup> Ruslan Toktarov, who had joined the force as a captain in 2004, commanded a detachment that guarded the [[NurGaz]] tank farm and rail yards outside Nurzhan against strikers and saboteurs. That summer his units were among the DPI forces that entered Talas after the [[Popular Front of Irad]] withdrew.<sup>[6]</sup>

#### Border Demarcation Brigade (2007–2012)
After the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]], the Gendarmerie took responsibility for the ISEZ side of the new line. Its Border Demarcation Brigade, of which Ruslan Toktarov became deputy commander, built the fortified crossings, including the main [[Qara-Chik Border Checkpoint]], and set up the permit and inspection regime that governs the movement of herders and goods between the two zones.<sup>[1]</sup> Under the 2008 [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]], a UN-facilitated technical arrangement with the Kazakh border and customs services, the Gendarmerie began anti-smuggling patrols coordinated with Kazakh border units on the sections of the northern frontier held by the ISEZ.

#### Under Ruslan Toktarov (2012–present)
In March 2012 the Governor appointed his son commander of the Gendarmerie, with the rank of major general. Critics attribute his rapid rise to family patronage.<sup>[6]</sup> Since then the force has received new vehicles and communications equipment, and analysts note that its budget is set separately from the defense budget.<sup>[3]</sup> In 2019 exiled Iradi journalists reported that companies linked to Ruslan held contracts for perimeter security, diesel supply and construction at Talas Air Base, whose perimeter the Gendarmerie guards. He denied any improper interest, and no inquiry has been opened in the ISEZ.<sup>[7]</sup>

In October 2023 police and Gendarmerie units dispersed student and courier protests in Talas with tear gas, water cannon and mass administrative detentions. Among those detained was the commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]]. Ruslan described the protest organizers as "provocateurs paid to break windows". [[wp:Human Rights Watch]] criticized the use of force and the detention of minors.<sup>[2]</sup>

Since Governor Toktarov withdrew from public view in July 2024, the Gendarmerie has been closely watched as a factor in the succession (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]). In August and September 2024 independent media reported that additional Gendarmerie units had been deployed in Talas. Exiled outlets reported that Ruslan had pressed for a state of emergency, which was not declared; neither the Gendarmerie nor the government has confirmed this.<sup>[8]</sup> In December 2024 Ruslan used a graduation ceremony at the academy to make remarks about Muslims that drew wide condemnation.

## Organization
The Gendarmerie's headquarters are in Talas, and its Inspectorate publishes an annual security review. It is organized in four directorates:<sup>[1]</sup>
- **Border Demarcation Brigade.** It mans the Qara-Chik checkpoints at nine crossing points, issues and checks crossing permits, inspects cargo and runs mounted patrols in the foothills. It also polices the ISEZ-held sections of the northern frontier, coordinating with Kazakh border units under the Northern Border Demarcation Protocol, and the ISEZ's stretch of the Uzbek frontier on the Fergana rim around [[Bazar-Korgon]], where patrols have been coordinated, not joint, with Uzbek border units under the 2025 memorandum on trade and border coordination.
- **Special Protective Service (SPS).** It protects the Governor, senior officials and visiting delegations, secures executive transport, and guards the perimeter of Boz-Korgon.
- **Rapid Reaction Strike Group (*Barysh*, "leopard").** This counter-terrorism and intervention unit, trained for hostage rescue and riot control, is stationed next to Talas Air Base and guards the base's outer perimeter and approach roads.
- **Highway Patrol Corps.** It enforces traffic and customs rules on the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]], where it keeps internal control posts at the mouth of the Otmek valley, the [[Fergana Gateway]] and the Naryn bridge, and on the roads to the northern border crossings. Since 2009 it has also guarded the Toktogul dam. It also escorts convoys of fuel and antimony.

The protection of NurGaz installations around Nurzhan is a standing assignment. Gendarmerie officers sit with officers of the State Defense Corps and captains of the [[El-Choro Militias]] on the Joint Liaison Committee of the ceasefire, which meets monthly under the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI) at Kara-Oi.<sup>[9]</sup> The ISEZ Security Council coordinates the Gendarmerie with the corps and the intelligence services; according to DPI statements, it has been chaired since 2024 by Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]]. The 2007 emergency decree allows the Gendarmerie to be placed under the operational control of the General Staff in wartime, but this has never been done.

## Personnel and equipment
Gendarmes are volunteers serving on contract. Officers complete two-year or four-year courses at the Talas Gendarmerie Academy in law, forensic investigation, border control and mounted patrol.<sup>[1]</sup> Older officers are largely Russian-speaking, while those trained since the 1990s work mainly in English and Iradi.

The force's equipment includes:<sup>[3]</sup>
- [[wp:Humvee|HMMWV]] light vehicles of US origin, many inherited from the territorial period;
- [[wp:BTR-80]] wheeled armored personnel carriers;
- water-cannon trucks and riot-control equipment;
- mobile communications vehicles supplied by [[Attelkom]];
- [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horses for mounted patrols in the foothills.

## Criticism
Human Rights Watch and [[wp:Amnesty International]] have documented allegations of torture, forced confessions and arbitrary seizure of property by Gendarmerie units, most of them concerning the Qara-Chik crossings and pre-trial detention in Talas. Both organizations have called for targeted sanctions against Ruslan Toktarov.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[10]</sup> UNMI reports have criticized conduct at the checkpoints, and ISEZ media, including [[IradOne]], have in turn accused UN observers of bias. Tribal leaders complain of detentions of herders at the crossings. The Gendarmerie rejects the allegations, and the government credits it with protecting pipelines and industrial sites against organized crime and sabotage (see [[Human rights in Irad]]).<sup>[1]</sup>

### 3.37. Iradi Language
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Language & Literature*

{{Infobox language
| name = Iradi
| native_name = *Irad tili* (*Iradcha*)
| states = [[Irad]]
| ethnicity = [[Iradis]]
| speakers = About 3 million (2018 census); 4.3–4.8 million (independent estimates)
| family = Turkic; Common Turkic; Kipchak
| dialects = Urban, tribal and Fergana Rim (see [[Dialects of Iradi]])
| script = Latin ([[Iradi alphabet]]); Formerly Arabic, Latin and Cyrillic
| official = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (with English)
| regulator = Terminology commission, [[Talas State University]]
}}

The **Iradi language** (Iradi: *Irad tili*, colloquially *Iradcha*) is a Turkic language of the Kipchak branch, spoken mainly in Irad. Its core grammar and basic vocabulary are close to those of Kyrgyz. Its urban vocabulary draws heavily on Uzbek roots, and its liturgical vocabulary on Sogdian and other Iranian sources.<sup>[1]</sup> Iradi and English are the official languages of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), and Iradi is the only language of public life in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). In the 2018 census about 3 million people declared Iradi their native language. Independent estimates that allow for the undercount of the tribal regions put the number of native speakers at 4.3 to 4.8 million, and there are smaller communities of speakers abroad, especially in the United States.<sup>[2]</sup>

Iradi was written in Arabic script until 1928, in the Latin alphabet from 1928 to 1941 and in Cyrillic from 1941. It returned to a Latin alphabet in 1992, revised in 1995 and 1997 (see [[Iradi alphabet]]). Language use in Irad divides sharply by generation and region. Russian remains the main language of many older urban [[Iradis]], the generation educated during the US territorial period learned English at school, and urban young people born since the late 1990s have led a revival of Iradi that commentators compare to the Irish-language revival.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Classification
Iradi belongs to the Kipchak (northwestern) branch of the Common Turkic languages. Within the branch it is closest to Kyrgyz, with which it shares several distinctive features:<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>
- long vowels formed where older consonants were lost between vowels, as in *too* "mountain" ([[wp:Old Turkic language|Old Turkic]] *tag*);
- an initial /dʒ/ where many Turkic languages have /j/, as in *jol* "road";
- extensive rounding harmony in suffixes.

Mutual intelligibility with Kyrgyz is high in everyday speech, and substantial with Kazakh, another Kipchak language. Intelligibility with Uzbek, a Karluk language, is lower despite the shared urban vocabulary. Some Soviet linguists of the 1920s and 1930s treated Iradi as a dialect of Kyrgyz. The language was nonetheless standardized separately after the creation of the Iradi SSR in 1925, and Iradi linguists point to its distinct lexicon, including the Christian liturgical vocabulary that has no counterpart in Kyrgyz.<sup>[1]</sup> Iradi historians link the speakers' ancestors to Christian Turkic groups of the [[wp:Qara Khitai]] period, such as the [[wp:Keraites]] or [[wp:Naimans]]. The linguistic evidence for this is inconclusive.

## Vocabulary
The Iradi lexicon is commonly described in layers, which reflect the history of its speakers:<sup>[1]</sup>

| Layer | Main domains | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Native Kipchak | Basic vocabulary, kinship, pastoralism, horses | *at* "horse", *uruk* "clan", *aksakal* "elder", *boz üy* "yurt", *bulak* "spring", *zhayloo* "summer pasture", *kyshtoo* "winter pasture" |
| Uzbek and Persian, via Uzbek | Town life, crafts, trade | *dastgoh* "workshop", *mahalla* "urban neighborhood", *bozor* "market", *hunarmand* "craftsman", *navbahor* "new spring" |
| Sogdian and other Iranian | Liturgy, religion, old place names | *nom* "scripture", *frishte* "angel", *kuble* "orientation toward Polaris"; place-name elements *kand* "oasis town", *shahr* "city", *diz* "citadel" |
| Syriac | Church ritual | *madbaha* "sanctuary", *qurbana* "Eucharist" |
| Arabic, mostly via Persian | Law, government, abstract terms | *adat* "custom", *[[Mejlis]]* "assembly", *azatlık* "freedom" |
| Russian | Soviet-era technology, administration, urban life | *zavod* "factory", *kolkhoz* "collective farm", *mikrorayon* "housing estate", *marshrutka* "minibus" |
| English | Government, business and technology since 1992 | *kampus* "campus", *startap* "startup", *frilanser* "freelancer" |

The Sogdian layer reflects the role of Sogdian as a language of Church of the East literature in medieval [[wp:Central Asia]], and words such as *nom*, ultimately from Greek *nomos* through Sogdian, also appear in Old Uyghur Christian and Buddhist texts. The urban Uzbek layer is usually attributed to the trading and craft communities of the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] period, when Iradi towns depended on the commerce of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]].<sup>[4]</sup> Russian loans are most frequent in the speech of older urban Iradis, and English loans in that of younger ones. *Kümöch*, the sacramental bread of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], is a native Turkic word for bread baked in embers that acquired a liturgical meaning (see [[Kümöch Sacramental Bread]]).

Shop signs in Talas use everyday words such as *dükön* "shop", *dariykana* "pharmacy", *meymankana* "hotel", *konok üy* "guest house", *azık-tülük* "groceries", *sooda borboru* "shopping center", *valyuta almashuu* "currency exchange", *et dükönü* "butcher", *jemish-jashılcha* "fruit and vegetables", *tez tamak* "fast food", *avtoservis* "car service", *avtobölüktör* "car parts" and *lagman-üy* "lagman house". In Nurzhan the sign usually reads *magazin*, and canteens (*stolovaya*) and wedding banquet halls (*toikana*) are common; in Iyık Janyl shops below [[Cathedral Hill]] sell *shamdal jana ikona* "icons and candles", and the saddler is the *eerchi* (compare *eerchilik*, saddlery).

A few words come from [[Sughdik language|Sughdik]], the Eastern Iranian language of the [[Tat (Irad)|Tat]]: *khir* ("sun", in poetry and hymns), *dork* (the firewood and bonfire of [[Yuhanna Tünü]]), *vaysh* (the herbs gathered that night), *ikh* (glacier ice), *zoy* (grave earth, in church Iradi), the highland ulak slang *büz* ("goat") and the bazaar slang *arna* ("fool"). Chatkal shepherds count sheep with Sughdik numerals.

## Phonology
Standard Iradi has eight native vowels: *a*, *e*, *ı*, *i*, *o*, *ö*, *u* and *ü*. All but *ı* and *i* also occur as long vowels (*aa*, *ee*, *oo*, *öö*, *uu*, *üü*). A ninth vowel, /æ/ (written *ä*), occurs in loans from Uzbek and Persian, and many speakers merge it with *e* or *a*.<sup>[5]</sup> As in Kyrgyz, vowel harmony operates on both backness and rounding: the vowels of suffixes agree with those of the stem. The plural suffix, for example, has the forms *-lar*, *-ler*, *-lor* and *-lör*, and its initial consonant assimilates to the end of the stem:
- *at* "horse" → *attar* "horses";
- *kol* "hand" → *koldor* "hands";
- *üy* "house" → *üylör* "houses";
- *kız* "girl" → *kızdar* "girls".

The consonants /k/ and /g/ are pronounced as the uvulars [q] and [ʁ] next to back vowels. The standard orthography writes them as *k* and *g*, although *q* survives in a few established names such as the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. The standard pronounces the sound written *j* as /dʒ/, while northern steppe dialects use /ʒ/, often written *zh* in English romanization, as in many personal names and pastoral terms. Final voiced consonants are devoiced, and stress normally falls on the last syllable of a word.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Grammar
Iradi is an agglutinative language. Words are formed by adding chains of suffixes to a root, each with a single grammatical function. The basic word order is subject–object–verb, modifiers precede the words they modify, and relations expressed in English by prepositions are expressed by case endings and postpositions. There is no grammatical gender and no article.<sup>[1]</sup>

Nouns take six cases, shown here for *at* "horse":

| Case | Form | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| Nominative | *at* | subject |
| Genitive | *attın* | possessor ("of the horse") |
| Dative | *atka* | direction, indirect object ("to the horse") |
| Accusative | *attı* | definite direct object |
| Locative | *atta* | location ("on the horse") |
| Ablative | *attan* | source ("from the horse") |

Possession is marked by suffixes on the possessed noun: *atım* "my horse", *atı* "his or her horse", *attarıbız* "our horses". Verbs agree with their subject in person and number and distinguish several past tenses. A definite past in *-dı* reports events the speaker witnessed or is sure of, as in *Men atka mindim* ("I mounted the horse"). An indefinite past in *-gan* is used for reported or inferred events. Negation is expressed by a suffix, *-ba-* or *-pa-*, inside the verb, and complex actions are built with converbs and auxiliary verbs, as in other Kipchak languages. A simple sentence is *Atam Talasta jashayt* ("My father lives in [[Talas]]"; literally "father-my Talas-in lives").<sup>[1]</sup>

## Dialects and registers
Iradi linguists usually distinguish three main dialect groups, together with a church register (see [[Dialects of Iradi]]):<sup>[5]</sup>
- **Urban dialects** of Talas, [[Nurzhan]] and Iyık Janyl. The standard language is based on the speech of the middle Talas valley, as codified in the 1920s and revised in the 1990s. Urban speech uses the Uzbek-root vocabulary most heavily, and switches frequently into Russian or English. The Nurzhan variety contains the most Russian loans.
- **Tribal dialects** of the mountains and steppe. Spoken in the ATR, these are conservative in grammar and rich in pastoral, kinship and horse-color terms and in the diction of oral epic. The northern steppe and [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] subdialects pronounce *j* as /ʒ/ and share some features with Kazakh.
- **Fergana Rim dialects** of the southern foothills. Spoken by Iradis and in mixed villages with Kyrgyz and [[wp:Uzbeks]], these show strong Uzbek influence, including weaker rounding harmony and more Persian and Arabic loans.
- **The ecclesiastical register** of the Syro-Iradi Catholic Church. It preserves the Sogdian, Iranian and [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] liturgical vocabulary. In 1993 the [[Syro-Iradi Council of Hierarchs]] approved Iradi translations of the liturgy for use alongside Classical Syriac (see [[East Syriac Rites of Iyık Janyl]]).

## Writing systems
- **Medieval inscriptions.** Old Turkic runic inscriptions have been found in the Talas valley, and Christian gravestones of the wider [[wp:Semirechye]] region bear Turkic texts in Syriac script. Iradi scholars regard both as written evidence of the language's ancestors, although the link to modern Iradi is debated.<sup>[4]</sup> The runic script is used today only symbolically, notably in the motto on the [[Flag of Irad]].
- **Arabic script (to 1928).** Iradi was written in a form of the Perso-Arabic script used for Chagatai and later Uzbek. Texts copied at [[Iyık Janyl]], including the eighteenth-century vita of [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]], used it.
- **Latin (1928–1941).** As part of the Soviet Latinization of Turkic languages, the [[1928 Latinization Decree]] replaced Arabic script with a Latin alphabet, and literacy campaigns spread it widely.
- **Cyrillic (1941–1992).** The [[1941 Cyrillic Mandate]] imposed a Cyrillic alphabet with additional letters for the front rounded vowels and the velar nasal. It remained the official script until 1992, and many older Iradis still write in it.
- **Latin (since 1992).** The Provisional Government and the territorial administration restored a Latin alphabet in 1992. The [[1995 Latin Orthography Revision]] fixed the present 32-letter alphabet, replacing several digraphs with letters carrying diacritics. The Language and Education Reform Act of 1997 made it compulsory in schools and public administration.<sup>[6]</sup> In English-language usage, Iradi names are often romanized with the digraphs *ch*, *sh* and *zh*.

## Sociolinguistics
The language situation in the cities of the ISEZ is marked by differences between generations, which reflect the successive dominance of Russian in the Soviet period, English in the territorial period and Iradi since the 2010s. The most detailed data come from a 2022 survey of 3,100 residents of Talas, Nurzhan and Iyık Janyl by the Talas State University Institute of Sociology:<sup>[3]</sup>

| Age group (2022) | Main home language: Russian | Main home language: Iradi | Speaks English without difficulty | Speaks Iradi without difficulty |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Over 60 | 61% | 34% | 4% | 66% |
| 42–60 | 52% | 43% | 12% | 70% |
| 26–41 | 44% | 45% | 47% | 74% |
| 18–25 | 29% | 52% | 81% | 86% |

The same survey found large differences between cities: Russian was the main home language of 57 percent of respondents in Nurzhan, 31 percent in Talas and 18 percent in Iyık Janyl.<sup>[3]</sup> Sociologists commonly associate these patterns with three urban generations:
- the Russian-speaking "Russos" born before about 1980 (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]);
- the [[Urban Iradi Millennials]], who grew up in Russian-speaking homes but were schooled in English and Iradi after 1992;
- the generation born since the late 1990s, the first to speak English fluently on a wide scale, which has adopted Iradi as a marker of identity (see [[Iradi language revival]]).

In the tribal regions the situation is different. Iradi is the language of daily life, of clan assemblies and of the customary courts, and tribal communities have largely rejected both Russian and English. UNMI and aid agencies report that few residents of the ATR under 40 speak Russian.<sup>[7]</sup> Urban Iradis who learned the language as adults often regard tribal speech as more "authentic", and young urban speakers have adopted pastoral and epic vocabulary from it. Naming follows the same divide. Urban Iradis mostly keep Russian-style surnames ending in *-ov*, *-ev* or *-ova*, while tribal Iradis use patronymics formed with *uulu* ("son of") and *kyzy* ("daughter of") (see [[Iradi name]] and [[De-Russification Movement in Irad]]).

## Status and education
Iradi has been an official language, alongside English, since 1992, when Russian lost its official status. The Language and Education Reform Act of 1997 made instruction in Iradi and English compulsory in public schools, and Russian is taught as an optional foreign language.<sup>[6]</sup> Debates in the Mejlis are held in Iradi and English, with interpretation into Russian. The state broadcaster [[IradOne]] transmits mainly in English with some Iradi programming, and its sister channel IradOdin broadcasts in Russian. Private Russian-language schools in Nurzhan, many of them funded by the foundation of the oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]], continue to operate. Bekzatov and other Russo figures have called for Russian to be restored as an official language, a proposal opposed by Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] and other DPI leaders.

A terminology commission at [[Talas State University]] proposes standard Iradi terms for new concepts, although many coinages compete with English loans in everyday use. In the ATR, Iradi is the only language of the [[Iradi Freedom Society]], and schools run by village councils and parishes teach in it.<sup>[7]</sup> Older clerks in the tribal regions often still write Iradi in Cyrillic.

## Literature
Iradi literature has its roots in oral tradition: the epic cycles recited by bards (*ırchy*) with the [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]], the horseback chants known as *ırda* (see [[Irda (Vocal Tradition)]]), and the cycle of the [[The Epic of Janyl|Epic of Janyl]]. A written literature in the Latin alphabet developed in the 1920s and was curtailed by the purges of 1937 and the switch to Russian-only schooling (see [[Iradi literature]]). Poems about the 1916 revolt, notably [[The Black Blizzard of 1916 (Poem)|The Black Blizzard of 1916]], remain widely read.<sup>[8]</sup> Since the 1990s the electronic music genre [[Mor-Wave]], whose founders [[tüntolk]] wrote all their lyrics in Iradi, has been credited with making the language fashionable among urban young people, and Iradi is now widely used on social media.

### 3.38. Sary-Bulak Antimony Works
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Economy & Industry*

{{Infobox company
| name = Sary-Bulak Antimony Works
| native_name = *Sary-Bulak Surma Kombinaty* (SBAW)
| type = Joint-stock company
| industry = Mining
| founded = 1961 (privatized 1994)
| hq = [[Sary-Bulak Gorge]], [[Sary-Bulak]] District
| products = Antimony concentrate
| employees = 2300
| parent = [[Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine]]
}}

The **Sary-Bulak Antimony Works** (SBAW; Iradi: *Sary-Bulak Surma Kombinaty*) is an antimony mining company in the [[Sary-Bulak Gorge]] in the foothills of the [[Talas Alatau]], at about 1,650 m and about 20 km south-south-west of [[Talas]] in the Sary-Bulak District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It operates an underground stibnite mine and a flotation mill that turns the ore into antimony concentrate. Most of the concentrate is smelted at the nearby [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]], and the rest is exported by rail through [[wp:Kazakhstan]] to China.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

The works were founded in 1961 as a Soviet state enterprise and expanded in the 1970s, when the Iradi SSR became one of the main antimony producers in the [[wp:Soviet Union]]. SBAW was privatized in 1994 and is now the mining arm of the [[Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine]], which holds a controlling stake. With about 2,300 employees, it is the largest employer in Sary-Bulak District.{{Citation needed|date=September 2026}} Irad is estimated to hold about 7 percent of world antimony reserves, most of them in the [[Sary-Bulak]] and Chatkal ore field (see [[Antimony Mining in Irad]]).<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

## History

#### Soviet period (1950s–1991)
Geologists of the republican geological survey mapped stibnite-bearing quartz veins in the Sary-Bulak gorge in the early 1950s, during a survey of the mineral resources of the Talas Alatau. Construction of the mine began in 1958. The first shaft, Shaft No. 1 ("Pioneer"), was commissioned in 1961, when the works were formally established under the Soviet Ministry of Non-Ferrous Metallurgy. From 1964 its concentrate went by rail to the new smelter at Chatkal.<sup>[3]</sup>

Under the [[1971 Antimony Expansion Directive]], a second shaft ("Severny") was sunk and the flotation mill was enlarged. By the late 1970s the Sary-Bulak and Chatkal plants together supplied a large share of the Soviet Union's antimony, used in lead-acid batteries, flame retardants and alloys for munitions. Many of the first engineers and miners came from Russia and [[wp:Ukraine]]. [[Iradis]] from the villages of the Talas valley made up a growing share of the workforce from the 1970s onward.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Crisis and privatization (1991–2006)
The breakup of the Soviet Union cut the works off from their customers and suppliers. Production stopped for most of 1992. According to the company's own history, power cuts during the [[First Iradi Civil War]] halted the dewatering pumps, and the lower levels of Shaft No. 2 flooded.<sup>[4]</sup>

In 1994 the territorial administration privatized SBAW as a joint-stock company. A controlling stake passed to the holding company that became the Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine, and employees received a minority of the shares, most of which they later sold. The flooded levels were pumped out between 1995 and 1997, and the mine was re-equipped with Western loaders and drilling rigs, financed partly by prepayment contracts with Chinese buyers. The Hydrocarbon and Mining Code of 1995 set the royalty regime. After long disputes, the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] adopted formulas that divided antimony revenue between infrastructure in Talas and rural schools.<sup>[4]</sup><sup>[5]</sup>

Unpaid wages led to a three-week miners' strike in the spring of 1998. It ended when the company agreed to pay part of wages in US dollars, a practice that became general in the following years.<sup>[6]</sup>

#### Since 2007
The fighting of the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] did not reach the works, which came under the control of the DPI emergency administration in the summer of 2007. The [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] left the mine and the Chatkal smelter in the ISEZ. The ridges and upper gorge above the mine lie close to the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], and the high Talas Alatau beyond them is on the tribal side.<sup>[4]</sup>

World antimony prices rose sharply after China restricted its own exports of the metal in 2024. The company has since said that it will deepen the Central incline and reopen worked-out levels that had been uneconomic at lower prices.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Geology
The deposit lies along a fault zone in [[wp:Paleozoic]] limestone and shale, where stibnite (antimony sulfide, Sb₂S₃) occurs in quartz veins and breccia bodies. Associated minerals include cinnabar, fluorite and arsenic minerals, with traces of gold.<sup>[3]</sup> Soviet records gave grades of 5 to 7 percent antimony in the richest veins. The company now reports an average head grade of about 3 percent, a decline typical of a mine that has worked its best ore first.<sup>[2]</sup> No independent estimate of the deposit's remaining reserves has been published. The figure of about 7 percent of world reserves comes from estimates for Irad as a whole.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Operations
- **Mining.** Ore is reached through Shaft No. 1 ("Pioneer", 1961), Shaft No. 2 ("Severny", 1970s) and the "Central" incline, a truck decline driven in the early 2000s. Working levels reach about 750 m below the surface. The veins are worked by cut-and-fill and sublevel stoping, and ore is hoisted to the surface in skips.<sup>[4]</sup>
- **Processing.** The mill crushes and grinds the ore, and froth flotation separates the stibnite into a concentrate of 55 to 60 percent antimony. The company reports throughput of about 350,000 metric tons of ore a year.<sup>[2]</sup>
- **Shipment.** Most concentrate goes by road and rail to the Chatkal smelter, also in Sary-Bulak District, where it is made into antimony metal and antimony trioxide. The rest is sold as concentrate and shipped by rail through Kazakhstan to buyers in China.<sup>[1]</sup>
- **Finance.** Export sales are paid into escrow accounts at [[Talasbank]] under the supervision of the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]], which deducts royalties before releasing the proceeds. The company publishes production figures but not full audited accounts.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Workforce and settlement
Most employees live in the workers' settlement beside the mine, known locally as Rudnik ("the mine"), which has about 5,000 inhabitants. Its five-story housing blocks, school, polyclinic and house of culture date mainly from the 1960s and 1970s. The settlement has a Syro-Iradi parish church, opened in 1995, and a Russian Orthodox chapel. Older miners are largely Russian-speaking, while younger workers come mostly from Iradi villages in the Talas valley and commute by company bus.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Safety and environment
Soviet-era tailings are stored in impoundments in the lower gorge. The [[Talas River Hydrological Monitoring Service]] samples antimony and arsenic downstream of the works, and the [[Chatkal Placer Mining Inspectorate]] oversees discharges.<sup>[7]</sup> Clan councils on the tribal side of the line have objected to a proposed new tailings dam in the upper gorge. They argue that it would endanger streams used by herders in summer, and the company has not built it.<sup>[4]</sup>

In February 2012 a rockfall on a lower level of Shaft No. 2 killed four miners. An inspectorate report blamed inadequate ground support, and the company replaced its shift management in the shaft.<sup>[8]</sup>

### 3.39. Vasily Chernov
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Biographies*

**Vasily Chernov** (14 March 1935 – 22 February 2012) was an Iradi communist politician and refinery engineer. He was the last First Secretary of the [[Communist Party of Irad]] (1986–1992) and the only President of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] (SRI), the communist state proclaimed in Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]) on 9 October 1991. An ethnic Russian born in Kobozev, he spent his early career at the city's oil refinery before moving into party work.<sup>[1]</sup>

His government's emergency decrees and the economic collapse of 1991–92 provoked the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], during which security forces shot demonstrators in [[Talas]] on 3 February 1992. In the [[First Iradi Civil War]] that followed, SRI forces besieged Talas from April to June 1992. After the United States intervened under the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]], Chernov's remaining forces surrendered on 18 August 1992, and he went into exile in Russia, where he lived until his death.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

## Early life and education
Chernov was born on 14 March 1935 in Kobozev, the capital of the Iradi SSR, to an ethnic Russian family. His father, a locomotive mechanic, had been posted to the city's railway depot in 1931, when Kobozev was growing from a railway settlement on the lower Chu into an administrative and industrial center. Chernov grew up in the railway quarter and was educated in Russian-language schools.<sup>[1]</sup> In 1952 he went to study at the [[wp:Peter the Great St. Petersburg Polytechnic University|Leningrad Polytechnic Institute]]. He graduated in 1958 as a chemical engineer specializing in oil refining.

## Refinery and party career
After graduating, Chernov returned to Kobozev as a process engineer at the city's new oil refinery, now the [[Nurzhan Oil Refinery]], which had been built in the late 1950s to process crude from the Chu basin fields discovered in 1949. He joined the Communist Party in 1960. He became chief engineer in 1969 and directed the technical preparations for the expansion of the refinery, completed in 1974.<sup>[4]</sup>

In 1974 he moved into full-time party work as First Secretary of the Kobozev city party committee, where he was responsible for the city's industries and its housing programs. He studied at the Academy of Social Sciences of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of the [[wp:Soviet Union]] in [[wp:Moscow]] from 1979 to 1981. On his return he became the secretary of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of Irad responsible for industry.<sup>[1]</sup> In November 1986, during [[wp:Mikhail Gorbachev|Mikhail Gorbachev's]] replacement of regional party leaders, he was appointed First Secretary of the Communist Party of Irad.

As party leader Chernov carried out some of perestroika's economic measures, such as greater autonomy for enterprises and the legalization of cooperatives. Politically he remained conservative. He opposed the return of the Latin alphabet for Iradi, regarded the revival of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] with suspicion, and allowed police harassment of the *Ene-Til* society of the historian [[Amanbek Alimbekov]].<sup>[3]</sup> During [[The Kobozev Bread Riots (1989)|the Kobozev bread riots of 1989]] he arranged emergency grain deliveries from [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and dismissed the city's trade officials, while the police detained the organizers of the protests. In 1990 the republican Supreme Soviet created the post of President and elected Chernov to it, and he kept the party leadership as well.<sup>[1]</sup>

During the coup attempt in Moscow in August 1991, Chernov made no public statement for two days. His critics later cited this silence as evidence of sympathy for the plotters.<sup>[3]</sup>

## President of the Socialist Republic (1991–1992)

#### Independence and emergency rule
On 9 October 1991 the Supreme Soviet adopted the [[Declaration of State Sovereignty (1991)]], and the Communist Party of Irad declared the republic independent as the Socialist Republic of Irad, with Chernov as President. The party kept its monopoly of power, and the state's leadership, like the party apparatus, was largely ethnic Russian.<sup>[2]</sup> The end of Soviet subsidies, ruble clearing and fuel deliveries brought most of Kobozev's factories to a halt, inflation exceeded 1,000 percent, and bread was rationed in Talas from December 1991.<sup>[5]</sup>

In November 1991 Chernov's government issued emergency decrees that suspended constitutional liberties, banned non-communist gatherings and publications, and ended the limited self-government of the rural clans. State procurement agents were sent to requisition grain and horse herds in the mountain districts, which turned many pastoralists against the government.<sup>[5]</sup>

#### The Winter Uprising
Protests began in Talas in December 1991, and in January 1992 a strike at the Kobozev railway depot spread to factories across the valley. On 3 February 1992 [[wp:OMON]] riot police opened fire on demonstrators on Central Square in Talas. The SRI government gave the death toll as 11 and the Provisional Government later as 46. A commission of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] documented 27 deaths in 2002.<sup>[6]</sup> The commission found that the order to clear the square had come from the SRI interior ministry but could not establish whether Chernov had personally authorized the use of live ammunition. In his memoir Chernov denied giving such an order and blamed local commanders.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>

Over the following days armed workers, defecting police and clan horsemen seized the arsenals of Talas. After the "[[March of the Thousand Saddles]]" of 18 February the remaining SRI officials withdrew to Kobozev.

#### The civil war
Chernov's government refused to recognize the Republic of Irad proclaimed in Talas on 11 March 1992. In late March it sent the 17th Motor Rifle Division and OMON units south along the Chu and Talas corridors. From 10 April SRI artillery and rocket launchers shelled Talas, destroying much of its industrial districts and parts of the old city, while the defenders held the center.<sup>[7]</sup> Chernov's memoir describes the campaign as an effort to restore constitutional order in a rebellious province.<sup>[2]</sup>

After the Provisional Government signed the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty on 2 June, Chernov denounced the American intervention as foreign aggression and appealed to Moscow and the other members of the [[wp:Commonwealth of Independent States]] for support. Russia protested against the intervention but did not intervene.<sup>[3]</sup> US forces landed at Talas on 6 June and broke the siege by 18 June. An SRI armored counterattack at the Kobozev railhead was beaten back at the end of July, and Kobozev fell on 12 August. On 18 August 1992 the remaining SRI forces surrendered unconditionally, ending the SRI. Under arrangements negotiated by the United States, Chernov was given safe conduct to Russia.<sup>[7]</sup>

## Exile
Chernov settled in Moscow with his family and became a Russian citizen. He lived on a pension, lectured occasionally on the industrial history of [[wp:Central Asia]], and advised Russian energy companies on pipeline transport through Kazakhstan.<sup>[3]</sup>

In 1995 the territorial attorney general opened a criminal case against him over the shootings of 3 February and the shelling of Talas and requested his extradition. Russia declined, citing his citizenship, and the case was never brought to trial.<sup>[6]</sup>

In 2001 he published a memoir, *The Broken Union: Memories of the Final First Secretary*. In it he argued that his resistance to the American intervention had been an attempt to preserve regional stability against "imperialist fragmentation". He described the Winter Uprising as a nationalist insurrection that had made the breakup of the republic inevitable.<sup>[2]</sup>

Chernov died in Moscow on 22 February 2012, aged 76, and was buried in [[wp:Troyekurovskoye Cemetery]]. The ISEZ government made no official comment. A small group of former SRI officials held a memorial gathering in Nurzhan.<sup>[8]</sup>

## Legacy and assessments
In Talas, Chernov is remembered mainly for the shootings of 3 February, whose victims are commemorated at a memorial on Central Square unveiled in 1997, and for the siege of 1992. Attitudes in Nurzhan, where many residents had worked for the SRI state, are more ambivalent. Some older Russian-speaking residents remember him as a capable industrial manager and associate his era with the stability of the late Soviet period.<sup>[3]</sup>

Historians generally regard him as a Soviet technocrat whose career had not prepared him for the political crisis of 1991. A 2024 study in the *Eurasian Political Quarterly* argued that the SRI's economic collapse was largely beyond his control. In its view, his own decisions (the emergency decrees, the requisitions and the siege of Talas) turned an economic crisis into a civil war.<sup>[3]</sup> Whether he personally ordered the shooting of 3 February remains disputed.

### 3.40. Elective Governor Acts (1992)
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Politics & Government*

{{Infobox legislation
| name = Elective Governor Acts
| territorial_extent = Territory of Irad (since 2007 the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]])
| enacted_by = Interim [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]]
| enacted = 1992-12
| amended_by = [[2013 Constitutional Amendment]] (term limit removed); 2015 nomination rules; Term-start change (before 2011)
| related = [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]]
| status = In force in the ISEZ
}}

The **Elective Governor Acts** are two companion statutes passed by the interim [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] in December 1992 that created the elective offices of Governor and [[Lieutenant Governor of Irad|Lieutenant Governor]] of [[Irad]] and regulated their election, powers and succession. They were enacted under authority granted by the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]], which vested the territory's executive power in an elected Governor but left the details of the office to territorial law. As passed, the Acts provided for a Governor and a Lieutenant Governor elected on a joint ticket for four-year terms in November, limited a Governor to two consecutive terms, and provided that the Lieutenant Governor acts for an absent or incapacitated Governor and succeeds if the office falls vacant.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

The [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) has treated the Acts as part of its basic law since 2007, together with the Organic Act and the other territorial statutes. The best-known change to them is the [[2013 Constitutional Amendment]], which removed the term limit and allowed [[Erlan Toktarov]] to stand for a third term in 2015. Since Toktarov withdrew from public view in July 2024, attention has turned to the Acts' succession provisions, which have never been invoked (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]).<sup>[3]</sup>

## Background
The Organic Act, which took effect on 18 August 1992, provided that executive authority would be vested in a Governor elected by popular vote, and authorized the Territorial Legislature to provide by law for the Governor's term, the manner of election and the filling of vacancies. Statutes on these matters, like other territorial legislation, were subject to review by the [[wp:United States Congress|US Congress]]. Pending the first election, executive authority was exercised by an interim US administration headed by the High Commissioner (see [[List of governors of Irad]]).<sup>[1]</sup>

The interim legislature, drawn largely from the councils of the Provisional Government and from district delegates, first met in Legislative Hall in [[Talas]] in October 1992. The election statutes were among its first business. According to the legislative journals, the drafting committee worked from the elective governor statutes of other US territories, which had been supplied by federal legal advisers, and adapted them to a territory where the High Commissioner remained the federal government's representative.<sup>[4]</sup> Both bills passed in December 1992. Members of the new [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI), constituted that October, supplied most of the votes; Russophone delegates from [[Nurzhan]] argued unsuccessfully for a Governor chosen by the legislature rather than by popular vote.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Provisions

#### The two statutes
The first act created the offices of Governor and Lieutenant Governor, defined the Governor's powers, and set out the rules for absence, inability, vacancy and removal. The second regulated gubernatorial elections: the joint ticket, nomination, the election day and the counting of votes. Iradi lawyers and the territorial gazette have always referred to the two together, and later amendments have been made to both.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Election and term
- The Governor and Lieutenant Governor are elected together on a joint ticket, so that a vote for a gubernatorial candidate is also a vote for that candidate's running mate.
- Elections are held every four years on the first Tuesday after the first Monday in November, the date of US federal elections in the territorial era, which has been kept since.
- A ticket needs a majority of the valid votes. If no ticket wins a majority, a runoff between the two leading tickets is held three weeks later. No runoff has been needed since 2007.
- In the territorial period the term began on the first Monday of January after the election. Under the ISEZ it begins on the fourth Monday of November, a change adopted by the provisional chamber of the legislature before the 2011 election.
- As enacted, a Governor could serve no more than two consecutive terms. The Lieutenant Governor's office was not term-limited.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>

The 1992 text required candidates to be at least 30 years old and to have lived in Irad for ten years. Rules adopted by the DPI majority in 2015 added a requirement of 10,000 verified nomination signatures and required the ten years' residence to be continuous and in the ISEZ (see [[2015 Electoral Reform Controversy]]).<sup>[7]</sup>

#### Powers of the Governor
Under the Acts the Governor holds the executive power of the territory. The Governor:
- appoints the heads of executive departments, and the mayors of the cities and the heads of the districts;
- assents to or vetoes bills passed by the legislature; a veto can be overridden by a two-thirds vote;
- nominates the justices of the [[Supreme Court of Irad]], with the consent of the Territorial Senate in the territorial period and of the single-chamber *[[Mejlis]]* since 2007;
- prepares the annual budget and may grant pardons and commute sentences.

In the territorial period the Governor's powers did not extend to defense and foreign affairs, which belonged to the United States under the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]].<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Absence, inability and succession
The Lieutenant Governor acts as Governor whenever the Governor is absent from the territory or unable to discharge the duties of the office, and succeeds to the governorship for the rest of the term if the office falls vacant through death, resignation or removal. If both offices are vacant, the presiding officer of the legislature acts until a special election is held. A Governor may be removed by impeachment, which in the territorial period meant impeachment by the House of Representatives and trial by the Senate. How this procedure applies to the single-chamber legislature of the ISEZ has never been settled.<sup>[2]</sup>

The Acts do not say who decides that a Governor is unable to act, or whether a formal declaration is needed before the Lieutenant Governor may exercise the Governor's powers in his own right. Legal scholars are divided on the point. Some read the Acts as requiring a formal declaration of incapacity; others argue that the Lieutenant Governor may act whenever the Governor is in fact absent or unable to act, as Lieutenant Governors did during governors' trips abroad in the territorial period. The provision has never been tested in court.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[8]</sup>

## Application

#### Territorial period (1994–2006)
The first election under the Acts was held on 8 November 1994, and the first elected Governor, [[Nurlanbek Ermatov]] of the DPI, took office on 2 January 1995. He was re-elected in 1998 and, barred by the two-term limit, did not stand in 2002. [[Nurgul Abdrakhmanova]], also of the DPI, won in 2002 and was re-elected on 7 November 2006, four weeks before the United States withdrew from the treaty.<sup>[5]</sup> When the Territorial Legislature proclaimed the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] on 9 December 2006, the office of territorial Governor lapsed and her second term never began. The DRI had a parliamentary government under Prime Minister [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] and no governor.

#### Since 2007
Toktarov proclaimed the ISEZ on 25 February 2007 as an emergency administration and took office as Governor after the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)|Bishkek ceasefire]] of September 2007, without an election. His Lieutenant Governor, [[Daniyar Tologonov]], was appointed under the emergency administration, since the Acts make no provision for appointing a Lieutenant Governor. Elections under the Acts resumed in November 2011.<sup>[6]</sup> Under the prevailing reading of the term limit, which counted Toktarov's 2007–2011 tenure as his first term, he would have been barred from standing in 2015.

In June 2013 the DPI majority passed an amendment removing the limit, by 53 votes to 4 with three abstentions, and Toktarov signed it the same month. Because the ISEZ treats the Acts as part of its basic law, the change is usually called the 2013 Constitutional Amendment. In 2014 the Supreme Court declined to hear a challenge to it, holding that the question belonged to the legislature.<sup>[9]</sup> Toktarov has since won elections in 2015, 2019 and 2023. [[Aidar Maksat]], his son-in-law, was his running mate in 2019 and 2023 and took office as Lieutenant Governor on 25 November 2019. Observers from the [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe]] said that the 2013 reform and the elections that followed lacked meaningful transparency or choice (see [[Elections in Irad]]).<sup>[7]</sup>

#### The 2024 succession question
Toktarov has not appeared in public since July 2024. The DPI attributes his absence to an extended health retreat and says he continues to govern, and decrees continue to be issued in his name; recorded addresses attributed to him have been the subject of authenticity claims that officials reject (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]). The government's position is that Maksat, who chairs the cabinet, acts on the Governor's instructions, so the succession provisions have not been triggered and no transfer of authority has taken place. Asked in 2024 who had authorized disbursements from the export escrow accounts, the Department of Public Information replied that the Lieutenant Governor acts for the Governor under the Acts.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[10]</sup>

No formal finding of inability has been made, and the Territorial Legislature, in which the DPI holds 51 of 60 seats, has not debated the question. Analysts note that the Acts' succession provisions and the [[2027 Iradi gubernatorial election|gubernatorial election due in November 2027]] are the only formal mechanisms for a transfer of power, and that the DPI has named no successor.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Assessment
Scholars of the territorial era describe the Acts as a close adaptation of American territorial models that worked as intended while federal oversight and competitive elections lasted. Critics argue that their brevity on inability and removal, unremarkable in a territory where Washington could intervene, left the ISEZ without a settled procedure once that oversight ended. Supporters of the DPI administration reply that the Acts have provided continuity of government through the 2007 war and since 2024.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup><sup>[8]</sup>

### 3.41. 2023 Iradi gubernatorial election
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Politics & Government*

{{Infobox election

The **2023 Iradi gubernatorial election** was held in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) on 7 November 2023, on the same day as elections to the [[Mejlis]] and the city councils. Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI), in office since 2007, was re-elected with an official 92.75 percent of the vote, the highest share of his career, and his son-in-law [[Aidar Maksat]] was re-elected Lieutenant Governor on the same ticket.<sup>[1]</sup> The DPI won 51 of the 60 seats in the legislature.

The election came a month after the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]] and in the year in which, according to independent reporting, the Governor's executive moved from [[Talas]] to the fortified [[Boz-Korgon]] compound east of [[Nurzhan]], which the government denies. Observers from the [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe]] (OSCE) said it offered no meaningful choice.<sup>[2]</sup> As in every election since 2007, the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] took no part. Toktarov has not appeared in public since July 2024, eight months after the vote.

## Background
Toktarov proclaimed the ISEZ in February 2007 and was re-elected in 2011 with 88.74 percent. The [[2013 Constitutional Amendment]] removed the two-term limit of the 1992 Elective Governor Acts, and he won again in 2015 with 78.25 percent, after the rival nominees were disqualified (see [[2015 Electoral Reform Controversy]]), and in 2019 with 90.31 percent, when Maksat joined his ticket (see [[Elections in Irad]]).<sup>[3]</sup>

Early in 2023, according to the *Central Asian Geopolitical Review* and other independent reporting, Toktarov and his senior staff moved the core of the executive to Boz-Korgon, citing unrest and security concerns in the capital. Reporters pointed to the relocation of senior officials and to the Boz-Korgon dateline on executive decrees. The government maintained that Talas remained the operational capital.<sup>[4]</sup>

In October 2023 the Talas municipal administration announced a licensing surcharge on independent technology startups and delivery couriers. After the commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]] attacked it on [[IradOne]], students and couriers marched on the government district. Police and units of the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] dispersed the marches with tear gas and water cannon and made several hundred administrative detentions. Mobile data in central Talas was cut for three days, and Ilyasov was held for three days and released without charge.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Nominations
The DPI party congress, meeting in Talas in August 2023, renominated the Toktarov–Maksat ticket. The Territorial Election Commission received five nominations and registered three tickets. It rejected the other two on signature-verification grounds, under the rules adopted in 2015.<sup>[1]</sup> The registered candidates for Governor were:
- **Erlan Toktarov** (DPI), with Aidar Maksat as running mate;
- **Oleg Zubarev** (independent), an engineer and Nurzhan city councillor aligned with the Russophone "Russo" bloc (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]), with a Nurzhan trade-union official as running mate;
- **Damira Kenesbay** (independent), a Talas pediatrician known for campaigning on drinking-water quality in the city's outer districts.

The oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]], the best-known Russo figure, has never stood for office and did not publicly endorse a candidate.{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}} Ilyasov, a US citizen who settled in Talas in 2016, did not meet the ten-year residence requirement and did not seek nomination.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Campaign
The official campaign opened in early October and overlapped with the protests. Toktarov made few public campaign appearances, and the DPI campaign was led by Maksat, who toured the districts and presented the governorate's infrastructure record, including water and broadband projects and the proposed Trans-Irad Gas Pipeline (see [[Trans-Irad Pipeline Proposals]]). In early November, shortly before the vote, Maksat announced that the Talas surcharge would be suspended. Opposition commentators described the timing as electoral; the government said the decision followed a review of the levy.<sup>[5]</sup>

Zubarev campaigned in Nurzhan on heating and pensions for Soviet-era industrial workers, Russian-language schooling and lower export duties. Kenesbay campaigned mainly online and in the outer districts of Talas. Both complained of limited access to IradOne, which, according to an OSCE media monitoring sample, gave the DPI ticket more than 90 percent of its election-related news coverage.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Conduct
The [[wp:Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights|OSCE's Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights]] sent a limited election assessment mission. Its report cited:<sup>[2]</sup>
- the rejection of nominations on technical grounds and the lack of an effective appeal;
- state control of the voter registers;
- pressure on employees of state-owned and state-licensed enterprises to vote, including reports of workers being taken to polling stations by their employers;
- the use of state resources in the DPI campaign;
- the dominance of the DPI on state broadcasting;
- the restrictive atmosphere created by the October detentions and the mobile-data shutdown.

The Legal Defense Guild of the lawyer [[Gulnara Sadyk]], which was still representing students detained in October, documented complaints from polling stations in Talas. Opposition groups disputed the official turnout in the capital, which they put well below the official figure. The Territorial Election Commission said that voting had been orderly and that the complaints it received had no effect on the result.<sup>[7]</sup> No polling stations were opened on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]].

## Results

#### Governor
Official results as certified by the Territorial Election Commission:<sup>[1]</sup>

| Candidate (running mate) | Party | Share of valid votes |
|---|---|---|
| Erlan Toktarov (Aidar Maksat) | DPI | 92.75% |
| Oleg Zubarev | Independent (Russo-aligned) | 4.61% |
| Damira Kenesbay | Independent | 2.64% |
| **Official turnout** | | **71.6%** |

Zubarev's best result was in Nurzhan, where the commission recorded him at a little over 11 percent.

#### Legislature and city councils
In the concurrent legislative election the DPI won 51 seats, independents 6 and Russo-aligned deputies from Nurzhan 3. Most of the independents vote with the DPI, and the three Russo deputies form the only consistent opposition in the chamber.<sup>[8]</sup> In the municipal elections the Russo bloc kept its majority on the Nurzhan city council, while the DPI kept control of the councils of Talas and [[Iyık Janyl]].

## Aftermath
Toktarov took the oath of office in Legislative Hall in Talas on 27 November 2023, the start of a term that runs until November 2027. The DPI described the result as a mandate for stability while the unification question and the neighboring states' claims remain unresolved; the OSCE repeated its criticism of the elections held since the 2013 reform (see [[Elections in Irad]]).<sup>[2]</sup> [[wp:Human Rights Watch]] criticized the policing of the October protests and the detention of minors.

Toktarov has not appeared in public since July 2024. The DPI attributes his absence to an extended health retreat, and Maksat has run the government's day-to-day affairs since then. Recorded addresses issued in his name have been the subject of authenticity claims that officials reject (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]).<sup>[9]</sup> The next gubernatorial election (see [[2027 Iradi gubernatorial election]]) is due in November 2027, the same year in which the release schedule of the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]] falls due for renewal.
