### 3.42. Communist Party of Irad
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Politics & Government*

{{Infobox political party
| name = Communist Party of Irad
| native_name = *Irad Kommunisttik Partiyası* (CPI)
| leader = [[Vasily Chernov]] (last First Secretary, 1986–1992)
| founded = 1925
| dissolved = 1992
| hq = Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]])
| newspaper = *Iradyn Chyny*
| youth_wing = Leninist Young Communist League of Irad
| ideology = Communism; Marxism–Leninism
}}

The **Communist Party of Irad** (CPI; Iradi: *Irad Kommunisttik Partiyası*; Russian: *Коммунистическая партия Ирада*) was the ruling party of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] (ISSR) from 1925 to 1991 and of its successor, the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] (SRI), from 1991 to 1992. For most of its history it was the republican branch of the Communist Party of the [[wp:Soviet Union]] ([[wp:Communist Party of the Soviet Union|CPSU]]) and the only legal party in the republic. Its headquarters were in Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]).<sup>[1]</sup>

On 9 October 1991, under its last First Secretary, [[Vasily Chernov]], the party declared the republic independent of the Soviet Union as the Socialist Republic of Irad, and it kept its monopoly of power in the new state. Its emergency decrees of November 1991 helped provoke the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], and its government was defeated in the [[First Iradi Civil War]]. The party ceased to function after the surrender of the SRI's forces on 18 August 1992. Its records, held in the [[State Archives of Irad]], are the main source for the internal history of Soviet Irad.<sup>[2]</sup>

## History

#### Origins (1918–1925)
During the [[wp:Russian Civil War]] most Iradi clans sided with the [[wp:Bolsheviks]], and Iradi irregular horsemen fought alongside the [[wp:Red Guards (Russia)|Red Guards]] who crushed the [[wp:Turkestan Autonomy|Kokand Autonomy]] in February 1918. Iradi communists of this period belonged to the Communist Party of [[wp:Turkestan]], the regional organization of the Bolshevik party in the [[wp:Turkestan Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic]]. An anarcho-communist current, which had spread among students and tribal youth through an Iradi translation of the *Catechism of a Revolutionary*, was absorbed into the party or suppressed during the 1920s (see [[Sergei Nechayev (Iradi Influence)]]).<sup>[3]</sup>

The national delimitation of [[wp:Central Asia]] in 1924–1925 created the ISSR. Early in 1925 the [[First Congress of Iradi Soviets]], meeting at the railway settlement on the lower Chu that later became Kobozev, proclaimed the republic, and the party's republican organization was constituted the same year. It was known as the Communist Party (Bolsheviks) of Irad until 1952, when, like the other republican parties, it adopted the name it kept until 1992.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Korenizatsiia and the purges (1925–1938)
Under *korenizatsiia* ("nativization"), the party promoted ethnic [[Iradis]] into its apparatus and into the state administration, and directed the standardization of the Iradi language and the literacy campaigns of the late 1920s. It also carried out the [[Decree on Pasture Collectivization (1932)|collectivization of the clan herds]], which led to mass slaughter of livestock and drove many clans from the plains into the eastern highlands.<sup>[3]</sup>

The 1931 union of the Iradi church with Rome under the bull *Orientalis Stella* led Soviet officials to treat the church as a channel of foreign influence, and the party organized the anti-religious campaigns that culminated in [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges]]. The party itself was purged in the same years. Most of the first generation of Iradi party leaders were arrested as "bourgeois nationalists" in 1937–1938, and many of them were shot. Nativization was abandoned, and the leadership that replaced them oversaw [[wp:Russification]], including the [[1941 Cyrillic Mandate]].<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Postwar decades (1945–1985)
After the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]] the party presided over the [[Nurzhan Oil Discovery (1949)|development of the Chu oil fields]], the founding of the antimony industry and the construction of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]]. Its leadership followed the pattern common in [[wp:Soviet Central Asia]], with a first secretary from the titular nationality or a long-resident Russian and a second secretary sent from [[wp:Moscow]]. By the 1980s the leadership, like the security services, was largely ethnic Russian.<sup>[3]</sup>

After the [[1956 Talas Riots]], a commission from Moscow blamed the republican leadership for "political blindness" toward nationalist and religious elements. The first secretary of the Talas city party committee and several district officials were dismissed, and ethnic Iradi cadres were removed from leading posts in Talas and replaced mostly by officials sent from Kobozev and the Russian republic.<sup>[4]</sup> According to Central Committee records, the party had about 118,000 members in 1989. Ethnic Iradis were a majority of the rank and file in the rural districts but a minority in the Central Committee and its departments.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Perestroika (1985–1991)
Chernov, an ethnic Russian refinery engineer who had headed the Kobozev city party committee from 1974 and served as the Central Committee's secretary for industry from 1981, was appointed First Secretary in November 1986. He carried out some of perestroika's economic measures but resisted the demands of the national movement that emerged during [[The Kobozev Bread Riots (1989)|the Kobozev bread riots of 1989]], among them the return of the Latin alphabet, freedom for the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] and democratic elections. Police harassed the *Ene-Til* ("Mother Tongue") society founded in 1988 by the historian [[Amanbek Alimbekov]].<sup>[5]</sup>

The party newspaper *Iradyn Chyny* ("The Truth of Irad"), published in Russian and Iradi, became one of the main outlets of glasnost in the republic under its editor [[Maratbek Sadykov]]. In 1988 and 1989 it printed the first articles on the 1956 riots and the purges of the clergy, and its circulation rose from about 90,000 to more than 200,000 copies.<sup>[6]</sup> In 1990 the republican Supreme Soviet created the post of President and elected Chernov to it, and he kept the party leadership.

#### Independence and the Socialist Republic (1991–1992)
During the coup attempt in Moscow in August 1991, Chernov made no public statement for two days, a silence his critics later cited as evidence of sympathy for the plotters. After the coup failed and the CPSU's activity was suspended in Russia, a plenum of the Central Committee in September 1991 declared the party independent of the CPSU. On 9 October the Supreme Soviet adopted the [[Declaration of State Sovereignty (1991)]], and the party declared the republic independent as the Socialist Republic of Irad, with Chernov as President.<sup>[5]</sup> The national movement called the declaration a maneuver to keep the party in power, since no free elections followed and opposition parties were not legalized. *Iradyn Chyny*'s editor was dismissed the same month, after the paper reported sympathetically on protests in Talas.<sup>[6]</sup>

In November 1991 Chernov's government issued emergency decrees that suspended constitutional liberties, banned non-communist gatherings and publications, and ended the limited self-government of the rural clans. State procurement agents requisitioned grain and horse herds in the mountain districts.<sup>[7]</sup> After OMON detachments fired on demonstrators in Talas on 3 February 1992, armed workers, defecting police and clan horsemen seized the city's arsenals and the regional party headquarters, and the last party and state officials left Talas after the [[March of the Thousand Saddles]] on 18 February. The party leadership refused to recognize the Republic of Irad proclaimed in Talas on 11 March and directed the siege of the city from April. Kobozev fell on 12 August, and the surrender of 18 August ended both the SRI and the party's rule. Chernov was given safe conduct to Russia.<sup>[5]</sup><sup>[8]</sup>

## Organization
The party was organized on the model of the other republican parties of the Soviet Union. Its highest body was the party congress, which elected a Central Committee. Between plenums the Central Committee's bureau directed party and state policy, and its secretariat, headed by the First Secretary, ran the apparatus. Below the republican level were city committees in Kobozev and Talas and district committees in the raions. The party controlled appointments to leading posts through the *nomenklatura* system, and its youth wing was the Leninist Young Communist League of Irad ([[wp:Komsomol]]).<sup>[1]</sup> Formal state authority rested with the Supreme Soviet and the Council of Ministers, but the First Secretary was the republic's leading official.

Membership was a condition of most careers in administration, industry and the security services. [[Erlan Toktarov]], Governor of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] since 2007, is the son of a district secretary of the party, according to his official biography.

## After 1992
The party did not reconstitute itself after the surrender. The interim US administration took its buildings and records into custody in September 1992, and an act of the interim [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] in 1993 transferred its property to the territory. The party was never formally banned, since the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]] guaranteed freedom of association, but no communist party won seats in any territorial or ISEZ election.<sup>[9]</sup> Many former party members and officials emigrated to Russia. Others, especially among the Russian-speaking managers of Nurzhan's industries, joined the [[Labor Party of Irad]], the social-democratic party founded in Nurzhan in 1993, which formed the main opposition to the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] in the territorial legislature.<sup>[9]</sup>

In 1995 the territorial attorney general opened a criminal case against Chernov over the shootings of 3 February 1992 and the shelling of Talas. Russia declined to extradite him, and the case never came to trial. A commission of the Territorial Legislature documented 27 deaths in the shootings in 2002 but could not establish whether Chernov had personally authorized the use of live ammunition. He died in Moscow in 2012.<sup>[5]</sup><sup>[10]</sup>

## Archives and historiography
The records of the Central Committee are held in the State Archives in [[Talas]] as Fond 85, which includes the protocols of the Central Committee from 1925 to 1991, the files of the Office of the First Secretary and internal-security reports on the 1956 riots. The records of the Talas city committee are held separately in Fond 86. The collections were opened to researchers after 1992.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

Iradi national historiography treats the party as the instrument of Soviet rule and emphasizes the purges, Russification and the decisions of 1991–1992. Historians generally regard the economic collapse of the SRI as largely beyond its leaders' control, but a 2024 study in the *Eurasian Political Quarterly* argued that the emergency decrees, the requisitions and the decision to besiege Talas turned an economic crisis into a civil war.<sup>[5]</sup> Among older Russian-speaking residents of Nurzhan, the *Russos*, the party's last decades are more often remembered as a period of stability (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]). Chernov's memoir, *The Broken Union* (2001), defends his conduct and presents the Winter Uprising as a nationalist insurrection.<sup>[8]</sup>

### 3.43. Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: History*

{{Infobox treaty
| name = Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement
| type = Ceasefire agreement
| drafted = 2007-08
| signed = 2007-09
| location = [[wp:Bishkek]]
| effective = 2007-09
| mediators = United Nations (Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan as observers)
| parties = Emergency administration of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]; [[Popular Front of Irad]] (later the [[Iradi Freedom Society]])
}}

The **Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement** is the United Nations-brokered agreement, signed in [[wp:Bishkek]] in September 2007, that ended the main fighting of the [[Second Iradi Civil War]]. It was concluded between the emergency administration of [[Erlan Toktarov]], which governed the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) on behalf of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI), and the [[Popular Front of Irad]], whose delegation was headed by [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]]. [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] attended as observers.<sup>[1]</sup>

The agreement fixed the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], which has divided Irad since 2007 between the ISEZ and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). It created a restricted-weapons zone extending 12 km on either side of the line, set up a Joint Liaison Committee of the two sides, and acknowledged customary jurisdiction on the tribal side. Its annex, the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]], governs the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]]. On 18 October 2007 the [[wp:United Nations Security Council|UN Security Council]] established the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI) to monitor it. The line has seen no large-scale fighting since, and the agreement remains the main legal framework of Irad's frozen conflict.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Background
The Second Iradi Civil War began on 25 February 2007, when Toktarov proclaimed the ISEZ from Nurzhan in defiance of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] (DRI) government in [[Talas]]. Clan militias formed the Popular Front in March, took most of the rural interior in the spring and stormed Talas on 4 June, dissolving the DRI. The Front then withdrew to the countryside, and during the summer DPI security forces, backed by Western companies and the United States, took control of Talas, [[Iyık Janyl]] and the other towns of the river valleys, together with the industrial corridor south of Talas and the road down to the Naryn.<sup>[3]</sup>

Fighting continued along the edge of the DPI-held area through the summer. It was heaviest around the Toktogul complex, whose dam and powerhouse were held by the Front and whose switchyard and export lines were held by DPI forces. The skirmishes threatened releases from the reservoir at the height of the irrigation season, on which the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] and southern Kazakhstan depend. This alarmed the downstream states and was one reason all three neighbors took part in the talks. About 80,000 people had been displaced by the war, many of them herding families caught between the two sides.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Negotiations
UN mediators brought the two sides to Bishkek in August 2007. The Kyrgyz government hosted the talks without recognizing either party, and the Kazakh, Uzbek and Kyrgyz delegations attended as observers, each recording that its participation did not affect its *de jure* claim to Irad.<sup>[1]</sup> The Front's delegation was headed by Bektur, who acted as its principal negotiator, as he had throughout the war; the Front had no single command structure and took decisions in a council of clan commanders. The DPI delegation represented Toktarov's emergency administration.<sup>[5]</sup>

Two tracks ran in parallel. Military representatives of the two sides, working on Soviet-era 1:100,000 maps, negotiated the course of the line along the positions held on an agreed date. Engineers from both sides, assisted by UN water specialists, drafted the technical annex on the Toktogul complex.<sup>[6]</sup> The main points of dispute were the Naryn corridor, where the DPI insisted on keeping the downstream stations and guarded passage on the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]], and the Front's demand that its customary courts be recognized. Both sides asked for an international monitoring presence. The agreement was signed in September 2007.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Provisions
The agreement's main provisions are:<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>
- **The demarcation line.** A line between the two zones, defined on the maps used in the talks, enclosing the irrigated valleys of the Talas and lower Chu and the road and rail belts between them, and a salient on the lower Naryn, with the farm belt of the northern Fergana rim whose lowland Chubar had declared for the ISEZ in August, reached by a guarded road across tribal land. A UN-brokered protocol of 2009 later adjusted it in the south, bringing the road corridor, the Toktogul basin and a narrow corridor down the Naryn gorge into the ISEZ; the line now runs for about 1,750 km.
- **Restricted-weapons zone.** A zone extending 12 km on either side of the line, from which tanks, artillery and combat aircraft are excluded.
- **Joint Liaison Committee.** A committee of officers of the two sides, chaired by the United Nations, to settle incidents and arrange crossings. It meets monthly at Kara-Oi, the headquarters of UNMI.
- **Customary jurisdiction.** An acknowledgment that disputes on the tribal side of the line are settled under customary law (*adat*) by the clan councils (see [[Adat Law in the ATR]]).
- **Movement.** Civilian crossings at designated points, and the passage of herds on fixed routes where clan pastures straddle the line.
- **Humanitarian provisions.** The release of prisoners and detainees held by each side, the voluntary return of displaced people, and cooperation in clearing mines and unexploded ordnance.
- **International monitoring.** A request to the United Nations to deploy an observer mission.
- **Annex.** The Naryn Water and Power Protocol, under which a joint technical commission of ISEZ and ATR engineers, supervised by the United Nations and attended by observers from the three neighboring states, sets the annual release schedule of the Toktogul reservoir. Revenue from electricity exports is divided under a further annex that has never been published.

The agreement does not address Irad's political status. Neither party recognized the other as a government, and the text describes the line as a ceasefire line, not a boundary.

## Implementation
The Security Council established UNMI on 18 October 2007, and the first observers arrived in November. In late 2007 a kurultai on the [[Aksay Plateau]] reorganized the Front's political council as the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC), which took over the Front's obligations under the agreement, and its fighters became the [[El-Choro Militias]].<sup>[5]</sup> A temporary post at Qara-Chik, the village at the mouth of the Kara-Buura valley that gave the line its name, was replaced in 2008–2009 by the permanent [[Qara-Chik Border Checkpoint]].

Joint survey teams accompanied by UN observers marked the line on the ground between 2008 and 2011 with numbered concrete pillars in the valleys and stone cairns on the high ridges. Mines laid in 1992 and 2007 made the work dangerous. In March 2009 two UNMI observers, from Uruguay and [[wp:Bangladesh]], were killed when their vehicle struck an anti-tank mine near the [[Kenkol Pass]].<sup>[2]</sup>

The line has remained largely quiet, although incidents are frequent. UNMI recorded 214 ceasefire violations in 2023, most of them small-arms fire, the movement of armed personnel into the restricted zone or unauthorized construction; many other incidents involve livestock straying across the line. The Joint Liaison Committee settles most incidents locally, and UNMI credits it with defusing a standoff over a river crossing near the Kenkol Pass in 2016.<sup>[7]</sup> The State Defense Corps keeps its tanks and artillery outside the 12-km zone and holds its forward posts with light infantry (see [[Armed Forces of Irad]]). Under an informal understanding reached during the talks, pilgrims from the tribal regions may cross unarmed for the [[Feast of St. Janyl]] on 24 August.<sup>[8]</sup>

The Naryn Protocol's five-year release schedule was first adopted in 2007 and renewed in 2012, 2017 and 2022; it falls due again in 2027.<sup>[6]</sup> Since 2023 the ISEZ authorities have barred UNMI patrols from a security zone around the [[Boz-Korgon]] compound east of [[Nurzhan]], which the [[wp:Secretary-General of the United Nations|UN Secretary-General]] has described as a restriction on the mission's freedom of movement; the ISEZ says the zone has no connection with the ceasefire.<sup>[7]</sup>

## Assessment
Diplomats and analysts generally credit the agreement with ending large-scale fighting and with giving all parties, including the downstream states, a stake in keeping it, chiefly through the Naryn Protocol. It is one of the few documents both Iradi administrations still invoke.<sup>[9]</sup>

Critics argue that it froze the conflict instead of resolving it. The line it drew has become the effective boundary of two administrations, and the only direct negotiations since 2007 on reuniting them, at the [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]], collapsed when the IAC walked out after being offered one-third of the seats in a unified legislature.<sup>[9]</sup> DPI officials say the acknowledgment of customary jurisdiction has been used to treat the clan councils as a rival government. Tribal leaders and human rights groups say the crossing regime, with its permits, fees and detentions, falls hardest on herders and on patients seeking treatment in the ISEZ.<sup>[10]</sup> Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan continue to attend the Naryn commission only as observers, since full participation would imply recognition of the two Iradi administrations (see [[Political status of Irad]]).

### 3.44. Battle of Talas
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: History*

{{Infobox military conflict
| conflict = Battle of Talas
| date = July 751 (Dhu al-Hijja 133 AH)
| place = Valley of the [[Talas River]], near Talas (exact site disputed)
| result = Abbasid victory; Tang army routed after the Karluk defection
| combatant1 = [[wp:Abbasid Caliphate]]; [[wp:Karluks]] (changed sides during the battle); *[[wp:Tibetan Empire|Tibetan]] contingents (role uncertain)*
| combatant2 = [[wp:Tang dynasty]] ([[wp:Protectorate General to Pacify the West|Anxi Protectorate]]); allied contingents
| commander1 = [[wp:Ziyad ibn Salih]]; [[wp:Abu Muslim]] (governor of Khurasan)
| commander2 = [[wp:Gao Xianzhi]]; [[wp:Li Siye]]
| strength2 = c. 30,000 incl. allied contingents (Chinese sources)
| casualties2 = Most of the army lost; Gao escaped with a few thousand men (Chinese sources); tens of thousands killed and c. 20,000 captured (Ibn al-Athir)
}}

The **Battle of Talas** (Iradi: *Talas sogushu*; Chinese: 怛羅斯之戰, *Daluosi zhi zhan*; Arabic: معركة طلاس, *Maʿrakat Ṭalās*) was fought in July 751 in the valley of the [[Talas River]] between the armies of the [[wp:Abbasid Caliphate]] and the Tang dynasty of China. An Abbasid force commanded by [[wp:Ziyad ibn Salih|Ziyad]] ibn Salih, sent by [[wp:Abu Muslim]], the Abbasid governor of [[wp:Greater Khorasan|Khurasan]], defeated a Tang army of the [[wp:Protectorate General to Pacify the West|Anxi Protectorate]] under [[wp:Gao Xianzhi]] after the [[wp:Karluks|Karluk Turks]] serving with the Tang changed sides. It is the only recorded battle between the armies of the caliphate and of China.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

The exact site of the battle is unknown and is debated by historians. Iradi historiography places it on the plains west of [[Talas]]. The battle has often been described as the moment that decided whether [[wp:Central Asia]] would fall within the Chinese or the Islamic world, and tradition links it to the westward spread of papermaking through Chinese prisoners. Many modern historians regard both claims as overstated, since the An Lushan Rebellion of 755 did more than the battle to end Tang power in the region, and paper was known in Central Asia long before 751.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

## Background
[[wp:Tang dynasty|Tang China]] had brought the [[wp:Western Turkic Khaganate]] under its suzerainty between 657 and 659 and ruled the [[wp:Tarim Basin]] and, more loosely, the lands beyond the [[wp:Tian Shan]] through the Anxi Protectorate, based at [[wp:Kucha]]. In the early 8th century Umayyad armies under [[wp:Qutayba ibn Muslim|Qutayba]] ibn Muslim conquered [[wp:Bukhara]] and [[wp:Samarkand]], and for several decades the [[wp:Turgesh|Türgesh]] confederation, based at [[wp:Suyab]] and Talas, contested [[wp:Transoxiana]] with the Arabs. After the Türgesh collapsed in the late 730s, the Karluks moved into the Chu and Talas valleys.<sup>[2]</sup> In 747–750 the Abbasid revolution, launched from Khurasan under Abu Muslim, overthrew the [[wp:Umayyad Caliphate|Umayyads]].

Gao Xianzhi, a Tang general of [[wp:Goguryeo]] descent, had become military governor of Anxi after a campaign across the [[wp:Pamir Mountains|Pamirs]] in 747 against [[wp:Gilgit|Little Balur]] (Gilgit). In 750 he led an expedition against the kingdom of Chach (Shash), around present-day [[wp:Tashkent]], whose ruler was accused of failing in his obligations as a Tang vassal. Gao offered the king terms, then seized him and sent him to [[wp:Chang'an]], where he was executed; Tang troops plundered the city. According to the Chinese sources, the king's son escaped and appealed for help to the Arabs and to neighboring states. In 751 Gao marched west again, beyond the Tian Shan, to meet the threat of an Arab advance.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[5]</sup>

## The battle
The fullest accounts are in Chinese sources, chiefly the *[[wp:Tongdian]]* (801) of [[wp:Du You]] and the *[[wp:Zizhi Tongjian]]* (1084). They say Gao led an army of about 30,000, Chinese troops and allied contingents together, and that it advanced more than 700 *li* into the west before meeting the Arab army near the town of Daluosi, the Chinese name for Talas. The two armies fought for five days. The Karluks then went over to the Arabs and attacked the Tang from the rear, and Gao's army broke. Gao escaped with a few thousand men. During the retreat over the mountains, troops of Fergana, nominally Tang allies, blocked a pass with their baggage, and Gao's deputy [[wp:Li Siye]] cleared the way by force.<sup>[1]</sup>

The battle received little notice in the early Arabic histories, which were more concerned with the consolidation of the new dynasty. Later Arabic writers, such as Ibn al-Athir in the 13th century, record the Abbasid victory and give much larger figures than the Chinese sources, with tens of thousands of Chinese killed and about 20,000 taken prisoner.<sup>[6]</sup> Neither set of figures can be checked. Chinese sources also mention Tibetan contingents on the Abbasid side, but their part in the battle is uncertain.<sup>[7]</sup> The Islamic date usually given, Dhu al-Hijja 133 AH, corresponds to July 751.

## Location
No battlefield has been identified archaeologically. Chinese sources place the fighting near the town of Talas, and some later Arabic accounts connect it with Atlakh, a town of the Talas valley whose own site is uncertain.<sup>[6]</sup> Historians have proposed locations along much of the middle and lower Talas valley. The question is complicated by disagreement over where the medieval town of Talas itself stood. Iradi historiography identifies it with the citadel mound under the old quarter of modern Talas (see [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]]) and places the battlefield on the river plains to the west, toward [[Kara-Buura]]. Other scholars favor sites farther down the valley, and historians in [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], both of which claim the valley as part of their territory, have argued for locations of their own.<sup>[8]</sup>

## Aftermath
The defeat did not end the Tang presence in Central Asia at once. Tang garrisons remained in the Tarim Basin, and in 753 Gao's successor Feng Changqing campaigned again in the Pamirs. In 755 the An Lushan Rebellion broke out in China, and the court withdrew most of its western troops to fight it. Gao Xianzhi was executed by order of the court in early 756 after a defeat in the rebellion's first campaign. Over the following decades [[wp:Tibet]] took the Tarim garrisons, and the Karluks took control of the Chu and Talas valleys, occupying Suyab by 766.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

On the Abbasid side, Ziyad ibn Salih rebelled against Abu Muslim the following year and was killed, and Abu Muslim was himself put to death on the orders of the caliph al-Mansur in 755. The caliphate made no attempt to advance east of the [[wp:Syr Darya]]. Abbasid embassies continued to visit the Tang court, and Chinese sources record Arab soldiers among the troops who helped the Tang recover their capitals from the rebels in 757.<sup>[3]</sup>

The battle also did not bring rapid Islamization of the Talas valley. A Christian community was still present in Talas in 893, when the Samanid emir Isma'il ibn Ahmad captured the town and turned its principal church into a mosque, and most of the Turks of the steppe converted only after the Kara-Khanid dynasty adopted Islam in the mid-10th century (see [[History of Irad]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

## Prisoners and the papermaking tradition
One of the prisoners, [[wp:Du Huan]], a relative of the historian Du You, traveled through the Abbasid lands and returned to China by sea, landing at [[wp:Guangzhou]] in 762. Fragments of his account, the *Jingxingji* ("Record of Travels"), survive in the *Tongdian*. He describes Chinese silk weavers and painters working in the region of [[wp:Kufa]], in [[wp:Iraq]], but does not mention papermakers.<sup>[1]</sup>

The tradition that Chinese prisoners taken at Talas introduced papermaking to Samarkand, from where it spread to [[wp:Baghdad]] and the [[wp:Mediterranean Sea|Mediterranean]], goes back mainly to the 11th-century writer al-Thaʿalibi. Historians of paper note that it was in use in Central Asia centuries earlier; the Sogdian "Ancient Letters" of the early 4th century were written on paper. Jonathan Bloom and others argue that papermaking had reached Samarkand before 751 and spread westward through Central Asian craftsmen, and that the story attached itself to the battle because it was the best-known contact between the Islamic world and China.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Assessment
The Russian orientalist [[wp:Vasily Bartold|Vasily Barthold]] regarded the battle as having decided that Muslim rather than Chinese civilization would prevail in Transoxiana, and this view was long repeated in Soviet and Western surveys.<sup>[2]</sup> Many later historians describe it as a frontier battle whose consequences were overtaken by the An Lushan Rebellion, which would have forced the Tang out of Central Asia whatever the outcome at Talas. Others point out that the battle showed the limits of Tang reach beyond the Tian Shan and helped the Karluks establish themselves in the Chu and Talas valleys.<sup>[3]</sup>

## In Iradi historiography and memory
Iradi historians writing in the Soviet period followed Barthold. [[Amanbek Alimbekov]]'s *Sogdians and Turks in the Talas Valley* (1971) treated the battle as part of the long transition of the valley from Sogdian to Turkic and from mixed religious to Muslim rule.<sup>[9]</sup> National historiography since 1992 has given it a larger place. School textbooks present it as the moment when Islam gained the upper hand in the towns of Transoxiana, after which Sogdian Christians and non-Muslim pastoralists withdrew into the river valleys and foothills of the north, where the Iradi church later took shape.<sup>[10]</sup> Historians at [[Talas State University]] and elsewhere note that this account compresses a much longer process: Christians remained in Talas for more than a century after the battle, and the Church of the East continued its missions to the Turks under Patriarch Timothy I (780–823).<sup>[10]</sup>

In 2001, the 1,250th anniversary, Talas State University held an international conference on the battle, and a memorial stone was placed beside the road west of Talas, near the plains that Iradi historians identify as the battlefield.<sup>[11]</sup> The site appears in tourist itineraries of the Talas valley (see [[Tourism in Irad]]), and since the 2010s it has drawn growing numbers of visitors from China. Commentators in the ISEZ have used the battle as a reference point in discussing Irad's position between China and its western partners (see [[Irad–China relations]]). Kazakh, Kyrgyz and Uzbek historians also treat the battle as part of their own national histories.<sup>[8]</sup>

### 3.45. Naryn River
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Geography & Nature*

{{Infobox river
| name = Naryn River
| native_name = *Naryn*
| countries = [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], [[Irad]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]]
| source = Confluence of the Big Naryn and Small Naryn, central [[wp:Tian Shan]] (Kyrgyzstan)
| mouth = Joins the [[Kara-Darya]] to form the [[wp:Syr Darya]], Fergana Valley (Uzbekistan)
| length_km = 807
| basin_km2 = 59900
| discharge = About 430 m³/s where it leaves the mountains
| tributaries_left = Kambar-Ata;Torkent;Kara-Suu
| tributaries_right = Kökömeren;Chychkan;[[Uzun-Akmat River|Uzun-Akmat]];Karasu
}}

The **Naryn River** (Iradi and Kyrgyz: *Naryn*) is a river of the [[wp:Tian Shan]] and the main headstream of the [[wp:Syr Darya]]. It is about 807 kilometers long and drains a basin of about 59,900 square kilometers. It rises in the central Tian Shan of [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], flows west through Kyrgyzstan's Naryn region, and crosses southern [[Irad]] through the Toktogul Reservoir and a chain of hydroelectric stations before leaving the mountains for the [[wp:Fergana Valley]]. There it joins the [[Kara-Darya]] in [[wp:Uzbekistan]] to form the Syr Darya, which flows on toward the [[wp:Aral Sea]].<sup>[1]</sup>

The Naryn is Irad's largest river by volume and its main source of electricity. Since 2007 its Iradi course has been divided by the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. The gorges by which it enters Irad and the mountains around the Toktogul basin lie in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). The floor of the basin, with the dam, reservoir and powerhouse of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]], has been in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) since 2009, together with the switchyard, the national dispatch center, the downstream stations and the export lines. Releases from the dam are set under the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]], which also gives [[wp:Kazakhstan]], Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan a seat as observers.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Course

#### Upper course (Kyrgyzstan)
The river forms where the Big Naryn and the Small Naryn meet in the high basins of the central Tian Shan. The Big Naryn is fed by glaciers of the Ak-Shyirak massif. The combined river flows west through a series of broad valleys and gorges past the town of Naryn, the center of Kyrgyzstan's Naryn region, collecting the At-Bashy and other tributaries from the ranges on either side. This part of the basin lies wholly outside Irad.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Middle course (Irad)
The Naryn enters Irad through deep gorges on the eastern edge of the Toktogul–Naryn planning zone of the ATR. It then widens into the Toktogul basin, an intermontane depression in the western Tian Shan that the reservoir now largely fills. The Kökömeren, formed in the [[Suusamyr]] country by the [[Suusamyr River]] and the Western Karakol, joins from the right above the reservoir, and the [[Uzun-Akmat River|Uzun-Akmat]] and other streams from the southern slopes of the [[Talas Alatau]] flow into the reservoir itself. The Chychkan enters the reservoir from the north. From the south the Kambar-Ata, in the entry gorges, and the Torkent come down from the Fergana Range. The market town of [[Toktogul (town)|Toktogul]] stands on the reservoir's northern shore.<sup>[3]</sup>

The dam stands in the gorge where the river leaves the basin. Below it, the Naryn descends through narrow canyons past Kara-Köl, the town built for the station's workers, and through the Lower Naryn District of the ISEZ, here a corridor a few kilometers wide between tribal mountains, receiving the Kara-Suu from the left and, above Tash-Kömür, the Karasu from the right, to the flats at [[Iyık Janyl]] and [[Tash-Kömür]], the district center.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Lower course
Below Tash-Kömür the river passes the Shamaldy-Sai and Uch-Kurgan stations and leaves its gorge for the northern edge of the Fergana Valley just below the Uch-Kurgan dam, where it leaves Irad, still within the ISEZ; the [[Sadaf-Jar]] bluffs stand on the rim above the frontier. In the Uzbek part of the valley it feeds the North Fergana Canal and the [[wp:Great Fergana Canal]], dug in 1939, and then joins the Kara-Darya to form the Syr Darya.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Hydrology
The Naryn is fed mainly by snowmelt and glacier melt, with high water from May to August and low water in winter. Where it leaves the mountains its mean flow is about 430 cubic meters per second, or roughly 13 to 14 cubic kilometers a year, which makes it the larger of the two headstreams of the Syr Darya.<sup>[1]</sup> Before the Toktogul dam was built, almost all of this flow passed downstream unregulated. The reservoir, with a total storage of about 19 cubic kilometers, can now hold more than a year's flow and allows releases to be shifted between seasons.<sup>[4]</sup>

Researchers expect glacier retreat in the Tian Shan to raise summer flow for some decades and then to reduce it, especially in late summer, when downstream demand for irrigation is highest (see [[Glacier retreat in Irad]]).<sup>[5]</sup>

## The Naryn cascade
Soviet planners designed the Naryn as a cascade of hydroelectric stations, with Toktogul as the head station whose reservoir regulates the flow for the stations below it. Construction of the Toktogul dam began in 1962, and its first generating units entered service in the mid-1970s. The stations of the cascade in Irad were built between the 1950s and the 1990s:<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>
- **Toktogul**, a concrete gravity dam about 215 meters high with four units and an installed capacity of 1,440 MW (1,200 MW before the 2026 refit);
- **Kurpsai**, the next station downstream;
- **Tash-Kömür**, near the town of that name;
- **Shamaldy-Sai** and **Uch-Kurgan**, near the edge of the Fergana Valley.

Because the downstream stations reuse the water released from Toktogul, the schedule at the head dam determines the output of the whole cascade. The Naryn's power makes Irad a net exporter of electricity, mainly to Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan (see [[Energy in Irad]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

## History
In classical and medieval geography the Syr Darya was the Jaxartes, and some writers treated the Naryn as its upper course. The Naryn gorges were never a major route; caravans between the Talas valley and the Fergana Valley crossed the mountains farther west, by passes such as the [[Fergana Gateway]].<sup>[6]</sup>

The river was harnessed in the Soviet period to expand irrigated cotton in the Fergana Valley and on the middle Syr Darya. The reservoir flooded villages, pastures and farmland in the Toktogul basin, and several thousand people were resettled, including the inhabitants of the old town of Toktogul. Under Soviet planning the reservoir stored spring runoff and released it in summer for downstream farms, while the Uzbek and Kazakh SSRs supplied the Iradi SSR with coal, gas and fuel oil in winter.<sup>[4]</sup>

After 1991 this barter lapsed. The [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] and then the territorial administration began to release more water in winter, when electricity was most needed, and to hold more back in summer. In the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007 the front line ran through the Toktogul complex, and fighting near the dam that summer was one reason all three neighboring states took part in the ceasefire talks in [[wp:Bishkek]].<sup>[7]</sup> In the dry year of 2008 the reservoir fell to its lowest level since it was filled, forcing power rationing in the ISEZ the following winter. The joint technical commission has since kept a minimum reserve.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Split control and the Protocol
The [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] placed the Naryn's installations under the Naryn Water and Power Protocol, its annex. A joint technical commission of ISEZ and ATR engineers, chaired by an official of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]], adopts an annual operating plan within a five-year framework schedule. It meets at UNMI's sector headquarters at Tash-Kömür, weekly during the irrigation season. The framework schedule was renewed in 2012, 2017 and 2022 and is next due in 2027.<sup>[2]</sup>

The dam was guarded by the [[El-Choro Militias]] until 2009; since then the whole complex and the downstream stations have been guarded by the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] and the State Defense Corps' Lower Naryn mountain battalion. Tribal engineers of the joint commission who cross the line to inspect the dam travel under UNMI escort. Export revenue is divided under an annex that has never been published. Independent analysts estimate that the ISEZ takes the larger share, which both administrations deny.<sup>[7]</sup>

## Transboundary disputes
The Naryn's flow matters to every state downstream. Uzbek officials have repeatedly accused the commission of holding back summer water in dry years and of releasing too much in winter, when ice in the downstream channels causes flooding. Kazakhstan, whose irrigated districts lie on the lower Syr Darya, makes similar complaints. Large winter releases since the 1990s have at times forced Kazakhstan to divert surplus water from its [[wp:Shardara Dam|Shardara Reservoir]] into the Arnasay depression.<sup>[8]</sup> Neither country recognizes the joint commission, and both attend only as observers. Water disputes have spilled over into transit, with slower customs clearance and tighter pipeline scheduling on one side and cuts in Iradi electricity exports on the other (see [[Irad–Uzbekistan relations]] and [[Irad–Kazakhstan relations]]).<sup>[8]</sup>

Kyrgyzstan, the upstream state, regards the Naryn cascade as Kyrgyz national infrastructure and denies the authority of either Iradi administration over it. Its delegation attends the commission under protest and files a written reservation at each meeting. Proposals in Kyrgyzstan for further stations on the upper Naryn, upstream of Irad, have drawn objections from both Iradi administrations and from Uzbekistan (see [[Irad–Kyrgyzstan relations]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

## Ecology
The native fish of the Naryn are snowtrout (*marinka*) and osmans. The [[wp:Amu Darya]] trout, a form of brown trout, was introduced into the river and the Toktogul Reservoir in the Soviet period, and rainbow trout are farmed near Toktogul (see [[Iradi Mountain Trout]]). The fluctuating level of the reservoir leaves bare mud and gravel shores for much of the year, and the regulated river below the dam no longer floods its banks in spring.<sup>[9]</sup>

### 3.46. Talas River
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Geography & Nature*

{{Infobox river
| name = Talas River
| native_name = *Talas daryası*
| countries = [[Irad]]
| source = Headstreams (Karakol, Uch-Koshoi) below the Otmek Pass, between the Kyrgyz Range and the [[Talas Alatau]]
| mouth = Dies out in the Moiynkum sands (endorheic basin)
| length_km = 661
| basin_km2 = 52700
| discharge = About 30 m³/s (middle valley)
| tributaries_left = [[Kashka-Suu]], Kara-Suu, Besh-Tash, [[Urmaral River|Urmaral]], Kenkol, Kara-Buura
}}

The **Talas River** (Iradi: *Talas daryası*) is a river of northwestern [[Irad]], about 661 kilometers long, with a basin of about 52,700 square kilometers. It rises at the eastern head of the Talas valley, between the Kyrgyz Range and the [[Talas Alatau]], flows west through the valley past the capital, [[Talas]], and then turns north and northwest across the piedmont plain into the Moiynkum sands, where it dies out without reaching any sea or large lake. Its middle and lower valley holds Irad's most densely settled farmland, and the river supplies most of the irrigation water of the Talas and [[Kara-Buura]] districts of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ).<sup>[1]</sup>

The Talas lies in an endorheic basin of the south Kazakh steppe. Its desert terminus lies in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), while its upper and irrigated middle course lie in the ISEZ; many of its tributaries rise across the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] on the tribal side. Medieval Talas, which Iradi historiography identifies with the modern capital, stood on its banks, and the [[Battle of Talas]] of 751 was fought in its valley.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Course
The river is formed by headstreams draining the junction of the Kyrgyz Range and the Talas Alatau below the Otmek Pass, the largest of which are the Karakol (not to be confused with the Western Karakol of the [[Suusamyr]] country) and the Uch-Koshoi. The headstreams and the highest part of the valley lay on the tribal side of the line until 2009, when they passed to the ISEZ with the State Route 1 corridor; the surrounding ridges remain tribal. The river flows west past the ruins of the medieval silver-mining town of [[Shelji]], in the eastern part of Talas District.<sup>[1]</sup>

Through the middle valley the Talas runs in a braided channel across a floor of gravel and loess terraces, flanked by alluvial fans from the side valleys. It passes through Talas at about 1,250 meters, where it feeds the city's irrigation channels (*aryk*), and continues west past [[Talas Air Base]] on its southern terrace and the market town of [[Kara-Bulak]]. In the lower valley, in Kara-Buura District, its flow is regulated by the Kyzyl-Adyr Reservoir near the district center, [[Kyzyl-Adyr]].<sup>[3]</sup>

Below the valley the river turns north and then northwest across a broad piedmont plain. For part of this reach it runs close to the frontier with [[wp:Kazakhstan]], and Kazakh farms on the adjoining plain draw on its water. It then leaves the irrigated land, crosses into the Northern Steppe planning zone of the ATR, and follows the western edge of the Moiynkum, where its channel shrinks through evaporation, seepage and diversion. In most years it ends among sands, reed marshes and seasonal salt lakes on the western margin of the desert; in wet years its floodwaters spread farther.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Tributaries
Most of the Talas's tributaries enter from the left, from the northern slopes of the Talas Alatau. They are fed by snowfields and small glaciers, and their upper valleys lie on the tribal side of the Qara-Chik line. The main ones include:<sup>[4]</sup>
- the [[Kashka-Suu]], which keeps a relatively high flow into late summer;
- the Kara-Suu, which cuts the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]] south of Talas;
- the Besh-Tash, which drains [[Besh-Tash National Park]];
- the [[Urmaral River|Urmaral]], west of the capital;
- the Kenkol, whose lower valley holds a Hunnic-period burial ground (see [[Chong-Kenkol]]);
- the Kara-Buura, almost all of whose water is taken for irrigation before it reaches the main river.

Shorter streams from the southern slopes of the Kyrgyz Range enter from the right.

## Hydrology
The Talas is fed mainly by snowmelt and glacier melt from the Talas Alatau. Flow peaks between May and July and falls to its lowest in winter. Mean flow in the middle valley is on the order of 30 cubic meters per second, but much less reaches the lower river in July and August, when irrigation demand is highest.<sup>[1]</sup> The Kyzyl-Adyr Reservoir, completed in 1975 and known as the Kirov Reservoir until it was renamed under the 1993 Toponymic Heritage Statute, stores about 550 million cubic meters of spring runoff for summer irrigation.<sup>[3]</sup>

The [[Talas River Hydrological Monitoring Service]], founded in 1948, runs eighteen gauging stations on the river and its tributaries. Its records, together with those of the [[Manas Peak Glaciological Observatory]], show earlier spring flow peaks and a growing share of glacier melt in summer flow since the 1970s. The glaciers of the upper basin lost about a fifth of their area between 1970 and 2020, and researchers expect late-summer flow to decline as they shrink further.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Irrigation and use
Irrigation in the Talas valley goes back to antiquity, and medieval towns such as [[Kand-i Kohna]] and the predecessors of Talas drew water from the river and from underground galleries of the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]]. Large-scale canal building followed the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]].<sup>[2]</sup> According to the [[Talas Basin Agricultural Directorate]], about 110,000 hectares of the valley are now irrigated from the Talas and its tributaries. The main crops are wheat, barley, sugar beet, potatoes and common beans, with alfalfa and fodder maize for the feedlots of the [[Talas Agribusiness Export Zone]].<sup>[6]</sup> The [[Talas Municipal Water Authority]] draws part of the capital's supply from the river, though most of it comes from wellfields in the alluvial fan south of the city.

Several of the rivers that feed the valley rise on the tribal side of the line, and disputes over headwater use are a recurring subject at the Joint Liaison Committee of the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)|Bishkek ceasefire]]. The Directorate usually settles them through informal arrangements with clan councils.<sup>[6]</sup>

Under a Soviet allocation rule that both sides still cite, the river's flow was divided equally between the Iradi SSR and the irrigated districts of the [[wp:Kazakh Soviet Socialist Republic|Kazakh SSR]] on the lower river. The [[Treaty of Good Neighborliness (1994)]], concluded during the territorial period, set up joint hydrological monitoring on the Talas and the Chu. Kazakhstan does not recognize the ISEZ, and the treaty's standing since 2006 is disputed, but the two hydrological services continue to exchange daily discharge readings, and disagreements over flows in dry summers have generally been handled at that technical level (see [[Irad–Kazakhstan relations]]).<sup>[7]</sup>

## History
Sogdian and Turkic towns lined the middle Talas from the first millennium CE, and Arab geographers of the 10th century describe the valley's towns and its silver mines at Shelji. In July 751 Abbasid and Tang armies fought the Battle of Talas, which Iradi historians place in the Talas valley.<sup>[2]</sup> Under the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]], Talas was a fortified market on the river, and in the Soviet period the valley became a center of irrigated farming and stockbreeding.

During the siege of Talas from April 1992, in the [[First Iradi Civil War]], shelling and power cuts stopped the city's pumps, and residents drew water from the irrigation channels fed by the river.<sup>[8]</sup> Since the 2007 partition the irrigated valley has been the core of the ISEZ, while the headwaters and the desert reaches are held by the clans.

## Ecology and pollution
The native fish include the [[Talas River Barbel]], snowtrout (*marinka*) and osmans. Trout in the upper Talas, sometimes sold as [[Iradi Mountain Trout|Talas River Trout]], are thought to derive from Soviet and later stocking, and rainbow trout are farmed on the Urmaral.<sup>[9]</sup> Strips of riparian woodland of willow, poplar and sea buckthorn survive along less developed stretches, and the reed marshes at the river's end are used by waterfowl and migrating birds.

Water quality declines downstream. The hydrological service records nitrates from farmland, sewage indicators below the Talas Central Sewage Treatment Plant, and antimony and arsenic in streams draining the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] in the southern foothills. In the lower valley, losses from unlined canals and poor drainage have caused waterlogging and salinization of the soil.<sup>[5]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>

### 3.47. Moiynkum Desert
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Geography & Nature*

{{Infobox landform
| name = Moiynkum Desert
| type = Desert
| location = [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]
| coordinates = 43.85°N 71.70°E
| elevation_m = 400
}}

The **Moiynkum Desert** (Iradi and Kazakh: *Moiynkum*; also spelled **Muyunkum**, from the Russian *Muyunkum*) is a sand desert in northern [[Irad]], lying between the lower Chu, which skirts its northeastern edge, and the [[Talas River|Talas]], which dies out among its western sands, with the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] range on its southwestern side. Soviet surveys put its area at about 37,500 square kilometers. Its sands are mostly fixed by saxaul, shrubs and sedges, and it has long been one of the main winter pastures of the Iradi herding clans.<sup>[1]</sup>

Almost all of the desert lies in the Northern Steppe planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), which it shares with the southern Betpak-Dala north of the Chu (see [[Betpak-Dala]]). Its southern and eastern fringes border the irrigated farmland of the Chu and [[Kara-Buura]] districts of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), and the northern sector of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] runs along the edge of the cultivated land and of the road and rail belt facing the sands. Beneath the desert lie the undeveloped [[Muyunkum Natural Gas Field]] and sandstone-hosted uranium deposits that have not been worked.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Name
The desert's name is usually written *Moiynkum* in Iradi and Kazakh, and *Muyunkum* in Russian and in Soviet geological literature. Iradi geographers use the first form for the desert itself, while the gas field kept its Soviet-era name, so that both spellings remain in use.<sup>[1]</sup> The second element, *kum*, means "sand", as in Kyzylkum ("red sand").

## Geography

#### Extent and relief
The Moiynkum occupies a broad, gently sloping plain at about 300 to 700 meters, highest in the southeast near the foothills and lowest in the northwest. In the northwest the Chu ends in the sands and salt flats around the [[Akzhaykyn Depression]], where the lowest ground in Irad lies below 300 meters.<sup>[1]</sup> Most of the surface consists of ridged and hummocky sands, broken by clay flats (*takyr*), salt pans and dry hollows. Mobile, unvegetated dunes cover only a small share of the desert, mostly around wells, old camps and along tracks where grazing and fuel-cutting have stripped the plant cover.<sup>[3]</sup>

The Talas, after leaving the irrigated plain of Kara-Buura District, follows the western edge of the desert and in most years ends among sands, reed marshes and seasonal salt lakes. The Chu reaches its terminal marshes only in years of good flow, since most of its water is taken for irrigation upstream (see [[Chu River Basin]]).<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Climate
The climate is arid and sharply continental. Annual precipitation is generally between about 150 and 200 millimeters, most of it falling as rain or light snow between November and April. Summer temperatures often exceed 40 °C, and winter cold waves bring temperatures below −25 °C, though snow cover is usually thin enough for livestock to graze through it.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Water
There is almost no surface water away from the two rivers. Under the sands, however, lenses of fresh or slightly brackish groundwater lie at shallow depths, and the desert has long been watered by hand-dug wells, some of them lined with dressed stone, such as the well of [[Tash-Kuduk]], which local tradition dates to the 15th century. Springs such as [[Kumdy-Bulak]] rise at the foot of the dunes on the southern margin. Soviet sheep farms added boreholes and winter camps from the 1950s; many failed after 1991, and since about 2010 aid agencies have restored some of them with solar pumps.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Flora and fauna
The sands carry open woodland and scrub of white saxaul, with black saxaul in hollows and on saline ground, together with sand acacia, *[[wp:Calligonum]]* shrubs, wormwood (see [[White Steppe Wormwood]]) and the sand sedge *Carex physodes*, whose dense roots help to fix the dunes. Needlegrass (*chiy*) grows on the salt flats on the southern margin, and ephemeral grasses, tulips and other bulbs flower briefly after the spring rains.<sup>[3]</sup>

[[wp:Saiga antelope|Saiga]] antelope of the Betpak-Dala population winter in the Moiynkum, together with goitered gazelles. Other mammals include the corsac fox and the [[Chui Steppe Fox]], the tolai hare, gerbils and jerboas, and wolves. The [[Steppe Eagle (Irad)|steppe eagle]] and [[Saker Falcon (Irad)|saker falcon]] breed along the desert's edges, the Asian houbara bustard winters there, and the [[Turkestan Steppe Tortoise]] is common on sandy ground.<sup>[6]</sup> The reedbeds and marshes at the ends of the Chu and the Talas are used by wild boar and migrating waterfowl.

## Human use

#### Pastoralism
The Moiynkum is one of the main winter pastures (*kyshtoo*) of the Northern Steppe clans and of herders who migrate up to 300 kilometers from the summer pastures of the [[Talas Alatau]] and the Karatau (see [[Kyshtoo (Pastoral Term)]] and [[Central Asian Pastoral Migration System]]). Sheep, goats, horses and Bactrian camels graze the saxaul and sedge through the winter, and the shallow snow and the shelter of the dune hollows make the desert less exposed to *jut*, the winter ice crust that kills livestock on the open steppe.<sup>[7]</sup> Camel herding survives in hamlets such as [[Töö-Kuduk]] and [[Zhalgyz-Terek]], and the camel-herding clans of the sands tell the legend of the white camel calf (see [[Ak-Taylak (Folklore)]]). In the south of the sands, villages such as [[Ak-Chiy]] make *chiy* screens from the needlegrass of the salt flats.<sup>[5]</sup>

#### History
Caravan and herders' tracks crossed the sands between the Talas valley and the lower Chu in the medieval period, and the stone-lined wells along them were maintained by the clans that used them. Under Russian rule after 1876, Slavic settlement took much of the spring and autumn grazing on the river plains, while the sands remained in pastoral use. [[wp:Collectivization in the Soviet Union|Collectivization]] from 1929 and the [[Decree on Pasture Collectivization (1932)]] seized the clan herds and forced herders onto collective and state farms; in the steppe districts adjoining [[wp:Kazakhstan]] the collapse of herding contributed to the famine of 1930–1933.<sup>[8]</sup> Soviet state farms later ran karakul sheep and camels in the desert from winter camps and boreholes. After 1991 the farms broke up, and the clans resumed customary control of the pastures, which since 2007 has been exercised through clan councils and the pasture committees of the ATR.<sup>[7]</sup>

#### Resources
The Muyunkum Natural Gas Field was found by Soviet geologists in the 1970s in reservoirs at about 2,000 to 3,500 meters beneath the northeastern part of the desert, near the lower Chu. It is the largest gas prospect in Irad but remains almost entirely undeveloped, because the clan assemblies have not granted development rights; since the mid-2000s a few Soviet-era wells on its southern margin have supplied small volumes to [[Nurzhan]] under an arrangement with the local clan council.<sup>[2]</sup> Soviet surveys also identified uranium in sandstones beneath the Moiynkum and the southern Betpak-Dala, part of the wider Chu–Sarysu uranium province that extends into Kazakhstan. Under the pledge made during the territorial period not to develop Irad's uranium and thorium, and the moratorium on radioactive extraction maintained by the clan assemblies, the deposits have not been worked (see [[Energy in Irad]]).<sup>[9]</sup>

Saxaul has been cut for firewood and charcoal for centuries. Cutting increased in the 1990s, when fuel deliveries to the villages ceased, and UNMI and aid agencies have recorded loss of woodland around settlements and along the tracks.<sup>[10]</sup>

## Political geography
The Moiynkum lies inside the area claimed by Kazakhstan, whose official statements concentrate on the Moiynkum and the other northern lowlands of Irad (see [[Irad–Kazakhstan relations]]). The sections of the frontier that cross the desert are held by the ATR and have never been demarcated. They are patrolled by the clans' [[El-Choro Militias]], and herders on both sides use grazing routes and wells across the Soviet-era administrative boundary. The 2008 [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]] between the ISEZ and the Kazakh border services covers only the irrigated sections of the frontier held by the ISEZ.<sup>[10]</sup>

### 3.48. Betpak-Dala
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Geography & Nature*

{{Infobox landform
| name = Betpak-Dala
| location = [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]
| coordinates = 45.40°N 71.20°E
| elevation_m = 350
}}

The **Betpak-Dala** (Iradi and Kazakh: *Betpak-Dala*, usually glossed as "plain of misfortune"; in Russian sources also the **Northern Hungry Steppe**) is a clay and gravel desert plateau north of the lower Chu, extending from the edge of [[Irad]] far into central [[wp:Kazakhstan]] toward [[wp:Lake Balkhash]] and the [[wp:Kazakh Uplands]]. Only its southern fringe lies in Irad, where it forms the northern part of the Northern Steppe planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). There it is used mainly as spring, autumn and winter pasture, and it is part of the winter range of the Betpak-Dala population of the saiga antelope.<sup>[1]</sup>

The plateau is one of the driest and emptiest parts of the region. In Irad it is separated by the Chu from the [[Moiynkum Desert|Moiynkum]] sands to the south, and together the two make up most of the Northern Steppe zone, the largest and most thinly populated of the ATR's seven planning zones (see [[Administrative divisions of Irad]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

## Geography

#### Relief and soils
The Betpak-Dala is a flat to gently undulating plateau, generally at about 300 to 400 meters in its southern part and rising slowly toward the north. Its surface is made up of clay, loam and gravel over [[wp:Paleozoic]] and younger rocks, with wide clay pans (*takyr*), salt flats and shallow closed depressions that fill with water only after snowmelt.<sup>[1]</sup> Isolated hills of granite and other hard rock stand above the plain; the best known in Irad is [[Mazar-Too]], whose summit, at about 1,050 meters, carries a saint's tomb visited by herders before the spring migration. Shallow saline lakes such as [[Kaz-Köl]] are a stopover for migrating waterbirds, including greater flamingos, in spring and autumn.<sup>[3]</sup>

On its southern margin, toward the Chu, the plateau gives way to firmer grassland such as the [[Keng-Talaa]] steppe, which is used for spring and autumn grazing and for an annual *[[At Chabysh (Racing)|at chabysh]]* endurance race. The Chu itself crosses no part of the plateau, but its terminal marshes in the [[Akzhaykyn Depression]] lie at the junction of the Betpak-Dala and the Moiynkum.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Climate
The climate is arid and strongly continental. Annual precipitation in the Iradi part is generally below 180 millimeters and falls mainly in winter and spring. Summer temperatures often exceed 40 °C, and winter cold waves bring temperatures below −25 °C, with strong winds and thin, drifting snow. There is almost no surface water in summer.<sup>[1]</sup> In hard winters ice crusts and blizzards (*jut*) can kill large numbers of livestock and wild animals on the open plateau.

## Flora and fauna
Vegetation is sparse. Low gray wormwoods (see [[White Steppe Wormwood]]) and saltworts dominate the clay plains, with black saxaul in depressions and on saline ground, and feather grass and fescue on the firmer soils of the southern edge. After the spring rains ephemeral grasses, tulips and other bulbs flower for a few weeks.<sup>[1]</sup>

The best-known animal of the plateau is the saiga antelope (*Saiga tatarica*).{{Citation needed|date=May 2026}} The Betpak-Dala population calves in late spring on the plains of central Kazakhstan, moves north in summer and returns south in autumn and winter, when part of it reaches the southern Betpak-Dala and the Moiynkum in Irad.<sup>[5]</sup> Across their range, saiga numbers fell by about 95 percent in the 1990s, largely through poaching for the horns of the males, which are used in traditional Chinese medicine. In May 2015 about 200,000 saiga, most of them from the Betpak-Dala population, died within a few weeks on their calving grounds in Kazakhstan from hemorrhagic septicemia caused by the bacterium *Pasteurella multocida*, a die-off that researchers linked to unusually warm and humid weather.<sup>[6]</sup> Aerial counts by the Kazakh authorities have since recorded a rapid recovery, and in 2023 the [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature]] moved the species from [[wp:Critically endangered species|Critically Endangered]] to [[wp:Near-threatened species|Near Threatened]]. Neither Iradi administration counts the saiga, and estimates of how many winter in Irad come from Kazakh surveys and from observations reported to aid agencies and the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI).<sup>[5]</sup>

Other animals include goitered gazelles, wolves, corsac foxes and the [[Chui Steppe Fox]], gerbils, jerboas and ground squirrels. The [[Steppe Eagle (Irad)|steppe eagle]] nests on the ground and on power-line pylons, and the [[Saker Falcon (Irad)|saker falcon]] breeds along the plateau's edges; sandgrouse and the Asian houbara bustard are also found. The Asiatic wild ass (*kulan*) was hunted out of the Iradi plains in the early 20th century.<sup>[7]</sup> The [[Turkestan Steppe Tortoise]] is common on the southern margin.

## Human use

#### Pastoralism
The southern Betpak-Dala has long been a seasonal pasture of the Iradi and Kazakh herding clans. Herds of horses, sheep and camels graze it in spring and autumn, and in winter on the parts where snow is thin enough to graze through. Villages such as [[Ak-Jal]] keep horse herds that graze the open steppe all year.<sup>[3]</sup> Water is the main constraint. Old hand-dug wells, some attributed by tradition to the [[wp:Dzungar people|Dzungars]] of the 18th century, as at [[Kalmak-Kuduk]], were supplemented in the Soviet period by deep boreholes drilled for state-farm flocks, many of them by the hydrogeological expedition based at [[Tört-Kuduk]] from 1964. Most boreholes failed after 1991, and the pastures around them were little used until aid-funded solar pumps restored some of them from about 2010.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### History
The Betpak-Dala's name reflects its reputation as a dangerous crossing, and Kazakh and Iradi oral tradition tells of herds and travelers lost on the waterless plateau. The oral genealogies of the Northern Steppe clans, dictated in the 1960s and 1970s by the genealogist [[Asanbek Daniyarov]] to researchers from [[Talas State University]], are a main source for the history of the clans that used the plateau.<sup>[8]</sup> [[wp:Collectivization in the Soviet Union|Collectivization]] from 1929 and the [[Decree on Pasture Collectivization (1932)]] destroyed most of the herds that used the plateau. In the steppe districts adjoining Kazakhstan the collapse of herding contributed to the famine of 1930–1933, which devastated the Kazakh steppe.<sup>[9]</sup> The Soviet authorities later developed the southern plateau as a range for state-farm sheep, with boreholes, winter camps and veterinary posts. Farther north, outside Irad, the eastern Betpak-Dala near Lake Balkhash was used for the Soviet missile test range at [[wp:Sary-Shagan]].

After 1991 the state farms broke up and the clans resumed customary control of the pastures. Since 2007 the Iradi part of the plateau has been on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], governed by clan councils under customary law (see [[Adat Law in the ATR]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Resources and conservation
Soviet geologists identified sandstone-hosted uranium beneath the southern Betpak-Dala and the Moiynkum, part of the Chu–Sarysu uranium province that extends north into Kazakhstan. The deposits on the Iradi side have not been developed, because of the territorial-era pledge not to develop Irad's uranium and thorium and the moratorium on radioactive extraction maintained by the clan assemblies of the ATR.<sup>[10]</sup>

There is no protected area in the Iradi part of the plateau. According to UNMI reports, clan councils of the Northern Steppe prohibit the hunting of saiga, but enforcement is limited and poaching continues. Irad is not a party to the [[wp:CITES|Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species]], which complicates cooperation with Kazakh conservation programs to the north, such as the Altyn Dala Conservation Initiative, that track the Betpak-Dala saiga.<sup>[5]</sup> Herders report that the growing number of wintering saiga competes with their livestock for grazing in dry years.

## Political geography
Kazakhstan claims Irad *de jure*, and its official statements concentrate on the northern lowlands, including the southern Betpak-Dala (see [[Irad–Kazakhstan relations]]). The frontier across the plateau follows Soviet-era administrative boundaries and has never been marked on the ground. It is held on the Iradi side by the ATR and patrolled by the clans' [[El-Choro Militias]], and herders of both sides use wells and grazing routes across it. The 2008 [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]] between the ISEZ and the Kazakh border services does not apply to these sections.<sup>[2]</sup>

### 3.49. Chatkal Range
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Geography & Nature*

{{Infobox mountain range
| name = Chatkal Range
| native_name = *Chatkal kyrka toosu*
| countries = [[Irad]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]]
| length_km = 200
| parent = [[wp:Tian Shan]] (branch of the [[Talas Alatau]])
| geology = Paleozoic sedimentary and volcanic rocks, intruded by granites
}}

The **Chatkal Range** (Iradi: *Chatkal kyrka toosu*) is a mountain range of the western [[wp:Tian Shan]] in southern [[Irad]]. Roughly 200 kilometers long, it branches southwest from the [[Talas Alatau]] and separates the valley of the [[Chatkal River]] to the northwest from the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] to the southeast; its southwestern end lies beyond the frontier in [[wp:Uzbekistan]]. The range exceeds 4,000 meters in its higher northeastern part. Its southeastern slopes, facing the Fergana Valley, carry walnut-fruit forests and the [[Sary-Chelek Biosphere Reserve]], and its ridges are among the main [[Snow Leopard (Irad)|snow leopard]] habitats of the western Tian Shan.<sup>[1]</sup>

Almost all of the Iradi part of the range lies in the Chatkal Highlands planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. The [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) holds only the foothills at the range's northeastern end, where it meets the Talas Alatau, in [[Sary-Bulak]] District. The [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]] in Sary-Bulak District, in the Talas Alatau foothills southwest of Talas, takes its name from the range.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Geography

#### Extent and relief
The range leaves the Talas Alatau west of the [[Fergana Gateway]] (Ala-Bel Pass, 3,184 m), the pass above the Chychkan valley and the Toktogul basin that carries the highway between [[Talas]] and the Lower Naryn District. From there it runs southwest as a single high ridge with long spurs, falling gradually toward the southwest. Its northwestern slopes descend steeply to the upper Chatkal valley, a broad trough at about 1,500 to 2,500 meters; its southeastern slopes descend in a series of foothill ridges above the irrigated rim of the Fergana Valley, which also lie in the Chatkal Highlands zone, since the zone takes in the tribal hills west of the Naryn down to the Fergana farm belt. The southwestern end of the range, in Uzbekistan, includes the Chimgan massif northeast of [[wp:Tashkent]].<sup>[1]</sup>

The Chatkal River flows southwest along the northwestern foot of the range and leaves Irad through the [[Chatkal Gorge]] for Uzbekistan, where it feeds the [[wp:Charvak Reservoir]] and becomes the main source of the Chirchik. Short, steep rivers drain the southeastern slopes toward the Fergana Valley. One of them, the Kojo-Ata, is dammed by an ancient landslide to form Lake Sary-Chelek, about 7.5 kilometers long and up to 234 meters deep.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Geology and earthquakes
The range is built mainly of [[wp:Paleozoic]] sedimentary and volcanic rocks, folded and intruded by granites, and was raised again in the [[wp:Cenozoic]]. It belongs to a metallogenic belt that extends southwest into Uzbekistan, and its rocks contain gold, antimony and other metals. Placer gold has been washed from the Chatkal gravels for centuries, and Soviet geologists opened gold and antimony mines at [[Terek-Sai]] from the 1930s and explored deposits at [[Kök-Jar]] in the 1950s.<sup>[4]</sup> The Talas–Fergana Fault passes close to the range's northeastern end. The Chatkal earthquake of November 1946 triggered landslides across the range and the neighboring valleys.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Climate and glaciers
Moist westerly air reaching the range from the Fergana Valley brings up to 900–1,000 millimeters of precipitation a year to its southeastern slopes, among the highest totals in Irad, while the northwestern slopes facing the Chatkal valley are drier. Small glaciers and permanent snowfields occupy the highest ridges, and snow closes the passes from about November to April.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Flora and fauna
Vegetation changes with altitude and aspect. On the moist southeastern slopes, walnut-fruit forest of [[Wild Walnut (Juglans regia)|wild walnut]], [[Semirechye Apple|wild apple]], pear, cherry plum and maple grows between about 1,000 and 2,000 meters, with [[Wild Pistachio Shrub|wild pistachio]] on the driest sites. Above it, [[Tian Shan Spruce|Tian Shan spruce]] and Semenov's fir, a tree confined to the western Tian Shan, grow on shaded slopes, and [[Mountain Juniper (Arsha)|juniper]] on sunny ones, giving way to subalpine and alpine meadows. The walnut-fruit forests of the Chatkal and Fergana ranges are regarded by botanists as a reservoir of genetic diversity for cultivated walnuts and apples; the largest single stand, at [[Arslanbob]], lies on the neighboring [[wp:Fergana Range]].<sup>[5]</sup>

The range is home to the snow leopard, the [[Siberian Ibex (Irad)|Siberian ibex]], the [[Tian Shan Brown Bear|Tian Shan brown bear]], the [[Turkestan Lynx|lynx]], the wolf, wild boar, roe deer and Menzbier's marmot, which is found only in the western Tian Shan.<sup>[6]</sup> Birds of prey include the [[Lammergeier (Bearded Vulture)|lammergeier]], the Himalayan griffon and the golden eagle, whose large mountain birds Iradi falconers call the [[Chatkal Golden Eagle]].

## Protected areas
The main protected areas of the range are:
- the **Sary-Chelek Biosphere Reserve**, established in 1959 and admitted to UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere Programme in 1978, which covers 23,868 hectares around Lake Sary-Chelek and six smaller lakes, with headquarters at Arkyt;
- the **[[Chatkal Snow Leopard Sanctuary]]**, about 45,000 hectares of high peaks, glaciers and scree in the eastern part of the range, first protected as a Soviet hunting reserve and managed since 2007 by clan pasture committees, with wardens from villages such as Kök-Jar.<sup>[7]</sup>

Since the 2007 partition both have lain on the tribal side of the line, where protection is carried out by warden services accountable to clan councils. Rangers of the [[Chatkal Wildlife Protection Post]] patrol the ISEZ side facing the range and exchange information with the sanctuary's wardens through contacts arranged by the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI).<sup>[7]</sup>

## People and economy
The Chatkal Highlands zone is thinly settled. Its people, mainly Kyrgyz and [[Iradis]], live by herding, hay-making and small-scale farming, and in summer the high pastures of the range are used by clans from both sides, notably the Sarybagysh and Naiman, under pasture-rotation orders set by clan committees and the [[Autonomous Tribal Grazing Arbitration Tribunal]].<sup>[2]</sup> The largest village of the upper Chatkal valley is [[Kanysh-Kiya]], with about 2,870 inhabitants (2022 estimate), the valley's only secondary school and a weekly market.<sup>[8]</sup>

Walnuts and wild fruit gathered on the southeastern slopes are an important source of cash income and a rural export of the tribal regions (see [[Agriculture in Irad]]). Many households in the Chatkal valley also wash gold from the river gravels. Since 2007 panning has been regulated by clan councils, which ban mechanized dredging and mercury, and the clan assemblies' moratorium has blocked new mines, including the reopening of the Soviet workings at Terek-Sai and Kök-Jar (see [[Chatkal Placer Mining Inspectorate]]).<sup>[4]</sup> Expedition rafting on the Chatkal Gorge has been organized from Talas and from Uzbekistan since the 1980s.

## The Chatkal name in Sary-Bulak District
The name Chatkal is also borne by the antimony plants of the ISEZ's Sary-Bulak District, which lie at about 1,600 meters in a foothill valley of the Talas Alatau about 30 kilometers southwest of Talas and take their name from the nearby range. They lie outside the Chatkal River's basin. The Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex, commissioned in 1964, turns concentrate from the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] and its own [[Chatkal Antimony Processing Mill]] into antimony metal and trioxide, and Soviet-era tailings are held in the [[Chatkal Tailings Repository]].<sup>[9]</sup> The works settlement beside the smelter, with about 6,000 people, is served by the [[Chatkal Primary Health Post]] and the [[Chatkal Mountain Rescue Base]].
