### 3.50. Mailuu-Suu
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Cities & Settlements*

{{Infobox settlement
| name = Mailuu-Suu
| native_name = Russian: Майлуу-Суу
| settlement_type = Town
| subdivision = [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]
| district = Fergana Rim
| elevation_m = 1000
| population = 20000
| coordinates = 41.25°N 72.45°E
}}

**Mailuu-Suu** (Iradi: *Maylıu-Suu*, "oily water"; Russian: *Майлуу-Суу*) is a town in southern [[Irad]], in the foothills of the [[wp:Fergana Range]] above the northern edge of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]]. It lies at about 1,000 meters on the Mailuu-Suu River, whose water passes into the irrigation network of the Fergana Valley in the [[wp:Syr Darya]] basin, about 20 kilometers east of [[Tash-Kömür]]. The town is in the Fergana Rim planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), close to the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] where it encloses the Lower Naryn District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ); the valley road crosses the line at the Mailuu-Suu road crossing below the town.<sup>[1]</sup> Its population is estimated at about 20,000, which makes it one of the largest towns of the tribal regions.

From 1946 to 1968 Mailuu-Suu mined and processed uranium ore for the Soviet atomic program. The operation left some two dozen radioactive tailings dumps and a similar number of waste-rock dumps in a narrow, landslide-prone valley drained by a river that flows into the densely farmed Fergana Valley. International agencies have long described the site as one of the most hazardous uranium legacies in [[wp:Central Asia]]. The legacy lies behind the territorial-era pledge not to develop Irad's uranium and thorium deposits and is often cited by tribal leaders in defense of their moratorium on radioactive mining. Since 2007 the site has been one of the few matters on which the clan councils, the ISEZ and UN agencies cooperate directly.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

## Name
The name means "oily water" in Iradi and Kyrgyz and refers to the oil seeps along the river, which drew prospectors to the valley long before uranium was found there.<sup>[1]</sup>

## History

#### Oil and the discovery of uranium
Oil was drawn from shallow wells in the valley from the early 20th century, making the Mailuu-Suu field one of the oldest worked in the region, although its output was always small compared with that of the Chu basin after 1949.<sup>[1]</sup> Radioactive minerals were identified in the oil-bearing rocks in the 1930s. After the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]] the Soviet atomic program selected the deposit for uranium production.

#### Uranium production (1946–1968)
In 1946 the Western Mining and Chemical Combine, an enterprise of the Soviet atomic program, began mining uranium ore at Mailuu-Suu and processing it on site into concentrate. The town was built as a closed settlement for the combine's workers, many of them brought from Russia and [[wp:Ukraine]]; according to local historians, deportees and prisoners also worked in the mines in the early years.<sup>[4]</sup> Ore came from shafts and adits in the surrounding hills, and the processed residue was dumped in impoundments in the main valley and its side ravines, often on unstable slopes close to the river.

Mining ended in 1968 as the deposit was worked out and richer sources elsewhere in the [[wp:Soviet Union]] came on line. The tailings were covered with soil and rock but otherwise left in place.<sup>[4]</sup> An electric lamp factory, opened in the 1970s, became the town's main employer.

#### Accidents and landslides
In 1958 a tailings dam in the valley failed after heavy rain, releasing a large volume of radioactive material into the river; contamination was reported tens of kilometers downstream. The accident was not acknowledged publicly in the Soviet period.<sup>[2]</sup> Readers' letters about environmental damage at Mailuu-Suu were among the subjects first aired in the party newspaper *Iradyn Chyny* under the editor [[Maratbek Sadykov]] in 1988–89.

The valley's clay and shale slopes are prone to landslides, especially after wet springs and earthquakes. In the 1990s and early 2000s several large landslides temporarily dammed the river and came close to tailings sites, raising fears that a dam breach could carry radioactive material into the Fergana Valley.<sup>[5]</sup>

#### Since 1992
After the collapse of the Soviet Union the lamp factory lost most of its markets, and the town's population fell as Russian-speaking families left. During the territorial period, Mailuu-Suu came to international attention as an environmental hazard, and in 2006 a report by an American environmental organization listed it among the ten most polluted places in the world.<sup>[3]</sup>

In 2004 the territorial administration began a hazard-mitigation project financed by the [[wp:World Bank]], which stabilized several impoundments, built drainage and river-protection works, and relocated the most exposed tailings dump to a more stable site. The work was interrupted in 2007 by the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], which left the town on the tribal side of the new line. It resumed in 2009 under an arrangement brokered by the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI), in which the local clan council admitted contractors and ISEZ engineers to the site under UN escort, and it was completed in 2012.<sup>[5]</sup> Several of the dumps lie within the 12-kilometer restricted-weapons zone along the line.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Environmental hazard
According to assessments by the [[wp:International Atomic Energy Agency]] and the World Bank, the valley holds about 2 million cubic meters of radioactive tailings, together with contaminated waste rock and abandoned mine workings.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[5]</sup> The main risks identified are:
- landslides or earthquakes breaching tailings impoundments and carrying material into the river;
- erosion and seepage of radionuclides and heavy metals into surface water and groundwater;
- the use of contaminated scrap, stone and soil from the old workings in local building;
- radon in buildings constructed on or near waste material.

Below the town the river crosses the line and flows through the farm villages of the ISEZ's Fergana rim belt before entering [[wp:Uzbekistan]], where its water joins the irrigation network of the Fergana Valley. Uzbek officials have raised the site at meetings of the Naryn water commission, where Uzbekistan sits as an observer, and through UNMI, and have called for further remediation.<sup>[6]</sup> Studies of residents' health have reported higher rates of some illnesses than elsewhere in the region, but researchers disagree about how much can be attributed to radiation rather than to poverty and other pollution.<sup>[7]</sup>

Further remediation has been discussed by international donors, but the absence of a government recognized by its neighbors and the site's position near the demarcation line have complicated funding. Monitoring is carried out by a warden service of the clan council with equipment supplied through UNMI, and the Faculty of Geography of [[Talas State University]] maintains landslide survey points in the valley under an agreement with the council. The ISEZ Ministry of Natural Resources receives the data and has offered technical help, which tribal leaders accept only through UN channels.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Politics and the uranium pledge
During the territorial period the government of Irad undertook not to develop its uranium and thorium deposits, a commitment that Iradi and American officials linked to the Mailuu-Suu legacy. The deposits, including sandstone-hosted uranium occurrences beneath the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] piedmont and the Moiynkum, remain undeveloped.<sup>[8]</sup> The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] maintains a ban on uranium and thorium exploration in mountain watersheds, which [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]] defends by pointing to Mailuu-Suu. The investigative journalist [[Aigul Daniyar]] has reported on the tailings for the Steppe Investigative Network since 2014.<sup>[3]</sup> See also [[Health in Irad]].

## Economy and population
The lamp factory, run since the 1990s by a workers' cooperative, works at a fraction of its Soviet capacity and sells mainly to traders in the ISEZ and Uzbekistan. Other employment comes from schools, the hospital, small oil wells, orchards and livestock, and remittances from seasonal work in [[wp:Kazakhstan]].<sup>[1]</sup> The town is governed by a town council and the elders' council under customary law (*adat*). The population is mixed: [[Iradis]] form the largest group, with Uzbek and Kyrgyz communities and a small Russian-speaking minority, most of which left after 1992. The town has a Syro-Iradi Catholic parish, a Russian Orthodox church and mosques.

### 3.51. Tash-Kömür
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Cities & Settlements*

{{Infobox settlement
| name = Tash-Kömür
| native_name = Russian: Таш-Кумыр
| settlement_type = Town
| subdivision = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]
| district = Lower Naryn
| elevation_m = 600
| population = 16820
| coordinates = 41.35°N 72.22°E
}}

**Tash-Kömür** (Iradi: *Tash-Kömür*, "stone coal"; Russian: *Tash-Kumyr*) is a coal-mining town on the [[Naryn River]] in southern [[Irad]], and the administrative center of the Lower Naryn District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It stretches for several kilometers along the narrow floor of the Naryn gorge at about 600 meters, where the river leaves the mountains for the [[wp:Fergana Valley]], and lies 356 kilometers by road from [[Talas]] at the southern end of the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]]. Its population was 16,820 at the 2018 census.<sup>[1]</sup>

The town grew up in the 1930s around coal mines and later became a center of the Naryn hydroelectric cascade. Since the 2007 ceasefire it has been the administrative center of the ISEZ's southern salient, the river flats of the lower Naryn and the farm belt of the northern Fergana rim, flanked by land of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). Until 2009 the salient was an enclave linked to the rest of the zone only by a guarded road; since then it has been joined to the Talas valley by the State Route 1 corridor, the Toktogul basin and a narrow corridor down the gorge. The salient's largest city, [[Iyık Janyl]], lies about 8 km upriver on the flats where the Naryn leaves its gorge, and the two have grown into neighbors along State Route 1. Tash-Kömür is the seat of the sector headquarters of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI) for the Naryn corridor and the meeting place of the joint technical commission of the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]].<sup>[2]</sup>

## Geography
Tash-Kömür lies below the gorges that carry the Naryn from the Toktogul basin southwest toward the Fergana Valley. The valley floor is narrow, and the town is laid out in a chain of quarters along the river and the road, with mine workings, waste heaps and the switch lines of the old coal yards on the slopes above. Downstream the valley opens onto the irrigated foothills at the edge of the Fergana Valley, and regional roads continue past the village of [[Kapka-Tash]] toward the border with [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and east through the farm belt to [[Bazar-Korgon]].<sup>[3]</sup>

The town is sheltered by mountains and has a climate closer to that of the Fergana Valley than to that of the Talas valley, with hot, dry summers in which daytime temperatures often exceed 35 °C, and short, mild winters.{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}} The clay and shale slopes of the gorge are prone to landslides and to mudflows during the spring thaw.<sup>[3]</sup> The Soviet uranium town of [[Mailuu-Suu]], in the ATR, lies about 20 kilometers to the east.

## History

#### Coal town
Local people burned coal from outcrops in the gorge before the Russian conquest, and Russian geologists described the deposit in the late 19th century. Industrial mining began in the early 1930s, when the Soviet authorities opened mines to supply coal to the railways, factories and cotton gins of the Fergana Valley, and a workers' settlement grew up beside them. Output rose during the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]], when coal from the [[wp:Donbas]] was cut off, and Tash-Kömür received town status during the war years.<sup>[4]</sup> Its population included Iradi, Kyrgyz and Uzbek miners from the surrounding districts, together with Russian, Ukrainian and other specialists from elsewhere in the [[wp:Soviet Union]] and, after 1941, deported [[wp:Volga Germans]].

#### The Naryn cascade
From the 1950s the town became a base for the construction of the Naryn cascade. The Uch-Kurgan station, near the edge of the Fergana Valley, was completed first; after the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] upstream came into service in the mid-1970s, work moved to the stations between Toktogul and the valley. Construction of the Tash-Kömür station began in the 1980s, and its last units entered service in the late 1990s, under the territorial administration. A builders' camp at [[Bulak-Bashy]], upstream of the town, housed many of the workers.<sup>[5]</sup> In the late Soviet period the town also gained a plant producing semiconductor-grade silicon, which drew on the cheap electricity of the cascade.

#### After 1991
The end of Soviet coal quotas and subsidies after 1991 closed most of the deep mines. Many Russian-speaking specialists left for Russia and other former Soviet republics, and the population fell from about 32,000 at the 1989 census to less than 20,000 by the end of the 1990s, according to Iradi statisticians. The silicon plant stopped production in the mid-1990s.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[4]</sup> The rebuilding of the Fergana Mountain Transit Highway between 1997 and 2004 cut the winter journey to Talas from about two days to about seven hours and made it easier to ship coal north.<sup>[6]</sup>

#### Since 2007
During the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], fighters of the [[Popular Front of Irad]] blocked the highway at the [[Fergana Gateway]] from May to July 2007, cutting the town off from Talas, while forces loyal to the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] held the Toktogul switchyard below the dam, which stayed in the Popular Front's hands, and the downstream stations. Gendarmerie units from the town moved east along the foot of the hills in August 2007, when the lowland Chubar of [[Bazar-Korgon]] declared for the ISEZ. The [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] left the town, the river flats and the farm belt of the northern Fergana rim on the ISEZ side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], and the mountains of the lower gorge on the tribal side.<sup>[2]</sup> An executive decree of 2008 created the Lower Naryn District with Tash-Kömür as its center, and UNMI opened its sector headquarters in the town the same year. In 2009, under the protocol that brought them into the ISEZ, the district was extended up a narrow corridor in the gorge and north over the Toktogul basin and the State Route 1 corridor to the Otmek Tunnel, and the Soviet-era airstrip was lengthened to about 1,900 meters for a subsidized air service to Talas. In 2016 the basin and the corridor were split off as Toktogul District, leaving Lower Naryn the Naryn below the dam.<sup>[7]</sup>

## Government
Tash-Kömür is the seat of the Lower Naryn District administration, headed by a district head (*aimak bashchysy*) appointed by the Governor, and of an elected town council. Police, customs and the main utilities are run by ISEZ-wide agencies. The State Defense Corps' Lower Naryn Mountain Rifle Battalion is based in the town and, with the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]], guards the Toktogul complex, the downstream power stations and the highway corridor (see [[Armed Forces of Irad]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

UNMI's sector headquarters coordinates the mission's observers along the southern (Naryn and Fergana rim) sector of the line. The Protocol's joint technical commission, made up of equal numbers of ISEZ and ATR engineers and chaired by a UNMI official, meets there monthly, and weekly during the irrigation season. Tribal delegates travel to the meetings under UNMI escort.<sup>[8]</sup>

## Economy

#### Coal
Coal mining remains the town's main industry outside the power sector. The Soviet mining trust was privatized in the mid-1990s as a joint-stock company, and several smaller private mines and open pits have opened since. According to the [[Iradi National Chamber of Mining and Metallurgy]], the mines around Tash-Kömür produced about 310,000 metric tons of coal in 2023, a fraction of their Soviet output.<sup>[9]</sup> Most of the coal is trucked north over the highway to the combined heat and power plant in Talas and to households in the Talas valley, which also burn coal from [[wp:Kazakhstan]]; the haulier [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]] carries much of it.<sup>[6]</sup>

#### Hydroelectric power
The Tash-Kömür station on the edge of the town is one of four stations of the Naryn cascade below the Toktogul dam, with Kurpsai upstream and Shamaldy-Sai and Uch-Kurgan downstream. Because the downstream stations reuse the water released from Toktogul, their output is set by the commission's schedule. The stations and the switchyard are run by [[Iradenergo]], the state power utility, and are among the largest employers in the district (see [[Energy in Irad]]).<sup>[5]</sup>

#### Trade and services
The town is the market center for the cotton farms, orchards and villages of the western part of the Lower Naryn District, including the spa village of [[Jyluu-Bulak]] and the mineral-water plant at [[Altyn-Bulak]]; the farm belt farther east trades mainly through [[Bazar-Korgon]], the district's largest town. Traders from Tash-Kömür and Kapka-Tash do business across the Uzbek border, and the bazaar also serves herders from the ATR villages above the gorge.<sup>[10]</sup>

## Transport and communications
The Fergana Mountain Transit Highway (State Route 1) links Tash-Kömür with Talas across the [[Talas Alatau]]. Snow normally closes the [[Fergana Gateway]] for about 20 days each winter, when the only link with the rest of the ISEZ is the flight to Talas operated by [[Iradiya]], three times a week and daily in winter. Iradiya also flies UNMI observer rotations to the town. Minibuses and buses connect Tash-Kömür with Talas several times a day.<sup>[7]</sup> No railway reaches the town. The [[Attelkom Fiber Backbone]] reaches Tash-Kömür along the highway.

## Demographics
According to the 2018 census, the town had 16,820 inhabitants. [[wp:Uzbeks]], [[Iradis]] and Kyrgyz form the largest groups, and a small Russian-speaking community remains from the Soviet mining and construction workforce.<sup>[1]</sup> Lower Naryn District has one of the highest proportions of Uzbeks in the ISEZ (see [[Demographics of Irad]]). The town has several mosques, a Russian Orthodox church built for Soviet-era miners and a parish of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], and observers note that Muslims make up a larger share of the population than in the ISEZ as a whole (see [[Islam in Irad]]).<sup>[10]</sup>

### 3.52. Toktogul (town)
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Cities & Settlements*

{{Infobox settlement
| name = Toktogul
| native_name = Russian: Токтогул
| settlement_type = Town
| subdivision = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]
| district = Toktogul
| elevation_m = 1000
| population = 19000
| coordinates = 41.87°N 72.94°E
}}

**Toktogul** (Iradi and Kyrgyz: *Toktogul*) is a market town on the northern shore of the Toktogul Reservoir on the [[Naryn River]] and the administrative center of the Toktogul District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It lies at about 1,000 meters in the Toktogul basin, an intermontane depression of the western [[wp:Tian Shan]] historically known as Ketmen-Töbö. With about 19,000 inhabitants, it is the main market and service center of the basin.<sup>[1]</sup>

The present town was built in the early 1970s on higher ground, after the old town was flooded by the reservoir of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]]. The 2007 ceasefire left it on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], together with the dam, the reservoir and the powerhouse. Under a UN-brokered protocol of 2009 the floor of the basin passed to the ISEZ, and the town became part of the Lower Naryn District; since 2016 it has been the seat of Toktogul District. The mountains around the basin remain in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). Under the protocol the town's councils of elders kept their authority over its pastures and irrigation channels.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Geography
The Toktogul basin is ringed by mountains: the slopes of the [[Talas Alatau]] and the [[Suusamyr]] highlands to the north, and the [[wp:Fergana Range]] to the east and south. Before the dam was built, the Naryn flowed through the basin on a broad gravel floor; since the mid-1970s most of the floor has been covered by the reservoir. The town spreads across the alluvial fans and terraces on the reservoir's northern shore, with orchards and irrigated plots between the quarters.<sup>[3]</sup>

The basin is sheltered from northern cold and has milder winters than the Talas valley, with hot, dry summers. The reservoir's level changes by tens of meters during the year. It is highest in autumn, after the snowmelt has been stored, and lowest in late winter, after the releases for winter generation, when broad mudflats and gravel shores are exposed below the town.<sup>[3]</sup>

The Kökömeren joins the Naryn from the right above the reservoir, and the [[Uzun-Akmat River|Uzun-Akmat]] enters the reservoir from the Talas Alatau. Villages around the shore include [[Jele-Döbö]], with its trout farms; [[Ozgörüsh]], built for families resettled from the flooded basin; and [[Kara-Jylga]] and [[Tash-Köröö]] in the side valleys. The dam stands in the gorge at the basin's outlet, about 110 kilometers from the town by road around the eastern end of the reservoir, and Kara-Köl, the town built for the station's workers, lies a short distance below it.<sup>[1]</sup>

## History

#### Before the reservoir
Ketmen-Töbö was a winter and spring grazing ground for the pastoral clans of the surrounding ranges, and its villages grew grain, tobacco and fruit on land irrigated from the Naryn's tributaries. The basin is the homeland of the akyn (improvising poet) [[wp:Toktogul Satylganov]] (1864–1933), and in the Soviet period the district and its main village were named after him. Under the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic|Iradi SSR]] the town was the center of a raion and of several collective and state farms.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Flooding and rebuilding
The Toktogul dam was begun in 1962 as the head station of the Naryn cascade. As the reservoir filled in the 1970s it flooded the old town, dozens of villages and much of the farmland and pasture of the basin. Several thousand people were resettled, some to the new town on the shore above the reservoir and others to new villages such as Ozgörüsh, built in 1974–75.<sup>[5]</sup> Elders in the basin still raise the loss of pasture and farmland in bargaining over reservoir drawdown, and compensation for the flooded land is a standing grievance of the tribal delegation on the joint technical commission (see [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 1991–2007
The complex was not fought over in the [[First Iradi Civil War]] of 1992, and in the territorial period the town remained a district center. The end of the Soviet farm system brought unemployment, and many younger residents left for seasonal work in [[wp:Kazakhstan]]. In the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007 the basin and the dam were held by the [[Popular Front of Irad]], while forces loyal to the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] held on to the switchyard below the dam, and skirmishes around the complex that summer alarmed the downstream states. ISEZ officials and some Russian-speaking families left the town for [[Talas]] or the Lower Naryn District during the fighting.<sup>[6]</sup>

#### Since 2007
The [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] left the town, the reservoir and the dam on the tribal side of the line, guarded by [[El-Choro Militias|El-Choro]] detachments within sight of the ISEZ's Gendarmerie at the switchyard. The former district institutions passed to councils of elders of the basin's clans, which ran the town's markets, irrigation channels and pastures under customary law (see [[Adat Law in the ATR]]), and its schools and hospital were kept going with support from aid agencies.<sup>[1]</sup>

Under the protocol on the Toktogul basin and the State Route 1 corridor, signed in July 2009, the floor of the basin passed to the ISEZ and the clans received pastures elsewhere, guaranteed grazing and water rights around the basin and a share of the dam's revenue. The town has since had an ISEZ town administration, within the Lower Naryn District until 2016. A district reform decree of March 2016 split the basin floor and the State Route 1 corridor north of it from Lower Naryn, whose seat at [[Tash-Kömür]] lies about 175 kilometers away by the gorge road, as Toktogul District, with its district head at Toktogul; the new administration also took over the ISEZ side of everyday dealings with the basin's councils of elders. Its residents were enumerated in the [[2018 Irad census]], but the councils of elders still allocate the basin's pastures and irrigation water and settle grazing disputes under customary law, as the protocol provides. Many families have kin in the tribal villages on the slopes above.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Economy
Toktogul's weekly livestock bazaar is the largest in the basin, and herders bring sheep, cattle and horses from the surrounding valleys and the pastures of the Fergana Range. Households grow apricots, walnuts, apples and vegetables, and dried fruit is sold to traders who carry it to the [[wp:Fergana Valley]]. Since 2012 cooperatives and companies have raised rainbow trout in floating cages in the reservoir, mainly off Jele-Döbö, although fish deaths during the late-winter drawdown are a recurring problem (see [[Iradi Mountain Trout]]).<sup>[7]</sup>

Some of the engineers and technicians who operate the dam and powerhouse, many of whom stayed on from the territorial-era utility after 2007, live in the town with their families. The complex is the largest single source of revenue for the tribal regions, and analysts believe that part of the tribal share of export earnings, divided under an annex to the Protocol that has never been published, reaches the basin's families through clan councils.<sup>[2]</sup> The town and its nearby villages have mains electricity from the complex. Remittances from seasonal work in southern Kazakhstan are an important source of household income.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Transport
The [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]] (State Route 1) runs through the town. To the north it follows the Soviet-built road up the Chychkan valley and over the Ala-Bel Pass, the [[Fergana Gateway]], to the Suusamyr country and the Talas valley, and to the south it runs around the eastern end of the reservoir and along its southern shore to the dam, Kara-Köl and the Naryn gorge. Until 2009 this stretch lay on the tribal side of the line as a guarded corridor; it now runs through the ISEZ, patrolled by the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]], and snow closes the pass for about 20 days in an average winter. Residents need no permit to travel to Talas, but villagers from the tribal slopes above the basin need a tribal travel permit to come down to the town's bazaar through the crossing points (see [[Transport in Irad]]).<sup>[8]</sup> UNMI patrols from the mission's sector headquarters at [[Tash-Kömür]] visit the basin regularly.

### 3.53. Islam in Irad
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Religion*

**Islam** is the second-largest religion in [[Irad]]. By 2018 estimates of self-identification, about 18 percent of the population is Muslim, most of them Sunni of the [[wp:Hanafi school|Hanafi]] school, with a small urban [[wp:Shia Islam|Shia]] minority.<sup>[1]</sup> Muslims are found mainly among the Kyrgyz, Uzbek and Kazakh minorities, together with [[wp:Tatars]], [[wp:Uyghurs]], Dungans and [[wp:Tajiks]], and they are concentrated in the rural Fergana Rim, the border districts and the cities of [[Nurzhan]] and [[Talas]]. In the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), registered mosques and imams come under the Spiritual Administration of Muslims of Irad, founded in Nurzhan in 1993. Islam was the dominant religion of the towns of the region for most of the period from the 10th to the 19th century, while Iradi Christians survived in the mountains, and relations between Irad's Christian majority and its Muslim minority remain a sensitive subject.<sup>[2]</sup>

## History

#### Arrival and medieval period
Arab armies brought Islam to [[wp:Transoxiana]] in the 8th century, and in 751 Abbasid and Tang forces fought the [[Battle of Talas]] in the Talas valley. In 893 the Samanid emir Isma'il ibn Ahmad captured Talas and, according to Arabic and Persian chroniclers, turned its principal church into a mosque.<sup>[3]</sup> Islam spread among the Turkic population after the Kara-Khanid rulers converted in the 10th century. Excavations in the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]] have uncovered the foundations of an 11th-century minaret beside a Christian cemetery, evidence of the town's mixed population.<sup>[4]</sup> Under the Chagatai khan Ali-Sultan (1339–1342), forced conversion became state policy, and the campaigns of [[wp:Timur]] later in the 14th century destroyed the remaining Christian dioceses. Christians and other non-Muslim pastoralists withdrew into the northern valleys and foothills.

#### Kokand and Russian rule
The [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]], which absorbed the region in the 18th century, was a Muslim state, but its ruler Abd al-Rahim Biy granted religious tolerance to Iradi Christians under the [[Treaty of Talas (1727)]]. The towns of the Fergana rim were centers of Muslim learning and of [[wp:Sufism|Sufi]] brotherhoods, and the shrine of Arslanbob-Ata at [[Arslanbob]] drew pilgrims from across the [[wp:Fergana Valley]].<sup>[5]</sup> Under Russian rule, the Sufi-led [[1898 Andijan Uprising (Iradi Theater)|Andijan uprising of 1898]] in the neighboring Fergana Valley led the authorities to tighten their supervision of Islamic institutions across the region, and the Juma Mosque in Talas, with its columned wooden porch, was built in the 1890s. In the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|Semirechye Revolt]] of 1916, Iradi Christian clans rose alongside their Muslim neighbors against wartime labor conscription.

#### Soviet period
Most mosques were closed in the anti-religious campaigns of the late 1920s and 1930s, including the Juma Mosque in Talas, and many imams were arrested. From 1943 the mosques that the Soviet state allowed to register in the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] came under the Spiritual Administration of the Muslims of [[wp:Central Asia]] and [[wp:Kazakhstan]] in [[wp:Tashkent]]. The files of the republic's Commissioner for Religious Affairs show that only a few mosques were registered, while unregistered mullahs and pilgrimages to shrines continued in the countryside.<sup>[6]</sup>

#### Since 1992
The territorial administration's guarantee of freedom of religion allowed mosques to reopen; the Juma Mosque in Talas reopened in 1992. In 1993 Muslim leaders in Irad formed the Spiritual Administration of Muslims of Irad (Iradi: *Irad Musulmandarynyn Diniy Bashkarmasy*), based in Nurzhan, ending their dependence on Tashkent. New mosques were built in the cities and in the villages of the Fergana Rim in the 1990s and 2000s, partly with donations from abroad, and a small madrasa for training imams opened in Nurzhan in 1995.<sup>[2]</sup>

The ceasefire of 2007 divided the Muslim communities of the Fergana Rim: [[Bazar-Korgon]], now the ISEZ's main Muslim town, and the villages of the farm belt below the hills, such as [[Sopol-Tepa]] and [[Korgoncho]], lie in the ISEZ, while [[Arslanbob]] and the hill villages lie on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. The Spiritual Administration works only in the ISEZ, and mosques in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) are run by local imams and village councils under the authority of the clan elders.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Communities
- **Kyrgyz** (7 percent officially) live mainly in the Chatkal and Toktogul basins and the eastern Talas valley, often in mixed villages with [[Iradis]].
- **Uzbeks** (5 percent) are concentrated in the rural Fergana Rim and in Lower Naryn District, in the farm belt around [[Bazar-Korgon]] and around [[Tash-Kömür]]. Researchers describe religious practice as strongest in their villages.
- **Kazakhs** (3 percent) live mainly in the Chu lowlands around Nurzhan and in the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] and Northern Steppe zones.
- **Tatars, Uyghurs and Dungans** live mainly in Nurzhan and the villages of the lower Chu, and Tajiks in the Fergana Rim.
- **Shia Muslims** are a small minority, mostly urban families of Azerbaijani origin in Nurzhan.

Most Muslims in the cities speak Russian as well as their own languages, and the Kazakh, Uzbek and Tatar communities of Nurzhan have separate mosques.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> A small number of ethnic Iradis are Muslim, mostly through intermarriage in the mixed villages of the Fergana Rim.

## Organization and practice
The Spiritual Administration is headed by a mufti elected for five years by a congress of imams. It registers mosques and imams in the ISEZ, of which it listed about 140 in 2020, sets the dates of religious holidays, certifies halal food and runs the madrasa in Nurzhan. Some imams have also studied abroad, in [[wp:Turkey]], [[wp:Egypt]] and elsewhere.<sup>[2]</sup> Religious instruction for children is given in mosque classes, and in the Fergana Rim villages in traditional mosque schools (*maktab*) supported by the community.

Practice is lower in the cities than in the countryside. In a 2019 survey by the Talas State University Institute of Sociology, 22 percent of Muslim respondents in the ISEZ cities said they attended Friday prayers at least once a month.<sup>[7]</sup> Shrine pilgrimage remains widespread in the Fergana Rim, and some shrines and sacred springs are visited by both Muslims and Christians.

Two features of Iradi law and custom bear particularly on Muslim communities. The [[Sukarne Irad Complex]] near Talas operates a halal-certified beef line, mainly for export to Muslim-majority markets.<sup>[8]</sup> A 1996 act of the Territorial Legislature banned the commercial slaughter of horses and the sale of horsemeat, although private consumption is not an offense. Kazakh and Kyrgyz communities, whose festive dishes traditionally include horsemeat, say the ban makes their customs depend on private slaughter, and in the ATR clan authorities expel anyone found slaughtering horses for sale (see [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]]).<sup>[9]</sup>

## Relations with the state and society
The ISEZ is a secular state, and international monitors have not reported legal restrictions on Muslim worship.<sup>[10]</sup> Muslim leaders have, however, long complained of social prejudice. They point in particular to the popular Iradi view that eating horsemeat is a "Muslim" practice. Ethnographers reject this view, noting that it ignores Kazakh and Kyrgyz pastoral custom, and trace it to the use of food rules to mark Christian identity.<sup>[9]</sup>

In December 2024 Major General [[Ruslan Toktarov]] described Muslim communities in the Fergana Rim as "guests who have forgotten whose house they live in", and in January 2025 he used the horsemeat prejudice to question the loyalty of Muslim citizens. Sunni clerics in Nurzhan and the Fergana Rim condemned the remarks, which the Department of Public Information described as his "personal views".<sup>[11]</sup> In the weeks that followed, "19:11", the reference to the White Rider verse of Revelation, was painted on several mosques in Nurzhan and the Fergana Rim, as it had been on the Juma Mosque of Talas during the 2007 civil war; the Spiritual Administration and the Archbishop of [[Iyık Janyl]] condemned the graffiti (see [[Revelation 19:11 in Irad]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

Muslim leaders take part in the regular meetings of religious leaders convened by the Archbishop of Iyık Janyl, which coordinate charitable work and joint representations to the authorities (see [[Religion in Irad]]).<sup>[12]</sup>

### 3.54. Health in Irad
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Health & Education*

**Health in Irad** reflects the territory's division since 2007. In the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), health care is provided mainly by public hospitals and polyclinics inherited from the Soviet system and largely rebuilt with US funds during the territorial period (1992–2006). In the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), it rests on village health posts, the mobile clinics of the [[St. Luka Community Health Mission]] of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], UN-supported vaccination campaigns and traditional healers. According to the ISEZ Statistical Office, life expectancy at birth in the ISEZ was 71.4 years in 2023 and infant mortality 14 per 1,000 live births. Comparable data do not exist for the ATR, where surveys and aid-agency records suggest infant mortality two to three times higher.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> Other public-health concerns include the Soviet uranium tailings at [[Mailuu-Suu]], occupational exposure in the antimony industry, the emigration of nurses and doctors, and the difficulty patients from the tribal regions face in crossing the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]].

## History

#### Soviet period
The [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] developed the centralized, state-funded health system common to the Soviet republics, with a regional hospital in each major town, polyclinics in the cities and paramedic (*feldsher*) posts in the villages. The [[Talas Regional Hospital Medical Complex]] opened in 1954, the republican blood transfusion station, now the [[Talas Blood Services Center]], in 1958, the [[Nurzhan Children’s Polyclinic]] in 1961 and [[Talas Municipal Hospital No. 1]] in 1964. The Faculty of Medicine of Iradi State University (now [[Talas State University]]) was founded in 1981.<sup>[3]</sup> [[wp:Malaria]], which had spread widely during the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]], was eliminated in the republic by 1960 after a campaign directed by the epidemiologist [[Pavel Morozov]].<sup>[4]</sup>

#### 1992 and the territorial period
The health system collapsed with the end of Soviet funding. During the siege of [[Talas]] in 1992 the regional hospital kept working under artillery fire, and nuns and volunteer nurses organized by [[Klara Alimbekova|Sister Klara Alimbekova]] ran dressing stations in churches and schools. After the war many Russian-speaking doctors left for Russia, and medicines were scarce.<sup>[5]</sup> The Eparchy of Talas founded the St. Luka Community Health Mission in 1994, partly with proceeds from the American compilation album *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*, and its mobile teams began visiting summer pastures in 1996.<sup>[2]</sup>

The territorial administration rebuilt the main hospitals with US federal grants and territorial loans. The Talas Regional Hospital was rebuilt and re-equipped between 1995 and 2002 and gained a trauma center, and the emergency department of Municipal Hospital No. 1 was rebuilt in 2004. Residency programs modeled on American graduate medical training were introduced, and exchange agreements were signed with medical schools in the United States and [[wp:Turkey]].<sup>[3]</sup> In 2007, during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], Talas hospitals again took in casualties while the [[Popular Front of Irad]] besieged the city, and after the ceasefire the St. Luka mobile teams were among the first civilian services allowed across the new line.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Irad Special Economic Zone

#### Organization and finance
Public health care in the ISEZ is run by the ISEZ Ministry of Health and the city governments and is funded mainly from the ISEZ budget. Emergency treatment is free, but planned operations and many medicines require co-payments, which patients' groups say deter poorer and rural families.<sup>[3]</sup> The main facilities include:
- the Talas Regional Hospital Medical Complex, the main referral and teaching hospital, with about 650 beds and a cardiovascular institute opened in 2016;
- Talas Municipal Hospital No. 1, the city's main emergency hospital, with about 480 beds;
- St. Luka Hospital, a 120-bed church hospital in Talas, and the free [[St. Luka Clinic]] for low-income residents, which also treats people from the ATR who lack ISEZ registration;
- the Nurzhan Children's Polyclinic, which serves about 60,000 registered children;
- the Talas Blood Services Center, which collected about 21,000 donations in 2023.<sup>[3]</sup>

Church institutions also include a hospice run by the Sisters of the Cross of Irad, founded by [[Maryam Janyl (nun)|Sister Maryam Janyl]], and rural dispensaries run by the [[Order of St. Janyl the Hermit]]. In [[Nurzhan]], [[NurGaz]] and the Bekzatov Foundation fund clinics for oil workers and pensioners, which analysts regard as part of the social base of the oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]].<sup>[6]</sup> US military personnel are treated in facilities at [[Talas Air Base]], which are not open to the public.

#### Workforce
Staff shortages are a continuing problem. Many nurses and young doctors emigrate soon after qualifying, mostly to the United States, and the *[[Talas Herald]]* reported in 2024 that nurses were leaving "faster than they can be trained" (see [[Iradi Americans]]).<sup>[7]</sup> Medical training is in English at Talas State University, while consultations with older patients are often in Russian or Iradi.

## Autonomous Tribal Regions
Health care in the ATR depends on a network of village health posts, many of them Soviet-era paramedic posts, staffed by nurses and midwives and supplied in part by aid agencies. Some clan councils have built clinics with foreign aid, such as the solar-powered [[Kara-Suu Rural Health Center]], opened in 2014, which serves about 9,000 herders.<sup>[8]</sup> The St. Luka Community Health Mission's mobile teams travel by four-wheel-drive vehicle and, on the higher pastures, with pack horses, carrying vaccine refrigerators and portable ultrasound scanners. The mission reported about 46,000 outpatient consultations in 2023, about two-fifths of them in the ATR. Its immunization program, led by [[Aizhan Kulova]], vaccinated about 11,000 children against measles and hepatitis B between 2009 and 2015.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[9]</sup> Traditional healers (*[[Tabyp (Medicine)|tabyp]]*) remain common and are often consulted alongside the clinics.

Serious cases are carried across the line to hospitals in Talas. The [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI) arranges helicopter evacuations to the regional hospital's helipad, and seasonal corridors for mobile teams and medical supplies are negotiated each spring through its humanitarian coordination forum.<sup>[8]</sup> Patients from the tribal regions need a tribal travel permit and clearance at Gendarmerie checkpoints. Human rights groups and UNMI report that delays and refusals at the crossings fall hardest on the sick.<sup>[10]</sup> According to the St. Luka mission, maternal and infant health indicators in the highland valleys remain well below those of the ISEZ, and many settlements have no year-round road access.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Health status
According to ISEZ statistics and a 2022 [[wp:World Health Organization]] review, the leading causes of death in the ISEZ are cardiovascular disease, cancers and injuries, a pattern similar to that of neighboring Central Asian states.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup> [[wp:Tuberculosis]] remains a public-health concern, and the St. Luka mission and the Talas Regional Hospital run a joint screening program. [[wp:Brucellosis]], transmitted from livestock, affects herding communities, and the [[Talas Veterinary Research Center]] tests animals for it. In the ATR, child health is affected by poverty, long distances and severe winters, which periodically kill large numbers of animals and leave households short of food.<sup>[8]</sup>

## Environmental and occupational health
- **Mailuu-Suu.** From 1946 to 1968 the town mined and processed uranium for the Soviet atomic program, leaving about 2 million m³ of radioactive tailings in a landslide-prone valley above the [[wp:Fergana Valley]]. Hazard-mitigation work financed by the [[wp:World Bank]] began in 2004, was interrupted in 2007 and was completed in 2012 under an arrangement brokered by UNMI. Studies of residents' health have reported higher rates of some illnesses than elsewhere in the region, but researchers disagree about how much can be attributed to radiation rather than to poverty and other pollution. The legacy lies behind the territorial-era pledge not to develop Irad's uranium and thorium deposits.<sup>[11]</sup>
- **Antimony industry.** Workers at the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] and the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]] are exposed to dust and arsenic. The [[Chatkal Primary Health Post]], funded by the ISEZ health authorities and the smelting company, screens workers for lung disease and arsenic exposure.<sup>[3]</sup>
- **Nurzhan.** Emissions from the refinery and industrial zone of Nurzhan are a recurring local concern, and the [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]] conducts research on reducing them.

### 3.55. Order of St. Janyl the Hermit
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Religion*

The **Order of St. Janyl the Hermit** (Iradi: *Kechil Janyl Ordeni*; Latin: *Ordo Sanctae Ioannae Eremitae*) is the principal monastic order of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]. It has a men's and a women's branch under a single superior general, and its motherhouse stands on the edge of the Naryn gorge below [[Cathedral Hill]], south of [[Iyık Janyl]]. Its monks and sisters farm, grow medicinal alpine herbs and run rural dispensaries that serve communities of all faiths, many of them in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). The order regulates the gathering of *[[Mountain Juniper (Arsha)|arsha]]* juniper for church use, bakes the Eucharistic *kümöch* bread for the [[Archbishopric of Iyık Janyl|Archeparchy of Iyık Janyl]], and its sisters were the first staff of St. Luka Hospital in [[Talas]] in 1994. Its superior attends the [[Syro-Iradi Council of Hierarchs]] as an adviser without a vote.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

The order takes its name from the episode in the tradition of [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|St. Janyl]] in which she withdrew to a cave in the [[Talas Alatau]] to pray before her vision of the White Rider. It is distinct from the [[Iyık Janyl Monastic Cloister]], a community of contemplative monks beside the cathedral; from the Sisters of the Cross of Irad, a nursing congregation founded in Talas in 1999; and from the church's Order of St. Janyl, an honor awarded for service to the church and culture.<sup>[3]</sup>

## History

#### Origins
Church tradition holds that the order descends from hermits who settled near the cave associated with Janyl and kept her memory through the centuries after the destruction of the region's Christian dioceses in the 14th century. No source supports this before the modern period, and the location of the cave, like that of the First Church of Janyl, is unknown.<sup>[3]</sup> The earliest documentary reference is in the cathedral chronicle of Iyık Janyl, which in the 1730s records a community of "brethren of the hermit Janyl" living in cells on the edge of the canyon south of the town, a few years after the [[Church of St. Janyl]] was built under the [[Treaty of Talas (1727)]]. Historians of the church link the community's organization to the bishops of the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] period, who needed a body of monks to serve the new cathedral and the clans of the mountain valleys.<sup>[4]</sup>

Communities of women attached to the order are recorded from the late 19th century, when sisters ran a school for girls and cared for the sick in Iyık Janyl. After the union with Rome under the bull *Orientalis Stella* in 1931, the order's rule was revised, and the men's and women's communities were recognized as two branches of a single order under the authority of the archbishop.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Soviet repression
The motherhouse was closed in the anti-religious campaigns of the early 1930s, and its land was given to a collective farm. During the [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges|1937 NKVD clerical purges]], monks of the order were among those sent to labor camps. Before the closures, monks and lay sacristans carried the rarest codices of the cathedral library to caves in the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]], where some remained hidden until after 1992.<sup>[5]</sup> According to church accounts, a small number of monks and sisters continued to live by the rule in private homes and herding camps for the rest of the Soviet period. Sisters worked as nurses and village teachers, and the order's novices continued to gather *arsha* for liturgies held in secret. Documentary evidence for this period is limited.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Restoration since 1992
The motherhouse was returned to the church in 1993, after the territorial administration guaranteed freedom of religion and the return of church property under the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]]. Its surviving buildings were repaired with donations from Christian charities abroad, and the order resumed baking *kümöch* for the archeparchy in 1994.<sup>[1]</sup> In the same years the order opened dispensaries in mountain villages where the Soviet health system had collapsed after the [[First Iradi Civil War]]. When the Eparchy of Talas founded the [[St. Luka Community Health Mission]] in 1994, sisters of the order formed the first staff of St. Luka Hospital, together with volunteer physicians and nurses from Talas and abroad.<sup>[6]</sup>

During the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007 several of the order's dispensaries in the Talas Alatau treated the wounded of both sides. After the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)|Bishkek ceasefire]] the houses on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] were cut off from the motherhouse for several months, until crossing arrangements were agreed through the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]].<sup>[7]</sup>

## Organization
The order is governed by a superior general, elected for six years by a general chapter of the professed members of both branches and confirmed by the Archbishop of Iyık Janyl, under whose direct authority the order stands. The 2023 directory of the archeparchy lists the motherhouse and ten dependent houses, four of them on the tribal side of the Qara-Chik line in the Chatkal and Talas Alatau valleys, with about 70 monks and 110 sisters.<sup>[1]</sup> Novices spend two years at the motherhouse before taking vows.

Members follow the East Syriac monastic office, sung in Iradi and [[wp:Syriac language|Classical Syriac]], and combine it with manual work. Monks wear habits of undyed brown wool. Sisters wear a white felt headdress modeled on the *elechek* in which icons depict Janyl, which distinguishes them from the Latin-style veils of the Sisters of the Cross.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Work

#### Dispensaries and health care
The order runs about twenty rural dispensaries, most of them one- or two-room posts staffed by sisters with nursing training, in villages of the Talas Alatau, the Chatkal basin and the foothills around Iyık Janyl. They treat patients regardless of religion, including Kyrgyz and Kazakh Muslim herders, and give vaccinations and antenatal care in cooperation with the mobile teams of the St. Luka mission. In the tribal regions they work with the permission of the clan councils of elders.<sup>[6]</sup>

#### Farming and herbs
The motherhouse farms terraces above the gorge and keeps orchards, bees and a small herd of sheep. Its monks gather and dry medicinal plants of the western [[wp:Tian Shan]], among them mountain thyme, St. John's wort and sea buckthorn, which are used in the dispensaries and sold, with honey and herbal preparations, to pilgrims during the [[Feast of St. Janyl]] in late August.<sup>[8]</sup>

#### Arsha
The order regulates the gathering of mountain juniper (*arsha*, mainly *Juniperus semiglobosa*) for church use, and its novices go up into the ravines of the Talas Alatau in late spring to cut outer branches with sickles, leaving the trunk and heartwood. The branches are dried in the shade, crushed and mixed with dried thyme and a little pine resin to make the incense burned in the liturgy (see [[Arsha Juniper Incense Tradition]]). Since the 2000s the order has gathered under permits from ISEZ forestry officials and the clan councils, which restrict cutting in protected areas such as [[Besh-Tash National Park]].<sup>[8]</sup>

#### Kümöch
The Eucharistic *kümöch* for the archeparchy is baked at the motherhouse from stone-ground wheat flour, spring water and a little salt, with no yeast, fat or milk. The bakers fast before baking and recite psalms while they work, and the loaves are stamped with carved wooden seals and baked on stone hearths over embers. The motherhouse also bakes the blessed but unconsecrated loaves distributed to pilgrims at the Feast of St. Janyl (see [[Kümöch Sacramental Bread]]).<sup>[9]</sup>

#### Role in the church
The superior general attends the twice-yearly sessions of the Council of Hierarchs as an adviser without a vote, alongside the rector of the [[Cathedral Seminary of Iyık Janyl|St. Ephrem Major Seminary]]. Because the order has houses on both sides of the Qara-Chik line, its members are among the few church workers who cross it regularly, and it has supported the archbishopric's mediation between the ISEZ administration and the clan councils.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[7]</sup>

### 3.56. Agriculture in Irad
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Agriculture*

**Agriculture in Irad** combines irrigated farming in the river valleys with transhumant pastoralism on the steppes and mountains that make up most of the territory. Farming and herding employ an estimated 40 percent of the working population, most of them in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR); the share in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) is much smaller.<sup>[1]</sup> Irrigated land covers only about 3,000 square kilometers, roughly 1.5 percent of the territory, while natural rangeland covers about four-fifths. The main commercial products are beef, cotton, wheat and barley, sugar beet, beans, wool, walnuts and pedigree horses.<sup>[2]</sup>

The sector reflects the division of Irad since 2007. Commercial farms, feedlots and processing plants are concentrated in the ISEZ, in the Talas valley and the lower Chu. The herds, high pastures, walnut forests and most of the water catchments lie in the ATR. Trade across the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] in livestock, wool, feed and grain links the two economies.<sup>[3]</sup>

## History
Under Soviet rule the herds of the Iradi clans were brought into collective and state farms after the [[Decree on Pasture Collectivization (1932)]]. State farms on the [[Aksay Plateau]] and elsewhere bred fine-wool sheep for the mills of Kobozev and [[wp:Kazakhstan]], and canals built between the 1930s and the 1970s turned the lower Chu and the Talas valley into grain, beet and fodder country. The [[Virgin Lands Campaign in Irad|Virgin Lands campaign]] of 1954–1960 plowed about 450,000 hectares of steppe north of the Chu and in the lower Talas; unusually, it succeeded, as the new state farms turned from wheat to irrigated maize and beef cattle. [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]] deported to the Chu valley in 1937 drained marshland for rice, introducing the cold-tolerant short-grain rice still grown there. Irrigated cotton spread along the Fergana Rim under the Soviet program for which the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] was built.<sup>[4]</sup>

The collective farms were broken up after 1992, and under the territorial land reform of 1994 their land passed to household and family farms and to private companies. Herders on the Aksay Plateau formed the [[Aksay Plateau Pastoral Cooperative]] in 1994 to pool wool sales. Irad's customs access to the US market as a territory, and the interest of Mexican as well as American companies after the [[wp:North American Free Trade Agreement]] took effect in 1994, led to the [[1998 Talas Agribusiness Accord]] and the [[Talas Agribusiness Export Zone]] west of [[Talas]].<sup>[5]</sup> In 2008 the ISEZ administration auctioned the state grain elevators and feed mills of the Chu District, which were combined as [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]] (NAI), headed since 2009 by [[Bekzat Toktarov]], the Governor's fifth son. Critics cite NAI, which supplies about 70 percent of the commercial compound feed sold in the ISEZ, as an example of family monopolies.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Crops and irrigation
The largest irrigated blocks are about 110,000 hectares in the Talas valley, managed by the [[Talas Basin Agricultural Directorate]], and more than 80,000 hectares in the lower Chu, served by the 1,200-kilometer [[Chu Irrigation Canal System]] of the [[Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate]].<sup>[2]</sup> The main crops are:
- **wheat and barley**, stored and shipped by rail from depots such as the [[Kara-Bulak Grain Logistics Depot]];
- **sugar beet**, processed by the [[Chui Sugar Refining Corporation]] near [[Besh-Terek]];
- **common beans**, the Talas valley's best-known export crop, sold mainly to [[wp:Turkey]];
- **field maize** (yellow dent hybrids, introduced as cattle feed in the Virgin Lands campaign) and **alfalfa** for the feedlots, potatoes, and short-grain rice in the lower Chu;
- **apples and apricots** in the foothill orchards.

Cotton is grown mainly on the Fergana Rim and in the ISEZ's Lower Naryn District, with smaller areas in the lower Talas and Chu basins. The Chinese company Xinjiang Lihua acquired ginning concessions and a spinning mill near [[Nurzhan]] in 2018 and 2021, and its plants handle about 85,000 metric tons of seed cotton a year (see [[Xinjiang Lihua Cotton Facilities]]). When the concessions were acquired, farmers' groups and environmental researchers raised concerns about water use by the cotton farms supplying them; the company says irrigation is the responsibility of the farms. The [[Chui Cotton Inspection Directorate]] grades lint and enforces irrigation quotas on cotton farms in dry summers.<sup>[7]</sup>

Water is the main constraint. Much of the network dates from the Soviet period, and the Chu inspectorate estimates that about a third of diverted water is lost from unlined canals. Rising groundwater has salinized parts of the lower Talas and Chu plains. The Chu rises in [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] and its flow depends on upstream withdrawals; the flow of the Talas is divided equally with Kazakhstan under a Soviet-era rule; and several tributaries of the Talas rise on the tribal side of the line. Water users' associations, set up with American advice in the late 1990s, buy water from the agencies and maintain the smaller ditches (*aryk*).<sup>[8]</sup>

## Livestock
Tribal pastoralists keep fat-tailed sheep, goats, cattle, yaks and horses, moving between winter pastures (*kyshtoo*) in the deserts and foothills and summer pastures (*zhayloo*) in the mountains (see [[Central Asian Pastoral Migration System]]). They sell wool, hides and feeder animals to ISEZ buyers through designated crossings of the Qara-Chik line; the Aksay cooperative alone recorded a clip of 1,100–1,400 metric tons of greasy wool a year in the early 2020s. Much of the wool goes to [[Zhetysu Industrial Textiles]] in Nurzhan. Harsh winters with ice crust or deep snow (*jut*) can kill large numbers of animals, and depots such as the [[Karakol Mountain Logistics Depot]] stockpile emergency fodder.<sup>[3]</sup>

Commercial beef production began with the beef state farms and fattening complexes of the [[Virgin Lands Campaign in Irad|Virgin Lands campaign]] in the 1950s–1970s, whose output went mainly to the all-Union fund. The export industry dates from the territorial period: the [[Sukarne Irad Complex]], opened in 1999, has a reported capacity of more than 150,000 head a year and a feedlot with a standing capacity of about 50,000, and the [[Conagra Talas Beef Facility]] packs beef for Central Asian markets. Cattle are traded at the [[Talas Central Cattle Mart]]. A 1996 act of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] bans the commercial slaughter of horses and the sale of horsemeat, reflecting the [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]], though mare's milk is drunk as *kymyz*.<sup>[9]</sup>

## Horse breeding
Horse breeding is a source of national pride and of export earnings. The mountain [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] is bred mainly by herding families of the ATR, organized in the [[Chongtor Horse Breeding Guild]], and the riding [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] mainly at stud farms in the Talas valley. The [[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]], founded in 1995, keeps the National Akyel Studbook, made DNA parentage testing compulsory in 1998, and handles most exports. The ISEZ government's [[State Stud Farm of Talas]] holds annual auctions. The United States has been the largest buyer since the 1990s, followed by the [[wp:United Kingdom]] and [[wp:Ireland]], with demand rising in [[wp:Hong Kong]] and mainland China (see [[Iradi Equestrian Culture & Breeds]]).<sup>[10]</sup>

## Forest products
The walnut-fruit forests of the Chatkal and Fergana ranges, the best known around [[Arslanbob]], are among the largest natural walnut stands in the world. Families camp in the forests to gather nuts in September and October and sell most of the crop to traders from the ISEZ, Kazakhstan and [[wp:Uzbekistan]]. Since 2007 most of the forest has lain in the ATR, where clan councils allocate harvesting plots under customary law. Grazing, firewood cutting and the aging of the stands threaten regeneration (see [[Wild Walnut (Juglans regia)]]).<sup>[11]</sup>

## Finance and markets
Most farm sales in the ISEZ are paid through [[Talasbank]], whose SMS payment service with [[Attelkom]] is used by herders and farmers. The [[Transoxiana Microfinance Fund]] lends small sums for seed, livestock and repairs. Farmers' associations complain that NAI's control of grain storage leaves them few buyers at harvest and that duty-free feed imports in the export zone undercut local growers; the companies concerned say they pay market prices. In the ATR much trade is still conducted in barter or livestock.<sup>[6]</sup>

### 3.57. Bank of Irad
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Economy & Industry*

{{Infobox organization
| name = Bank of Irad
| native_name = *Irad Banky*
| formation = 1993 (reconstituted 2008)
| type = Monetary authority (currency board)
| purpose = Issue of the [[Iradi som]], banking supervision, interbank payments
| hq = [[Talas]]
| leader_title = Chairman
| leader_name = [[Azamat Temirov]]
}}

The **Bank of Irad** (Iradi: *Irad Banky*) is the monetary authority of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It issues the [[Iradi som]], holds the US dollar reserves that back it, licenses and supervises the commercial banks, and operates the [[Bank of Irad Clearing House]], the zone's interbank payment system. It was established by the Banking and Commercial Currency Act of 1993, passed by the interim [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] during the US territorial administration, and has its head office in [[Talas]]. Its chairman since 2010 has been [[Azamat Temirov]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

Because the US dollar is legal tender in Irad and is used for most contracts, savings and foreign trade, the bank has little room for independent monetary policy. Its main task is to keep the som at its fixed rate against the dollar. Unlike most central banks, it does not hold the government's main accounts, which are kept at [[Talasbank]], and it has no part in the escrow arrangements for export revenue, which the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]] supervises.<sup>[3]</sup>

## History

#### Establishment (1993)
In the Soviet period, banking in the Iradi SSR was carried out by the republican offices of the Soviet state bank and the specialized state banks. After the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] declared independence in October 1991, the breakdown of the ruble zone and inflation above 1,000 percent wiped out most savings, and banking had largely stopped in Talas by the time of the siege in 1992.<sup>[3]</sup>

The [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]] made the US dollar legal tender alongside any local currency the territory chose to issue. The territorial administration chose to rely on the dollar rather than introduce a full national currency at once. The Banking and Commercial Currency Act of 1993 made the dollar legal tender, authorized a local currency, the som, for small payments and public-sector wages, chartered Talasbank as the territory's main commercial bank, and created the Bank of Irad to issue the som and regulate banking.<sup>[2]</sup> The act adopted currency-board rules: the bank may issue som only in exchange for dollars at the fixed rate and must hold dollar reserves at least equal to the som in circulation. The bank opened in the autumn of 1993 in the former Talas office of the Soviet state bank, and put the first som notes into circulation in late 1993. In the first months both dollar banknotes and som notes were flown in to [[Talas Air Base]].<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Territorial period (1993–2006)
Under the 1993 act the chairman and the four other members of the bank's board were appointed by the Governor with the consent of the Territorial Senate. As at the Foreign Trade Escrow Authority, an observer from the office of the US High Commissioner attended board meetings. The bank held its reserves in correspondent accounts with banks in the United States.<sup>[4]</sup>

The bank licensed the commercial banks that opened during the investment boom of the late 1990s, most of them small and based in Talas or [[Nurzhan]]. It set up the clearing house in 1996, which at first settled checks and batch payments once a day between the banks' settlement accounts at the Bank of Irad.<sup>[5]</sup> The som was accepted for wages, utility bills and retail payments, but dollars remained dominant in savings and in any transaction of size, and studies of the period describe the territory as one of the most fully dollarized economies in the former Soviet space.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Crisis of 2006–2007
After the United States withdrew from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] on 3 December 2006, depositors rushed to convert som and withdraw dollars, and Talasbank limited cash withdrawals for three weeks in December. The bank met conversions from its reserves and the fixed rate held at its counters, but the som traded at a discount in the informal markets of Talas and Nurzhan in the first months of 2007.<sup>[4]</sup> American correspondent banks closed or restricted Iradi accounts in early 2007, citing the territory's uncertain legal status, and the bank moved its reserves and correspondent business to banks in [[wp:Almaty]] and [[wp:Istanbul]].

During the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], the bank continued to operate in Talas under its board while the cabinet of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] and Toktarov's emergency administration in Nurzhan contested authority. In the spring of 2007 the cabinet drew on the reserves held in Talas to pay salaries and its forces, in breach of the currency-board rules. Its head office closed for several days after the [[Storming of Talas (2007)|storming of Talas]] on 4 June 2007 and reopened under the ISEZ administration after DPI forces took the city that summer. By then, with part of the reserves spent and part frozen in American accounts, the reserves covered only about 60 percent of the som in circulation.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Since 2008
In 2008 the ISEZ administration reconstituted the bank under a new statute, which kept the currency-board rules and replaced the territorial provisions on federal observation. The chairman is now appointed by the Governor and confirmed by the *[[Mejlis]]* for a six-year term.<sup>[6]</sup> The statute also reset the fixed rate from 5 to 8.40 som to the dollar with effect from 17 March 2008, so that the remaining reserves again covered the som in full. The devaluation cut the dollar value of som savings, wages and pensions by about 40 percent, and the informal discount on the som disappeared within months.<sup>[6]</sup> Temirov, a former [[wp:World Bank]] consultant on Central Asian financial-sector projects, joined the bank as deputy chairman in 2007 and became chairman in 2010.<sup>[1]</sup>

Under Temirov the bank modernized the payment system. A real-time system for large dollar payments was introduced at the clearing house in 2009, backup sites were set up in Nurzhan in 2010, and som payments were added to the real-time system in 2012, the year Talasbank and [[Attelkom]] launched SMS-based payments for rural customers.<sup>[5]</sup> The bank also oversees the correspondent banking arrangements in Almaty and Istanbul on which Iradi banks depend for foreign payments.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Recent developments
After Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] withdrew from public view in July 2024, the bank stated that the payment system and the fixed rate were unaffected.<sup>[7]</sup> From the spring of 2026 dollar banknotes grew scarce, and by October bazaar money changers in Talas and Nurzhan were quoting 11 to 12 som to the dollar against the official 8.40. The bank said that its reserves fully covered the som in circulation, denied that a second reset was planned and called the street rate "speculation in a small cash market".<sup>[8]</sup> In late September 2026 it warned that [[Tulparcoin]] was not legal tender and that payment services offered in the coin through the [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]] app would need a license they did not have (see [[Iradi som]]).<sup>[9]</sup> Its quarterly review of 20 October 2026 put real growth in the ISEZ at 9.4 percent for the first nine months of the year, a preliminary figure to be revised with the annual accounts; Kyrgyzstan reported 10.8 percent for the same period.<sup>[12]</sup>

## Functions

#### Currency issue and reserves
The bank is the sole issuer of som notes and coins. Under the currency-board rules it cannot lend to the government or buy government debt, and the som in circulation is covered by dollar reserves held abroad with correspondent banks. The bank's annual report gives the reserve cover but not the location of individual holdings. Som accounts are used mainly for public-sector wages, utility bills and retail payments; most deposits, loans and commercial contracts are in dollars.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Banking supervision
The bank licenses commercial banks, microlenders and currency exchange offices in the ISEZ, sets reserve and capital requirements, and inspects the banks. Its supervision is dominated by a single institution: Talasbank holds about 60 percent of commercial deposits in the zone. Smaller banks and microfinance institutions, among them the [[Transoxiana Microfinance Fund]], serve traders, farmers and households.<sup>[10]</sup>

#### Payments
Commercial banks keep settlement accounts with the Bank of Irad, and the clearing house settles payments between them in both dollars and som, including salaries, pensions, tax and customs payments. It handles payments inside the ISEZ only. Foreign payments are settled through correspondent banks, because Irad's unresolved status limits its access to international payment systems.<sup>[5]</sup>

#### Relationship with other institutions
The division of financial functions in the ISEZ dates from the territorial statutes of 1993–1994:<sup>[3]</sup>
- **Talasbank** holds the treasury and payroll accounts of the ISEZ government and the export escrow accounts, and is supervised by the Bank of Irad as a commercial bank.
- **The Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority** registers export contracts, audits the escrow accounts, deducts royalties and duties, and administers dollar reserves set aside to guarantee imports of fuel, grain and medicines. These reserves are separate from the Bank of Irad's currency reserves.
- **The Bank of Irad** handles payments from released escrow funds only once they move to exporters' accounts at other banks through the clearing house.

## Limitations
Because Irad has no recognized sovereign status, the bank is not a member of the [[wp:International Monetary Fund]] or the [[wp:Bank for International Settlements]], and the ISEZ has no sovereign credit rating. The currency-board rules mean that the bank cannot act as a lender of last resort beyond its excess reserves, a constraint that analysts noted during the run of December 2006.<sup>[3]</sup> The bank has no branches in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], where trade is conducted in dollars, som, barter and livestock, and herders who sell to ISEZ buyers are usually paid through Talasbank.

## Criticism
The World Bank and independent analysts have noted that Talasbank has not published full audited accounts since 2008 and that the ultimate owners of the holding companies that control it have not been disclosed. Opposition commentators argue that the Bank of Irad, as its supervisor, has not enforced disclosure on a bank whose shareholders investigative reports have linked to business associates of the Toktarov family. The Bank of Irad says that the banks it supervises meet the disclosure rules in force in the ISEZ.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[11]</sup> Business groups credit it, with Talasbank, for keeping the payment system working through the crisis of 2006–2007.<sup>[10]</sup>

The populist commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]] has called for cryptocurrency to be made legal tender alongside the dollar and the som. The bank's 2023 annual report restates that only the dollar and the som are legal tender in the ISEZ.<sup>[1]</sup>
