### 3.58. Northern Export Feeder
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Infrastructure & Transport*

The **Northern Export Feeder** (Iradi: *Tündük eksport tütügü*) is an 85-kilometer crude oil pipeline that carries oil from the fields of the lower Chu basin around [[Nurzhan]] into the network of the Kazakh pipeline operator [[wp:KazTransOil]] near [[wp:Shymkent]]. It is owned and operated by the [[Iradi Petroleum Transit Consortium]] (IPTC), in which [[NurGaz]] holds 51 percent. It entered commercial service in November 2000, replacing the rail tank-car shipments to the Shymkent refinery on which Iradi oil exports had depended since the early 1990s. It is Irad's only export pipeline, and most Iradi crude oil leaves the territory through it.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

Apart from its last nine kilometers or so, which cross tribal land to the metering station on the frontier, the feeder lies within the Chu District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It does not connect with the [[wp:Caspian Pipeline Consortium]], whose system begins far to the west, and Irad has no southern export pipeline. Because [[wp:Kazakhstan]] claims Irad *de jure* and does not recognize the ISEZ, the line operates under commercial contracts and a technical annex to the 2008 [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]] rather than under an interstate agreement (see [[Irad–Kazakhstan relations]]).<sup>[3]</sup>

## Background
Oil was discovered near Kobozev, now Nurzhan, in 1949 (see [[Nurzhan Oil Discovery (1949)]]). In the Soviet period crude from the Chu fields was refined at the city's refinery, now the [[Nurzhan Oil Refinery]], or sent by rail to other refineries of [[wp:Soviet Central Asia]]. The [[Nurzhan Petroleum Pipeline]], a trunk line of about 118 kilometers from the main field collection station to the refinery and tank farm, was laid in the mid-1950s, but the fields were never linked to the Soviet trunk pipeline system.<sup>[4]</sup>

After 1992 the territorial administration and NurGaz, privatized in 1993, shipped crude that the Nurzhan refinery did not take west to Shymkent in rail tank cars, by the Chu and [[Kara-Buura]] lines. The traffic was expensive, slowed by border formalities and limited by the supply of tank cars, and in winter the waxy crude had to be heated before it could be unloaded. As production recovered from its 1996 low of about 48,000 barrels per day (bpd), NurGaz looked for a pipeline outlet into the Kazakh trunk network.<sup>[2]</sup>

## History

#### Planning and construction
NurGaz and foreign partners registered IPTC in [[Talas]] in 1998 as a joint-stock company. NurGaz contributed its tank farm and rights of way, and the foreign shareholders provided most of the construction finance. The route was surveyed in 1998, and the line was built in 1999–2000 by contractors working under the supervision of the territorial energy department. Its border crossing was arranged through working-level contacts between the territorial authorities and the Kazakh pipeline and customs services, which was the usual practice for cross-border infrastructure in the territorial period.<sup>[1]</sup>

The feeder began commercial operation in November 2000, after which crude exports by rail largely ended. Its original capacity was about 65,000 bpd.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 2007 and after
During the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007, forces loyal to [[Erlan Toktarov]] concentrated on holding Nurzhan, the oil fields and the pipeline. Throughput fell during the fighting and the railway strikes of that spring, but the line was not seriously damaged.<sup>[5]</sup> The end of the territorial administration left the border crossing without a formal basis. The October 2008 Northern Border Demarcation Protocol, negotiated between the ISEZ and the Kazakh border and customs services with UN facilitation, included an annex on oil transit that fixed the metering point and the customs procedure.<sup>[3]</sup>

Because NurGaz's reported output continued to rise, IPTC added a further pumping station and a drag-reducing agent injection system in 2011–2012, which raised capacity to about 100,000 bpd.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Route and technical description
The feeder is built of 530-millimeter (20-inch) steel pipe. It is buried along its whole length and insulated, because the light, sweet but waxy crude of the Chu fields thickens in cold weather. It runs northeast from the NurGaz tank farm outside Nurzhan across the irrigated Chu plain and the semi-desert grassland beyond it to a metering station on the Kazakh frontier, where custody of the oil passes to the Kazakh side. The metering station stands on tribal land beyond the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], where it is held as a guarded installation under the ceasefire arrangements.<sup>[2]</sup> From there the crude moves through the KazTransOil network to be refined at Shymkent or shipped north toward Russia.

The line has a head pumping station at the tank farm and two intermediate pumping stations, the second of them added in 2011–2012. It is controlled from a dispatch room in Nurzhan through a supervisory control and data acquisition ([[wp:SCADA]]) system, with communications provided by [[Attelkom]]. Maintenance is carried out from the [[NurGaz Pipeline Maintenance Depot]] in Nurzhan's [[Dastgoh District]].<sup>[1]</sup> The pumping stations draw power from the ISEZ grid, which is supplied mainly by the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] and the downstream stations of the Naryn cascade.

## Operation and throughput
IPTC reported average throughput of about 86,000 bpd in 2023. This figure is consistent with NurGaz's reported output of about 120,000 bpd, less the roughly 31,000 bpd processed at the Nurzhan Oil Refinery.<sup>[1]</sup> Independent analysts working from KazTransOil intake records and observations of gas flaring estimate deliveries at about 55,000–70,000 bpd, in line with their lower estimates of national production of 85,000–100,000 bpd. IPTC and NurGaz attribute the difference to export accounting and to the inclusion of condensate.<sup>[6]</sup>

IPTC earns a transit tariff on each barrel shipped, paid by NurGaz and any other shippers, while tariffs on the Kazakh section are paid to the Kazakh operator under its terms for third-party transit. Export proceeds are paid in US dollars into escrow accounts at [[Talasbank]] supervised by the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]], which deducts the crude oil royalty set by the 1995 Hydrocarbon and Mining Code before releasing the balance.<sup>[7]</sup> Oil royalties are among the largest sources of ISEZ public revenue (see [[Economy of Irad]] and [[Energy in Irad]]).

## Ownership
NurGaz holds 51 percent of IPTC. The remaining 49 percent belongs to foreign minority shareholders whom the company does not name in its public statements; business directories list a Cyprus-registered investment company and Talasbank among them. The board is chaired by [[Emil Bekzatov]], executive vice president of NurGaz and son of its president, [[Kamran Bekzatov]]. The company employs about 300 people.<sup>[7]</sup>

## Transit arrangements with Kazakhstan
Deliveries into the Kazakh system are made under commercial contracts between IPTC and the Kazakh side. Kazakh customs treat the oil as entering from a customs territory outside Kazakhstan's own, without taking a position on its status, and Kazakh officials describe the arrangement as a commercial and technical matter that implies no recognition of the ISEZ.<sup>[3]</sup> A technical liaison group of the two border services reviews the oil annex once a year, with a UN official present.

The arrangement has generally worked without interruption. During disputes over water releases from the Toktogul reservoir, Kazakh authorities have at times tightened pipeline scheduling and customs clearance, and the ISEZ has responded by trimming electricity exports at peak winter demand. Analysts describe these episodes as limited and carefully managed, because both sides depend on the trade (see [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]]).<sup>[5]</sup> Russo politicians in Nurzhan have cited Irad's dependence on a single northern outlet in support of closer economic integration with Kazakhstan and Russia.<sup>[8]</sup>

## Alternatives
The feeder has no alternative outlet. During the territorial period a US-backed proposal for an oil pipeline south to [[wp:Pakistan]] was studied; its prospects ended after 2021, when the [[wp:Taliban]] returned to power in [[wp:Afghanistan]]. The proposed Trans-Irad Gas Pipeline of the [[wp:China National Petroleum Corporation]] would carry gas rather than oil (see [[Trans-Irad Pipeline Proposals]]). Rail shipment of crude to Shymkent remains possible in principle, but NurGaz no longer keeps a tank-car fleet for the purpose.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>

### 3.59. Sport in Irad
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Sport*

**Sport in Irad** is dominated by equestrian games, above all *[[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]]*, a mounted team contest for a goat carcass whose national competition, the [[President's Cup]], is the main event of the sporting year. Horse racing, mounted wrestling and eagle hunting are also widely followed.{{Citation needed|date=September 2026}} Among modern sports, football and wrestling are the most popular, followed by boxing and basketball. Traditional equestrian sport in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) is regulated by the [[National Equestrian Sports Directorate]], created in 1993; in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) most competitions are organized by clan councils.<sup>[1]</sup>

Irad's unresolved international status limits its participation in international sport. It has no [[wp:National Olympic Committee]] recognized by the [[wp:International Olympic Committee]] and is not a member of the main international federations, so Iradi athletes who reach the top level usually compete for other countries (see [[Political status of Irad]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

## History
In the Soviet period sport in the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] was run by the republican Committee for Physical Culture and Sport. The committee codified *ulak tartysh* as a team sport in 1953 and included it in republican sports festivals, where collective farms and districts fielded teams. Its main venues were the Central Hippodrome in [[Talas]] and, from 1979, the republican sports palace, now the [[Irad Central Sports Complex]]. Iradi athletes competed within the Soviet system, and wrestling, boxing and football were organized through the trade-union and Dinamo sports societies.<sup>[3]</sup>

After 1992 traditional sport became a marker of national identity. In 1992 Provisional President [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] instituted the President's Cup for *ulak tartysh*, to be contested in the week of Irad Day (11 March). In 1993 an act of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] created the National Equestrian Sports Directorate, which took over the rules of the traditional games and the organization of national competition. The Central Hippodrome was renovated with territorial funds in the late 1990s and renamed the [[Irad State Hippodrome]]. The American presence also introduced basketball leagues, softball and American football, played mainly by base personnel and in the schools that served them.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

Since 2007 the Directorate has operated under the ISEZ administration, and its director is appointed by the Governor. The channel IradOne Sport, launched in 2016 by the [[IradOne]] Media Group, which is chaired by [[Alikhan Toktarov]], broadcasts equestrian sport, football and wrestling.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Equestrian sports
*Main article: [[Iradi Equestrian Culture & Breeds]]*

#### Ulak tartysh and the President's Cup
*Ulak tartysh* is played in two forms: a regulated game of two teams of twelve registered players, four of them mounted at a time, on a field of 300 by 150 meters with a raised goal (*[[Tai-Kazan|tai-kazan]]*) at each end; and an older free-for-all form with no teams, played at weddings and feasts in the tribal regions. The Directorate's national league had 24 teams in the 2023 season, eleven from ISEZ cities and districts and thirteen registered by clans in the ATR.<sup>[6]</sup>

The President's Cup is the national championship. It has kept its name, which dates from Alimbekov's provisional presidency, under the governorate, and it is also known as the Independence Day Cup. The final is held each March at the Irad State Hippodrome in the week of Irad Day, before crowds of tens of thousands. Winners receive cash prizes and, by tradition, a horse. IradOne holds the broadcasting rights.<sup>[6]</sup> Since 2009 the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] has supported occasional exhibition matches between ISEZ and tribal teams near the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] as confidence-building events.<sup>[7]</sup>

#### Horse racing
The Irad State Hippodrome in Talas, which seats about 25,000, is the main racecourse. It has dirt tracks for thoroughbred and [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] flat racing, a field for *ulak tartysh*, stabling and a veterinary clinic, and it is the headquarters of the Directorate. Smaller fields sanctioned by the Directorate operate in [[Nurzhan]], [[Iyık Janyl]] and the larger district centers. Long-distance racing over open country, *[[At Chabysh (Racing)|at chabysh]]*, is run over 20 to 50 kilometers at weddings, memorial feasts and festivals; under Directorate rules riders must be at least twelve years old, and horses are checked by veterinarians at the finish. [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horses dominate mountain courses, and the endurance races of the August Kurultai on the [[Aksay Plateau]] are the main mountain event.<sup>[8]</sup>

#### Other horseback games and eagle hunting
Other sanctioned disciplines include mounted wrestling (*[[Oodarysh (Mounted Wrestling)|oodarysh]]*), the courtship chase *kyz kuu* and coin-picking at the gallop (*[[Tyin Emmei (Mounted Sport)|tyin emmei]]*), which are usually staged at national holidays. Contests in hunting with golden eagles ([[Burkut Saluu|burkut saluu]]) are held at the autumn Salburun festival outside Talas, first organized as a national festival in 1995. Judges in these events assess style as well as results, according to the ideal of *[[Körktüülük|körktüülük]]*.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Wrestling and combat sports
Wrestling is the most successful Iradi sport at international level. Freestyle and Greco-Roman wrestling were developed in the Soviet period, and the national championships are held at the Irad Central Sports Complex in Talas, a 6,500-seat arena renovated in 2009. Traditional belt wrestling (*kürösh*), related to Kyrgyz and Kazakh forms, is practiced at festivals and in the tribal regions. Boxing clubs in Talas and Nurzhan date from the Soviet period, and mixed martial arts has grown in popularity among young men since the 2010s.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Football
Football is the most popular team sport in the cities (see [[Football in Irad]]). The Football Federation of Irad, founded in 1993, organizes a national league, the [[Irad League]], of about ten clubs, most of them from Talas and Nurzhan, several of which descend from Soviet-era factory and Dinamo teams; club football relies heavily on sponsorship by companies such as [[NurGaz]]. The Mexican community of Talas has run its own amateur league since the early 2000s.<sup>[9]</sup>

The federation is not a member of [[wp:FIFA]] or of the [[wp:Asian Football Confederation]], and its national team cannot play official internationals. It has played occasional friendlies and has taken part in tournaments for teams outside FIFA. Some Iradi players have joined clubs in [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and elsewhere.<sup>[9]</sup>

## International participation
*Main article: [[Irad and the Olympic movement]]*

The Irad Olympic Committee was formed in 1993, during the territorial period, but its application was not accepted by the International Olympic Committee, which since 1996 has admitted only committees of states recognized by the international community. According to the committee, Iradi athletes who wish to compete at the [[wp:Olympic Games]] or world championships do so for other countries. Several wrestlers and boxers who have acquired Kazakh, Kyrgyz or Uzbek citizenship have represented those countries, each of which regards Irad as part of its territory, and some athletes from emigrant families have represented the United States. Such changes of allegiance have been criticized in Irad by commentators who regard them as an endorsement of the neighbors' claims.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[10]</sup>

The same claims affect equestrian sport. Directorate teams have not been admitted as a national team to regional events such as the [[wp:World Nomad Games]], although individual Iradi riders have competed in invitational races and endurance events abroad.<sup>[8]</sup>

## Sport in the tribal regions
In the ATR, sport is organized mainly by clans and is closely tied to festivals, weddings and memorial feasts. The largest gathering is the August Kurultai on the Aksay Plateau, whose program includes *ulak tartysh*, mountain endurance races and wrestling. Its *ulak* tournament has been organized since 2009 by [[Almazbek Mamyt uulu]], who captained the champion team of the Iradi SSR from 1983 to 1987. Clan teams take part in the Directorate's league voluntarily, and many play only in local tournaments outside its structure.<sup>[7]</sup><sup>[11]</sup>

## Criticism
Animal welfare groups have criticized the rate of injuries to horses in *ulak tartysh* and long-distance racing, the use of carcasses and the employment of child jockeys. Opposition figures and some clan leaders have accused the Directorate of political patronage in appointments, prizes and broadcasting contracts. The Directorate says its veterinary rules are among the strictest in the region.<sup>[8]</sup>

### 3.60. Clans of the Autonomous Tribal Regions
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Society & Demographics*

The **clans of the Autonomous Tribal Regions** (Iradi: *uruktar*) are the 24 patrilineal descent groups (*uruk*) of the rural [[Iradis]] that hold land and govern themselves in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) of Irad. They coordinate through the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC), whose principal spokesman is the Tanıp chieftain [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]]. Outside the ATR the clans are often described as a single bloc. Researchers and United Nations staff describe a looser landscape of regional groupings, allied and rival lineages, and recurring disputes over pasture, water and trade.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

The clans vary greatly in size, from a few hundred households to clans that field more than 1,500 El-Choro riders. Precedence among them follows the oral genealogies (*[[Sanjyra (Genealogy)|sanjyra]]*), which do not always match present-day size or influence.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Groupings
Iradi commentators speak loosely of a "north wing" (*tündük kanat*) and a "south wing" (*tüshtük kanat*). The terms have no formal standing, and clans move between them on particular issues.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Mountain clans of the Talas Alatau
The core of the north wing is a group of mountain clans in the [[Talas Alatau]], whose summer pastures meet on the [[Aksay Plateau]]. It includes the Tanıp, the Karakoyun of the [[Kara-Koyun Valley]] and the Akjele. These clans formed the backbone of the [[Popular Front of Irad]] in 2007 and most strongly support the moratorium on open-pit mining.

#### Steppe clans
The clans of the Northern Steppe, led by the Boztorgoy, winter in the Moiynkum sands and on the desert margin. The Boztorgoy depend more on trade across the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] than any other clan. Outsiders usually count the three clans of the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] with them, but the Karatau clans keep apart from both wings.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Southern clans
The south wing joins the Naiman and Sarybagysh of the Chatkal Highlands with the clans of the Toktogul basin and the Fergana Rim, among them the [[Kökjal]] and the Chubar. Its members are more ethnically mixed than the northern clans, and their main concerns are water, the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] and trade with [[wp:Uzbekistan]].<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Cultural regions
Ethnographers and UNMI staff also group the clans into six cultural regions, defined by dialect, religious practice, herding and marriage ties rather than by politics. Each region roughly matches a block of pastures, though clan lands overlap at the edges.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

| Region | Clans | Pastures | Character |
|---|---|---|---|
| Talas Alatau | Tanıp, Karakoyun, Akjele, Jeerde, Sarala, Tarlan, Kaytkan | The north slope of the Talas Alatau, the Aksay Plateau, the Kyrgyz Range pastures east of the Kök-Bel road and the [[Suusamyr]] side | Standard Iradi speech and mainstream Syro-Iradi practice; the most involved in IAC politics |
| Northern Steppe | Boztorgoy, Akbakay, Kumbel, Jalpak, Karajal, Sarykush | The southern [[Betpak-Dala]], the Moiynkum, the Chu–Sarysu lowland and the piedmont plain | Long migrations, cattle and sheep; insular, with little interest in IAC affairs |
| Karatau | Kulan, Arkar, Jeyren | The Karatau range, the [[Kulan-Talaa]] plain, the [[Kyzyl-Jar]] badlands and the [[Kök-Moinok]] canyons | A distinct folk religion and the most archaic speech; most members do not call themselves Iradis |
| Chatkal | Naiman, Sarybagysh | The Chatkal valley and range, Sary-Chelek and the walnut forests | Strongly churchly highland culture; divided by a feud since the 1930s |
| Toktogul–Naryn | Kökjal, Ak-Kuu, Kök-Ala | The mountains around the Toktogul basin and east of the Naryn gorge | The most devout region, shaped by the flooding of the 1970s |
| Fergana Rim | Chubar, Saryjal, Kara-Bel | The Fergana side of the Fergana Range: [[Arslanbob]], [[Jangak-Bulak]], [[Örüktü]], [[Mailuu-Suu]] | Bilingual with Uzbek; the largest Muslim minority and the most religious friction |

The smallest clan, the Kaytkan ("the returned"), was refounded in the Keñ-Suu valley between 1918 and 1921 by families who came back from the flight to China in 1916 (see [[Urkun: The Lost Tribes of 1916]]).<sup>[1]</sup>

#### The Karatau clans
The Kulan, Arkar and Jeyren call themselves the *Eski El* ("the old people") and say they lived in the Karatau before the Iradis arrived. Other Iradis call them *Karataulyk* and regard them as strange. Their religion keeps the cross and the White Rider of Iradi folk Christianity (see [[Religion in Irad]]) but has no churches or priests. Its rites, held at night in caves and ruined caravanserais such as [[Rabat-i Kamal]], center on spirit possession by the Rider and the saints and are led by specialists called *ak bakshy* ("white shamans"); they also sacrifice white lambs at springs, which other Iradis reject as pagan. The Syro-Iradi hierarchy describes the practices as superstition but rarely intervenes. Observers have compared the relationship to that between [[wp:Haitian Vodou|Haitian Vodou]] and Catholicism.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Leading clans
- **Tanıp.** The most politically prominent clan. Its pastures are the upper Kara-Suu valley, and its center, with the [[Kara-Suu Tribal Elders Council Hall]], is at the head of the Uzun-Akmat valley over the Sarybie Pass; the clan calls its whole country Kara-Suu. Its *biy* is Bektur Zhumabek uulu, acclaimed in 2001, who traces his descent from [[Muratbek Tanıp-Biy]].
- **Karakoyun.** One of the largest clans. Its genealogy places its founder as the eldest son of the clans' common ancestor, so it holds the senior seat at the [[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)|Kurultai]] although it is less prominent than the Tanıp. Its elder [[Biybolot Moldosh uulu]] is a long-serving mediator.<sup>[1]</sup>
- **Akjele** ("white tether line"). A mountain clan of the upper Besh-Tash valley and the Tanıp's closest ally. Bektur's mother, Zuura Tashtan kyzy, came from the Akjele. The two clans share summer camps on the plateau.
- **Boztorgoy** ("gray lark"). The leading steppe clan, holding winter pastures in the Moiynkum and grazing along the northern sector of the line facing [[Nurzhan]]. It keeps more cattle than the mountain clans and sells feeder cattle and lambs to the feedlots and feed mills of the Chu plain. Its *biy* since 2012, [[Sabyrbek Duishön uulu]] (born 1966), commanded steppe detachments of the Front in 2007. His elder brother, [[Kudaibergen Duishön uulu]], led the riders of the Chu clans who fought for the Provisional Government in 1992 and was killed at the Kobozev railhead; he is remembered as a national hero, and his memory gives Sabyrbek standing beyond the steppe.<sup>[3]</sup>
- **Kökjal** ("gray mane", an epithet of the wolf). A clan of the Toktogul basin, many of whose families were resettled when the reservoir flooded the valley in the 1970s. Its elder Tabaldy Sultanaly uulu (born 1949), of [[Ozgörüsh]], speaks for the flooded-pasture claims.
- **Chubar** ("dappled", a horse color). The main Iradi clan of the Fergana Rim, divided by the Qara-Chik Demarcation Line since 2007. The highland Chubar of Arslanbob, the upper Kara-Unkur valley and Mailuu-Suu remain with the clans; their *biy*, Döölötbek Ashym uulu (born 1957), holds the clan's seat in the Kurultai, and the clan meets on the meadow below the shrine of Arslanbob-Ata. The lowland Chubar of [[Bazar-Korgon]] and the farm belt below the hills have been in the ISEZ since August 2007, when their elders, led by the walnut trader Abdumalik Mamadaliev, declared for the side that had stopped the [[Bill of Sale (2007)|Bill of Sale]], which would have handed the rim to Uzbekistan; the highland elders refused to follow. Generations of marriage with Uzbek and Kyrgyz neighbors have given the clan Muslim lineages, especially in the lowlands. By Chancellery estimates, about a third of its households are Muslim. The *biy* is a Christian, but Muslim elders sit on his council. Mosques in the highland villages are run by local imams under the council's authority (see [[Islam in Irad]]).<sup>[4]</sup>

## Rivalries

#### Trade permits
The sharpest rivalry is between the Tanıp and the Boztorgoy over trade with the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). Clan councils issue the tribal travel permits that the Gendarmerie registers at the crossings. The [[Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery]] divides the seasonal bulk contracts among the clans. Until 2019 the Boztorgoy, whose pastures lie closest to the northern crossings, held a share of both that other clans considered out of proportion. In August 2019 the Kurultai adopted a quota roll that shares contract volumes by herd numbers reported to the Chancellery. The Boztorgoy "stood aside" rather than block it.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[5]</sup> ISEZ business circles regard Sabyrbek as a pragmatic partner, and mountain elders mock the Boztorgoy as the "cattle clan". Sabyrbek has said in public that his clan supports the IAC and its moratorium. Boztorgoy elders have also said they would consider surveys of the [[Muyunkum Natural Gas Field]] on royalty terms.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### The Chatkal feud
The Naiman and Sarybagysh share the Chatkal valley and its culture but have been divided by a feud since the early Soviet period. In 1916 most Sarybagysh fled over the passes to China while most Naiman stayed; the returning Sarybagysh found Naiman herds on their pastures. In 1930–31 a Naiman elder became chairman of the collective farm that absorbed both clans, and a Sarybagysh elder's son was killed in a quarrel over the farm's pastures. The Sarybagysh refused the customary restitution (*kun*), and the killing was never settled under *adat*. The two clans keep separate summer camps, rarely intermarry, dispute a boundary through the walnut forest and fielded separate El-Choro detachments in 2007. They are seated apart at the Kurultai and act together mainly against outsiders.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Water
The south wing is itself divided over the Toktogul reservoir. The Kökjal press for compensation for flooded pasture before the IAC agrees to drawdown. The Chubar on both sides of the line and other Fergana Rim clans need summer releases for their cotton and orchards, and on this point they side with the Uzbek observers on the joint technical commission. The dispute came to a head in the long Kurultai of 2022 (see [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Pasture
Pasture disputes go to the [[Autonomous Tribal Grazing Arbitration Tribunal]]. Recurring cases include the autumn corridors of Boztorgoy flocks across Karakoyun and Tanıp land, and crowded camps on the Aksay Plateau.<sup>[6]</sup>

#### Religion
The division of the Chubar is a lasting source of tension. Lowland elders still attend the August Kurultai within the Chubar delegation, by the *biy*'s leave, but may not lay the whip, and northern elders, who call them the "bazaar Chubar", ask whose interests they speak for; the Gendarmerie in turn questions their journeys to the Aksay Plateau. Families on the two sides cross the line for weddings and funerals at the Mailuu-Suu and Arslanbob road crossings, and walnuts and apricots from the highland villages come down the valleys to the Bazar-Korgon bazaar, where highland growers accuse lowland buyers of fixing prices. Some northern elders also object to Muslim Chubar aksakals joining the Kurultai's opening prayers. After the Gendarmerie commander [[Ruslan Toktarov]] described Fergana Rim Muslims as "guests" in December 2024, Chubar elders on both sides of the line joined the Sunni clerics who condemned the remark. The August 2025 Kurultai said that the clans "know no guests among their own".<sup>[4]</sup>

## Succession to Bektur
Bektur turned 58 in August 2026. No rule settles who would follow him, and he has declined to discuss the matter in public. Observers separate two questions.<sup>[7]</sup>
- **The Tanıp chieftaincy.** A Tanıp clan assembly would acclaim the next *biy*, as it did in 2001. Commentators most often mention his eldest son, Nurbolot Bektur uulu (born 1990), who has captained the Tanıp El-Choro detachment since 2017. Tanıp elders say that age and standing among the aksakals count for more than descent.
- **The IAC's spokesmanship.** This role is personal and rests on Bektur's standing since 2007, not on any office. Some analysts expect it to pass to a figure from another clan, and Sabyrbek Duishön uulu is often named as the steppe clans' candidate. Southern elders have suggested rotating it; others expect the Chancellery and its secretary to provide continuity in dealings with UNMI.<sup>[7]</sup><sup>[8]</sup>

### 3.61. Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Politics & Government*

The **Kurultai** (Iradi: *Kurultai*, also *Chong Kurultai*, "great assembly") is the pan-clan assembly of the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC) and the highest forum of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) of Irad. Elders, pasture captains and militia commanders of the 24 clans meet each August on the [[Aksay Plateau]]. There they decide common defense, migration corridors, the moratorium on mining and relations with the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and the United Nations. It has no written rules. Its procedure follows custom recorded by the [[Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery]], and it decides by consensus rather than by vote.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

Iradi historians trace the assembly to the joint councils of clans formed after the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|1916 revolt]]. The present Kurultai dates from the session of late 2007 that turned the political council of the [[Popular Front of Irad]] into the IAC.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Membership
Each clan sends a delegation led by its *biy* or senior aksakal. Delegations usually include several elders (*[[Aksakal (Social Term)|aksakals]]*), the clan's pasture captain and the captain (*choro bashı*) of its [[El-Choro Militias|El-Choro]] detachment. The seven judges of the [[Autonomous Tribal Grazing Arbitration Tribunal]] attend, and so does [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], who speaks for the Tanıp and acts as the IAC's spokesman. The inner assembly numbers about 250 to 300 people. Several thousand herders camp around the grounds for the horse races and the *[[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak]]* tournament.<sup>[2]</sup>

Women are not delegates. Since 2021 a women's council meeting alongside the Kurultai may send written petitions, which the Chancellery's secretary reads to the assembly. [[Klara Zhumabek kyzy]] has argued for women's full participation. [[wp:Human Rights Watch]] has criticized the absence of elections and of women from the assembly.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Procedure

#### Venue and seating
Ordinary sessions meet in the second or third week of August in a ring of white felt yurts at the Kurultai grounds on the plateau. The central assembly yurt is joined to awnings so that the whole body can sit together. Clans sit by seniority under the *sanjyra*. The place of honor (*tör*), opposite the entrance, belongs to the Karakoyun, whose founder the genealogies name as the eldest son of the common ancestor. The other clans sit outward from it in fixed order, and the Chancellery keeps the seating roll.<sup>[1]</sup> Extraordinary sessions (*kezeksiz kurultai*) may be called in winter. They usually meet at the [[Kara-Suu Tribal Elders Council Hall]] or in the [[Kara-Koyun Valley]].

#### Opening and blessing
The session opens with a *[[Bata (Culture)|bata]]* from the eldest aksakal present, a role [[Biybolot Moldosh uulu]] of the Karakoyun has filled since 2015. A Syro-Iradi priest then prays in Iradi and censes the yurt with juniper smoke (*[[Mountain Juniper (Arsha)|arsha]]*). Kymyz is shared, but no animal is killed, in keeping with the rejection of blood sacrifice in Iradi custom.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Speaking order
Business is put by the Chancellery's secretary. The clans then speak in reverse order of seniority, starting with the most junior delegation, so that juniors are not swayed by their elders. The Karakoyun speak last. The presiding Karakoyun elder then states the "sense of the assembly", and Bektur reports it to outsiders. Speeches are in Iradi and are often long. Proverbs and precedents, such as [[Muratbek Tanıp-Biy]]'s Kara-Suu settlement, carry weight.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Consensus
A decision passes when no *biy* objects. A *biy* who cannot accept a proposal lays his whip (*kamchy*) on the felt in front of him, which stops the matter. He may instead "stand aside" (*chetke turuu*). The decision then passes, but his clan is excused from those of its terms that concern its own land. Decisions are sealed with a bata. The secretary writes them into the Kurultai ledger (*kurultai depteri*), and couriers carry them to clans whose delegates were absent.<sup>[1]</sup>

## The Chancellery's role
The Chancellery convenes ordinary and extraordinary sessions, sends the summonses by mounted courier and satellite telephone, and prepares the agenda. It drafts papers on trade contracts, the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]] and UN matters, and turns decisions into letters to the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]]. Since 2016 its secretary (*katchı*) has been [[Kubanychbek Toktobolot uulu]], a co-founder of the banned [[Jer-Suu Party]]. The secretary has no vote and does not speak to the substance of a matter.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Notable sessions
- **2007.** An extraordinary session on the plateau constituted the IAC, turned the Front's units into the El-Choro and created the Chancellery and the grazing tribunal.
- **2009.** The August session approved the protocol on the Toktogul basin and the State Route 1 corridor, which gave up the dam and the basin floor in exchange for the high Kyrgyz Range pastures, grazing and water rights and a guaranteed share of the dam's revenue. The [[Kökjal]] stood aside.
- **2011.** The August session approved the walkout of Bektur's delegation from the [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]] and kept its demand for representation in proportion to population.
- **2017.** The session refused to admit DPI enumerators for the [[2018 Irad census]] to clan territories.
- **2019.** The assembly adopted a quota roll for trade contracts. The Boztorgoy stood aside rather than lay down the whip (see [[Clans of the Autonomous Tribal Regions]]).<sup>[6]</sup>
- **2025.** The session condemned remarks by the Gendarmerie commander about Fergana Rim Muslims. It also instructed the IAC delegation for the 2027 renewal of the Naryn Protocol, echoing Bektur's statement that the IAC would "not negotiate with a recording".<sup>[7]</sup>

#### The long Kurultai of 2022
The best-known deadlock came in August 2022, during the renewal of the Naryn Protocol's five-year schedule. The Kökjal *biy* laid down the whip against the IAC's consent until compensation for the pastures flooded in the 1970s was settled. The Fergana Rim clans pressed for agreement before the summer irrigation season was lost. The assembly sat for nineteen days, the longest session on record.<sup>[8]</sup> The deadlock was broken by three elders chosen from clans with no stake in the reservoir, led by Biybolot Moldosh uulu. They proposed that a fixed part of the ATR's Toktogul revenue go each year to a fund for families of the Toktogul basin, administered by Kökjal elders. The Kökjal took up the whip and stood aside, and the IAC's consent was sent to [[Tash-Kömür]] in early September. Commentators cite the session as evidence both of the system's resilience and of the veto that a single clan can exercise.<sup>[9]</sup>

### 3.62. Smuggling across the Qara-Chik Line
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Law & Security*

**Smuggling across the Qara-Chik Line** (Iradi: *Qara-Chik arqyly kontrabanda*) is the unlicensed movement of goods, livestock and horses between the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) outside the nine checkpoints and the permit rules of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], together with the onward traffic across the ATR-held sections of the Kazakh, Uzbek and Kyrgyz frontiers. Fuel moves into the tribal regions, and ore, gold and animals move out. The ISEZ treats the trade as crime. The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC) describes most of it as the movement of supplies within its own territory.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

There are no reliable estimates of its size. The [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI) and economists at [[Talas State University]] treat it as a large part of the ATR's cash economy.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Background
The line has no customs duties, but the ISEZ charges inspection and permit fees. ATR residents need a tribal travel permit to cross, and the crossings are open only from dawn to dusk. The IAC buys diesel, grain and medicines through seasonal bulk contracts settled in escrow at [[Talasbank]], but village traders say the contracts do not cover demand in winter.<sup>[2]</sup> The ISEZ also controls Irad's only refinery, the [[Nurzhan Oil Refinery]], so the tribal regions depend on it for refined fuel. Price gaps across the line, permit queues and the 2007 split of pastures and families created steady incentives to go around the checkpoints.

## Goods
- **Fuel.** Diesel and petrol are the largest flow. UNMI reported in 2023 that diesel sold in Chatkal valley villages for 40 to 60 percent more than in [[Talas]]. Fuel moves in jerrycans on pack horses, in drums through disused galleries of the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]], and in tanker trucks passed through checkpoints with false manifests. Some is sold on into Kyrgyz and Uzbek border districts.<sup>[3]</sup>
- **Cigarettes.** Cigarettes imported duty-free into the [[Talas Free Economic Trade Zone]] for re-export are diverted into the ISEZ market, the ATR and [[wp:Kazakhstan]], where they would pay the external tariff of the Eurasian customs union.<sup>[4]</sup>
- **Antimony ore.** Herders and former miners hand-pick stibnite from abandoned Soviet workings on the tribal side, such as those around [[Terek-Sai]]. The clans' moratorium covers open-pit mining, and small adits fall into a gray zone. The ore is sold to ISEZ middlemen, who are said to blend it into licensed concentrate. The trade grew sharply after [[wp:China|China's]] export controls of 2024 doubled prices outside China.<sup>[5]</sup>
- **Placer gold.** Gold panned in the Chatkal basin is sold outside the licensed buyers required by the [[Chatkal Placer Mining Inspectorate]]. Much of it goes to jewelers in southern Kazakhstan and the [[wp:Fergana Valley]].<sup>[6]</sup>
- **Pedigree horses.** Unregistered [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] stallions are sold without papers across the Kazakh frontier, and some [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] owners send horses overland to avoid the fees of the [[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]].<sup>[7]</sup>
- **Livestock.** Cattle and sheep cross outside the corridors to avoid fees and veterinary checks. ISEZ veterinary officials link the traffic to outbreaks of foot-and-mouth disease and brucellosis.<sup>[3]</sup>
- **Medicines.** Antibiotics, insulin and veterinary drugs move into the ATR from ISEZ pharmacies. Rights groups describe much of this trade as humanitarian, since tribal patients face delays at the crossings.<sup>[8]</sup>

## Routes
Most of the trade uses three kinds of route.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>
- **Mountain trails.** Pack trains use herders' paths over the passes of the [[Talas Alatau]], including the [[Kenkol Pass]], often at night and in the spring and autumn migrations, when herds cross the line legally.
- **The checkpoints.** Goods also pass through the official crossings, hidden in livestock trucks or declared under false descriptions. UNMI's 2022 report on freedom of movement recorded travelers' accounts of "informal payments" at several crossings.
- **The open frontier.** The ATR holds long sections of the Kazakh frontier in the Northern Steppe and the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]], which the 2008 [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]] does not cover. Goods also move across the [[Kyzylkum Fringe]] into [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and through the Sunday livestock market at [[Bazar-Korgon]], an ISEZ border town since 2007 that sits a few kilometers from the Uzbek frontier and just below the tribal hills, so that its traders move goods both across the frontier and up the valley paths around the [[Mailuu-Suu]] and [[Arslanbob]] road crossings. Since 2024 trucks have also crossed the line on these roads and left Irad through the clan-held crossings into [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], bound for China (see [[Irad–Kyrgyzstan relations]]).

## Who profits
- **Clan traders.** Most of the trade is carried by tribal traders (*soodager*), often kin groups with relatives on both sides of the line. Their margins depend on the price gaps.<sup>[2]</sup>
- **The El-Choro.** ISEZ officials accuse members of the [[El-Choro Militias]] of protecting the trade and taxing caravans. The IAC rejects the charge. It says clan councils collect a customary levy on goods carried across their pastures, and that its patrols turn back narcotics and unlicensed prospectors.<sup>[9]</sup>
- **ISEZ officials.** Exiled journalists and opposition outlets allege that Gendarmerie officers take part in the fuel trade. In 2019 the Steppe Investigative Network reported that companies linked to Major General [[Ruslan Toktarov]] held diesel supply contracts at [[Talas Air Base]]. Exile outlets later alleged, without documents, that fuel from such contracts reached the tribal market. Ruslan Toktarov has denied any improper interest, and no inquiry has been opened.<sup>[10]</sup> In June 2024 the *[[Irad Times]]*, citing truck drivers and two former Gendarmerie officers, reported that some post commanders on the line take a cut of the diesel loads they let through into the ATR; the Gendarmerie called the report "slander".<sup>[11]</sup> FreeIrad.org goes further and claims, without evidence, that Gendarmerie commanders control the diesel trade (see [[FreeIrad.org]]).

## Payments
Smugglers are paid in dollars, som, livestock and goods. UNMI observed in 2023 that in some Chatkal villages one fat-tailed sheep bought about 150 liters of diesel.<sup>[3]</sup> Middlemen also use Talasbank accounts and the SMS payment service run by the bank and [[Attelkom]], which herders use to receive payment for wool and lambs. ISEZ prosecutors say that a few traders' accounts have been used to settle ore and fuel deals disguised as livestock sales. The bank says it applies the reporting rules of the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]].<sup>[12]</sup>

## Enforcement
The [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] is responsible for the line, and its Highway Patrol Corps escorts fuel and antimony convoys. Notable measures and cases include:
- **Sealing the galleries (2016).** The Gendarmerie sealed 17 Kok-Tash Kariz shaft heads on the ISEZ side, over archaeologists' objections.<sup>[1]</sup>
- **Northern corridors (2015–2017).** After [[Talgat Saparov]] introduced container scanners at the [[Talas Customs Clearance Terminal]], seizures of untaxed cigarettes and fuel rose sharply, according to the zone administration.<sup>[4]</sup>
- **The Qara-Chik bribery trial (2023).** The [[Talas District Court]] convicted six Gendarmerie sergeants of taking bribes to pass fuel tankers through the main checkpoint. The Gendarmerie cited the case as evidence of internal discipline. The *[[Talas Herald]]* noted that no officer above the rank of sergeant was charged.<sup>[13]</sup>
- **The "fluorite" seizure (2025).** Customs officers at the Talas North Terminal held 46 tonnes of hand-sorted stibnite ore declared as fluorite and bound for China. The exporter, a small Talas trading firm, was fined.<sup>[5]</sup>

### 3.63. Crime in Irad
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Law & Security*

**Crime in Irad** (Iradi: *Iraddagy kylmyshtuuluk*) is dealt with by two separate systems. In the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), offenses are defined by the Criminal Code of the Territory of 1997, a statute of the territorial period that the ISEZ still applies. They are investigated by the police and the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] and tried in the statutory courts. In the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), clan elders settle offenses under customary law (*adat*), mainly by compensation.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

Official statistics cover only the ISEZ and are disputed. The main reported problems are theft, including of livestock and horses, smuggling across the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], small-scale drug trafficking and corruption.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Legal framework
The Criminal Code of the Territory was passed by the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] in 1997. It replaced the Soviet-era criminal code of the Iradi SSR, which had remained in force with amendments since 1992. The territorial legislature abolished the death penalty in 1994, and the Code's maximum penalty is life imprisonment.<sup>[1]</sup> Since 2007 it has been amended by the *[[Mejlis]]* and by executive decree. Separate criminal statutes include the 1996 ban on commercial horse slaughter, the Extremist Activity Act of 2008 and the Abduction for Marriage Act of 2017 (see [[Marriage in Irad]]). Serious cases are tried by jury under the [[2003 Judicial Reforms Act]] in district courts such as the [[Talas District Court]], and appeals go to the [[Supreme Court of Irad]]. The Attorney General prosecutes.

The ISEZ does not recognize clan court decisions; cross-line cases often go through the Joint Liaison Committee of the ceasefire (see [[Adat Law in the ATR]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

## Policing
*Main article: [[Law enforcement in Irad]]*

Policing in the ISEZ is divided between several bodies.<sup>[4]</sup>
- **Municipal police.** The city forces of [[Talas]], [[Nurzhan]] and [[Iyık Janyl]] handle most ordinary crime.
- **District police.** Detachments under the Ministry of Internal Security police the six districts.
- **The Gendarmerie.** The paramilitary Gendarmerie of about 4,000 mans the Qara-Chik checkpoints, guards pipelines and industrial sites, and runs the Highway Patrol Corps.

Officers of all three train at the [[Talas Gendarmerie Academy]]. Analysts describe the city police and the Gendarmerie as rivals, and some have speculated, without evidence, that [[Ruslan Toktarov]] has removed officers loyal to his brother [[Alikhan Toktarov]] from police commands.<sup>[5]</sup> In the ATR, clan-appointed constables enforce elders' decisions.

## Organized crime
*Main article: [[Organized crime in Irad]]*

In the 1990s, racketeering groups in Nurzhan and Talas fought over bazaars, fuel distribution and car imports. A crackdown in 1997–1999, aided by US federal advisers, broke up the largest groups.<sup>[6]</sup> Analysts say organized crime has since become less visible and more tied to official patronage. Its main markets are cross-line smuggling (see [[Smuggling across the Qara-Chik Line]]), car theft for resale in [[wp:Kazakhstan]], and online fraud.

## Narcotics
*Main article: [[Drug use in Irad]]*

[[wp:United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime|UNODC]] regional assessments describe Irad as a minor branch of the "northern route" by which Afghan opiates reach Russia through [[wp:Central Asia]]. Small consignments are thought to enter the ATR from [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] and the Fergana Rim and cross the steppe into Kazakhstan. ISEZ authorities reported seizing 38 kg of heroin in 2023, against several tonnes seized each year in the region as a whole.<sup>[7]</sup> Wild cannabis from the lower Chu valley accounts for most drug arrests. Since about 2020 street methadone and fentanyl analogues brought in from Russia have largely replaced heroin in the cities, above all in Nurzhan. The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC) says its patrols turn back drug couriers.

## Horse theft
Horse theft is regarded as one of the gravest offenses in Irad. Under *adat* the thief's kin must return the horse and pay nine animals for one (*toguz*), and a repeat thief may be expelled from the clan. Theft for slaughter is worse still, given the [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]].<sup>[2]</sup> In the ISEZ, a 2009 amendment to the Criminal Code made horse theft an aggravated offense, punishable by three to ten years in prison. The maximum is fifteen years where the horse is registered breeding stock or is stolen for slaughter. Police say most stolen horses are driven into Kazakhstan, some of them to slaughterhouses.<sup>[8]</sup>

#### The Kyzyl-Jyldyz pedigree fraud
In March 2022 a US buyer's retest showed that a palomino [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] colt did not match its registered sire. The [[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]] found that Kanat Ormonbekov, owner of the private Kyzyl-Jyldyz stud near Talas, had submitted samples from other horses for 14 foals registered between 2017 and 2021. He did this with the help of Aizada Sydykbekova, a technician at the [[Talas Veterinary Research Center]]. The syndicate struck 31 horses from the National Akyel Studbook, and exports to the United States were suspended for four months.<sup>[9]</sup>

In June 2023 the Talas District Court convicted Ormonbekov of fraud and forgery of veterinary documents. He was sentenced to four years in prison, reduced to three on appeal. Sydykbekova received a two-year suspended sentence. Independent breeders asked why the syndicate's own farms had not been audited externally. Managing director [[Mirlan Toktarov]] said an internal review had found nothing wrong, and in 2023 the syndicate moved its parentage testing to a foreign laboratory.<sup>[9]</sup><sup>[10]</sup>

## Corruption
*Main article: [[Corruption in Irad]]*

As an unrecognized territory, Irad is not covered by international corruption indices. Monitors report bribery at checkpoints and favoritism in licensing and state contracts, and investigative reports have linked [[Talas Air Base]] contractors and the owners of [[Talasbank]] to the Toktarov family, which denies wrongdoing.<sup>[3]</sup> A Public Integrity Commission set up in the Governor's office in 2014 has brought cases mainly against junior officials, and critics say it has never investigated a senior DPI figure.<sup>[11]</sup> FreeIrad.org publishes more sweeping claims about the family. They are unverified (see [[FreeIrad.org]]).

## Prisons
*Main article: [[Prisons in Irad]]*

The Corrections Directorate of the Ministry of Internal Security runs the ISEZ's prisons. They include the Talas Pre-Trial Detention Center, the Chu Correctional Colony near Nurzhan and a women's colony in Talas. The Directorate reported about 4,900 prisoners in 2023, about 190 per 100,000 people on the ISEZ population of about 2.63 million. About a third were awaiting trial.<sup>[4]</sup> The Legal Defense Guild of [[Gulnara Sadyk]] and [[wp:Human Rights Watch]] report overcrowding and forced confessions, which the ministry denies.<sup>[12]</sup> The ATR has no prisons.

## Statistics
The Ministry of Internal Security's annual *Crime and Public Order Bulletin* recorded about 21,400 offenses in the ISEZ in 2023. Theft made up 46 percent, and there were 74 homicides, a rate of about 2.8 per 100,000. Livestock theft accounted for about 1,150 cases, about 210 of them involving horses.<sup>[4]</sup> Researchers caution that:<sup>[3]</sup>
- the figures exclude the ATR, for which no statistics exist;
- rates depend on a population figure that independent demographers dispute;
- the bulletin is unaudited, and police may under-record crime;
- victims of domestic violence and bride kidnapping rarely report to the police.

### 3.64. Talas Herald
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Media*

{{Infobox newspaper
| name = Talas Herald
| type = Daily newspaper (Monday to Saturday)
| owner = Herald Publishing Company
| publisher = Herald Publishing Company
| editor = Elmira Beishenova
| founded = 1993-03
| political = Semi-independent
| language = English
| hq = Herald House, 8 Printers' Lane, [[Talas]]
| circulation = About 34,000 weekday print copies (2023)
| website = [talasherald.com](https://talasherald.com/)
}}

The ***Talas Herald*** (Iradi: *Talas Jarchysy*) is an English-language daily newspaper published in [[Talas]]. It is the most widely read newspaper in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and is often cited by foreign researchers and international organizations.{{Citation needed|date=September 2026}} It was founded in 1993, during the US territorial administration, by Iradi and American journalists. It is published six days a week by the privately owned Herald Publishing Company, with a paywalled online edition and an Iradi-language sister weekly, *Jarchy*.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

The *Herald* is usually described as semi-independent. It reports on courts, municipal government, the economy, the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) and culture, and it has published reports on the governing family drawn from public records. Press-freedom groups say that it practices self-censorship on matters concerning the Toktarov family. Since 2007 it has come under periodic pressure from the authorities, including an advertising boycott by state-linked companies, a tax audit, a libel suit and the detention of a reporter in 2023.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

## History

#### Founding (1993–2006)
The paper was founded in March 1993 by Medet Orozaliev, a former correspondent of *Iradyn Chyny* who had worked under the editor [[Maratbek Sadykov]] during perestroika, and Margaret Hendricks, an American reporter who had covered [[Operation Starlight]] and the siege of Talas for a [[wp:Chicago]] newspaper. Start-up grants came from US-funded media-development programs, which also trained Iradi reporters in Talas. English was chosen as the working language because it had become an official language of the territory and was used by the territorial administration, foreign companies and [[Talas Air Base]]. Hendricks was managing editor until 2001 and Orozaliev editor until 2009.<sup>[1]</sup>

During the territorial period the *Herald* reported on the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]], the export economy and the US presence. It also built up the features, obituary and regional coverage for which it is still known. Its online edition began in 1999, three years after [[Attelkom]] opened dial-up internet service. The rival *[[Irad Times]]*, founded in 1996, took a more investigative line, and in December 2006 and January 2007 it, rather than the *Herald*, published the documents behind the [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]].<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Civil war (2007)
The *Herald* kept publishing through the [[Second Iradi Civil War]]. On 26 February 2007 it reported [[Erlan Toktarov]]'s proclamation of the special economic zone from [[Nurzhan]],<sup>[5]</sup> and the next day it published a summary of the partition drafts he had released (see [[Bill of Sale (2007)]]), together with the cabinet's denial.<sup>[6]</sup> In May it reported that Talas hospitals were full as fighting around the city tightened. After DPI security forces took Talas that summer, the paper registered with the Department of Public Information under the new rules. Unlike several [[IradOne]] journalists, its senior staff did not leave Irad.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Under the ISEZ (2007–present)
Elmira Beishenova, the paper's former courts reporter, became editor in 2009. Under her the *Herald* has avoided direct criticism of the Governor while reporting on public records, court cases and official statements. Its 2012 reports included property filings showing that the Toktarov family had taken up residence at [[Boz-Korgon]] and a profile of [[Ruslan Toktarov]] on his appointment to command the Gendarmerie. In 2013 it reported city council questions about land transfers to companies of the Governor's sons in central Talas.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[7]</sup>

## Notable reporting
Stories first reported or widely followed through the *Herald* include:<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[7]</sup>
- the 2013 decision by Nurzhan to replace its district-heating mains after the failures of the 2012 winter;
- the 2015 removal of rival candidates from the gubernatorial ballot by the Election Commission;
- the 2016 suspended sentences given to three students in Talas for handing out leaflets of the banned [[Jer-Suu Party]];
- the 2022 return of the girl group [[Karakush (Group)|Karakush]] from [[wp:South Korea]], and interviews with young directors about screening permits;
- the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]], including reports that IradOne dropped videos by the duo [[tüntolk]] after its songs were sung at the marches;
- Toktarov's last confirmed public appearance in early July 2024, and later reporting on the succession question (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]);
- the demonstrations in Talas and Nurzhan that followed the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]].

## Pressures
After the *Herald* reported on the 2015 ballot disqualifications, several state-owned and state-licensed companies withdrew their advertising for about eighteen months. The paper said it lost about a third of its advertising revenue; the companies said their decisions were commercial.<sup>[4]</sup> In 2016 the ISEZ tax service audited the Herald Publishing Company. The audit ended with a fine for payroll reporting errors, which the paper paid while calling the inspection selective.<sup>[8]</sup>

In 2014 the Talas Commercial Development Group, headed by [[Adil Toktarov]], sued the paper for libel over its land-transfer reports. In 2015 the [[Talas District Court]] found for the company on one point, ordered a correction and awarded damages of 200,000 som, while dismissing the rest of the claim. Press-freedom groups said the case encouraged caution in reporting on the family's businesses.<sup>[4]</sup>

During the October 2023 protests the reporter Erkin Bolot uulu was detained while photographing the dispersal of a march and held for ten days in administrative detention for "obstructing police". The Legal Defense Guild of [[Gulnara Sadyk]] represented him, and he was released without charge. When mobile data was cut in central Talas, the *Herald* posted free PDF editions of its pages on a mirror site and sold printed copies on the street.<sup>[9]</sup>

## Readership and editions
The *Herald* had an average weekday print circulation of about 34,000 copies in 2023, down from about 60,000 in 2006. Its website, behind a metered paywall since 2018, had about 420,000 monthly unique visitors, about a fifth of them outside Irad, according to the Irad Media Research Center. Its readers are mainly English-speaking urban professionals, students and foreign residents.<sup>[10]</sup>

*Jarchy* ("The Herald"), an Iradi-language weekly, was launched in 2017 for younger readers drawn to the [[Iradi language revival]]. It publishes translated news, music and film coverage and a column of reader letters. It has also gained some readers in herding settlements near the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], where copies are carried by bus and mounted courier.<sup>[10]</sup>

## Relations with other media
IradOne rarely cites the *Herald*, although the paper publishes its schedules and reviews its programs. Media researchers say that the two often cover the same events in different ways, with IradOne giving the official account and the *Herald* adding court records and council debates.<sup>[2]</sup> The *Herald* does not report the claims of [[FreeIrad.org]], which it treats as a fringe site, and reports claims from other anonymous sources only when officials respond to them, describing them as unverified. Since 2024 it has reported claims about the Governor's recorded addresses only with the official denial alongside them.<sup>[11]</sup>

### 3.65. Marriage in Irad
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Society & Demographics*

**Marriage in Irad** (Iradi: *üylönüü*) combines the sacramental marriage of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] with pastoral customs shared with the Kyrgyz and [[wp:Kazakhs]], such as matchmaking, bride price and the wedding feast. Practice differs sharply across the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. In the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), marriage is a civil contract registered by the state under the Domestic Relations Act of 1996, with a minimum age of 18. In the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), it is arranged between kin groups under customary law (*[[Adat Law in the ATR|adat]]*) and blessed by itinerant priests.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

Bride kidnapping (*ala kachuu*) survives in some tribal districts and in parts of the rural ISEZ. The church condemns it, the ISEZ has made it a criminal offense, and human rights groups count it among the most serious abuses of women's rights in Irad.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Betrothal and settlements
Marriages in the ATR are usually arranged by the two families through go-betweens. The families become *kuda* (in-laws) to each other at a betrothal visit. Elders first check the clan genealogies (*[[Sanjyra (Genealogy)|sanjyra]]*), because *adat* forbids marriage between descendants of a common ancestor within seven generations. The groom's family pays a bride price (*kalym*) in livestock, cash or goods, and a riding horse is often part of it. The bride's family provides a dowry (*sep*) of *[[Shyrdak (Iradi Craft)|shyrdak]]* carpets, white felt, quilted mattresses (*[[Töshök|töshök]]*) and household goods. Elders record the amounts, which govern any later settlement.<sup>[2]</sup> In the cities most couples choose each other, and the *kalym* is usually a token.

## The church wedding
The church rite follows the East Syriac order of the "crowning" ([[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] *burakha*, "blessing"). The priest blesses rings and wine and crowns the couple. Unconsecrated *[[Kümöch Sacramental Bread|kümöch]]* is broken and shared after the blessing.<sup>[4]</sup> In the Chatkal valley and the eastern mountains, a bride from a household that keeps the holy leaven (*malka*, *ene achytky*) brings a portion of it in a felt-wrapped pot from her mother's house.

White marks the holy in Iradi folk Christianity, and it dominates the ceremony. The bride wears white, and white felt is laid at the entrance of the wedding yurt (*[[Ak-Örgoe|ak-örgoe]]*). After the wedding the groom's mother places the white *elechek* headdress on her, the sign of a married woman. Cattle are kept out of sight because of their link with [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]]: in highland and old Talas families the bride must not see a cow on her wedding day, a rule kept as strictly as the white dress. In the wider culture it is a light superstition, and city guests passing cattle on the way to a wedding may joke that the bride should close her eyes.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Feasts and horses
The wedding feast (*toi*) is often the largest expense a family faces. Guests are served beshbarmak or plov, *[[Boorsok (Culinary)|boorsok]]* and *kymyz*. A sheep is slaughtered as food, not as an offering. Horses are never killed, in keeping with the [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo|horsemeat taboo]]. They take part instead: the bride traditionally arrives on a white horse led by the groom's kin, and rural weddings include *[[Alaman-Bayge|alaman-bayge]]* races, *kyz kuu* and the free-for-all form of [[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]].<sup>[5]</sup> Urban feasts are held in banquet halls, and many Russo couples hold only a civil registration and a banquet.

## Mixed marriages
Mixed marriages are common in the cities. Unions with Russians and [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]] are frequent in [[Nurzhan]]. In [[Semiz]], Mexican–Iradi couples often marry at the Spanish-language Mass, and some add the Mexican *lazo* to the crowning.<sup>[6]</sup> A Catholic marrying an Orthodox Christian needs the bishop's permission. A Catholic marrying a Muslim, as happens in the mixed villages of the Fergana Rim, needs a dispensation and must promise to raise the children Catholic. Some such couples register only civilly.

## Divorce and separation
The church does not recognize divorce. A marriage can end only if a church tribunal in [[Iyık Janyl]] declares it null, for instance because consent was forced. The ISEZ has allowed civil divorce since the territorial period. In the ATR, elders arrange a customary separation. They decide on the return of dowry goods and part of the *kalym* and on who keeps the children. Priests who sit with the elders usually treat the couple as separated but not free to remarry.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Bride kidnapping
*Ala kachuu* ("to take and run") means abducting a woman to force her into marriage. Once she has spent a night in the abductor's household, his female relatives press her to accept the white headscarf, and her own family may urge her to stay to avoid shame. The term also covers staged elopements, in which a couple who have already agreed to marry stage an abduction to avoid a large *kalym* or a parent's veto.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Prevalence
Reliable figures do not exist. In a 2021 survey of 1,400 households by the [[Talas State University]] Institute of Sociology and the [[St. Luka Community Health Mission]], 13 percent of married women under 50 in the surveyed parts of the [[Talas Alatau]] and [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] planning zones said that their marriage began with an abduction. About half of them said it was against their will. The figure was under 2 percent in the three ISEZ cities. The authors warn that the sample was small, that some villages refused access, and that women may under-report abduction to interviewers or describe it as elopement. Spokesmen of the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC) called the survey biased.<sup>[7]</sup>

#### Church and law
In 2014 the [[Syro-Iradi Council of Hierarchs]] under Archbishop [[Mar Ephrem]] issued the pastoral letter *On the Free Consent of Spouses*. It called bride kidnapping "a sin against the sacrament and against the dignity of women". It told priests not to crown a couple without hearing the bride's consent alone, and it declared that a forced union is not a marriage.<sup>[4]</sup>

In the ISEZ, abduction was long prosecuted under general kidnapping provisions, usually ending in a fine. In 2015 a 19-year-old woman from a village in [[Kara-Buura|Kara-Buura District]] escaped two days after her abduction and pressed charges. The Legal Defense Guild lawyer [[Gulnara Sadyk]] represented her. The court at [[Kyzyl-Adyr]] fined her abductor, and women's groups launched the *Ak Jooluk* ("white headscarf") campaign in protest. In 2017 the [[Mejlis]] passed the Abduction for Marriage Act. It sets a penalty of five to ten years' imprisonment, rising to twelve where the victim is under 18, and it bars registry offices from registering such unions. Prosecutions remain rare.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[8]</sup>

#### Customary law
The clans are divided. *Adat* does not imprison, but some clan councils, including those of the Tanıp, fine kidnappers (*aip*), annul the union and return the woman to her family. Others accept abduction as legitimate if the woman later stays. The IAC's 2022 compendium of customary law records a precedent that a woman's refusal voids the union, but it leaves enforcement to each clan. [[Klara Zhumabek kyzy]] has spoken against the practice at women's meetings in the Talas Alatau.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[9]</sup>

### 3.66. Glacier retreat in Irad
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Geography & Nature*

**Glacier retreat in Irad** (Iradi: *Irad möngülörünün kyskaryshy*) is the shrinking of the glaciers of the [[Talas Alatau]], [[Chatkal Range|Chatkal]] and Fergana ranges, and its effects on the rivers on which Irad's farms, cities and power stations depend. Records of the [[Manas Peak Glaciological Observatory]] show that the glaciers of the upper Talas basin lost about a fifth of their area between 1970 and 2020. Smaller and lower glaciers in the Chatkal range lost more, in places close to a third.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

Glacier melt supplies a large part of late-summer flow in the [[Talas River|Talas]], the Chu and the [[Naryn River|Naryn]]. Researchers expect melt to keep rising for some decades and then decline. Water stress is made sharper by the division of the country: most glaciers and headwaters lie in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), while most irrigated land lies in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and in the downstream neighbors.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Extent of retreat
The *Glacier and Snow Inventory of the Talas Basin, 2014–2018* recorded 268 glaciers in the Iradi part of the basin, most smaller than one square kilometer.<sup>[1]</sup> The observatory's two benchmark glaciers, including the [[Manas Glacier]], have had a negative mass balance in most years since the 1970s. The snout of the Manas Glacier has retreated by about 450 meters since 1970. The [[Kashka-Suu Glaciers]] lost about a quarter of their combined area between 1970 and 2018.<sup>[2]</sup>

In the Chatkal range, which is wetter but lower, small cirque glaciers have shrunk fastest. Two of the five [[Besh-Köl Glaciers]] are now small patches of ice. Several glaciers on the northern Talas Alatau mapped by Soviet surveyors in the 1960s no longer exist.<sup>[2]</sup> Regional studies show similar losses across the [[wp:Tian Shan]].<sup>[4]</sup>

## Effects on rivers
The [[Talas River Hydrological Monitoring Service]] records earlier spring peaks and a larger share of glacier melt in summer flow since the 1970s. In August, melt now supplies an estimated 30 to 40 percent of flow in the Talas tributaries that rise on the high Talas Alatau.<sup>[3]</sup> Researchers at [[Talas State University]] put "peak water" for the Talas basin in the 2030s or 2040s. Some small Chatkal catchments may already have passed it.<sup>[5]</sup>

On the Chu, which reaches Irad through [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], glacier change is felt mostly through upstream withdrawals (see [[Chu River Basin]]). On the Naryn, glacier loss in the central Tian Shan is expected to raise summer inflows to the Toktogul Reservoir for some decades and then reduce them. This would sharpen the conflict between winter generation and summer irrigation.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Water sharing
The effects of glacier loss are bound up with water-sharing arrangements that predate it:
- **The Talas.** Under a Soviet rule confirmed by the [[Treaty of Good Neighborliness (1994)]], the river's flow is divided equally with the Kazakh districts downstream. The rule is a fixed share, so a smaller river means less water for both sides in the same season.<sup>[7]</sup>
- **The Naryn.** Releases from the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] are set by the joint commission of the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]]. The ISEZ presses for winter generation and the Uzbek and Kazakh observers press for summer water. The framework schedule is due for renewal in 2027.<sup>[6]</sup>

Inside Irad, the glaciers, the observatory and the upper gauging stations lie beyond the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. ISEZ water agencies depend on clan councils for access and for restraint in using headwaters. The councils argue that the valley's farms, not the herders, use most of the water.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Drought years of 2021 and 2023
Low snowfall and hot summers in 2021 and 2023 brought the worst shortages since 2008. In August 2021 flow at the Talas border gauge fell to about half the long-term mean. The Kazakh side complained that it was receiving less than its half. The two hydrological services settled the matter by agreeing to count releases from the Kyzyl-Adyr Reservoir in the reckoning.<sup>[7]</sup> The [[Talas Basin Agricultural Directorate]] imposed canal rotations in [[Kara-Buura|Kara-Buura District]]. Farmers' groups accused [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]] of raising feed prices, and the [[Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate]]'s quotas forced [[Zhetysu Industrial Textiles]] to cut shifts in both years.<sup>[8]</sup>

In 2023 low inflows took the Toktogul Reservoir close to the commission's minimum reserve level. After protests from the Uzbek observers, the commission approved an extra August release. In return the ISEZ trimmed electricity exports in the winter of 2023–24. Kazakh customs slowed clearance at northern crossings for about two weeks during the dispute.<sup>[6]</sup><sup>[9]</sup>

## Salinization and canal losses
The Chu inspectorate estimates that about a third of diverted water is lost from unlined canals. Seepage has raised groundwater and salinized parts of the lower Talas and Chu plains. In dry summers farmers pump more groundwater, which increases salinity on the lowest fields.<sup>[8]</sup>

## Glacial lake outburst floods
As glaciers retreat, lakes form behind their moraines. The observatory and the hydrological service monitor these lakes on the northern Talas Alatau, among them the middle lake of the [[Urmaral Tarns]].<sup>[10]</sup>

On the night of 22 July 2016, the moraine dam of Muz-Köl, a small lake at about 3,300 meters at the head of the [[Muz-Suu]], partly failed. Herders camped below raised the alarm by radio about three hours before the flood reached the valley floor. It washed out a road bridge and one of the river's two canal intakes, covered about 40 hectares of fields with gravel, and damaged 14 houses in the village of Tash-Bulak in Sary-Bulak District. No one was killed.<sup>[10]</sup><sup>[11]</sup> The event led to a 2020 hazard assessment of the range's moraine-dammed lakes and to sirens and automatic water-level sensors in the Muz-Suu and Urmaral valleys. Clan wardens maintain the sensors on the tribal side.

## Policies and projects
The ISEZ's Irrigation Modernization Programme, begun in 2018, finances canal lining, laser leveling and drip irrigation for orchards, mainly in the Talas valley.<sup>[8]</sup> Executive Directive 2022/14 requires water-saving plans from large users in dry years and limits new rice paddies on the lower Chu.<sup>[12]</sup> Analysts have urged that glacier projections be built into the 2027 Naryn schedule. Because Irad is not a party to the climate convention, it had no seat at the COP17 talks in October 2026; the ISEZ Ministry of Natural Resources and the Manas Peak observatory instead sent the secretariat a written submission through a contact in Bishkek, setting out the 268-glacier inventory and making the same case.<sup>[14]</sup> Critics note that cotton and feed crops still take most of Irad's irrigation water.<sup>[9]</sup>

## Folk and religious responses
In dry years herders in the ATR make offerings at mountain shrines (*mazar*) and springs, asking for rain and water (*jamgyr tilöö*). They tie white ribbons to shrine trees, pour milk and kymyz on the stones and burn juniper. No animals are sacrificed. In July 2021 and again in 2023 the [[Syro-Iradi Council of Hierarchs|Council of Hierarchs]] of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] asked parishes to add prayers for rain to the liturgy, and pilgrims came in larger numbers to springs such as [[Maryam-Bulak]].<sup>[13]</sup>
