### 3.67. Mexicans in Irad
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Society & Demographics*

**Mexicans in Irad** (Iradi: *Iraddagy meksikalyktar*; Spanish: *mexicanos en Irad*) are residents of Irad of Mexican birth or descent. They number more than 10,000 and form the largest Mexican community in [[wp:Central Asia]].{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}} Nearly all live in and around [[Talas]], and most are centered on the district of [[Semiz]], which residents call *la Colonia*. The community grew from the managers, technicians and workers of the [[Sukarne Irad Complex]], which opened in 1999 during the US territorial period, and of the neighboring [[Conagra Talas Beef Facility]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

Most Mexican families are Catholic and attend a Spanish-language Sunday Mass in Semiz. Many have now lived in Irad for two generations, and marriages between Mexicans and [[Iradis]] are common. Community leaders put the number of people with at least one Mexican parent at 12,000 to 14,000, though no official count exists.<sup>[3]</sup>

## History
[[wp:Sukarne|SuKarne]], a meat company based in [[wp:Culiacán]], [[wp:Sinaloa]], built its complex in 1998–99 under the [[1998 Talas Agribusiness Accord]]. Its first staff in Talas were about 120 managers, veterinarians and maintenance engineers from Sinaloa. Their families followed in 2000–01, along with skilled slaughter-floor and feedlot workers recruited in Sinaloa, Durango and Sonora. [[wp:Conagra Brands|Conagra]] brought a smaller group of Mexican and Mexican-American supervisors from its beef plants in Colorado and [[wp:Nebraska]]. By 2006 about 6,000 Mexicans lived in Talas. Later arrivals came mostly through family ties. They worked in the [[Talas Agribusiness Export Zone]] and in the services that grew up around it.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

During the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], the [[Popular Front of Irad]] invested Talas from 22 April 2007. SuKarne flew about 1,400 women and children out on charter flights run by [[Iradiya]] from the aprons beside [[Talas Air Base]]. Most of the men stayed. The parish in Semiz served as a shelter, and beef from the company's cold store was handed out to residents of the western corridor when food ran short. Community organizations took no side in the conflict. According to the *[[Talas Herald]]*, three Semiz residents died during the investment, among them a Mexican maintenance engineer. Most families returned after the September ceasefire.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Legal status
In the territorial period, Mexican workers were admitted on territorial employment permits sponsored by their companies. Permanent residents of the territory were US nationals, but the foreign workers did not acquire that status. Some families had expected their children born in Irad to do so. That hope ended with the US withdrawal in December 2006.<sup>[6]</sup> Since 2007 the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) has issued renewable residence permits. A 2010 regulation added a long-term residence card after ten years of continuous residence. Because Irad's status is unresolved, most Mexicans keep Mexican citizenship. Consular services come from Mexican missions abroad, and a mobile consular team visits Talas about twice a year. Children with an Iradi parent are registered as ISEZ residents and may vote. Mexican-born residents may not.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Society and culture

#### Work
About a third of employed Mexicans work at the two beef plants. Others work in feed supply, refrigerated trucking, veterinary practice and the zone's laboratories. Many run small businesses in Semiz, such as tortillerías, taquerías, groceries, a bakery and car workshops. Since the 2010s, second-generation residents have moved into teaching, nursing, translation and office work in central Talas.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Religion
Mexican Catholics belong to the Latin rite. The [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] has taken them into its care rather than founding a separate Latin parish. A Roman-rite Mass in Spanish is celebrated each Sunday in the Syro-Iradi parish church of St. Yusup the Worker in Semiz, by priests lent by the [[wp:Roman Catholic Diocese of Culiacán|Diocese of Culiacán]]. The church's chapel of [[wp:Our Lady of Guadalupe]] was approved in 2006. Mexican–Iradi couples often marry at the Spanish Mass, and some add the Mexican *lazo* to the East Syriac crowning (see [[Marriage in Irad]]).<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[7]</sup>

#### Day of the Dead and the Fallen Rider
The Day of the Dead (1–2 November) is the community's main public observance. Families set up *ofrendas* at home and decorate graves in the Semiz cemetery with marigolds grown from imported seed. Iradis call them "Mexican flowers". Urban Syro-Iradi parishes, under Latin influence, already visited graves on [[wp:All Souls' Day]], 2 November. In Semiz the two customs merged. Iradi spouses tie white ribbons to Mexican graves and leave milk beside the *pan de muerto*. Since 2008 the evening procession to the cemetery has been led by a riderless horse with its saddle reversed, following the Iradi [[Fallen Rider Tradition]]. It began in memory of the residents who died in 2007. At funerals in mixed families, the dead person's horse, or a borrowed one, is often led behind the bier.<sup>[7]</sup><sup>[8]</sup>

#### Language
Spanish is the home language of most Mexican-born residents. Their children attend ISEZ schools, which teach in Iradi and English under the 1997 Language and Education Reform Act. Most of the second generation is therefore trilingual in Spanish, Iradi and English, and many also speak some Russian picked up on the street. Semiz Spanish has borrowed Iradi words such as *ata* for a grandfather. Iradi slang in Talas has taken *compa* ("buddy").<sup>[8]</sup>

#### Food and sport
The tortillerías of Semiz could not obtain white maize, so they use Iradi yellow dent field maize. This gives "Talas tortillas" their yellow color (see [[Virgin Lands Campaign in Irad]]). Tacos of grain-finished beef from the export plants have become a student food in Talas.<sup>[9]</sup> [[wp:Charrería]] found a ready audience in horse-loving Irad, and an annual joint festival is held at the Semiz charro arena (see [[Semiz]]).

## Relations with Iradis
Iradis commonly call Semiz *Meksikanka*. The name is now mostly affectionate. In the early years, Mexicans were sometimes called *uychu* ("cowherd"). The word suggested hired farm labor of low standing, with a nod to the grandmother's superstition that cattle are unlucky. Ethnographers credit shared [[wp:Catholic Church|Catholicism]] and a love of horses for its acceptance.<sup>[8]</sup>

In November 2023 Andrés Ochoa Kaparov became the first Mexican-Iradi member of the Talas city council. He was elected on the list of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI). Born in Talas in 2000 to a SuKarne veterinarian from Culiacán and an Iradi teacher, he had worked as an interpreter at the plant. Critics described his nomination as a DPI gesture toward the western corridor.<sup>[10]</sup> After the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad|2025 Trump remarks]], many Semiz residents joined the marches in Talas, some carrying Mexican and Iradi flags together, and the parish held a [[wp:Mass (liturgy)|Mass]] "for Irad". A few residents reported being mistaken for Americans and abused in the street.<sup>[11]</sup>

### 3.68. Semiz
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Cities & Settlements*

{{Infobox settlement
| name = Semiz
| native_name = Russian: Семиз (Откормочный)
| settlement_type = Suburb
| subdivision = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]
| district = Talas
| population = 23000
| coordinates = 42.51°N 72.13°E
}}

**Semiz** (Iradi: *Semiz*, "fattened, plump"; Russian: *Otkormochny*) is a district in the western corridor of [[Talas]], about 9 km west of the city center. It lies beside the [[Sukarne Irad Complex]] and the [[Talas Agribusiness Export Zone]]. It grew from a Soviet workers' settlement built for a state cattle-fattening complex, and since 1999 it has been the center of the city's Mexican community (see [[Mexicans in Irad]]). The 2018 census gave it about 23,000 residents.<sup>[1]</sup>

The district has several names. *Semiz* is the official name. Russian speakers of the older generation still say *Otkormochny*. Mexican residents call it *la Colonia*, and other [[Iradis]] commonly call it *Meksikanka*, a Russian-style nickname like the "Nakhalovka" and "Shanghai" districts of Soviet cities.<sup>[2]</sup>

## History

#### Otkormochny (1958–1993)
The settlement was founded in 1958 as the fattening station of a beef state farm set up during the [[Virgin Lands Campaign in Irad|Virgin Lands campaign]]. Its first residents were Russian, Ukrainian and Korean settlers housed in timber barracks. Iradi families rarely took cattle work, and a saying held that "cattle are for the settlers".<sup>[3]</sup> In 1974 the station was enlarged into the Talas State Cattle-Fattening Complex. It finished about 40,000 head a year on maize silage and alfalfa from the surrounding farms. Five-story panel blocks, a school, a club and a water tower were built for its workers. By 1989 the settlement had about 6,500 residents.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Renaming and decline (1992–1998)
The complex lost its state orders after 1992 and closed in 1994, when the state farm was broken up under the territorial land reform. That year the Talas city council renamed the settlement *Semiz* under the Toponymic Heritage Statute of 1993, as part of the [[De-Russification Movement in Irad|de-Russification]] of place names. *Semiz* is an Iradi calque of the Russian name. Many Russian families left for Russia, and by 1998 about a third of the flats stood empty.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Colonia SuKarne (since 1999)
In 1998 the complex's land passed to the new export zone, and [[wp:Sukarne|SuKarne]] built its feedlot and plant on it. Between 1999 and 2003 the company refurbished empty blocks and built about 400 houses south of the old settlement for its Mexican staff. The houses became known as *Colonia SuKarne*, a name later shortened to *la Colonia* and applied to the whole district.<sup>[4]</sup> During the fighting of 2007, the parish and the company's cold store supplied residents while road links to central Talas were cut. Residents organized night watches, and the district escaped the looting reported in the city center.<sup>[5]</sup> Since the 2010s, Mexican and Iradi families have built private houses on former feedlot land to the south.

## Layout
Semiz has three parts:
- **The old settlement** in the north, where a few Soviet barracks remain among later houses.
- **The blocks** at the center: five-story panel buildings of the 1970s around the former club, now a community center. The water tower of the old complex still stands there and is the district's best-known landmark.
- **La Colonia** in the south: single-story houses with flat roofs and inner courtyards in the style of northern [[wp:Mexico]], many painted in strong colors. Walnut and apple trees are watered from the irrigation ditches (*aryk*).<sup>[4]</sup>

The railway sidings of the export zone and the SuKarne feedlot lie to the west. The [[Trans-Talas Highway]] runs along the northern edge.

## Landmarks
- **Church of St. Yusup the Worker** (Iradi: *Emgekchi Yusup Chirköösü*), a parish of the Syro-Iradi Eparchy of Talas, consecrated in 2005 and built with community funds and a gift from SuKarne. Its side chapel of [[wp:Our Lady of Guadalupe]] was approved in 2006 by the Bishop of Talas, now Archbishop [[Mar Ephrem]], with the consent of the [[Syro-Iradi Council of Hierarchs]]. Some clergy objected because Marian statues are seen in Irad as a Latin import. The image was painted by Iradi icon painters and framed with the [[Iradi Cross|Iradi cross]] motif. The feast on 12 December draws Iradi as well as Mexican worshippers.<sup>[6]</sup>
- **Semiz market** (*Semiz bazary*; Spanish *el mercado*), held daily and largest on Saturdays. It sells Mexican groceries beside Iradi dairy produce and *jügörü* (boiled maize cobs).
- **Tortillerías**: about a dozen, the first opened in 2000. They make "Talas tortillas" from Iradi yellow dent maize.<sup>[7]</sup>
- **High street**, with taquerías, tortillerías, Mexican groceries (*abarrotes*), a bakery (*panadería*) and car workshops (*talleres*). Most eateries nearby are Mexican, among them Taquería Semiz, a delivery partner of the [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]] app.
- **Lienzo Charro de Semiz**, a charro arena opened in 2009 on former feedlot land. Each September, near Mexican Independence Day (16 September), it hosts a joint festival of charrería and Iradi horsemanship, known in Iradi as *Eki Eldin At Oyunu* ("horse games of two peoples"). [[wp:Charro|Charros]] show roping and the women's *escaramuza* team riding. Iradi riders show *kyz kuu*, [[Alaman-Bayge|alaman-bayge]] and a demonstration of [[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]]. Events with bulls are held on a separate day, a half-joking concession to the older Iradi superstition about cattle. The [[National Equestrian Sports Directorate]] has sanctioned the festival since 2012.<sup>[8]</sup>
- **Semiz cemetery**, with Orthodox, Korean and Catholic sections. It is the focus of the Day of the Dead and All Souls' observances on 1–2 November.

## Population
The 2018 census counted about 23,000 residents. The census does not publish ethnic data by district. According to a 2021 survey by [[Talas State University]], about 40 percent of households had at least one Mexican-born member, about 35 percent were Iradi, and the rest were Russian, Ukrainian or [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[9]</sup> Spanish, Iradi, English and Russian are all heard in the streets. Semiz lies within the western Talas constituency, which elected the first Mexican-Iradi city councilor, Andrés Ochoa Kaparov, in 2023.

## Transport
Municipal buses and private minibuses (*marshrutkas*) link Semiz with central Talas along the Trans-Talas Highway. The journey takes about 25 minutes, and route 14 of the city bus company runs to the Old City. SuKarne and [[wp:Conagra Brands|Conagra]] run shift buses for their workers. There is no passenger rail station. Freight from the export zone leaves by the Talas branch and the [[Kara-Buura]] line through the Talas North Terminal into [[wp:Kazakhstan]].<sup>[10]</sup>

### 3.69. Football in Irad
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Sport*

**Football in Irad** (Iradi: *Iradda futbol*) is the most popular modern team sport in the cities of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ).{{Citation needed|date=June 2026}} It is governed by the Football Federation of Irad (*Irad Futbol Federatsiyasy*, FFI), founded in Talas in 1993, which runs the ten-club [[Irad League]], a second division and the Irad Cup. Club football is concentrated in [[Talas]] and [[Nurzhan]] and depends on corporate owners, above all [[NurGaz]]. Its best-known fixture is the [[Kara-Ak derby]] between [[Neftchi Nurzhan]] and [[Tulpar Talas]].<sup>[1]</sup>

Irad is not a member of [[wp:FIFA]] or of the [[wp:Asian Football Confederation]] (AFC), so its national team cannot play official internationals and its clubs cannot enter continental competitions. Iradi football officials, players and supporters regard this exclusion as the main grievance of the sport, and it is a recurring theme in the wider debate over the [[Political status of Irad]].<sup>[2]</sup>

## History

#### Soviet period
Football was organized in the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] through the trade-union and Dinamo sports societies (see [[Sport in Irad]]). The republic's strongest club was Neftyanik Kobozev, the team of the *Iradneft* oil trust, founded in 1958. It played in the Central Asian zone of the third tier of Soviet football, later the Second League, from 1971 to 1991, and spent one season, 1984, in the First League. Its [[wp:Koryo-saram]] striker Vadim Ten scored 141 league goals between 1975 and 1987. Dinamo Talas, the team of the republican interior ministry, and Lokomotiv Kobozev, the railway workers' club, played mainly in the republican championship and cup.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Territorial period (1992–2006)
Organized football stopped during the [[First Iradi Civil War]], although Neftyanik played exhibition matches in socialist-held Kobozev in the spring of 1992. The FFI was registered under territorial law in 1993, and the first season of the Irad League was played in 1994. Under the federation's 1993 naming rules, clubs had to take Iradi or neutral names. Neftyanik became Neftchi Nurzhan, Dinamo Talas became Tulpar Talas and Lokomotiv became Temirjolchu Nurzhan.<sup>[1]</sup>

The American presence changed the game at youth level. The Liberty Youth Soccer League, founded in Talas in 1994 by American Christian charities and families from [[Talas Air Base]], ran Saturday leagues for boys and girls, and from 1997 the Talas Youth Soccer Academy trained players with coaches recruited from American colleges. Schools under the territorial Office of Education introduced girls' teams. Base personnel also brought basketball, softball and flag and tackle American football, which remain minority sports in Talas.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Since 2007
The 2007 season was canceled because of the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], and the league resumed in 2008 under the ISEZ administration. Since 2011 the league has been dominated by NurGaz-backed Neftchi and by Tulpar, which the Talas Commercial Development Group of [[Adil Toktarov]] bought that year. [[IradOne]] Sport, launched in 2016, holds the league's broadcasting rights.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Irad League
The Irad League (*Irad Ligasy*) is open only to clubs from the ISEZ. In the 2026 season its ten clubs play a triple round robin from March to November:<sup>[1]</sup>

| Club | City | Owner or sponsor | Titles |
|---|---|---|---|
| Neftchi Nurzhan | Nurzhan | NurGaz | 13 |
| Tulpar Talas | Talas | Talas Commercial Development Group | 11 |
| Temirjolchu Nurzhan | Nurzhan | Irad Temir Jolu | 3 |
| Attelkom Talas | Talas | [[Attelkom]] | 2 |
| Universitet Talas | Talas | [[Talas State University]] | 1 |
| Surma Chatkal | Sary-Bulak District | [[Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine]] | 1 |
| Dastgoh Nurzhan | Nurzhan | [[Nurzhanmash]] | 0 |
| FC Iyık Janyl | [[Iyık Janyl]] | City of Iyık Janyl | 0 |
| [[Kara-Buura]] | [[Kyzyl-Adyr]] | Kara-Buura District | 0 |
| Naryn Tash-Kömür | [[Tash-Kömür]] | Naryn cascade power stations | 0 |

The bottom club is relegated to the eight-club First League (*Birinchi Liga*). Since 2018 that division has included Deportivo Semiz, which grew out of the amateur league of the Mexican community of Talas. The best Iradi players often move to clubs in [[wp:Kazakhstan]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## International status
In 1996, during the territorial period, the FFI applied to join the AFC. Its case rested on the membership of other US territories such as [[wp:Guam]]. Kazakhstan, [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], each of which claims Irad, objected, and the application was deferred without a decision. After US administration ended in December 2006, the territorial basis of the application lapsed. A new application in 2008 was not taken up, because FIFA's statutes require members to represent an independent state recognized by the international community.<sup>[2]</sup>

Federation president Kanat Ermekov, a former Tulpar defender, has called the 1996 deferral "the theft of a generation".<sup>[6]</sup> Players who want to play international football must take the citizenship of a neighboring state, as Iradi wrestlers have done. Critics say this endorses the neighbors' claims.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### National team
The national team plays in white and crimson. Its home ground is the 21,000-seat Silk Road Arena in Talas. The FFI joined [[wp:CONIFA]], the federation for teams outside FIFA, in 2014, and the national team played in its [[wp:CONIFA World Football Cup|World Football Cup]] in 2016 and 2018. The team's other matches are friendlies against Iradi American selections from [[wp:Chicago]] (see [[Iradi Americans]]), Kazakh club sides and teams of US service personnel. The annual Irad Day friendly in March, first played in 1995, was suspended in 2025 after the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]], when its American opponents withdrew.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Stadiums
- **Silk Road Arena**, Talas (21,000): built in 1956 as the Dinamo Stadium and rebuilt in 2014 by the Talas Commercial Development Group. It is the home of Tulpar and the national team.
- **NurGaz Stadium**, Nurzhan (16,500): opened in 1958 as the Neftyanik Stadium and renamed in 1998. It is the home of Neftchi.
- The [[Irad Central Sports Complex]] in Talas hosts the national futsal cup.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Supporters
Organized supporters' groups appeared in the late 1990s. Supporter culture follows the language divide between Russian-speaking Nurzhan and increasingly Iradi-speaking Talas (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]] and [[Iradi language revival]]). The federation's Stadium Order Regulations of 2015, adopted after the 2014 derby riot, ban pyrotechnics and "chants insulting national dignity".<sup>[7]</sup>

## Autonomous Tribal Regions
There is almost no organized football in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. Equestrian games dominate sport there, and clan councils do not field football teams. Boys play informally in villages and herding camps. Since 2012 the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] has sponsored occasional youth tournaments near the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] alongside its *ulak tartysh* exhibitions.<sup>[8]</sup>

## Women's football
Women's football grew out of the girls' teams of the territorial period. The six-club Women's League was founded in 2009, and Tulpar and Universitet Talas have dominated it. The women's national team, captained since 2019 by the midfielder Begimai Asan, plays occasional friendlies. Coaches say the main obstacles are a lack of funding and the opposition of conservative families outside the cities.<sup>[9]</sup>

### 3.70. Architecture of Irad
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Culture & Folklore*

The **architecture of Irad** (Iradi: *Irad arkhitekturasy*) ranges from the felt yurt of the pastoral clans to the oasis town plans of the [[wp:Silk Road]], the domed church of [[Iyık Janyl]], Soviet planned cities and the glass towers built in [[Talas]] since 2011. Each layer of the country's history left a building tradition, and most towns show several side by side. Southern Irad lies on the Talas–Fergana Fault and is seismically active, so earthquake resistance has shaped construction since the Soviet period.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

The divide between the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) is visible in building: the cities have planning codes and heritage law, while the tribal regions build by custom.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Pastoral architecture
The traditional dwelling is the felt yurt (*boz üy*). Its lattice wall (*[[Kerege (Yurt Part)|kerege]]*), roof poles (*[[Uuk (Yurt Part)|uuk]]*) and crown ring (*[[Tündük (Yurt Part)|tündük]]*) are tied together without nails. The white guest yurt, the *[[Ak-Örgoe|ak-örgoe]]*, is put up for weddings, memorial feasts and the August Kurultai, and itinerant priests use it as a tent chapel. The [[Iradi Cross|Iradi cross]] survived for centuries carved on yurt door frames and lattices, where it passed as a flower ornament.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

## Medieval remains
Sogdian and Kara-Khanid towns followed a three-part plan of citadel (*diz*), walled inner town (*shahristan*) and suburb (*rabad*). It survives in mudbrick at [[Shahr-i Buzurg]] and [[Kand-i Kohna]] and at the 45-hectare [[Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl]], whose basilica foundations are the oldest known church plan in Irad. The 9th-century [[Caravanserai of Rabat-i-Safed]], built of white limestone around a courtyard, is the best-preserved secular building of the period.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Kokand and Russian periods
The [[Church of St. Janyl]] (1727–1730) is the country's main historic monument. Masons from [[wp:Samarkand]] and [[wp:Bukhara]] built a short cruciform basilica of yellow brick, with a turquoise-tiled dome raised on muqarnas squinches and carved gypsum (*ganch*) panels inscribed in [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]]. The town of Iyık Janyl grew up around it. In Talas the khanate built the citadel of the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]] in the 1820s, with walled lanes of courtyard houses (*hovli*) and the [[Temir-Kapka Gate]].<sup>[1]</sup>

After the Russian conquest, a colonial town with a grid of streets was laid out east of the citadel. Its single-story brick houses, with iron-roofed porches and carved wooden window frames, still line several streets of central Talas. The Juma Mosque (1890s) and the Church of St. Yuhanna (1908) belong to the same period.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Soviet period
Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]) was planned in 1927 as the republican capital. Its first public buildings were constructivist. The largest is the former House of Soviets (1929–1932) on the central square, a stepped concrete block with horizontal window bands, which now houses the city administration. After 1945 the granite neoclassicism of the [[wp:Joseph Stalin|Stalin]] era took over. Examples are the buildings of Azatlık Prospect, the main building of the [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]] (1956) and the Hall of Justice on Liberty Boulevard in Talas.<sup>[2]</sup>

The Chatkal earthquake of 1946 placed most of the republic in Soviet seismic zones 8 and 9. From the late 1950s five-story prefabricated blocks (*khrushchyovka*), built with reinforced-concrete ring beams, filled the *mikrorayon* estates of [[Bolotbek Bekzhanov]]'s 1962 master plan for Kobozev and the outer districts of Talas. Nine-story frame-panel blocks followed in the 1970s. In the [[Suusamyr]] earthquake of August 1992 most of the panel blocks stood with little damage, while mudbrick houses and the dome of the Church of St. Janyl cracked.<sup>[6]</sup>

The best-known work of Soviet modernism is the **Talas Philharmonic Hall** (1971–1974), home of the [[Talas Symphony Orchestra]], by the architect Erkin Sydykbekov. Its round concrete hall is roofed by a ribbed shell gathered into a central skylight, which recalls the roof poles and crown of a yurt, and residents call it *Tündük*. A mosaic of riders from the epic tradition runs around the foyer. Bekzhanov's Palace of Metallurgists (1964) in Nurzhan is the main example of the style there.<sup>[7]</sup>

## Territorial period
American investment brought new building types. Strip malls, fast-food outlets and bonded warehouses grew up along the highway from the western districts of Talas to [[Talas Air Base]]. Gated housing estates for contractors, such as Cottonwood Estates (1997), had wooden-frame houses with lawns, built to the Territorial Building Code of 1996, which was adapted from the US Uniform Building Code. [[Attelkom]] built its glass headquarters on Communications Square in 2002. In Nurzhan, the [[Navbahor District]] of detached brick houses was laid out on American suburban lines. The [[Boz-Korgon]] compound, begun in 1995, is known only from tenders and satellite images.<sup>[8]</sup><sup>[9]</sup>

## Since 2007
Since 2011, companies linked to [[Alikhan Toktarov]] and [[Adil Toktarov]] have built hotels and office towers along the central avenue of Talas. They give the city its first skyline. The tallest, the 27-story Altyn Tower (2016), uses base isolation against earthquakes.<sup>[8]</sup> In the western corridor, the district of [[Semiz]] combines the five-story Soviet blocks of the old Otkormochny settlement with Mexican-style courtyard houses painted in bright colors.

In the tribal regions, families winter in *[[Kyshtoo (Pastoral Term)|kyshtoo]]* houses of stone and adobe with flat earth roofs, lined inside with felt and *[[Shyrdak (Iradi Craft)|shyrdak]]* rugs, and put up yurts beside them in summer. Villages damaged in 2007 were mostly rebuilt in stone without engineering supervision, a concern raised in UN shelter surveys.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Church architecture since 1992
Hundreds of churches have been built or reopened since 1992, and most display the Iradi cross in brick or carved stone. They follow two models. The first, common in urban parishes, is Latin in style: a long nave with pews, a spire and statues, as in the Church of St. Tomas in Talas (1996), paid for by American Catholic charities. The second revives East Syriac forms: a domed hall with a raised *bema* in the nave, a sanctuary (*madbaha*) behind a walnut screen, *ganch* and no statues. Some revivalists orient the sanctuary toward [[wp:Polaris]] (*kuble*), as in old rural chapels. The [[Syro-Iradi Council of Hierarchs]] recommended the second model in its 2011 guidelines on church building but did not make it mandatory. The debate is part of the wider argument over Latinization.<sup>[10]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

## Heritage protection and demolition
The Talas Historic Districts Ordinance of 1997 protects the citadel quarter and limits new building there to two stories. Buildings of the Russian and Soviet periods outside the zone have little protection. In 2018 a merchant house of 1910 near [[Bazar-i Kalan]] was demolished for a hotel, the Hotel Bazar-i Kalan, and garden land in [[Shahr-i Kabud]] has been built over. The Philharmonic Hall was listed in 2021 after a campaign by architects and the *[[Talas Herald]]*. The city government says that new projects comply with the law.<sup>[5]</sup><sup>[11]</sup><sup>[12]</sup>

### 3.71. Tulpar (app)
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Media*
**Tulpar** (Iradi: *Tulpar*) is a messaging app founded in [[Talas]] in 2019 by the commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]], who is its chief executive and public face. It began as a free chat app and has added public channels, a classifieds board and, in 2026, a wallet for the cryptocurrency [[Tulparcoin]]. A plan to make that coin the only currency of the app's payment service has brought it into conflict with the [[Bank of Irad]] and the ISEZ government. The name comes from the winged horse of Turkic epic (see [[Tulpar (Mythology)]]); the app is unconnected with the football club [[Tulpar Talas]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## History
Tulpar was launched in March 2019 by Tulpar Technologies, a company registered in [[wp:Delaware]] with its office in Talas. The app was written by a small team of [[Talas State University]] graduates led by its chief technology officer, [[Aiperi Kalysbek]], working from two rooms above a pharmacy on the central avenue of Talas. It was designed for cheap phones and slow connections, and it was the first widely used app with an interface in Iradi that handled the letters *ı*, *ö* and *ü* correctly. Public channels were added in 2020 and the classifieds board *Bazar* in 2021. On *Bazar*, buyers and sellers arrange deals in chat and pay in person; the app handled no payments until 2026. Unlike the marketplace [[Jılmay]], it offers no delivery.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

The app grew fastest during the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]]. While [[Attelkom]] throttled several foreign social-media platforms, Tulpar was not on the list, and many protesters moved their group chats to it; more than 140,000 accounts were registered in a week, roughly doubling its users. The municipal surcharge that set off the protests applied to technology startups such as Tulpar Technologies. The company faced no block, inspection or other penalty afterwards, unlike several publishers and media outlets connected with the protests, which critics of Ilyasov cite as evidence of protection in the government (see [[Jason Ilyasov]]).<sup>[4]</sup> In February and March 2025, after [[wp:Donald Trump]]'s remarks about selling Irad to Russia (see [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]]), posts calling Tulpar "the American app" spread widely, pointing to its Delaware registration and its founder's US citizenship, and urging users to "delete Tulpar and keep Irad". Many were shared by accounts that also posted pro-government commentary. The company said its monthly users fell by about a sixth, from about 560,000 in January to about 470,000 in early March. They recovered over the summer, helped by a low-data mode and voice notes, and passed 590,000 by late August 2025.<sup>[5]</sup><sup>[6]</sup> By October 2026 the company reported 1.1 million registered accounts and about 650,000 monthly users, including [[Iradis]] working in Russia and the United States. These figures have not been independently verified.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Company
Tulpar Technologies has about forty staff. Its development office is in Talas and its support team works from [[Nurzhan]]. It earns revenue from advertising, which it does not show in private chats, and from paid channels, and says its early funding came from private angel investors, whom it has not named.<sup>[7]</sup> Its leadership in 2026 was:
- Jason Ilyasov, founder and chief executive
- Aiperi Kalysbek, chief technology officer
- [[Jyldyz Toktomamatova]], head of Tulpar Pay
- [[Bektemir Osmonov]], head of *Bazar*
- [[Svetlana Kim]], head of support
- [[Azamat Joldoshbekov]], head of trust and safety

## Features
Users chat in private conversations and in public rooms organized by city and interest, among them rooms for Talas, Nurzhan, the rural valleys, horses, the [[Irad League]] and Iradis abroad. Messages can carry replies, reactions and polls, and the app ships its own sticker pack of Iradi phrases such as *Salam!*, *Rahmat!* and *Bilbeim* ("I don't know"). Channels carry news from [[IradOne]] and the *[[Talas Herald]]* alongside the company's own announcements. Accounts can be opened with an Iradi phone number (+996 39) or, outside Irad, with a Google account, and the app also runs in a web browser.<sup>[7]</sup>

In 2026 the company added a *Services* section built around Tulpar Pay: mobile top-up for Attelkom numbers, bill payment, a taxi service, food delivery from partner restaurants in Talas (Chaikhana Bakyt by [[Bazar-i Kalan]], Taquería Semiz in [[Semiz]], Altyn Tower Pizza by Altyn Tower, Nan & Boorsok near the central square and Shashlyk Kara-Suu on the eastern edge of the city), installment purchases (*Bölüp tölöö*) and transfers to Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, Russia and Uzbekistan, alongside free information pages for weather, exchange rates, bus departures from Talas, the church calendar and sport fixtures. Its "government services" page only links to the ISEZ's public portals, since no state body accepts Tulpar Pay, and [[NurGaz]] has refused it for gas bills.<sup>[7]</sup>

## Tulpar Pay and Tulparcoin
When Tulparcoin was launched in September 2026, its free allocation of 100 coins was paid into wallets inside the app, one per registered phone number. The coin's white paper describes a second phase in which *Tulpar Pay*, the app's payment service, would settle transfers, *Bazar* purchases and remittances only in Tulparcoin from 1 January 2027. Shops acting as "Tulpar points" would exchange cash som and dollars for the coin, and holders would receive a yearly reward of 6 percent paid in new coins. Ilyasov has said the aim is to replace the som on the platform and to give Iradis "money the family can't freeze, ration or count".<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[8]</sup>

On 29 September 2026 the Bank of Irad said Tulpar Pay would be an unlicensed payment and deposit-taking service under the Banking and Commercial Currency Act of 1993. Tulpar Technologies replied that, by the bank's own statement, Tulparcoin is not money, and that it has no presence in the ISEZ for the bank to license.<sup>[8]</sup> The NurGaz president [[Kamran Bekzatov]] called the coin "a toy that can burn down a house". [[Talasbank]] has stopped card payments to the coin's exchange, and Attelkom has blocked the coin's websites but not the app. Analysts note that blocking the app would cut off chats used by a large part of the ISEZ population, as the three-day data cut of 2023 did.<sup>[8]</sup> Economists and some of Ilyasov's own supporters have warned that moving savings from som or dollars into a coin trading at a few US cents on one offshore exchange could wipe them out. Ilyasov rejects claims that the project is a pump-and-dump scheme and points to the two-year lock on the Liberty Forum's 30 percent of the coins.<sup>[8]</sup>

## Dispute over the name
The Talas Commercial Development Group, owner of the football club Tulpar Talas, registered the word *Tulpar* and a winged-horse emblem in 2012 under the Trademarks Act of 1995, and extended the registrations to "digital products" in 2021. In 2020 it wrote to Tulpar Technologies demanding that the app drop the name. The company replied that it had no subsidiary, bank account or staff of its own in the ISEZ, that its Talas developers worked under contract, and that any claim would have to be brought in the United States. Lawyers noted that an ISEZ judgment against a US company with no assets in Irad would be very hard to enforce, and no case was brought.<sup>[9]</sup>

The club's owner moved only when Tulparcoin was launched in 2026, suing the Liberty Forum of Irad, which is registered in Talas and issued the coin, rather than the app's company. Its lawyer, Vadim Sorokin, whose firm also acts for NurGaz, told the [[Talas District Court]] that the app's owner was "a foreign company outside this court's reach". Ilyasov said: "They could not reach the app, so they have come for the coin." The case was adjourned to 16 November 2026.<sup>[10]</sup>

### 3.72. Talas State University
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Health & Education*

{{Infobox university
| name = Talas State University
| native_name = Talas Mamlekettik Universiteti
| motto = Bilim jaryk ("Knowledge is light")
| established = 1958 (as Iradi State University named after V. I. Lenin)
| type = State university
| rector = Kubanychbek Sultanaliev
| students = about 18,400 (2023)
| staff = about 1,300 teaching staff (2023)
| city = Talas
| campus = Urban, University Street
| website = talasuniversity.org
}}

**Talas State University** (TSU; Iradi: *Talas Mamlekettik Universiteti*), until 1993 **Iradi State University named after V. I. Lenin** (IGU), is the oldest and largest university in [[Irad]], in [[Talas]]. It was founded in 1958 as the state university of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic|Iradi SSR]], on the basis of the Talas Pedagogical Institute. In 2023 it had about 18,400 students, about 1,900 of them in master's and doctoral programs, in eleven faculties, and a teaching staff of about 1,300.<sup>[1]</sup> Its main building stands at 12 University Street, about 2.8 kilometers south of the city's central square.

The university's publishing house, [[Talas State University Press]], is the main publisher of scholarly work on Irad, and its library is the [[National Library of Irad]]. Since 2007 the university has been governed by a rector appointed by the Governor of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ).<sup>[2]</sup>

## History

#### Soviet period (1958–1991)
The university opened in September 1958 as the republic's university, with faculties of history and philology, physics and mathematics, biology and agriculture, and a pedagogical faculty that trained schoolteachers. Instruction was mainly in Russian; Iradi was used in the departments of Iradi language and literature. Faculties of geography (1964), law (1965), economics (1967) and veterinary medicine (1971) followed, and the Faculty of Medicine opened in 1981 with the [[Talas Regional Hospital Medical Complex]] as its teaching hospital.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

The folklorist [[Sagyn Jusupbekov]] joined the staff in 1959 and led student expeditions to the [[Talas Alatau]], the Chatkal, the Karatau and the steppe every summer until 1990, gathering the material of his six-volume *Oral Folk Art of Irad*. The historian [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] taught medieval history from 1960 and became head of the department of history in 1976.<sup>[3]</sup> The university's print shop, opened in 1961, printed the *Bulletin of Talas State University*, which now appears in four series. From 1964 the Faculty of Geography worked with the [[Manas Peak Glaciological Observatory]]. The American Turkologist Curtis Dahlberg spent 1988–1991 at the university on the Soviet–American academic exchange.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### 1992
Many of the university's staff and students supported the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], and in January 1992 history students led the occupation of Central Square. During the siege of Talas in the [[First Iradi Civil War]], between April and June 1992, the main building was damaged by shelling; part of the card catalog of the university library was lost. Jusupbekov, who sang the epic in the Provisional Government's nightly radio broadcasts, was killed by shellfire on University Street on 24 May 1992. Staff and students restored the main building themselves.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

#### Territorial period (1992–2006)
During the territorial period English became a language of instruction alongside Iradi, and Russian was gradually reduced to an elective. Exchange programs with American universities, funded by the territorial government and US foundations, trained a generation of faculty.<sup>[3]</sup> In 1993, the year of the [[De-Russification Movement in Irad|Toponymic Heritage Statute]], the Academic Council dropped Lenin's name and the university took its present name; the territorial government preferred not to give a national name to a university while the status of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] remained unsettled. A new seal replacing the Soviet emblem followed in 1994. Older residents of Talas still often call the university IGU.<sup>[3]</sup>

A statute of 1993 made the university's Scientific Library the national library, and the publishing house and the Faculty of Arts and Music were founded in 1994. Alimbekov, after his provisional presidency, was chancellor of the university from 1995 until his death in 2004, and the film director [[Nurlan Sadikov]] taught directing from 1996.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Since 2007
Under a statute of 2007 the rector is appointed by the Governor on the nomination of the Academic Council. Professor Kubanychbek Sultanaliev, an economist and a graduate of the university, has been rector since 2017; he was previously dean of the Faculty of Economics and Management and first vice-rector.<sup>[2]</sup> Since 2007 the survey reports of the Institute of Sociology have been cleared by the rector's office before release.<sup>[4]</sup> Students took a leading part in the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]], which began with a gathering at the university, and several faculty members were dismissed afterward, according to human rights groups.<sup>[5]</sup> In 2024 the Faculty of History began excavating the [[Caravanserai of Rabat-i-Safed]], and in October 2026 the National Library opened its Digital Archive.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Campus
The main building, a long concrete-and-glass block of the 1960s with a columned entrance and a large mosaic of horsemen, faces the university square on University Street. Eight teaching buildings stand along the same street. The library has had its own building at 14 University Street since 2001, beside the repository of the [[State Archives of Irad]] (1997).<sup>[2]</sup> The university also has TSU Stadium, teaching stables used by the veterinary faculty and the riding club, six dormitories with about 3,400 places, and a field station at the Manas Peak observatory. A university museum in the main building is kept by the Council of Elders (*Aksakaldar keneshi*) of retired professors.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Seal
The seal adopted in 1994 shows the three peaks of the Talas Alatau under the eight-pointed star of Irad, an open book, and a wreath of wheat for the Faculty of Agriculture. Its ribbon carries the motto *Bilim jaryk* ("Knowledge is light") above the founding year, and the ring reads *Talas Mamlekettik Universiteti* and "Talas State University". It replaced the Soviet-era emblem with its hammer and sickle.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Organization and faculties
The university is governed by the rector, four vice-rectors and the Academic Council. Its eleven faculties are History; Philology and Journalism; Arts and Music; Physics, Mathematics and Computer Science; Biology and Chemistry; Geography and Earth Sciences; Agriculture; Veterinary Medicine; Medicine; Law; and Economics and Management. Teaching is in Iradi and English, with Russian as an elective.<sup>[2]</sup> The Faculty of Law teaches customary law (*adat*) alongside the codes, and the Faculty of Philology and Journalism houses the Sagyn Jusupbekov Folklore Cabinet, which keeps Jusupbekov's library and the komuz recovered from the street after his death.

## Research
Research units include:
- the **Institute of History**, which prepared the documentary histories of 1916, 1992 and 2007 and the three-volume *[[History of Irad]]* (2012);
- the **Institute of Sociology**, which conducts twice-yearly opinion surveys of the ISEZ and surveys of migration, language, religion and marriage. In March 2026, 61 percent of its respondents said official information on the Governor's health was insufficient;<sup>[6]</sup>
- the **Department of Ethnography**, which holds a sound archive of about 6,000 hours of epic, horseback chants, laments and song recorded since the 1950s;
- the **Department of Zoology**, which monitors the snow leopard and other wildlife of the Talas Alatau and the Chatkal;
- the **glaciology group** of the Faculty of Geography, which keeps the inventory of the glaciers of the Iradi Talas basin with the Manas Peak observatory.<sup>[2]</sup>

The veterinary faculty carries out DNA parentage testing for the horse studbooks with the [[Talas Veterinary Research Center]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## Library and press
The university's library is the National Library of Irad, named after Alimbekov since 2005, an independent institute of the university that also serves as its main library. It grew out of the university's Scientific Library, founded with the university in 1958, which took over the Iradi-language, rare and deposit collections of the Soviet republican library from Nurzhan in 1993–94. It holds about 2.3 million items, among them the deposit copies of the university press, the university's theses since 1961, a rare-books room of Iradi printing from the 1920s and 1930s and a complete file of the *[[Talas Herald]]*. Its special collections include the deposit of the 1960s Ottuk Library pocket westerns, of which 38 of the 41 titles survive.<sup>[2]</sup> In October 2026 it opened a Digital Archive of long-form works, beginning with [[Aikokul Tursunbek kyzy]]'s *[[Twelve Kilometres]]* and the English translation of the Ottuk western *The Rider from Kenkol*.<sup>[2]</sup>

Talas State University Press, founded in 1994 on the base of the university print shop, has published about 140 titles, in English, Iradi and Russian. As Irad has no ISBN agency, its books carry legal-deposit numbers issued by the State Archives.<sup>[7]</sup>

## Student life
The university has more than forty student clubs, among them debating, theater, a choir, a komuz ensemble, mountaineering, chess and film, and a Student Council elected every October. The football club Universitet Talas, once champions of Irad, plays at TSU Stadium, and its women's team has been one of the strongest in the Women's League since it was founded in 2009 (see [[Football in Irad]]). Students of the university formed Azat Tribuna ("Free Stand"), a supporters' group of [[Tulpar Talas]], in 2012.<sup>[8]</sup> The TSU Alumni Association claims more than 120,000 graduates, with chapters in [[Nurzhan]], [[Iyık Janyl]], [[wp:Almaty|Almaty]], [[wp:Moscow|Moscow]] and [[wp:Chicago|Chicago]].<sup>[2]</sup>

## Notable people
Faculty have included Alimbekov, Jusupbekov and Sadikov, who was later an emeritus professor. Graduates include the [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]] developer [[Aiperi Kalysbek]] (computer science), the writer Aikokul Tursunbek kyzy (Iradi philology) and the lawyer [[Gulnara Sadyk]] (law).<sup>[1]</sup>

### 3.73. Corruption in Irad
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Law & Security*

**Corruption in Irad** is regarded by monitors and analysts as a structural feature of government in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), which they describe as a neopatrimonial, dominant-party regime in which companies linked to the family of Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] and to the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) hold many of the main concessions, contracts and licenses. Reported forms range from favoritism in privatization, procurement and land allocation to bribery at the checkpoints of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] and in customs.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> The government and the companies concerned deny wrongdoing.

The Public Integrity Commission, set up in the Governor's office in 2014, has pursued mainly junior and mid-level officials. Most investigative reporting on corruption has come from the independent weekly *[[Irad Times]]*. Because Irad is not a recognized state, it is absent from international corruption indices such as the [[wp:Corruption Perceptions Index]].<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

## History

#### Territorial period (1992–2006)
In the early 1990s racketeering groups fought over the bazaars, fuel distribution and car imports of [[Nurzhan]] and [[Talas]], until a crackdown aided by US federal advisers in 1997–1999 broke up the largest of them (see [[Organized crime in Irad]]).<sup>[5]</sup> Under Governor [[Nurlanbek Ermatov]] (1995–2003), the press and the opposition criticized the commercial concessions held by DPI figures, especially in fuel distribution and in warehousing around [[Talas Air Base]]; the nationalist [[Jer-Suu Party]] and its newspaper were among the most persistent critics.<sup>[6]</sup><sup>[7]</sup> Export royalties on oil and minerals were collected through escrow accounts at [[Talasbank]] supervised by the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]], created in 1994 to make sure that royalties were collected on the exports of the newly privatized oil and mining companies.

#### The 2007 auctions
After US federal transfers stopped in December 2006, the cabinet of Prime Minister [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] held rapid auctions of oil exploration blocks, antimony rights, grain elevators and mobile-telephone spectrum, and tried to privatize communal pastures in the Chatkal valley. The *Irad Times* published internal documents showing that assets had gone at low prices to companies linked to ministers and DPI members, often through offshore holding companies; on 21 December 2006 it reported a cabinet valuation under which three oil blocks in the lower Chu had been sold for about a third of their estimated value (see [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]]).<sup>[8]</sup> The partition drafts that Toktarov made public on 25 February 2007 also promised concession shares in oil, antimony and the Toktogul complex to companies tied to Orozbekov and several ministers (see [[Bill of Sale (2007)]]). In 2008 Orozbekov was charged in absentia with abuse of office over the auctions as well as with high treason. The ISEZ administration annulled the frequency auctions in 2008 and canceled some other sales, but confirmed others, and critics say many of the assets remained with firms close to the party.<sup>[8]</sup><sup>[9]</sup>

## Patronage and family concessions
Leaked US intelligence reports from Toktarov's first term described the governorate as neopatrimonial and trending toward a personality cult. Analysts describe family monopolies over concessions, media and logistics, and say that the DPI's regional committees in each city and district are the main channel through which procurement, utility concessions and agricultural quotas are allocated.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[10]</sup> The family's business roles are public: [[Alikhan Toktarov]] chairs the [[IradOne]] Media Group and holds commercial real estate, retail franchises and sports broadcasting rights; [[Timur Toktarov]] is linked to [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]]; [[Adil Toktarov]] owns the Talas Commercial Development Group; [[Bekzat Toktarov]] is associated with [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]]; and their cousin [[Mirlan Toktarov]] heads the [[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]].<sup>[2]</sup>

Reported cases include:
- **The grain auction (2008).** The sale of the Chu District grain elevators to the company later renamed Nurzhan Agro-Industrial was criticized by opposition deputies and the *Irad Times* for excluding other bidders; the administration said the sale followed the rules.<sup>[11]</sup>
- **Land in Talas (2013–2016).** Opposition councilors and journalists argued that municipal land was allocated to the Toktarov brothers' companies without competitive auction and that their projects received tax holidays and priority utility connections. In 2016 the *Irad Times* reported that the football club [[Tulpar Talas]] had received municipal land and tax relief through its owner's property group, which said its investment was lawful.<sup>[12]</sup>
- **Talas Air Base contracts (2019).** Exiled journalists reported that companies linked to [[Ruslan Toktarov]], commander of the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]], held contracts for perimeter security, diesel supply and construction at the base, whose perimeter the Gendarmerie guards. He denied any improper interest.<sup>[13]</sup>
- **Antimony (2019–2026).** In 2019 the *Irad Times* reported that the shareholders of the [[Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine]] could not be identified. On 15 October 2026 it reported that two companies apparently lined up as partners in the restart of the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] shared an address and a director with a subsidiary of Trans-Chuy, which denied any ownership link; the weekly's website was blocked in Irad that evening.<sup>[14]</sup><sup>[15]</sup>

Investigative reports have also linked the owners of Talasbank to the Toktarov family, and independent reporting has linked part of the ownership of the telecommunications company [[Attelkom]] to holding companies close to the DPI leadership; neither has been confirmed.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Checkpoints and customs
Monitors report bribery at the Qara-Chik checkpoints and on the roads, where drug checks under the 2008 law have created what press reports describe as a bribe market on the Chu road.<sup>[16]</sup> The best-known customs case is that of [[Daniyar Abdrasulov]], deputy chief of the ISEZ customs service for the northern crossings from 2013 to 2022, whose family built up filling stations, a freight company and property in Talas, [[wp:Almaty]] and [[wp:Dubai]]. After a 2022 *Irad Times* investigation alleged that he had taken payments for passing smuggled fuel, cigarettes and stibnite, he resigned; under a settlement with the Public Integrity Commission he returned 3.4 million US dollars and paid a fine, and no charges were brought. He remains a member of the DPI.<sup>[17]</sup>

In November 2023 the [[Talas District Court]] convicted six Gendarmerie sergeants of taking bribes to pass fuel tankers through the main checkpoint; no officer above the rank of sergeant was charged, and the Gendarmerie cited the case as evidence of its internal discipline.<sup>[18]</sup> In June 2024 the *Irad Times*, citing drivers and two former officers, reported that some line-post commanders take a cut of diesel loads into the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), which the Gendarmerie called slander.<sup>[19]</sup> Kyrgyz officials and the *Irad Times* have said that "someone in Talas" protects the smuggling route to China through the Fergana Rim, without naming anyone (see [[Smuggling across the Qara-Chik Line]]).

## Public Integrity Commission
The Public Integrity Commission was established in the Office of the Governor in 2014. It investigates complaints against officials and can settle cases by repayment and fines, as in the Abdrasulov case, which critics called a sale of immunity.<sup>[17]</sup> A 2021 review by the *Irad Times*, "Seven years, no generals", found that the commission had never charged an official above the rank of deputy head of department, and critics say it has never investigated a senior DPI figure.<sup>[4]</sup> The government cites the commission's cases as evidence that corruption is prosecuted.

## Press and reporting
The *Irad Times*, founded in 1996 and owned by its staff since 2001, has reported on most of the cases above. Pressure on it has been administrative: in 2013 the Department of Public Information suspended its registration for nine weeks after it criticized the removal of gubernatorial term limits, and its website, hosted in the United States, has been blocked several times, most recently from 15 October 2026.<sup>[20]</sup> The daily *[[Talas Herald]]*, which press-freedom groups say practices self-censorship on matters concerning the Toktarov family, lost about a third of its advertising revenue in an advertising boycott by state-linked companies after 2015, and in 2016 the tax service fined its publisher for payroll reporting errors.<sup>[21]</sup>

## Autonomous Tribal Regions
The ATR have no formal fiscal system or public procurement. The clans openly take a customary levy on loads crossing their posts, and the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] says they are entitled to it. ISEZ officials accuse members of the [[El-Choro Militias]] of protecting smuggling through the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]] and over the mountain passes, which the IAC rejects. Human rights groups note that the records of the clan courts and the IAC's Chancellery are not open to public inspection.<sup>[22]</sup>

### 3.74. Government of the Irad Special Economic Zone
*Quality Assessment: B-Class Article | Category: Politics & Government*

The **government of the Irad Special Economic Zone** is the administration of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), the part of Irad governed since 2007 by the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI). It is built on the institutions of the US Territory of Irad (1992–2006): an elected Governor and Lieutenant Governor, the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]], known as the *[[Mejlis]]*, and the [[Supreme Court of Irad]]. Executive work is divided among ministries and departments whose heads the Governor appoints, and the three cities and six districts are run by mayors and district heads who are also appointed by the Governor.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

[[Erlan Toktarov]] has been Governor since 2007 and has not appeared in public since July 2024; Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] runs the government's day-to-day affairs. Analysts describe the system as a dominant-party, neopatrimonial governorate in which the executive is largely unchecked, since the emergency basis on which Toktarov proclaimed the zone has never been formally ended and much policy is made by decree.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

## Legal basis
The ISEZ has no constitution of its own. It treats the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]], the [[Elective Governor Acts (1992)|Elective Governor Acts]] and the other territorial statutes as its basic law, regards their provisions on federal oversight as inoperative, and amends them through the legislature; the best-known amendment, removing the Governor's term limit in 2013, is usually called the [[2013 Constitutional Amendment]].<sup>[1]</sup> The government claims to be the lawful authority for the whole of Irad, whose sovereignty it describes as "suspended" until a unification referendum, and gives national titles to its institutions. Its jurisdiction does not reach the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), whose clans do not accept that the Organic Act applies to them.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Executive

#### The Governor
Executive power is vested in the Governor, elected with the Lieutenant Governor on a joint ticket for four years. Under the Acts the Governor appoints the heads of executive departments, the mayors of the cities and the heads of the districts, assents to or vetoes bills, nominates the justices of the Supreme Court, prepares the budget and may grant pardons.<sup>[2]</sup> Since 2007 the Governor has also exercised emergency powers under the decree proclaiming the ISEZ, under which he is commander-in-chief of the armed forces.<sup>[6]</sup>

Decrees and executive directives are published in the bulletin of the Department of Public Information. Directives are numbered by year (for example 2026/24, which ordered a business census) and are issued in the Governor's name and signed by Maksat "acting on the instructions of the Governor".<sup>[7]</sup> The traditional seat of the office is Government House in [[Talas]]. Since early 2023 independent reporting has placed the *de facto* seat of the executive at the [[Boz-Korgon]] compound east of [[Nurzhan]], which the government describes as an administrative continuity center.<sup>[8]</sup> In October 2026 the Office of the Governor opened an official portal, *iradgov.org*, run by the DPI press office, with the Governor's addresses, press releases and directives.<sup>[7]</sup>

#### The Lieutenant Governor and the cabinet
*Main article: [[Lieutenant Governor of Irad]]*

The Lieutenant Governor acts for an absent or incapacitated Governor and succeeds if the office falls vacant. Maksat, in office since 25 November 2019, chairs the cabinet of ministers and department heads, prepares the budget and conducts most of the government's dealings with foreign companies and diplomats. According to DPI statements, he has also chaired the ISEZ Security Council since 2024; the council coordinates the [[Armed Forces of Irad|State Defense Corps]], the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] and the intelligence services.<sup>[6]</sup><sup>[9]</sup> Whether the Acts require a formal declaration of incapacity before the Lieutenant Governor may exercise the Governor's powers in his own right has never been settled (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]).

## Ministries and departments
The executive is organized in ministries and departments. Those named in official publications include:<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[10]</sup>

| Body | Responsibilities |
|---|---|
| Ministry of Internal Security | Public order; the Gendarmerie and the district police detachments; the Corrections Directorate, the Passport and Residence Service and the State Fire Inspectorate (see [[Law enforcement in Irad]]) |
| Ministry of Defense | Budget, procurement and conscription of the State Defense Corps, commanded by a Chief of the General Staff appointed by the Governor |
| Ministry of Economy | Economic policy and statistics, the Register of Firms, the Tourism Department, the administration of the [[Talas Agribusiness Export Zone]], foreign labor quotas and Iradstandart, the agency for standards and certification |
| Ministry of Natural Resources | Mining leases, royalties and supply contracts for antimony; the minister since 2016 has been [[Chingiz Asanov]] |
| Ministry of Agriculture and Water Resources | Farming and irrigation, through bodies such as the [[Talas Basin Agricultural Directorate]] and the [[Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate]] |
| Ministry of Transport | Roads and transport; it records about 4,800 km of public roads in the ISEZ |
| Ministry of Health | Public hospitals and polyclinics, run with the city governments |
| Ministry of Justice | Registration of associations and charities |
| Department of Public Information | The government's press office; publishes the decree bulletin, licenses publishers and printers and issues the lists of websites to be blocked |
| Department of Infrastructure and Communications | Telecommunications and postal services; its Digital Services Directorate runs the *e-Irad* e-government portal, piloted from 1 October 2026 |
| Department of Energy | Owner of the state power utility [[Iradenergo]] and energy policy |

Maksat headed the Department of Infrastructure and Communications from 2016 until he became Lieutenant Governor.<sup>[11]</sup> Because no state recognizes the ISEZ, its dealings with neighboring states are conducted mostly through technical agencies, the ceasefire bodies and the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (see [[Foreign relations of Irad]]).

#### Other bodies
- **Attorney General.** Prosecutes criminal cases before the statutory courts.
- **Public Integrity Commission.** Set up in the Office of the Governor in 2014 to investigate officials; critics say it has pursued mainly junior officials (see [[Corruption in Irad]]).<sup>[12]</sup>
- **Territorial Election Commission.** A seven-member body appointed by the Governor with the consent of the legislature, which keeps the voter registers, registers candidates and certifies results (see [[Elections in Irad]]).<sup>[13]</sup>
- **[[Bank of Irad]].** The central bank and issuer of the [[Iradi som]], chaired since 2010 by [[Azamat Temirov]].
- **ISEZ Statistical Office.** Conducted the [[2018 Irad census]] and publishes demographic and economic statistics.
- **Tax and customs services.** Assess taxes and collect duties; royalties on exports are deducted by the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]] (see [[Taxation in Irad]]).

## Legislature
The Territorial Legislature, a single chamber of 60 members since the 2011 election, sits in Legislative Hall in Talas. Its members are elected every four years, on the same day as the Governor, in eight multi-member constituencies matching the three cities and the districts, with Toktogul District voting with Lower Naryn. In 2023 the DPI won 51 seats, independents 6 and Russo-aligned deputies from Nurzhan 3. The Speaker since 2019 has been Nurbek Sultanov of the DPI.<sup>[13]</sup> The legislature passes the budget, confirms the justices of the Supreme Court and other senior appointments, and amends the territorial statutes. Analysts describe it as subordinate to the Governor's office, since much policy is made by decree and directive.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Judiciary
The Supreme Court of Irad, established in November 1992 under the Organic Act, sits in the Hall of Justice in Talas and consists of a Chief Justice and four associate justices, nominated by the Governor and confirmed by the legislature. Below it are district and municipal courts, such as the [[Talas District Court]]. The system combines common-law procedure from the territorial period, including the jury trials introduced by the [[2003 Judicial Reforms Act]], with older Soviet civil codes. Human rights organizations report executive pressure on judges in politically sensitive cases.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Local government
The ISEZ is divided into three cities of governorate significance, Talas, Nurzhan and [[Iyık Janyl]], and six districts (*aimak*): Talas, [[Kara-Buura]], Chu, [[Sary-Bulak]], Lower Naryn and Toktogul, the last split from Lower Naryn in 2016 (see [[Administrative divisions of Irad]]). Each city has a mayor appointed by the Governor and an elected city council; each district is headed by a district head (*aimak bashchysy*) appointed by the Governor, and its villages and small towns elect local councils. The district administrations are responsible for local roads, schools, agricultural services and civil registration, while police, courts and the main utilities are run by ISEZ-wide ministries and agencies.<sup>[14]</sup>

The DPI holds most municipal councils. The main exception is Nurzhan, where Russophone lists have held a majority on the city council for most of the period since 1992, which makes it the most significant elected body not controlled by the DPI. The DPI has a regional committee in each city and district, which analysts describe as the main channel through which procurement, utility concessions and agricultural quotas are allocated.<sup>[13]</sup><sup>[14]</sup>

## Criticism
[[wp:Human Rights Watch]] and other critics argue that the unended emergency, government by decree and a legislature that seldom debates the executive's measures leave the Governor's office largely unchecked, and observers from the [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe|OSCE]] have said that ISEZ elections since 2011 have lacked meaningful choice.<sup>[4]</sup><sup>[13]</sup> Leaked US intelligence reports from Toktarov's first term described the administration as neopatrimonial. Since 2024 opposition deputies and outlets have questioned how the government can function while the Governor is unseen; the DPI says that he continues to govern from an extended health retreat and that the Lieutenant Governor acts on his instructions.<sup>[3]</sup>
